lessons.title: Traduire: English and French at C2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 01 and 04 asked for the exact word and the unambiguous sentence in French. Translation
asks for both at once, with a second language pulling the other way. As a C2 learner whose first
language is probably English, you translate in your head all the time; this lesson gives you the
tools professionals use to do it well, and the names for what goes wrong.

You'll meet the seven procedures described by two French linguists working in Canada, Jean-Paul
Vinay and Jean Darbelnet, in their *Stylistique comparée du français et de l'anglais* (Paris,
Didier, and Montréal, Beauchemin, 1958), then the errors (false friends, the faux-sens, calques of
syntax), surtitling, and the old debate about how literal a translation should be. Every source
text in this lesson was written for it. Machine translation is the subject of honors lesson 93.

## Seven procedures, from closest to freest

Vinay and Darbelnet sort the procedures into two families. The *direct* ones keep the English
structure; the *oblique* ones change it, because French expresses the same thing differently.

![A map of translation procedures in two columns. The left column, "traduction directe", lists from top to bottom: l'emprunt (le week-end), le calque (gratte-ciel), la traduction littérale (le livre est sur la table). The right column, "traduction oblique", lists: la transposition (dès son arrivée), la modulation (c'est facile), l'équivalence (aïe !), l'adaptation (le 14 Juillet). An arrow along the bottom runs from "proche de l'anglais" on the left to "libre" on the right. A shaded box under the direct column adds two more: the chassé-croisé, a kind of transposition (swim across → traverser à la nage), joined to it by a dashed line, and l'étoffement (jusqu'à la gare).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| family | procedure | what it does | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| direct | borrowing (*l'emprunt*) | keeps the foreign word | *le week-end, le leadership* |
| direct | **[[calque]]** (*le calque*) | translates the parts of a foreign word or phrase one by one | *gratte-ciel* (skyscraper) |
| direct | literal translation | word for word, and it works | *The book is on the table* → *Le livre est sur la table* |
| oblique | **[[transposition]]** (*la transposition*) | changes the word class | *as soon as he arrived* → *dès son arrivée* |
| oblique | **[[modulation]]** (*la modulation*) | changes the point of view | *it's not difficult* → *c'est facile* |
| oblique | **[[equivalence]]** (*l'équivalence*) | the same situation in entirely different words | *it's raining cats and dogs* → *il pleut des cordes* |
| oblique | adaptation | replaces a situation the reader wouldn't know | *a Fourth of July barbecue* → *un barbecue du 14 Juillet* (with its risks) |

Two notes on the table. A calque can be a word (*gratte-ciel*) or a whole construction (*en charge
de*, from "in charge of", below); *le calque* also means tracing paper, which is the image behind
the term. And adaptation changes the facts of the text, so it is a choice for advertising,
children's books or theatre, not for a news report.

### Two procedures French needs constantly

The **[[chassé-croisé]]** (plural *les chassés-croisés*) is a double transposition that English and
French make in opposite directions. English puts the manner in the verb and the direction in a
particle (*swim across*); French puts the direction in the verb and the manner in an adverbial
phrase (*traverser à la nage*):

- *He limped out of the room* → *Il est sorti de la pièce en boitant.*
- *She ran down the stairs* → *Elle a descendu l'escalier en courant.*
- *The boat drifted away* → *Le bateau s'est éloigné au gré du courant.*

Outside translation, *un chassé-croisé* is a to-and-fro of people or traffic: *le chassé-croisé des
vacanciers* on the first Saturday of August, when July's holidaymakers drive home as August's set
off.

*Étoffement* (*l'étoffement*, "filling out") adds words that French often prefers where English
makes do with a preposition:

- *Walk to the station* → *Marchez jusqu'à la gare* (*à la gare* alone would say where you walk,
  not where you are going).
- *the train to Lyon* → in an announcement, *le train à destination de Lyon*
- *the road to the sea* → *la route qui mène à la mer*

## Errors: contresens, faux-sens, false friends

Translators grade errors by how far they lead the reader astray:

- *le contresens* (B2): the opposite or a wholly wrong meaning. *Eventually, the minister agreed*
  → ~~Éventuellement, le ministre a accepté~~ (possibly) instead of *Finalement, le ministre a
  accepté*.
- *le faux-sens* (plural *les faux-sens*): a slight error, a nearby but inexact meaning. *A
  grim smile* → ~~un sourire triste~~ instead of *un sourire amer* or *sans joie*.
- *le non-sens*: a sentence that means nothing at all.

The commonest cause is the **[[false friend]]** (*le faux ami*, also spelt *faux-ami*): a French word
that looks like an English one but means something else. These are the ones that still trap C2
learners:

| French | means | for the English word, say |
|---|---|---|
| *actuellement* | currently | actually → *en fait, en réalité* |
| *éventuellement* | possibly, if need be | eventually → *finalement, à terme* |
| *sensible* | sensitive | sensible → *sensé, raisonnable* (lesson 01) |
| *définitivement* | for good, permanently | definitely → *sans aucun doute, assurément* |
| *réaliser* (A2) | to carry out, to achieve | to realise → *se rendre compte* (B1) |
| *supporter* | to bear, to put up with; to support (a team) | to support (an idea, a person) → *soutenir* |
| *contrôler* | to check, to inspect | to control → *maîtriser, diriger* |
| *ignorer* | not to know | to ignore → *ne pas tenir compte de, faire comme si … n'existait pas* |

Several of these are moving. *Réaliser* for "to realise" is now very common and in dictionaries,
though some usage guides still criticise it; *ignorer quelqu'un* (to ignore someone) and
*contrôler* for "to control" are spreading too. In careful writing, prefer the safe column; in
speech, don't correct others.

### Anglicisms of syntax

Some calques copy an English construction with French words. They are common in the press and in
business, and usage guides criticise them:

- *être en charge de* (in charge of) → *être chargé de, être responsable de*
- *faire sens* (to make sense) → *avoir du sens, être sensé, se tenir*
- *adresser un problème* (to address a problem) → *traiter, aborder, s'attaquer à un problème*

*Faire sens* is now so frequent that some dictionaries record it; *adresser un problème* is still
widely rejected. As with lesson 01's improprieties, prefer the safe form when a reader may object.

## Surtitles, the untranslatable and the letter

*Surtitling* (*le surtitrage*) is the translation projected above the stage at the opera or the
theatre; *les sous-titres* (A2 honors) are for the screen. A surtitle has a line or two and a few seconds
of reading time, so the translator condenses: a five-line aria may become one sentence. The task
is the extreme case of a common choice: keep everything, or keep what the audience needs?

*L'intraduisible* (the untranslatable) names the words and turns with no one-word equivalent:
*le dépaysement* (the disorientation, often pleasant, of being somewhere new), *l'esprit de
l'escalier* (thinking of the right answer too late), English "fair play" or "serendipity". A
translator still translates them, with a phrase, a note or a borrowing; *intraduisible* is also an
adjective (*un jeu de mots intraduisible*). In 2004 a large *Vocabulaire européen des philosophies*,
edited by Barbara Cassin, took the subtitle *Dictionnaire des intraduisibles* and treated
untranslatable terms as the places where philosophies differ.

The debate on *la littéralité* (literalness) is older than the theory. In the 17th century, French
translators of Latin and Greek polished their authors to suit French taste, and the results were
nicknamed *les belles infidèles* ("beautiful and unfaithful"). In the 1980s the French translation
theorist Jean-René Ladmiral named the two camps: the *sourciers*, who stay close to the source text,
and the *ciblistes*, who write for the target reader. Antoine Berman, in the same decade, defended
a translation that lets the reader feel the foreignness of the original. Most working translators
move between the two depending on the text: a contract wants literalness, an advertisement wants
equivalence.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: an English notice into French

Source (written for this lesson): *As soon as the doors close, the train to Geneva will leave.
Passengers should not lean out of the windows. Wet paint on platform 2.*

1. *As soon as the doors close* → transposition (verb → noun): *Dès la fermeture des portes*.
2. *the train to Geneva* → étoffement: *le train à destination de Genève*.
3. *will leave* → literal translation: *partira*.
4. *Passengers should not lean out of the windows* → modulation: French notices state a
   prohibition impersonally: *Il est interdit de se pencher par les fenêtres.*
5. *Wet paint* → modulation (wet → fresh): *Peinture fraîche.*

Result: *Dès la fermeture des portes, le train à destination de Genève partira. Il est interdit de
se pencher par les fenêtres. Peinture fraîche, quai 2.*

### Example 2: correcting false friends

A draft translation of *The company currently employs 200 people. Eventually it will move. We
definitely realised the risk, but we ignored it*:

> ~~L'entreprise emploie actuellement 200 personnes. Éventuellement, elle déménagera. Nous avons
> définitivement réalisé le risque, mais nous l'avons ignoré.~~

- *actuellement* is right here (currently): keep it.
- *Éventuellement* means "possibly": contresens. → *À terme, elle déménagera.*
- *définitivement* means "for good": the English "definitely" is better rendered by *bien*.
- *réalisé le risque*: *réaliser* with this object reads as "to bring about". → *pris conscience
  du risque*.
- *nous l'avons ignoré* means "we didn't know it", the opposite of the context. → *nous n'en avons
  pas tenu compte*.

Corrected: *L'entreprise emploie actuellement 200 personnes. À terme, elle déménagera. Nous avions
bien pris conscience du risque, mais nous n'en avons pas tenu compte.*

### Example 3: a surtitle

A singer's line (written for this lesson), about ten seconds long: *Oh, how could I have known,
on that cold and rainy morning, that the man who smiled at me in the square would break my heart?*

A faithful translation runs to two long lines. The surtitle keeps the event and the feeling and
drops the scenery: *Comment aurais-je pu savoir qu'il me briserait le cœur ?* The morning, the rain
and the square are visible on stage, so they can go.

## Common mistakes

- Translating particle verbs word for word: ~~il a nagé à travers la rivière~~ → *il a traversé la
  rivière à la nage* (chassé-croisé).
- Forgetting étoffement where a bare preposition changes the sense: ~~marchez à la gare~~ for
  "walk to the station" → *marchez jusqu'à la gare*.
- The false friends: *éventuellement, définitivement, ignorer, sensible* for their English
  look-alikes.
- *En charge de, faire sens, adresser un problème* in formal writing.
- Calling every error a *contresens*: a near miss is a *faux-sens*.

## Key points

- Vinay and Darbelnet (1958): direct procedures (borrowing, calque, literal translation) and
  oblique ones (transposition, modulation, equivalence, adaptation).
- Chassé-croisé: *swim across* → *traverser à la nage*. Étoffement: *to the station* → *jusqu'à la
  gare*.
- Errors by degree: contresens, faux-sens, non-sens. False friends cause many of them.
- Calques of syntax (*en charge de, faire sens, adresser*) are common and criticised.
- Surtitling condenses; the untranslatable is translated with a phrase or a note; the debate on
  literalness opposes *sourciers* and *ciblistes*.

lessons.title: De Vaugelas au Bon Usage: who makes the norm?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module kept saying "careful usage", "usage guides criticise", "both are accepted". Who
decides? French has no single authority with legal power over the language as a whole, but it has
an unusually long tradition of people who described, judged and codified it. This lesson tells that
story from the 17th century to today's online dictionaries, separates the two attitudes a reference
work can take, and ends with the norm that governs the look of a printed page: typography.

Earlier words you'll need: *la norme* (the standard), *normatif* (prescriptive), *le purisme*, *le
barbarisme* (a wrongly formed word) and *le solécisme* (a grammatical error), all from B2 honors,
and *la ponctuation* (B1). The 1990 spelling reforms were C1 honors; the idea of several standard
Frenches comes in lesson 16.

## Vaugelas and the remarqueurs

In 1647 Claude Favre de Vaugelas published his *Remarques sur la langue françoise* (the old
spelling of *française*). It was not a grammar but a collection of short notes, each on one doubtful
point: which word, which construction, which pronunciation. His authority was usage, and he took as
his model the speech of the most refined part of the royal court, checked against the best writers
of his day. He presented himself as a witness to usage, not a lawmaker, but his book quickly became
a code.

He had successors, the **[[remarqueurs]]** (*les remarqueurs*): writers of further *Remarques* and
*Observations* in the second half of the 17th century, among them Gilles Ménage and Dominique
Bouhours, and Thomas Corneille, who published an annotated edition of Vaugelas. Their debates, one
point at a time, created the habit that still shapes French: asking whether a turn of phrase is
"correct" and looking for someone to say so.

## The Académie française

The Académie française received its letters patent in January 1635. Its task was to give the
language rules and to produce a dictionary; Vaugelas led the early work on it. The first
edition appeared only in 1694. The ninth, begun in the 1980s, was completed in November 2024 with
its fourth volume, and is free online. The Académie also publishes *Dire, ne pas dire*, short notes
on doubtful usage, very much in the remarqueurs' tradition.

The Académie's recommendations carry prestige, not legal force: no one is fined for *pallier à*.
Official terminology for the state is a separate matter, handled by a government commission in
which the Académie takes part.

## The great dictionaries and grammars

| work | maker | dates | what it brought |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Dictionnaire de la langue française* | Émile Littré | published from 1863 to 1872 (supplement 1877) | the classical language, illustrated with quotations from great writers, with word histories |
| *Grand Dictionnaire universel du XIXe siècle* | Pierre Larousse | 1866–1876 | an encyclopaedic dictionary; the *Petit Larousse* followed in 1905 |
| *Dictionnaire alphabétique et analogique* | Paul Robert | 1950s and 1960s | links between words (analogies, synonyms); the *Petit Robert* followed in 1967 |
| *Le Bon Usage* | Maurice Grevisse, then André Goosse | 1936; 16th edition 2016 | a grammar built on thousands of quoted examples from writers and the press |
| *Trésor de la langue française* (TLF) | a team at the CNRS in Nancy | 16 volumes, 1971–1994 | about 100,000 words with their history, based on a large corpus; free online as the TLFi |

A *lexicographer* (*un* or *une lexicographe*) writes dictionaries; *lexicography* (*la
lexicographie*) is the craft. A *grammarian* (*le grammairien*, *la grammairienne*) studies and
describes grammar. Grevisse was a Belgian grammarian, a schoolteacher by training; after his death
in 1980, his son-in-law André Goosse revised the book from its 12th edition (1986).

## Prescriptive and descriptive

A reference work can take one of two attitudes, and most mix them:

- **[[Prescriptive grammar]]** (*la grammaire normative*) says what you should write: it recommends,
  advises against, condemns. *Dire, ne pas dire* is prescriptive; so are most school grammars and
  usage guides.
- **[[Descriptive grammar]]** (*la grammaire descriptive*) says what speakers and writers do, with
  evidence. *Descriptif* (feminine *descriptive*) is the opposite of *normatif*; as a noun, *un
  descriptif* is a technical description (of a flat, a product).

*Le Bon Usage* is the classic example of the mix. Its title is prescriptive; its method is largely
descriptive: for a disputed construction, Grevisse and Goosse cite the writers who use it, the
grammarians who condemn it, and give their own judgement. That is why the book is so often quoted
on both sides of an argument. Modern dictionaries are also mixed: they record a use and label it
(*fam.*, *critiqué*, *anglicisme*).

The *puriste* treats every change as decay; the linguist treats usage as data. A C2 writer needs
both views: the descriptive one to understand what people say, the prescriptive one to know what a
given reader will accept.

## Typography: the norm of the printed page

*Typography* (*la typographie*) has its own norm, set by printers and publishers. In France the
reference most often cited is the *Lexique des règles typographiques en usage à l'Imprimerie
nationale* (its 2002 edition, reprinted since). Publishers and newspapers have house styles that
differ in details. The main French rules:

| point | French rule | example |
|---|---|---|
| spacing | a **[[non-breaking space]]** before *: ; ! ?* and inside guillemets (the thin non-breaking space before *; ! ?* in fine typography) | *Attention : travaux !* |
| quotation marks | *les guillemets* « » with spaces inside; " " for a quotation inside a quotation | *Il a dit : « Je reviens. »* |
| capitals | *les majuscules* keep their accents | *État, À bientôt, ÉCOLE* |
| capitals in names | lower case (*la minuscule*) for days, months, languages and nationality adjectives | *lundi, en mars, le français, un auteur français*; but *les Français* (the people) |
| italics | *l'italique* (*en italique*) for titles of works, foreign words, newspaper names | *Le Monde*, *a priori*, *Le Rouge et le Noir* |

A **[[non-breaking space]]** (*l'espace insécable*) is a space that keeps the two characters on the
same line, so that a colon or a closing guillemet never starts a new line. Note the gender: in
typography *espace* is feminine (*une espace insécable, une espace fine*); in everyday French it is
masculine (*un espace vert*). Switzerland's usage often drops the space before *; ! ?*, and many
websites ignore the rule, so you'll see all three practices.

![A short French magazine paragraph with typographic points marked. The heading "État des lectures d'hiver" starts with an accented capital É. The next line ends with the novel title Le Rouge et le Noir in italics. Then "La présidente annonce" is followed by a shaded non-breaking space, a colon and a quotation in French guillemets, « Nous lirons Stendhal. ». The last line, "Rendez-vous lundi, en janvier", is followed by a narrow shaded thin space and an exclamation mark. Labels name la majuscule accentuée, l'italique, l'espace insécable, les guillemets and l'espace fine.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The person who checks these points before printing is the *proofreader* (*le correcteur
d'épreuves*, *la correctrice d'épreuves*; *les épreuves* are the proofs). *Le correcteur* alone
(B2) also means an exam marker, and today a spell checker.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: correcting the typography of a paragraph

Draft (written for this lesson): *Le Ministre de l'education a declare: "Nous lirons Le Rouge et
le Noir en Janvier!"*

1. *Ministre*: a title in a sentence takes a lower case: *le ministre*.
2. *education*: the name of the ministry takes a capital, with its accent: *de l'Éducation
   nationale*; for the field in general, *de l'éducation*.
3. *declare*: missing accent: *a déclaré*.
4. *declare:* → non-breaking space before the colon: *a déclaré :*.
5. *"…"* → French guillemets with spaces: *« … »*.
6. *Le Rouge et le Noir* → italics: *Le Rouge et le Noir*.
7. *Janvier* → lower case: *janvier*.
8. *Janvier!* → space before the exclamation mark: *janvier !*

Result: *Le ministre de l'Éducation nationale a déclaré : « Nous lirons* Le Rouge et le Noir *en
janvier ! »*

### Example 2: one question, two kinds of answer

Question: is *pallier à un manque* correct? (lesson 01)

- A prescriptive answer: *pallier* is transitive; write *pallier un manque*. The construction with
  *à* is a mistake to avoid.
- A descriptive answer: *pallier à* is widespread in speech and in the press, probably on the model
  of *remédier à*; many usage guides condemn it, and careful writers avoid it.

Both answers are true. The first tells you what a demanding reader expects; the second tells you
what you will hear and why. A C2 writer uses the first in formal writing and the second to avoid
sneering at others.

### Example 3: reading a dictionary label

A dictionary entry gives *trivial* the sense "minor, unimportant" with the label *anglicisme* or
*critiqué* (lesson 02). The label is descriptive (the use exists) and prescriptive (it warns you).
Read the label as a map of readers: in a maths paper, *une solution triviale* is standard; in an
essay on style, *un mot trivial* means a coarse one.

## Common mistakes

- Believing the Académie can forbid a word. It recommends; its notes carry prestige, not law.
- Calling *Le Bon Usage* purely prescriptive. It quotes the usage of writers, including uses it
  advises against.
- Dropping accents on capitals: ~~ETAT~~, ~~A bientôt~~ → *ÉTAT, À bientôt*.
- English quotation marks and no spaces: ~~"Je reviens"~~ in French print → *« Je reviens »*.
- Capitals for months, days, languages and adjectives of nationality: ~~en Janvier~~, ~~le Français~~
  (the language) → *en janvier, le français*.
- *Un espace insécable* in a typography text: printers say *une espace*.

## Key points

- Vaugelas's *Remarques* (1647) founded the habit of judging usage one point at a time; the
  remarqueurs continued it.
- The Académie française: founded in 1635, first dictionary 1694, ninth edition completed in 2024;
  prestige, not law.
- Littré, Larousse, Robert, Grevisse's *Le Bon Usage* (1936) and the TLF (1971–1994, now the TLFi)
  are the great references.
- Prescriptive grammar says what to write; descriptive grammar says what people write. Most works
  mix both.
- French typography: non-breaking spaces before *: ; ! ?* and inside « », accented capitals,
  lower-case months and languages, italics for titles. *Une espace* in typography.

lessons.title: Il naquit, vécut et mourut: récit and discours
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 was about choosing the exact word. Module 2 turns to style, and it starts with the
tenses of literature. You met the **[[passé simple]]** for recognition in B2. At C2 you need to read
it without effort, irregular stems included, along with the **[[passé antérieur]]**, and to see what
a writer does by telling a story in one system of tenses rather than another.

This is a reading skill. You will never be asked to type a passé simple or a passé antérieur: you
identify them, understand them and turn them into the passé composé you write yourself. The
theme is a 19th-century chronicle from an invented village on an invented river: a wedding, a
flood and a family's emigration to America.

## The passé simple in one table

Two sets of endings cover the regular verbs. The *-er* verbs take *-a-*; the *-ir* verbs like
*finir* and most *-re* verbs take *-i-*.

| person | parler | finir | vendre |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | parlai | finis | vendis |
| tu | parlas | finis | vendis |
| il, elle | parla | finit | vendit |
| nous | parlâmes | finîmes | vendîmes |
| vous | parlâtes | finîtes | vendîtes |
| ils, elles | parlèrent | finirent | vendirent |

Three details help you read fast:

- The *nous* and *vous* forms carry a circumflex: *-âmes, -âtes, -îmes, -îtes, -ûmes, -ûtes,
  -înmes, -întes*. They are rare outside a first-person narrative and sound old-fashioned or comic
  today (*nous parlâmes*).
- The third person is the one you will meet most: *il parla, elle finit, ils vendirent*. The
  plural always ends in *-rent*.
- *-ger* and *-cer* verbs keep their soft sound before *a*: *il mangea, elle commença*. The *ils*
  form has no *e* or *ç*: *ils mangèrent, ils commencèrent*.

## The irregular stems a C2 reader meets

Irregular verbs fall into three vowel groups. Learn to recognise the stem: the ending then tells
you the person.

![A map of passé simple stems in three groups. The i group: fit, dit, vit, mit, prit, naquit, vainquit, s'assit, acquit, vêtit, rompit. The u group: fut, eut, sut, put, dut, crut, lut, plut, vécut, mourut, conclut, résolut. The in group: vint, tint and their compounds. A note in the corner shows two look-alikes: crut (believed) and crût (grew).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| group | third person singular (infinitive) |
|---|---|
| *-i-* | *fit* (faire), *dit* (dire), *vit* (voir), *mit* (mettre), *prit* (prendre), *naquit* (naître), *vainquit* (vaincre), *s'assit* (s'asseoir), *acquit* (acquérir), *vêtit* (vêtir), *rompit* (rompre) |
| *-u-* | *fut* (être), *eut* (avoir), *sut* (savoir), *put* (pouvoir), *dut* (devoir), *crut* (croire), *lut* (lire), *plut* (plaire, and pleuvoir), *vécut* (vivre), *mourut* (mourir), *conclut* (conclure), *résolut* (résoudre) |
| *-in-* | *vint* (venir), *tint* (tenir), and compounds: *survint, devint, revint, retint, obtint* |

The title of this lesson strings three of them together: *il naquit, vécut et mourut* (he was
born, lived and died), the shortest possible biography.

*Look-alikes.* Some passé simple forms are identical to the present: *il dit, il finit, il rit,
il conclut*; only the context (the other verbs, a date) tells you which it is. *Il lit* is present,
*il lut* is passé simple. *Il crut* (he
believed, from *croire*) and *il crût* (it grew, from *croître*) differ only by the circumflex,
and *il fut* (was) is not *qu'il fût* (subjunctive, lesson 06). *Il plut* can be "it rained" or
"he pleased": *le roman plut au public* (the public liked the novel).

## The passé antérieur

The **[[passé antérieur]]** is *avoir* or *être* in the passé simple plus the past participle: *il eut
fini, elle fut partie, ils se furent assis*. It marks an action completed just before another one
in the passé simple, and it lives almost only in two frames:

- after *quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, après que*: *Dès qu'il eut aperçu l'eau, il courut
  à la mairie.* — As soon as he had seen the water, he ran to the town hall.
- after *à peine*, with inversion, followed by *que*: *À peine fut-elle arrivée que l'orage
  éclata.* — She had hardly arrived when the storm broke.

The plus-que-parfait describes a state that was already in place (*l'eau avait envahi la cave*:
the water had flooded the cellar). The passé antérieur says one event was over before the next
one began. In your own writing, use the plus-que-parfait or *après avoir* + participle: *Après
avoir aperçu l'eau, il courut* becomes, in the passé composé, *Après avoir aperçu l'eau, il a
couru*.

## Récit and discours

In 1959 the linguist Émile Benveniste published an article on the French verb (reprinted in
*Problèmes de linguistique générale*, 1966) that is still the starting point for this question.
He described two ways of telling past events.

- In **[[récit]]**, which he called *histoire*, events seem to tell themselves. Nobody says "I" or
  "you"; the events are cut off from the moment of writing. Its tenses are the passé simple, the
  imparfait, the plus-que-parfait, the passé antérieur and the conditional for the future in the
  past. Its person is the third.
- In **[[discours]]**, a speaker addresses someone, and what is said is tied to the speaker's present.
  Its tenses are the présent, the passé composé, the imparfait, the plus-que-parfait and the
  future. Every person is possible.

![Two columns side by side. On the left, récit: the passé simple for events, the imparfait for background, the plus-que-parfait and passé antérieur for what came before, the conditional for what came after; third person; example Ils partirent à l'aurore. On the right, discours: the passé composé for events, the imparfait for background, the plus-que-parfait for what came before, the future for what comes next; I and you; example Nous sommes partis à l'aube.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The two systems share the imparfait and the plus-que-parfait. The difference is the tense of the
events: the passé simple in récit, the passé composé in discours. A letter, a conversation, a
blog post or a newspaper interview is discours; a novel, a tale or a history book is
traditionally récit.

*Mixing them is a choice.* A novelist who writes in the passé composé brings the story close to
the narrator's voice (lesson 08h2 shows what Camus did with this). A journalist who slips a passé
simple into an article gives an event the distance of history, sometimes with irony: *Le ministre
promit, le ministre partit, la réforme resta dans un tiroir.* And many contemporary novels are
told in the present.

## Foreground and background

Inside the récit, the two main tenses share out the work. The passé simple puts events in the
**[[foreground]]**: they happen one after another and move the story on. The imparfait paints the
**[[background]]**: the setting, the states, the habits, what was going on when the events came.

- *Il pleuvait depuis huit jours* (background). *La crue survint dans la nuit* (foreground).
- *Les femmes se hâtaient de monter le grain au grenier* (background: what was going on). *Étienne
  s'élança vers la maison* (foreground: the next event).

At C1 you met the *imparfait narratif* (*Le lendemain, il mourait*). Seen from here, it is a
deliberate breach of this sharing: an event in the foreground told in a background tense, so
that the camera stops on it.

## Where the passé simple lives today

You will meet it in novels and tales, in history books, in many biographies, and in some press
genres: obituaries, sports stories, magazine portraits. It is mostly in the third person. You
will not meet it in conversation, in letters and emails, or in most news writing, which uses the
passé composé and the présent. A first-person passé simple (*je partis, nous arrivâmes*) belongs
to the literary memoir; in an email it would sound like a joke.

## Reading: la crue de la Vaurelle

The text below is an original chronicle in the classical récit system. Read it once for the
story, then a second time looking only at the verbs.

> **La crue de la Vaurelle** (chronique de Saint-Aubin, 1857)
>
> Le village de Saint-Aubin s'étendait alors sur les deux rives de la Vaurelle, que reliait un
> vieux pont de bois. Les Morel, meuniers de père en fils, tenaient le moulin d'aval ; les Garnier,
> passeurs, vivaient dans une maison basse au bord de l'eau. On disait que les deux familles ne
> s'étaient jamais aimées. Ce fut pourtant au bal de la Saint-Jean, en 1856, que le jeune Étienne
> Morel s'éprit de Louise, la fille du passeur.
>
> Le père Morel s'opposa d'abord au mariage, puis se ravisa : la dot était maigre, mais Louise
> savait lire et compter. On célébra les noces le 2 juin 1857. Dans la pénombre de l'église, la
> mariée tressaillit au premier coup de cloche ; les vieilles y virent un mauvais présage. Le
> soir, on dansa dans la grange jusqu'à l'aurore.
>
> Il pleuvait depuis huit jours. Dans la nuit du 3 au 4 juin, la crue survint. Dès que le petit
> Garnier eut aperçu l'eau sous la porte, il courut à la mairie, où il arriva haletant, blême,
> incapable de parler. Le maire fit sonner le tocsin sur-le-champ. Tout le village accourut sur la
> digue. « Le pont ! » s'écria quelqu'un. Le vieux pont chancela, gémit, puis s'effondra dans un
> fracas que couvrit à peine le grondement du torrent. Un cri d'effroi traversa la nuit.
>
> Étienne s'élança vers la maison des Garnier, où Louise était retournée chercher sa mère. Il
> gravit le talus, entra dans l'eau jusqu'à la taille et ramena les deux femmes, qu'il étreignit
> longuement sur la berge. Pendant ce temps, les autres se hâtaient de monter le grain au grenier.
> À l'aube, les villageois découvrirent avec stupeur l'étendue du désastre : des vaches erraient
> dans les prés noyés, le moulin n'avait plus de roue, et, au milieu des eaux, seul le clocher se
> dressait encore au-dessus des toits à demi noyés.
>
> Ruinés, les Morel décidèrent de tenter leur chance en Amérique. Ils vendirent ce qui leur
> restait et partirent en septembre pour Le Havre. Le voyage fut riche en péripéties : une roue de
> la charrette se brisa près de Rouen, et la petite Rose, la sœur d'Étienne, qui sanglotait depuis
> le départ, tomba malade. À peine furent-ils arrivés au port qu'un agent leur proposa des billets
> à moitié prix ; Étienne flaira l'escroquerie et refusa. Le 2 octobre, le navire leva l'ancre.
> Louise frémit en voyant la côte disparaître. Elle ne revit jamais Saint-Aubin.

*Glosses:* *le moulin d'aval* the downstream mill; *le passeur* the ferryman; *la dot* the
dowry; *le présage* omen; *la grange* barn; *le tocsin* the alarm bell; *la digue* embankment;
*le fracas* crash; *le grondement* roar; *le talus* bank, slope; *la berge* riverbank; *flairer
l'escroquerie* to smell a swindle; *lever l'ancre* to weigh anchor.

*Summary, paragraph by paragraph.* (1) Saint-Aubin lies on both banks of the Vaurelle, joined by
a wooden bridge; the miller's family and the ferryman's family dislike each other, yet the miller's
son, Étienne, falls for the ferryman's daughter, Louise. (2) His father objects, then changes his
mind; the wedding takes place on 2 June 1857, and the bride's start at the first bell is taken as
a bad omen. (3) After a week of rain the flood comes in the night; the ferryman's boy raises the
alarm, the village runs to the embankment, and the bridge collapses. (4) Étienne rescues Louise and
her mother; at dawn the villagers find the meadows drowned, the mill wrecked and only the bell
tower standing. (5) Ruined, the Morels leave for America through Le Havre; after a broken wheel, a
sick child and a swindler, they sail on 2 October, and Louise never sees the village again.

*What the verbs do.* The imparfait sets the scene (*s'étendait, tenaient, vivaient, pleuvait,
se hâtaient, erraient*); the passé simple carries every event (*s'éprit, se ravisa, survint,
accourut, chancela, s'élança, partirent*). The plus-que-parfait looks back (*ne s'étaient jamais
aimées, était retournée*). The passé antérieur appears twice, in its two frames: *Dès que le petit
Garnier eut aperçu l'eau, il courut* and *À peine furent-ils arrivés au port qu'un agent leur
proposa*. Notice the run of three passés simples for the bridge (*chancela, gémit, s'effondra*):
three events in quick succession, joined by commas and one *puis*, which speeds the narrative up.

## The same events in discours

A year later, Louise writes to her mother. The events are the same; the system is not.

> *New York, le 12 mars 1858.* Ma chère maman, nous sommes arrivés le 20 novembre, après sept
> semaines de mer. La traversée a été dure : Rose est restée malade jusqu'à Terre-Neuve, et j'ai
> cru plus d'une fois que nous ne verrions jamais la terre. Étienne a trouvé du travail dans une
> minoterie dès la première semaine ; moi, je fais des ménages chez une dame de Lyon qui s'est
> installée ici il y a dix ans. Je pense souvent à la nuit de la crue. Depuis, je n'ai jamais eu
> aussi peur. Dites à Pierre que nous lui enverrons l'argent du passage au printemps. Je vous
> embrasse de tout mon cœur. Votre fille, Louise.

*New York, 12 March 1858.* My dear mother, we arrived on 20 November, after seven weeks at sea.
The crossing was hard: Rose was ill all the way to Newfoundland, and more than once I thought we
would never see land. Étienne found work in a flour mill in the very first week; as for me, I do
housework for a lady from Lyon who settled here ten years ago. I often think of the night of the
flood. I have never been so frightened since. Tell Pierre that we will send him the money for his
passage in the spring. I send you all my love. Your daughter, Louise.

The letter speaks in the first person to someone (*Ma chère maman, Dites à Pierre*). Its events
are in the passé composé (*nous sommes arrivés, j'ai cru, Étienne a trouvé*), measured from the
moment of writing (*il y a dix ans, Depuis*) and continued into the future (*nous enverrons*). In
the chronicle, the same arrival would read *ils arrivèrent le 20 novembre*, and *il y a dix ans*
would become *dix ans plus tôt*.

## Reading the frame

The chronicle you read is not the whole book. In our invented village, a schoolteacher finds it in
1912 in an attic, with Louise's letter, and tells in a short *récit-cadre* (frame story) how he found it; an
*épilogue* then says what became of the Morel children. The frame story is told in the passé
composé (*j'ai trouvé ces pages dans le grenier de l'école*), the chronicle in the passé simple:
the change of system marks the change of narrator. Look out for this in 19th-century novels, which
sometimes open with a narrator who finds a manuscript.

## Turning a récit into your own French

When you summarise or retell a literary text, write in the présent or the passé composé:

| in the text | in your summary |
|---|---|
| *La crue survint dans la nuit.* | *La crue est survenue dans la nuit.* / *La crue survient dans la nuit.* |
| *Tout le village accourut.* | *Tout le village a accouru* (or *est accouru*). |
| *Dès qu'il eut aperçu l'eau, il courut à la mairie.* | *Dès qu'il a aperçu l'eau, il a couru à la mairie.* |
| *À peine furent-ils arrivés qu'un agent leur proposa des billets.* | *À peine étaient-ils arrivés qu'un agent leur a proposé des billets.* |

*Accourir* is one of the few verbs found with both auxiliaries: *avoir* is the usual choice,
*être* is common in literary French. Both are correct; the drills of this course use *avoir*.

## Common mistakes

- *Reading il fit as "he did" only.* *Faire* + infinitive is causative: *Le maire fit sonner le
  tocsin* means the mayor *had* the bell rung.
- *Confusing il vint and il vit.* *Vint* is *venir*; *vit* is *voir* (or *vivre* in the
  present: *il vit à Lyon*). The *n* makes the difference.
- *Reading the passé antérieur as a state.* *Dès qu'il eut fini* is "as soon as
  he had finished", one event before the next, not a description.
- *Writing the passé simple in a letter or an email.* *Je reçus votre lettre* in a reply sounds
  like a novel or a joke. Write *j'ai reçu*.
- *Mixing systems by accident* in a summary: *Étienne s'élança et a ramené Louise*. Choose the
  passé composé, or the présent, and keep it.

## Key points

- The passé simple has two regular ending sets (*-a-, -i-*); irregular verbs add *-u-* and the
  *-in-* of *venir* and *tenir*. Learn the irregular stems by their vowel.
- The passé antérieur (*il eut fini, elle fut partie*) follows *dès que, quand, lorsque, après que*
  and *à peine … que*, for an event completed just before another.
- Benveniste's **[[récit]]** (passé simple, third person, cut off from the present) and **[[discours]]**
  (passé composé, tied to the speaker's present) are two systems; mixing them is a stylistic choice.
- The passé simple sets events in the foreground; the imparfait paints the background.
- Read these forms; write the passé composé or the présent when you retell.

lessons.title: Qu'il fût, eût-il su: the literary subjunctive and the second conditional
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 05 gave you the passé simple. Its stem is also the key to a family of forms that modern
speech has dropped but literature, old letters and some columnists still use: the imperfect and
pluperfect subjunctive, and a second form of the conditionnel passé. If you took B2's honors
lesson on the literary subjunctive, this goes much further; if not, everything starts from zero
here.

Like the passé simple, these forms are for recognition: you read them, understand them and
know what they would be in modern French. You never have to type them. What you *do* use are
their everyday equivalents, which this lesson also teaches: *ne serait-ce que, même si, même au
prix de, il aurait fallu*. The theme is letters: an invented correspondence of 1853 between a
novelist and her publisher, and a modern columnist who borrows its style to make fun of a minister.

## The imperfect subjunctive

The **[[imperfect subjunctive]]** is built on the passé simple. Take the *tu* form, drop the final
*-s*, and add *-sse, -sses, -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent*. The third person singular has no *-sse*:
its last vowel takes a circumflex and a *-t* follows (*-ât, -ît, -ût, -înt*).

![A table showing how the imperfect subjunctive is formed. Six verbs: parler (tu parlas, que je parlasse, qu'il parlât), finir (tu finis, finisse, qu'il finît), recevoir (tu reçus, reçusse, qu'il reçût), venir (tu vins, vinsse, qu'il vînt), être (tu fus, fusse, qu'il fût), avoir (tu eus, eusse, qu'il eût). A note at the bottom: il fut (passé simple) is not qu'il fût (subjunctive); il eut is not qu'il eût.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | parler | finir | être | avoir | venir |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| que je | parlasse | finisse | fusse | eusse | vinsse |
| que tu | parlasses | finisses | fusses | eusses | vinsses |
| qu'il, qu'elle | parlât | finît | fût | eût | vînt |
| que nous | parlassions | finissions | fussions | eussions | vinssions |
| que vous | parlassiez | finissiez | fussiez | eussiez | vinssiez |
| qu'ils, qu'elles | parlassent | finissent | fussent | eussent | vinssent |

Two things follow from the table.

- Only the third person singular is still met often (*qu'il fût, qu'elle eût, qu'il vînt*). The
  other persons sound stiff or comic today, partly because *-asse* and *-usse* rhyme with words
  nobody wants in a sentence: *que je parlasse, que nous reçussions*. Writers have long joked about them.
- For *finir*-type verbs most persons look exactly like the present subjunctive (*que je finisse,
  qu'ils finissent*). Only *qu'il finît*, with its circumflex, gives the tense away.

The circumflex is the whole difference between two pairs you must not confuse: *il fut* (passé
simple: he was) and *qu'il fût* (subjunctive); *il eut* (he had) and *qu'il eût*. A *que* or a
subjunctive trigger in front usually confirms it.

## The pluperfect subjunctive

The **[[pluperfect subjunctive]]** is *avoir* or *être* in the imperfect subjunctive plus the past
participle: *qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie, qu'ils se fussent trompés*. It is the past of the
imperfect subjunctive: something completed before the time of the main verb.

## The classical concordance

Everyday modern French uses only the present and past subjunctive, whatever the tense of the main verb
(C1 taught this). Classical prose, and much careful writing well into the 20th century, followed the
**[[classical concordance]]**: after a main verb in a past tense or the conditional, the subjunctive
shifted back too.

| main verb | same time or later | earlier |
|---|---|---|
| *Je veux que …* (present) | *qu'il vienne* | *qu'il soit venu* |
| *Je voulais que …* (classical) | *qu'il vînt* | *qu'il fût venu* |
| *Je voulais que …* (modern) | *qu'il vienne* | *qu'il soit venu* |

- *Je doutais qu'il fût venu.* — I doubted that he had come. (Modern: *qu'il soit venu*.)
- *On voudrait que mon roman ne parût jamais.* — They would like my novel never to appear.
  (Modern: *ne paraisse jamais*.)

A few writers and some journalists keep the third person singular by choice (*il fallait qu'il
fût là*), as a mark of elegance or of irony. It is never a mistake to read it; you are never
required to write it.

## The second conditional

The **[[conditionnel passé deuxième forme]]** has exactly the form of the pluperfect subjunctive but
the meaning of the ordinary conditionnel passé:

- *Il eût fallu le prévenir.* = *Il aurait fallu le prévenir.* — He should have been told.
- *On eût dit un enfant.* = *On aurait dit un enfant.* — You would have thought he was a child.
- *J'eusse aimé vous l'annoncer moi-même.* = *J'aurais aimé …* — I would have liked to tell you
  myself.

It lives in literary narrative and in a handful of set phrases, above all *il eût fallu, on eût dit,
il eût mieux valu, j'eusse préféré*. The classical hypothetical sentence could use it in either
clause, or both:

- *S'il l'eût su, il fût venu.* = *S'il l'avait su, il serait venu.* — If he had known, he would
  have come.

Notice that *si* is followed by *eût* here, a combination modern French forbids with the
conditional (*si j'aurais* is a classic error). The literary form is a subjunctive in shape, which
is why *si* accepts it.

## Hypothetical inversion

**[[Hypothetical inversion]]** puts the verb before its subject, without *si*, to make a condition or a
concession. With the literary forms it is the most frequent survivor today:

- *Eût-il su la vérité, il ne serait pas venu.* — Had he known the truth, he would not have come.
- *Fût-elle ministre, elle devrait répondre.* — Even if she were a minister, she would have to
  answer.
- *Dût-il y passer la nuit, il finira.* — Even if it takes him all night, he will finish.

English does the same with *had he known, were she to*. In your own writing, use *si* + plus-que-parfait
(*S'il avait su la vérité*) or *même si*. The conditional with inversion is also current for a
concession: *Aurait-elle tous les diplômes du monde, elle ne trouverait pas ce poste* (even if she
had every degree in the world).

## Reading the forms: which eût is it?

The same few letters can be four different things. A short checklist sorts them out.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to identify eut and eût
  accDescr: Start with the form. Without a circumflex, eut or fut is a passé simple, or a passé antérieur when a participle follows after dès que or quand. With a circumflex, ask what comes before. After que and a subjunctive trigger, it is an imperfect subjunctive, or a pluperfect subjunctive when a participle follows. At the head of a clause with the subject after it, it is a hypothetical inversion. Elsewhere, meaning would have, it is the second conditional.
  A["eut / fut, or eût / fût?"] --> B["no circumflex"]
  A --> C["circumflex"]
  B --> D["passé simple: il eut peur"]
  B --> E["+ participle after dès que: passé antérieur"]
  C --> F["after que + trigger: imperfect subjunctive"]
  F --> G["+ participle: pluperfect subjunctive"]
  C --> H["verb first, subject after: hypothetical inversion"]
  C --> I["means would have: second conditional"]
```

## Living formulas

Some of these forms survive as fixed formulas in journalism, essays and speeches. You will meet
them often; read them, and use the everyday equivalent in your own writing.

| formula | meaning | everyday equivalent (productive) |
|---|---|---|
| *fût-ce* | be it, even | *même* |
| *ne fût-ce que* | if only, even just | *ne serait-ce que* |
| *dût-il …* | even if he had to | *même s'il devait* |
| *dussé-je …* | even if I had to | *même si je devais* |
| *qui que ce fût* | whoever it was | *qui que ce soit* |
| *quoi qu'il en fût* | be that as it may | *quoi qu'il en soit* |
| *on eût dit* | it was as if | *on aurait dit* |
| *plût au ciel que …* | if only … (wish) | *si seulement* |

*Dussé-je* has an acute accent, not the *dusse* you would expect: two silent *e*'s in a row
(*dusse-je*) were thought ugly, so usage changed the first one (the 1990 spelling
recommendations write *dussè-je*, as it is pronounced). *Ne serait-ce que*, with the
ordinary conditional, is fully current and the form to write: *Répondez-lui, ne serait-ce que par
politesse* (answer her, if only out of politeness).

## Reading: three letters of 1853

The letters below are invented. Hortense Valmont, a novelist living on her family's estate in
Touraine, waits for news of her manuscript from her Paris publisher, Anatole Brunet.

> **I.** *La Garenne, près de Loches, le 14 octobre 1853.* Monsieur, voilà trois semaines que je
> me morfonds dans la maison de mes aïeux sans recevoir de vous la moindre missive. J'avais espéré
> que vous me répondriez avant la fin de septembre ; je craignais même que mon manuscrit ne se fût
> égaré. On m'écrit de Paris qu'une cabale s'ourdit contre moi dans certains salons, et que l'on
> voudrait que mon roman ne parût jamais. Je ne crois pas que ce soit votre dessein. Mais sachez-le
> : je publierai ce livre, fût-ce à mes frais, dussé-je vendre pour cela les dernières terres de mon
> père. Écrivez-moi, ne fût-ce que deux lignes ; votre silence me fait languir plus que l'opprobre
> dont on me menace. Votre très humble servante, Hortense Valmont.
>
> **II.** *Paris, le 20 octobre 1853.* Madame, votre épître m'a mis dans un grand émoi, et je vous
> dois des excuses. Votre manuscrit n'est point perdu : je l'ai lu deux fois, avec une ardeur que je
> n'avais pas éprouvée depuis longtemps. Il eût fallu que je vous l'écrivisse sur-le-champ ; une
> affliction de famille m'en a empêché. Quant à la cabale, n'en ayez aucun souci : eût-elle tout le
> faubourg Saint-Germain pour elle, elle ne ferait pas reculer ma maison. J'eusse aimé vous annoncer
> de vive voix que nous imprimerons en janvier ; je vous mande donc à Paris pour la fin du mois, si
> votre santé le permet. Croyez, Madame, à ma respectueuse sollicitude. A. Brunet.
>
> **III.** *La Garenne, le 2 novembre 1853.* Monsieur, je ne pourrai venir à Paris avant l'hiver :
> ma vieille tante est passée de vie à trépas la semaine dernière, et je dois rester auprès de ma
> mère. Votre lettre a pourtant été, au milieu de cette infortune, un instant de félicité. Quant à
> mon soupirant de Tours, qui voulait que je renonçasse à écrire, il a dû apprendre la nouvelle avec
> courroux : on eût dit, à le voir dimanche à la messe, un homme qu'on venait de voler. Je
> m'épanche trop ; pardonnez à une épistolière que la langueur de la campagne rend bavarde. H. V.

*Glosses:* *la cabale* a plot by a group; *le faubourg Saint-Germain* the aristocratic quarter of
Paris, here its salons; *ma maison* my publishing house; *de vive voix* in person; *bavard*
talkative.

*Summary.* (I) Hortense has heard nothing for three weeks and feared her manuscript was lost; a
cabal in the Paris salons wants the novel suppressed; she will publish it even at her own expense
and begs for two lines. (II) Brunet apologises: a family sorrow kept him from writing, he
loved the manuscript, the cabal can do nothing, the book will be printed in January, and he
summons her to Paris. (III) Her aunt has died, so she can't come before winter; his letter was a
moment of bliss, and the suitor who wanted her to stop writing looked as if he had been robbed.

*What to notice.* The classical concordance after past or conditional main verbs: *je craignais
que mon manuscrit ne se fût égaré* (pluperfect subjunctive, with the expletive *ne* after *craindre*),
*l'on voudrait que mon roman ne parût jamais, il voulait que je renonçasse* (imperfect). But after
a present main verb, the present: *Je ne crois pas que ce soit votre dessein*. The second
conditional: *Il eût fallu, J'eusse aimé, on eût dit*. Hypothetical inversion: *eût-elle tout le
faubourg pour elle* (even if it had). And three living formulas in one paragraph of Hortense's
letter: *fût-ce, dussé-je, ne fût-ce que*. *Que je renonçasse* and *que je vous l'écrivisse* are
there on purpose: a modern reader smiles at them, as Hortense's suitor never would have. Brunet,
the publisher, writes as an *épistolier* of his time; nobody would write *je vous mande à Paris*
today except as a joke.

## Reading: a modern column

The columnist below, also invented, uses the same forms for effect in a newspaper of today.

> **Concertation.** Le ministre a donc reçu les syndicats. Il les a reçus longuement, aimablement,
> et sans rien leur promettre, fût-ce une date. On eût dit un châtelain de 1850 recevant des cousins
> pauvres : du thé, des sourires, et la porte. Eût-il fallu, pour obtenir une réponse, écrire au
> ministère sur papier vergé et signer « votre très humble servante » ? Peut-être. J'ai pour ma part
> envoyé trois courriels, ne fût-ce que pour savoir si quelqu'un les lisait. On m'a répondu, le
> surlendemain, par un message automatique qui me remerciait de ma sollicitude. Il eût été plus
> simple de dire non. Mais un non, de nos jours, exige du courage, et le courage, dussé-je passer
> pour une vieille grincheuse, se fait rare dans les antichambres. Je propose donc une réforme
> modeste : que les ministres répondent, ne serait-ce que par oui ou par non. La langue qui a
> inventé l'imparfait du subjonctif saura bien s'en accommoder.

*Concertation.* So the minister received the unions. He received them at length, kindly, and
without promising them anything, not even a date. It was like a lord of the manor in 1850
receiving poor cousins: tea, smiles, and the door. Should one have written to the ministry on laid
paper and signed "your most humble servant" to get an answer? Perhaps. For my part, I sent three
emails, if only to find out whether anyone was reading them. Two days later, I received an
automatic reply thanking me for my concern. It would have been simpler to say no. But a no, these
days, takes courage, and courage, even if I am taken for a grumpy old woman, is in short supply in
the ministers' waiting rooms. So I propose a modest reform: that ministers answer, if only with a
yes or a no. The language that invented the imperfect subjunctive will cope with it.

The column works by contrast. The literary forms (*fût-ce, on eût dit, eût-il fallu, il eût été,
dussé-je*) belong to the world of châteaux and laid paper; the facts (emails, automatic replies,
unions) belong to ours. The gap is the joke: the minister's politeness is as outdated as the
grammar. Notice the last proposal, which switches to the modern *ne serait-ce que*: the columnist
asks for something plain, in plain French.

## Common mistakes

- *Reading qu'il fût as the passé simple.* The circumflex and the *que* mark a subjunctive: *Il
  fallait qu'il fût là* means "he had to be there".
- *Taking il eût fallu for a subjunctive after a trigger.* With no *que* before it, *il eût fallu*
  is the second conditional: "it would have been necessary".
- *Copying the forms into your own writing.* An *eût-il fallu* in a cover letter or a DALF essay
  sounds affected unless the irony is obvious. Write *il aurait fallu*, *ne serait-ce que*, *même
  si*.
- *Writing si + conditional because the literary sentence has si + eût.* *S'il l'eût su* is
  literary; *s'il l'avait su* is the modern form; *s'il l'aurait su* is wrong in careful French.
- *Dusse-je.* The literary form is *dussé-je*, with an acute accent.

## Key points

- Imperfect subjunctive: the *tu* passé simple without *-s* + *-sse, -sses, -ssions, -ssiez,
  -ssent*, and for *il* a circumflex + *-t*; only *qu'il parlât, fût, eût, vînt* are still common.
- Pluperfect subjunctive: *qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie*; the same shape is the
  conditionnel passé deuxième forme (*il eût fallu = il aurait fallu*).
- The classical concordance shifts the subjunctive back after a past main verb; modern French
  doesn't.
- Hypothetical inversion (*Eût-il su …, Dût-il …*) replaces *si*.
- Read *fût-ce, ne fût-ce que, dussé-je, on eût dit*; write *même, ne serait-ce que, même si je
  devais, on aurait dit*.

lessons.title: Cadence, rythme, sonorité: the music of the sentence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A C2 reader notices not only what a sentence says but how it moves: where it speeds up, where it
breathes, where it lands. A C2 writer can make those choices on purpose. This lesson gives you the
French terms for them (the ones used in a *commentaire de texte*) and shows how rhythm, sound,
syntax, adjective position and punctuation shape a page of prose. Unlike lessons 05 and 06, all of
this is for your own writing too.

The theme is a walk along the quays of a city at dusk, described three times: once with care, once
flatly, once with far too much. B2's honors lesson on figures of speech covered the *métaphore*,
the *comparaison* and their cousins; we use them here without defining them again.

## Rhythm: groups, lengths and landings

French prose is read in groups (*les groupes rythmiques*): stretches of words between two pauses, usually marked by a
comma or by a natural break. Counting their syllables, roughly, shows the rhythm.

- A **[[binary rhythm]]** (*un rythme binaire*) balances two groups: *lent et lourd* ; *Le fleuve s'assombrit, la ville se
  tait*. It gives an impression of order, symmetry, sometimes opposition.
- A **[[ternary rhythm]]** (*un rythme ternaire*) lines up three: *Il hésita, se retourna, partit*. Three is the classic
  number of rhetoric: it feels complete.

The length of the groups matters as much as their number. In a **[[cadence]]** *majeure*, each group is
longer than the one before, and the sentence opens out: *La pluie glissait sur les pavés,
ruisselait le long des gouttières, se perdait lentement dans les caniveaux du quai* (after the
subject, roughly six, eight, then thirteen syllables). In a cadence *mineure*, the last group is shorter, and the sentence closes
sharply: *Elle avait tout prévu, tout préparé, tout vérifié avec soin : sauf lui.* A very short
sentence after long ones, the *chute*, has the same effect on a paragraph.

### The period

The **[[period]]** (*la période*) is the grand form of French prose rhythm: a long sentence that rises
through several subordinate clauses (the *protase*), reaches a high point (the *acmé*), and falls in
a shorter main clause (the *apodose*).

![A diagram of a period. Three boxes climb like stairs: Quand les cafés rentraient leurs chaises; quand le dernier autobus disparaissait au bout du quai; et que le fleuve, sous les ponts de pierre, se fondait peu à peu dans l'ombre. A dashed arc rises over them to a high point marked acmé, then falls to a fourth box, la ville, lentement, se taisait. Under the stairs a bracket reads protase (montée), under the last box apodose (descente).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Quand les cafés rentraient leurs chaises, quand le dernier autobus disparaissait au bout du quai et
que le fleuve, sous les ponts de pierre, se fondait peu à peu dans l'ombre, la ville, lentement, se
taisait.* — When the cafés were bringing in their chairs, when the last bus was disappearing at the
end of the quay and the river, under the stone bridges, was melting little by little into the
shadows, the city, slowly, fell silent.

The three temporal clauses (*quand, quand, et que*) grow longer (*cadence majeure* inside the rise); the expected main verb is
held back; then the apodose drops in a few words. Bossuet's funeral orations and Chateaubriand's
prose are the classic models of the period; you will meet it in speeches too (lesson 20).

## Sound

- **[[Alliteration]]** (*l'allitération*) repeats a consonant sound: *le fleuve, lent et lourd* (l);
  *sous les saules, le souffle du soir* (s).
- **[[Assonance]]** repeats a vowel sound: *la pluie fine glissait sur la vitrine* (i).
- **[[Euphony]]** (*l'euphonie*) is a pleasant flow of sounds. French grammar itself serves it: the *t*
  in *viendra-t-il*, the *l'* in *si l'on*, *cet* before a vowel. Its opposite, *la cacophonie*, is
  a harsh or comic clash: *Ton thé t'a-t-il ôté ta toux ?* is the textbook example.
- A **[[hiatus]]** is two vowels meeting, between words or inside one: *il alla à Arles*, *il a été*,
  *poète*. Classical verse forbade it between words; careful prose avoids piling them up.

Together, rhythm and sound make the *musicalité* of a passage of prose. Sound should support meaning, not
decorate it. An alliteration in *s* can suggest wind or a
whisper; the same *s* in a sentence about a tax reform is just a tongue-twister.

## Syntax as style

- **[[Parataxis]]** (*la parataxe*) places clauses side by side without subordination: *Il pleuvait.
  Elle partit.* The reader supplies the link (cause? sequence?). Effect: sober, fast, sometimes
  brutal.
- **[[Hypotaxis]]** (*l'hypotaxe*) subordinates: *Comme il pleuvait, elle partit.* The writer states
  the link. Effect: explanation, nuance, the long sentences of Proust.
- **[[Asyndeton]]** (*l'asyndète*) leaves out the linking words in a list: *Il vint, il vit, il signa.*
  Its opposite, *la polysyndète*, repeats them: *Et la pluie, et le vent, et la nuit.* The first
  speeds up; the second insists, slows down, accumulates.
- The **[[nominal sentence]]** (*la phrase nominale*) has no conjugated verb: *Novembre, déjà. Silence.
  Puis un rire.* It sets a scene in a few strokes, as stage directions and headlines do.
- *Fronting and stylistic inversion* move a complement to the head of the sentence and the subject
  after the verb: *Au-dessus des toits scintillaient les premières étoiles.* The subject arrives
  last, like a reveal. (C1 taught the formal inversions after *peut-être, aussi, ainsi*; this one is
  free and purely stylistic.)
- *Apposition and detachment* (C1) slow a sentence down: *La ville, lentement, se taisait.*

## Adjective position

Most adjectives follow the noun and simply classify it (*une lumière verte*). Placed before, an
adjective often becomes subjective, emotional or literary: *une sombre histoire, un pâle sourire,
d'étranges lueurs*. Some adjectives change meaning with position:

| before the noun | after the noun |
|---|---|
| *un ancien élève* (former) | *un quartier ancien* (old) |
| *un cher ami* (dear) | *un repas cher* (expensive) |
| *ma propre voiture* (own) | *une voiture propre* (clean) |
| *un seul témoin* (only one) | *un témoin seul* (alone) |
| *un pauvre homme* (pitiable) | *un homme pauvre* (poor) |
| *un grand homme* (great) | *un homme grand* (tall) |
| *un curieux personnage* (odd) | *un personnage curieux* (inquisitive, or odd) |

For some of these, usage varies: *curieux* after the noun can mean either, and *seul* placed
before or after doesn't always change much. Check Le Robert before building an argument on a single
position.

## Punctuation as rhythm

The semicolon joins two clauses that belong together and makes a medium pause; the colon announces
an explanation, a list or a consequence, and creates suspense; the dash isolates an aside or a sudden
turn. French typography puts a non-breaking space before *; : ! ?* (lesson 04h2 owns the details).
In prose, punctuation is your score: a comma is a breath, a semicolon a pause, a full stop a silence.

## How to analyse a sentence's rhythm

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Analysing the rhythm of a sentence
  accDescr: First cut the sentence into groups at the pauses. Count the syllables of each group. Compare the lengths: groups that grow give a cadence majeure, a short last group gives a cadence mineure, two equal groups give a binary balance. Then listen for repeated sounds. Then look at the syntax: subordination or juxtaposition, links or no links. Finally, say what effect each choice has on the meaning.
  A[Cut into groups at the pauses] --> B[Count the syllables]
  B --> C{Compare the lengths}
  C --> D[growing: cadence majeure]
  C --> E[short last group: cadence mineure]
  C --> F[two equal groups: binary balance]
  D --> G[Listen for repeated sounds]
  E --> G
  F --> G
  G --> H[Look at the syntax and the links]
  H --> I[Say what each choice does to the meaning]
```

The last step is the one that counts. "There is an alliteration in *l*" is an observation; "the
alliteration in *l* and the two heavy syllables slow the river down" is an analysis.

## Reading: le soir sur les quais

> Novembre, déjà. Sept heures. Sur les quais, la lumière crépusculaire hésitait encore entre le gris
> et l'or ; le fleuve, lent et lourd, prenait des reflets mordorés sous les ponts. Les platanes
> bruissaient à peine. Une brume diaphane montait de l'eau, s'accrochait aux lampadaires, effaçait
> les façades de l'autre rive.
>
> Je marchais sans but. Il avait plu tout l'après-midi. La pluie glissait sur les pavés, ruisselait
> le long des gouttières, se perdait lentement dans les caniveaux du quai. Il flottait dans l'air humide des
> effluves de pain chaud, et de feuilles mouillées, et d'essence. Quand les cafés rentraient leurs
> chaises, quand le dernier autobus disparaissait au bout du quai et que le fleuve, sous les ponts de
> pierre, se fondait peu à peu dans l'ombre, la ville, lentement, se taisait.
>
> Rue des Tanneurs, les vitrines jetaient sur le trottoir des reflets chatoyants. Elles offraient des
> soies, des bijoux, des flacons aux formes compliquées : rien pour moi. Plus loin, la lumière
> blafarde d'une pharmacie de garde découpait sur la chaussée un rectangle vert. Dans la librairie
> où je suis entré un instant, les voix étaient feutrées, les pas aussi ; un vieil homme lisait
> debout, immobile, comme sorti d'un autre siècle.
>
> Puis la nuit est tombée. Une à une, les fenêtres se sont allumées. Au-dessus des toits
> scintillaient les premières étoiles ; des volutes de fumée montaient des cheminées, et d'étranges
> lueurs bleues dansaient sur l'eau noire. La ville sortait de la torpeur du jour pour entrer dans une
> autre, plus douce. Silence. Puis, très loin, le bruissement d'une fontaine, le rire d'une femme, un
> volet qui claquait. Personne.

*Glosses:* *le platane* plane tree; *la gouttière* gutter (on a roof); *le caniveau* gutter (in the
street); *la pharmacie de garde* the duty chemist; *la chaussée* roadway; *le volet* shutter.

*Summary.* (1) A November evening on the quays: the twilight wavers between grey and gold, the river
glints bronze under the bridges, a mist rises and blurs the far bank. (2) The narrator wanders; the
rain of the afternoon still runs into the gutters, the air smells of bread, wet leaves and petrol,
and as the cafés close and the last bus leaves, the city falls quiet. (3) Shop windows shimmer with
things he can't afford; a chemist's sign throws green light on the road; in a bookshop, voices are
hushed and an old man reads, motionless. (4) Night falls, windows light up, stars and smoke rise,
blue lights dance on the water; then silence, a fountain, a laugh, a shutter, and nobody.

*Reading the rhythm.* The text opens and closes on nominal sentences (*Novembre, déjà. Sept heures*;
*Silence. … Personne.*): a frame of short, verbless strokes. In paragraph 1, *lent et lourd* is
binary and alliterative, and the mist rises in an asyndeton of three verbs (*montait, s'accrochait,
effaçait*). Paragraph 2 builds a ternary *cadence majeure* (the rain), a polysyndeton (*et de
feuilles mouillées, et d'essence*) that makes the smells pile up, and then the period of the
diagram. Paragraph 3 ends a list on a *cadence mineure* (*rien pour moi*); the bookshop is *feutré*
in sound as in meaning, with a binary *les voix … les pas aussi*. In paragraph 4, the stylistic
inversion delays *les premières étoiles*, the adjective before the noun (*d'étranges lueurs*) is
subjective, and the last group, *Personne*, is the shortest of all: a *chute*.

## Two rewritings

The same walk, told flatly:

> Il est sept heures. Je marche sur les quais. Il a plu. La lumière est grise. Il y a de la brume.
> Les magasins sont éclairés. J'entre dans une librairie. Ensuite il fait nuit. On voit des étoiles.
> On entend une fontaine.

It's seven o'clock. I'm walking along the quays. It has rained. The light is grey. There's some
mist. The shops are lit up. I go into a bookshop. Then it gets dark. You can see stars. You can
hear a fountain.

And told with far too much:

> Ô soir ! Ô quais mordorés et crépusculaires, où la brume diaphane, chatoyante, mystérieuse et
> infiniment mélancolique ruisselait, scintillait et bruissait dans la torpeur feutrée d'une ville
> blafarde, tandis que mon âme éperdue, errante et solitaire cherchait, sous les volutes ineffables
> d'effluves inouïs, l'ombre d'un rêve à jamais évanoui !

O evening! O bronze-gold, twilit quays, where the diaphanous, shimmering, mysterious and infinitely
melancholy mist streamed, sparkled and rustled in the hushed torpor of a pallid city, while my
distraught, wandering and solitary soul sought, beneath the ineffable swirls of unheard-of scents,
the shadow of a dream forever vanished!

The first version is pure parataxis with no variation: every sentence has the same length and the
same shape, so nothing stands out. It is correct and dead. The second has every device at once:
four adjectives on one noun, three verbs that can't all apply to mist (a mist doesn't *ruisseler*),
a cascade of sounds (*-ait, -ait, -ait*), exclamations, abstract words (*ineffable, inouï*). Nothing
stands out there either, because everything shouts. Style is choice: one alliteration, one inversion,
one *chute*, placed where the meaning needs them.

## Common mistakes

- *Naming devices without an effect.* "Ternary rhythm" is not an analysis until you say what the
  three groups do.
- *Seeing a cadence majeure in any long sentence.* The groups must actually grow; count the
  syllables.
- *Calling every repeated letter an alliteration.* It is a repeated *sound*: *c* in *cela* and in
  *car* is not the same sound.
- *Over-writing.* In a DALF text, two or three well-placed effects are worth more than a page of
  adjectives.
- *Polysyndète for asyndète.* *Asyndète*: no links (*il vint, il vit*); *polysyndète*: links repeated
  (*et … et … et*).

## Key points

- Count the groups and their syllables: binary balances, ternary completes; a cadence majeure opens
  out, a cadence mineure closes sharply; the period rises and falls.
- Sound (alliteration, assonance, euphony, hiatus) should echo the meaning.
- Parataxis is sober and fast, hypotaxis explains; asyndeton speeds up, polysyndeton accumulates; the
  nominal sentence paints in strokes.
- An adjective before the noun is often subjective; some change meaning with position.
- Analyse by linking each device to an effect; write by choosing a few.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
