lessons.title: À la manière de: pastiche, parody and the analysis of style
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The three lessons before this one gave you the parts of a style: the tenses of the récit, the
literary moods, rhythm and sound. The best test that you can see a style is to reproduce it. French
literature has a long tradition of doing exactly that, for fun or for a fight: the **[[pastiche]]**, the
**[[parody]]**, the burlesque and the mock-heroic. This lesson shows what each one does, where French
law draws the line, how to turn a style into a recipe, and then asks you to write a pastiche of
your own, graded.

The theme is an invented literary magazine, *Contre-Jour*, which runs a pastiche competition every
spring. Its rules are simple: a period style, a modern subject, no copying.

## Five neighbours

| | what it does | attitude to the model |
|---|---|---|
| *le pastiche* | imitates a manner (an author, a genre, a period) | a game, often admiring |
| *la parodie* | imitates in order to mock, by exaggerating or by changing the subject | critical or comic |
| *le plagiat* (C1) | copies and signs the copy as one's own | a fault, not a style exercise |
| *l'hommage* | alludes to or imitates a model to honour it | respectful |
| *le détournement* | reuses a known text, slogan or image to give it another meaning | often political |

A **[[pastiche]]** succeeds when the reader recognises the manner without finding a single sentence of
the original: it copies a *way* of writing, not a text. It rests on a *connivence* (a shared understanding) between writer
and reader, who both know the model. A **[[parody]]** exaggerates the model's features until they become
visible, and usually laughable; it lives on *outrance*. To *pasticher* a writer is to write in his or her manner;
to *parodier* one is to mock that manner. The two overlap, and a pastiche that pushes
the model's habits a little too far is already half a parody. A **[[détournement]]** keeps the shape of
a known text and changes its message: an advertising slogan turned against the brand, a famous poster
with a new caption. The word also means a hijacking, and that is the idea.

*Le plagiat* is the opposite of all of these: it hides its model instead of showing it. A *faussaire*
(forger) does something else again: he imitates a work, a signature or a handwriting to pass the copy
off as genuine. An *imitateur*, on stage, imitates voices and *tics de langage*: a parodist of
speech.

## What the law says

French copyright law lets authors forbid most uses of their work. But the Code de la propriété
intellectuelle (article L122-5, point 4°) lists among the exceptions the parody, the pastiche and the
caricature, "taking into account the laws of the genre": once a work has been made public, its author
can't forbid them. Courts have generally looked for three things: a humorous or critical intent, no
risk that the public confuses the imitation with the original, and no intent to harm. Outside that
exception, reproducing a protected work without permission is a *contrefaçon* (infringement), whatever
it is called. Plagiarism as such is not a legal category in France; the offence is the infringement.

## High and low: the burlesque and the mock-heroic

Classical French theory ranked both subjects and styles as high or low. Crossing them gives two
comic genres, both popular in the 17th century.

![A two-by-two grid. Columns: sujet bas (trivial) on the left, sujet noble (héroïque) on the right. Rows: style bas at the top, style noble at the bottom. Top left: farce, a low subject in a low style, such as the deceived husband and the beatings. Top right: burlesque, a noble subject in a low style, Aeneas talking like a carter. Bottom left: héroï-comique, a low subject in a noble style, a quarrel between canons told as an epic. Bottom right: épopée, a noble subject in a noble style, heroes, gods and battles. A caption names Scarron's Virgile travesti for the burlesque and Boileau's Le Lutrin for the mock-heroic.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- The **[[burlesque]]** tells a noble subject in a low style: Paul Scarron's *Virgile travesti* (published
  from 1648) retells the *Aeneid* with its heroes speaking like market people. This *travestissement*
  pulls the great down.
- The **[[mock-heroic]]** (*l'héroï-comique*) does the reverse: a trivial subject in the style of the epic.
  In Boileau's *Le Lutrin* (1674), a quarrel between canons over where to put a lectern in a church
  becomes an epic war, with allegorical goddesses such as Discord and a battle fought with books. The trivial is pumped up until it bursts.

Both work by a gap between subject and style. The reader laughs at the gap.

## Bombast and its family

The epic style turned against itself produces **[[bombast]]**, *l'emphase*. Careful: *l'emphase* is a
false friend. It means pomposity, not emphasis (for that, say *l'insistance* or *la mise en relief*).
Its adjectives are worth having at C2, because critics use them constantly:

- *pompeux*: solemn and self-important (*un discours pompeux*);
- *grandiloquent*: using big words for small things;
- *ampoulé*: swollen with rare words and long periods (*un style ampoulé*);
- *boursouflé*: inflated, hollow inside (also *boursoufflé* in the 1990 spelling);
- *outrancier*: excessive, over the top.

At the other end of the scale, *mièvre* is sentimental and weak: sweet without force. Between the two
lie the *maniérisme* of a writer whose style has become a set of habits, the *tic de langage* (a pet
word or phrase repeated without thinking), and the *cliché*, a phrase used so often it no longer
means anything (*un silence de mort, une nuit d'encre*). Every one of these is raw material for
the pastiche writer.

## Three famous exercises

- Raymond Queneau's *Exercices de style* (1947) tells one trivial anecdote, a minor quarrel on a Paris
  bus followed by an overheard remark about a coat button, in 99 different ways: as a sonnet, an
  official letter, a list of exclamations, in slang, backwards. It is the best demonstration that
  style is a choice made on top of a story.
- Marcel Proust wrote pastiches of the "Lemoine affair", a swindle by a man who claimed he could make
  diamonds, in the manner of Balzac, Flaubert, Saint-Simon, Michelet, the Goncourt brothers and
  others. Most appeared in *Le Figaro* in 1908 and 1909; they were collected in *Pastiches et mélanges*
  (1919). Proust described his pastiches as literary criticism in action.
- Paul Reboux and Charles Muller published *À la manière de…* from 1908: pastiches of the writers of
  their day, gently mocking. The title became a common French name for the exercise.

None of them is imitated here; you will imitate a genre or a period, not a writer's text. One more
term belongs with these games of mirrors, the **[[mise en abyme]]**: a work that contains a smaller copy
of itself, like a novel about a writer writing that novel. (The image comes from heraldry, a small
shield set at the centre, the *abyme*, of a larger one; André Gide first applied it to literature, in
his journal for 1893.)

## How to turn a style into a recipe

Analysing a style means listing its features at every level and saying what each one does. The same
grid works for a page of Proust, a political speech or a ministry circular.

| level | questions to ask |
|---|---|
| lexicon | Which register? Rare or archaic words? Which fields (war, law, feelings)? Periphrases? |
| syntax | Long or short sentences? Subordination or juxtaposition? Inversions? |
| tenses | Récit or discours? Passé simple, présent, passive, impersonal *il*? |
| rhythm and sound | Binary, ternary, periods? A chute? Repeated sounds? |
| figures | Comparisons, epithets, hyperbole, apostrophe? |
| point of view | Who speaks to whom? A narrator who comments, or none? |
| clichés and tics | Which phrases come back every time? |

Then choose the four or five features that make the style recognisable, and use them steadily. A
pastiche fails in two ways: too few markers (the reader doesn't see the model) or one *anachronisme*
by accident (a modern word that breaks the spell). An anachronism *on purpose*, on the other hand, is
the main *procédé* (device) of the mock-heroic: the loyalty card in an epic battle.

## Model: le combat de la caisse numéro sept

This is the pastiche that won *Contre-Jour*'s competition: an ordinary supermarket queue in the style
of the classical epic. It uses the passé simple, which the course never asks you to write; you may
use it in your own pastiche if you want to, and you will be judged on it only if you do.

> **Le combat de la caisse numéro sept** (chant premier)
>
> Prête-moi ta voix, ô Muse, pour célébrer ce samedi funeste où le vaillant Gérard, chargé de
> victuailles, affronta la file immense ! Le soleil avait franchi déjà la moitié de sa course, et les
> portes de verre, s'ouvrant d'elles-mêmes, vomissaient sans trêve sur le parking une foule de héros
> chargés de sacs.
>
> Il s'avança, le fier Gérard, poussant devant lui son chariot aux roues rebelles, comme jadis le
> guerrier poussait son char sur la plaine de Troie. Dans ce char s'entassaient les trésors de la terre
> et de l'onde : la baguette dorée, le fromage odorant, le poulet rôti encore fumant, et six
> bouteilles d'une eau venue des cimes. Derrière lui grondait la tribu des Martin, avec ses enfants
> hurlants et ses montagnes de couches. Devant lui s'étirait la file, longue comme un fleuve, lente
> comme un remords.
>
> Soudain survint l'adversaire. Une dame au cabas fleuri, l'œil brillant d'audace, glissa son panier
> dans l'espace étroit que laissait l'imprudent. « Je n'ai qu'un article », dit-elle. Ô mensonge ! Ô
> perfidie ! Elle en avait trois. Gérard frémit ; son sang, tel un torrent d'avril, bouillonna dans
> ses veines. Il ouvrit la bouche pour lancer le défi ; les Martin retinrent leur souffle ; le rayon
> des surgelés lui-même parut frissonner.
>
> Alors la caissière, déesse impassible assise sur son trône de plastique, leva sur les combattants un
> regard plus froid que le surgelé. « Carte de fidélité ? » prononça-t-elle, et sa voix fit taire les
> clameurs. Le bip sacré retentit ; les articles défilèrent ; la dame passa.
>
> Gérard comprit que les dieux avaient choisi leur camp. Il paya, rangea ses trésors et s'en alla,
> vaincu mais digne, vers le parking où l'attendait, fidèle et cabossée, sa vieille Clio.

*Glosses:* *les victuailles* provisions (old, humorous); *l'onde* the waves (poetic for water); *le
cabas* shopping bag; *la perfidie* treachery; *les surgelés* frozen food; *cabossé* dented.

*Summary.* (1) The narrator calls on the Muse to sing of the Saturday when Gérard faced the queue; the
automatic doors pour heroes into the car park. (2) Gérard advances with his trolley like a warrior
in his chariot, loaded with bread, cheese, chicken and mineral water; a noisy family follows; the
queue is endless. (3) A woman with a flowery bag slips in front of him, claiming to have one item;
she has three; Gérard boils with rage and is about to protest. (4) The cashier, an impassive goddess,
asks for the loyalty card, and the woman goes through. (5) Gérard understands that the gods have
chosen their side, pays and leaves with dignity for his old dented car (named, like a Muse, Clio).

*The recipe.* Lexicon: noble and poetic words for ordinary things (*victuailles, l'onde, char,
trésors*), a periphrasis for mineral water (*une eau venue des cimes*), epic epithets (*le vaillant
Gérard, le fier Gérard*). Syntax: the subject held back (*Il s'avança, le fier Gérard*) or inverted
(*Devant lui s'étirait la file*; *Soudain survint l'adversaire*). Tenses: the récit, with the passé simple for events and the
imparfait for the scene, after an invocation in the imperative. Rhythm: a binary simile with a twist
(*longue comme un fleuve, lente comme un remords*), and an asyndeton of three short clauses for the
climax (*Le bip sacré retentit ; les articles défilèrent ; la dame passa*). Figures: the invocation
to the Muse, epic similes (*comme jadis le guerrier*), apostrophe and exclamation (*Ô mensonge !*),
hyperbole, divine intervention. The comic engine: deliberate anachronisms (*carte de fidélité, bip,
parking*) dropped into the epic, and the gap between three items and a war.

## The same anecdote in the administrative style

The competition's second prize went to the same story told as an internal memo: another period
style, the timeless French circular.

> *Objet : incident survenu le samedi 14 mars à la caisse n° 7.* Il a été porté à la connaissance de
> la direction qu'un différend a opposé deux usagers dans la file d'attente de la caisse n° 7, aux
> alentours de 15 h 30. Il ressort des premiers éléments recueillis qu'une cliente se serait insérée
> dans la file en faisant valoir le nombre réduit de ses articles. Il est rappelé que l'ordre d'arrivée
> constitue la règle en vigueur, sauf dérogation prévue à l'article 4 du règlement intérieur. Les
> responsables de secteur sont invités à veiller à la stricte application de la présente note.

*Subject: incident at checkout no. 7 on Saturday 14 March.* It has been brought to the management's
attention that a dispute arose between two customers in the queue at checkout no. 7 at around 3.30
p.m. It appears from the initial information gathered that a customer allegedly joined the queue
ahead of others, citing the small number of her items. Staff are reminded that order of arrival is
the rule in force, except where article 4 of the internal regulations provides otherwise. Section
managers are requested to ensure that this memo is strictly applied.

The markers here are the impersonal *il* (*Il a été porté, Il ressort, Il est rappelé*), the passive,
nouns instead of verbs (*l'application*, *une dérogation*), the conditional of hearsay (*se serait
insérée*), and set formulas (*sont invités à veiller à*). No colourful adjective, no feeling, no Gérard: the
comedy is that the epic and the memo describe the same three items.

## Your pastiche

Now it's your turn. Choose a period style, analyse it with the grid, pick your markers, and write.

```assignment
writing: fr6-m2-pastiche
```

## Common mistakes

- *Copying sentences from the model.* A pastiche imitates a manner; a sentence taken from a real text
  is plagiarism, and the competition (and the rubric) rejects it.
- *Mixing two styles by accident.* If the epic narrator suddenly writes *du coup* or *trop bien*, the
  spell breaks, unless that anachronism is the joke and is placed for effect.
- *Parody instead of pastiche.* Exaggerating every feature at once turns the text into a caricature.
  Keep most markers at their natural strength and push one or two.
- *Translating l'emphase as "emphasis".* It means pomposity.
- *Forgetting the subject.* The comic power of the héroï-comique comes from a clearly trivial subject;
  if the subject is vague, the gap disappears.

## Key points

- The **[[pastiche]]** imitates a manner, the **[[parody]]** mocks by exaggeration, the **[[détournement]]** reuses
  a text for another message; plagiarism hides its model.
- French law (CPI, art. L122-5, 4°) allows parody, pastiche and caricature within "the laws of the
  genre", which courts have generally read as humour, no confusion and no intent to harm.
- The **[[burlesque]]** lowers a noble subject; the **[[mock-heroic]]** raises a trivial one.
- **[[Bombast]]** (*l'emphase*) is pomposity: *pompeux, grandiloquent, ampoulé, boursouflé*.
- To analyse a style, go level by level (lexicon, syntax, tenses, rhythm, figures, point of view,
  clichés), then choose four or five markers and keep them steady.
- A work that contains a mirror of itself, like a pastiche competition inside a lesson on pastiche,
  is a mise en abyme.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: L'alexandrin: how French verse works
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 07 counted syllables in prose to hear its rhythm. French verse makes that count a rule. A
line of classical French poetry is defined by its number of syllables, not by stresses as in
English, and the rules for counting them are precise enough to learn in one lesson. Once you can
count, you can read Racine, La Fontaine or Baudelaire aloud as their lines were meant to sound, and
you can follow a *commentaire* that speaks of a *césure*, a *diérèse* or an *enjambement*.

This is a reading skill: nobody will ask you to write verse. Every example line below is original,
written for this lesson. Famous poems are named, never quoted.

## Counting syllables

The **[[syllable count]]** of a French line follows the spoken vowels, with three rules for the *e muet*
(the unstressed *e* of *une, belle, tombe*), which everyday speech often drops but verse does not.

1. *Before a consonant, the e muet counts.* *Une belle nuit*: *u-ne-bel-le-nuit*, five syllables
   (in conversation, three).
2. *Before a vowel or a mute h, it is elided* and doesn't count: in *une aube* the *e* of *une*
   disappears (*u-nau…*); *elle habite* begins *el-la…*.
3. *At the end of the line, it never counts*, nor does a final *-es* or the *-ent* of a verb:
   *ville, rimes, chantent* at the end of a line each count as one syllable.

Two vowels side by side can be counted as one syllable or two. Splitting them is a **[[diaeresis]]**
(*la diérèse*): *li-on, pas-si-on, nu-a-ge*. Merging them is a **[[synaeresis]]** (*la synérèse*): *lion*,
*hier*, *pied* in one syllable, as in speech. Classical poets had conventions for each word (*lion*
is usually two syllables, *pied* usually one), but some words vary, and a poet may use a diérèse to
stretch a word and give it weight. The count of the line tells you which reading the poet chose.

## The lines

The **[[alexandrine]]** (*l'alexandrin*) has twelve syllables. In the classical alexandrine a pause, the
**[[caesura]]** (*la césure*), falls after the sixth syllable and divides the line into two
**[[hemistichs]]** (*les hémistiches*) of six. The sixth and twelfth syllables carry the main stresses,
and the sixth must end a word. It was the line of French tragedy (Corneille, Racine) and of much of
the great poetry of the 19th century (Hugo, Baudelaire). Romantic poets loosened the caesura, and
some lines of Hugo fall more naturally into three groups of four.

Two shorter lines are common: the *décasyllabe* (ten syllables, often divided 4 + 6), the line of
medieval epic, and the *octosyllabe* (eight, with no fixed caesura), light and quick, used for medieval
romances, songs and much lyric poetry.

![An original alexandrine split into twelve numbered syllables: Le, soir, tom, be, sans, bruit, then a thick bar, then sur, les, toits, de, la, vil, followed by a greyed (le) that is not counted. Brackets under the two halves read premier hémistiche and second hémistiche. Labels point to the bar (césure), to the syllable be (e muet compté) and to the greyed le (e final muet, non compté).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: scanning an alexandrine

*Le soir tombe sans bruit sur les toits de la ville.* (Evening falls without a sound on the roofs
of the town.)

- Count: *Le (1) soir (2) tom (3) be (4) sans (5) bruit (6) | sur (7) les (8) toits (9) de (10) la
  (11) vil (12)*.
- *Tombe* is followed by a consonant (*sans*), so its *e* counts: syllable 4.
- *Ville* ends the line, so its *e* doesn't count.
- The caesura falls after *bruit*, at the end of a word: two hemistichs of six. Twelve syllables:
  an alexandrine.

Read aloud, the line has two heavy stresses, on *bruit* and on *ville*, and the first hemistich
(the silence) balances the second (the place).

### Example 2: when a diaeresis decides the count

*Le vieux lion dormait au soleil de midi.* (The old lion slept in the midday sun.)

- With a diérèse (*li-on*): *Le (1) vieux (2) li (3) on (4) dor (5) mait (6) | au (7) so (8) leil (9)
  de (10) mi (11) di (12)*. Twelve.
- With a synérèse (*lion* in one): eleven, one short. The count shows the poet means *li-on*.
- *Vieux*, by contrast, is one syllable here, as in speech.

And the other way round: *Hier, toute la ville a dansé sur le vieux port* (Yesterday, the whole town
danced on the old harbour) has twelve syllables only if *hier* is one (a synérèse). Note *toute la*
(*tou-te-la*: the *e* counts before *l*) and *ville a* (*vil-la*: elided).

## Running on: enjambment

When a sentence doesn't stop at the end of a line but runs into the next, the line has an
**[[enjambment]]** (*l'enjambement*). When only a short word or two spill over and then the sentence
stops, that short piece is a *rejet*: it gains weight by standing alone at the start of the line.

### Example 3: a rejet

> Elle avait attendu tout l'hiver sur le quai  
> Son fils. Le printemps vint, et le navire aussi.

(She had waited all winter on the quay / for her son. Spring came, and so did the ship.)

- Line 1: *El (1) l'a (2) vait (3) at (4) ten (5) du (6) | tout (7) l'hi (8) ver (9) sur (10) le (11)
  quai (12)*. *Elle avait* elides the *e*.
- Line 2: *Son (1) fils (2) Le (3) prin (4) temps (5) vint (6) | et (7) le (8) na (9) vi (10) r'aus (11)
  si (12)*.
- The object of *attendu*, *son fils*, is held back to the next line: a *rejet*. The reader waits,
  like the mother, and the two words land hard. (The passé simple *vint* is lesson 05's.)

## Rhyme

*Masculine and feminine rhyme.* A rhyme is feminine when the line ends in an *e muet* (*ville,
docile, rimes, chantent*) and masculine otherwise (*gris, cri, port*), whatever the gender of the
word. Classical poetry alternates them.

*Quality.* French manuals rank rhymes by the number of sounds they share at the end, though they
don't all draw the lines in the same place. Roughly: a *rime pauvre* shares one sound (*ami / pli*:
[i]); a *rime suffisante* shares two (*gris / cri*: [ʁi]); a *rime riche* shares three or more
(*lumière / chaumière*: [mjɛʁ]).

*Pattern.* Over four lines, rhymes can follow three patterns:

| pattern | name | scheme |
|---|---|---|
| two by two | *rimes plates* (or *suivies*) | aabb |
| alternating | *rimes croisées* | abab |
| one pair inside another | *rimes embrassées* | abba |

So a *rime croisée* is one rhyme of an *abab* stanza, and a *rime embrassée* one of an *abba* stanza;
both are usually named in the plural.

### Example 4: a quatrain in two patterns

Here is an original quatrain in alexandrines, with alternate rhymes:

> Le soir tombe sans bruit sur les toits de la ville ;  
> Le dernier tram s'en va, le quai devient tout gris.  
> Le vent pousse un journal le long du mur, docile,  
> Et la lune, au-dessus, monte sans faire un cri.

(Evening falls without a sound on the roofs of the town; / the last tram leaves, the quay turns
grey. / The wind pushes a newspaper along the wall, docile, / and the moon, above, rises without a
cry.)

- Rhymes: *ville (a), gris (b), docile (a), cri (b)*: *abab*, *rimes croisées*. *Ville / docile* is
  feminine and *suffisante* ([il]); *gris / cri* is masculine and *suffisante* ([ʁi]). Feminine and
  masculine alternate.
- Each line has twelve syllables: check *pousse un* (*pou-ssun*, elided), *lune, au-dessus*
  (*lu-nau*, elided), *monte sans* (*mon-te*, counted), *faire un* (*fai-run*, elided).
- Swap the last two lines and the pattern becomes *abba*: *ville, gris, cri, docile*, *rimes
  embrassées*.

## Stanzas and the sonnet

A *strophe* is a stanza: a group of lines set off by a blank line. A *quatrain* has four lines,
a *tercet* three. The **[[sonnet]]**, born in 13th-century Italy and made famous by Petrarch, came to France in the 16th century, and
Ronsard and Du Bellay made it a French form; Baudelaire wrote many in *Les Fleurs du mal* (1857). It
has fourteen lines: two quatrains, then two tercets. In the classical French sonnet the quatrains
share two rhymes in *rimes embrassées* (*abba abba*) and the tercets bring new ones (often *ccd eed*
or *ccd ede*); poets have bent these rules ever since. The last line, the *chute*, often turns or
sharpens the whole poem.

## Free verse

From the 1880s, poets such as Gustave Kahn and Jules Laforgue began to drop the fixed count, and
in the 20th century *le vers libre*, without regular count or rhyme, became the common form of French
poetry (Apollinaire, Éluard, Prévert). The vocabulary of this lesson still applies to it:
critics speak of *enjambement*, *rejet* and *diérèse* in free verse too, and free-verse poems often
hide alexandrines.

## Common mistakes

- *Counting the e muet as in speech.* In verse, *une belle nuit* has five syllables, not three.
- *Counting the final e.* *Ville* at the end of a line is one syllable.
- *Forgetting elision across words.* *Pousse un* is two syllables, not three.
- *Calling every pause a caesura.* The caesura of the classical alexandrine falls after the sixth
  syllable; a comma elsewhere is a pause, not the caesura.
- *Masculine rhyme = masculine noun.* No: it means no final *e muet*. *Cri* rhymes masculine and *ville* feminine, whatever
  their gender as nouns.

## Key points

- French verse counts syllables; the *e muet* counts before a consonant, is elided before a vowel,
  and is silent at the end of the line.
- Diérèse splits two vowels, synérèse joins them; the count tells you which the poet chose.
- The alexandrine has twelve syllables, a caesura after the sixth and two hemistichs.
- Enjambment runs a sentence over the line; a short word carried over is a *rejet*.
- Rhymes are masculine or feminine; pauvre, suffisante or riche; plates (aabb), croisées (abab) or
  embrassées (abba).
- The sonnet: two quatrains and two tercets, fourteen lines.

lessons.title: L'Étranger: Camus and the passé composé
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 05 set out the classical division: novels in the passé simple (récit), letters and
conversation in the passé composé (discours). In 1942 a young writer from Algeria published a novel
that broke it on purpose. *L'Étranger* is told in the first person and in the passé composé, in
short, flat sentences, by a man who seems to feel nothing much. It became one of the most widely
read French novels of the 20th century, and its grammar is part of its meaning.

This lesson retells the novel in original French (Camus's text is still under copyright, and we
quote none of it), looks at how its tenses work, introduces the philosophy of the **[[absurd]]** behind
it, and ends with the Algerian writer Kamel Daoud's answer, written some seventy years later.

## Albert Camus in brief

Albert Camus was born on 7 November 1913 in Mondovi (today Dréan), in French Algeria, and grew up
poor in Algiers. Journalist, playwright, novelist and essayist, he published *L'Étranger* with
Gallimard in 1942, and in the same year *Le Mythe de Sisyphe*, an essay on the absurd. His later
works include *La Peste* (1947) and *La Chute* (1956). He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in
1957 and died in a car accident on 4 January 1960.

## The novel, retold

> À Alger, Meursault, un modeste employé de bureau, apprend par un télégramme la mort de sa mère,
> qui vivait dans un asile de vieillards à Marengo. Il prend l'autobus, veille le corps, boit un café
> au lait, fume une cigarette et suit l'enterrement sous un soleil écrasant. Il ne pleure pas.
>
> Le lendemain, il se baigne au port, retrouve Marie, une ancienne collègue, et l'emmène voir un
> film comique. Les jours passent, tous semblables. Son voisin Raymond, un homme aux fréquentations
> douteuses, lui demande d'écrire une lettre pour piéger une maîtresse qu'il a battue ; Meursault
> accepte, sans y attacher d'importance. Marie veut savoir s'il l'aime ; la question ne lui paraît
> pas avoir de sens. Il accepte pourtant de l'épouser, puisqu'elle le souhaite.
>
> Un dimanche, Raymond invite Meursault et Marie au cabanon d'un ami, Masson, au bord de la mer. Sur
> la plage, une bagarre éclate avec deux hommes, dont le frère de la femme maltraitée ; Raymond est
> blessé au couteau. Plus tard, Meursault revient seul vers une source, ébloui, en sueur, avec le
> revolver de Raymond dans sa poche. L'un des deux hommes est là. La lame d'un couteau brille au
> soleil ; Meursault tire un premier coup de feu, puis, un moment plus tard, quatre autres sur l'homme à terre.
>
> La seconde partie raconte l'instruction et le procès. Devant la cour d'assises, on parle peu du
> meurtre et beaucoup de l'enterrement : il n'a pas pleuré, il a fumé, il est allé au cinéma le
> lendemain. L'accusation fait de lui un monstre sans âme ; la plaidoirie de son avocat ne convainc
> pas les jurés, qui ne lui accordent aucune circonstance atténuante. Il est condamné à mort. Dans sa
> cellule, il refuse de recevoir l'aumônier ; quand celui-ci vient malgré tout, Meursault explose de
> colère, puis trouve une paix étrange : il accepte un monde indifférent.

*Glosses:* *l'asile de vieillards* old people's home (today *la maison de retraite*); *veiller le
corps* to sit up with the body; *les fréquentations* the company someone keeps; *piéger* to trap;
*le cabanon* beach hut; *ébloui* dazzled; *l'instruction* the pre-trial investigation.

*Summary.* (1) In Algiers, Meursault, an office clerk, learns by telegram that his mother has died
in an old people's home at Marengo; he keeps vigil, drinks coffee, smokes, follows the funeral in
the heat, and doesn't cry. (2) The next day he swims, meets Marie and takes her to a comedy; he helps
his neighbour Raymond trap a mistress Raymond has beaten, and agrees to marry Marie though her
question about love means nothing to him. (3) On a Sunday at the beach, Raymond is wounded in a
fight; later, alone, dazzled by the sun, Meursault shoots one of the men once, then four more times.
(4) At the trial his behaviour at the funeral counts more than the killing; he is sentenced to death;
in his cell he rages at the chaplain, then finds peace in accepting an indifferent world.

Camus never names the man Meursault kills; the novel calls him only "the Arab". That silence is the
starting point of Daoud's novel, below.

![A schematic map, not to scale, of the places in the novel. The Mediterranean along the top. On the coast, Algiers, with Meursault's flat, the prison and the court. Further west along the coast, the beach with Masson's beach hut. Inland to the south-west, Marengo, with the old people's home, which the novel puts 80 km from Algiers. Dashed lines marked en autobus link Algiers to the beach and to Marengo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## A novel in the passé composé

The whole novel is a **[[first-person narration]]**: Meursault tells his own story, and we see nothing
he doesn't see. A classical novel in the first person would still have used the passé simple (*je
pris l'autobus, je ne pleurai pas*). Camus uses the **[[passé composé as a narrative tense]]**: the
tense of conversation and letters, tied to the speaker's present. The result is strange: a voice that
seems to speak, not to write, yet speaks to nobody in particular.

The passé simple links events in a chain: one thing leads to the next, and the narrator knows how the
story ends. The passé composé, used sentence after sentence, sets each event down on its own, as a
fact that is simply *there*. Add very short sentences, few linking words and almost no explanations
of motive, and you get a world without cause and effect. In 1943, in an essay called "Explication de
*L'Étranger*", published in *Cahiers du Sud*, Jean-Paul Sartre analysed exactly this: he argued
that the passé composé and the short sentences cut the narrative into separate moments with no causal
links between them, and he compared the technique to that of American novelists such as Hemingway.

### Example 1: the same events in two systems

Take a moment from lesson 05's chronicle, told in the classical récit:

*Étienne s'élança vers la maison. Il gravit le talus, entra dans l'eau jusqu'à la taille et ramena
les deux femmes.*

Now tell it as Étienne would, in the manner of a first-person narration in the passé composé, in
short sentences:

*Je me suis élancé vers la maison. J'ai gravi le talus. L'eau était froide. Je suis entré jusqu'à la
taille. J'ai ramené les deux femmes.*

- The *je* gives a point of view: we only know what Étienne knows.
- The passé composé puts each act next to the moment of speaking.
- The full stops replace the *et* and the commas of the récit: parataxis (lesson 07). The sentence
  about the cold water is a sensation with no comment.
- What's lost is the sense of a story already finished and shaped by a narrator who knows the end.
  What's gained is presence, and a kind of *détachement*: the speaker reports his own acts as if they
  were someone else's.

## The absurd

Camus wrote *L'Étranger*, *Le Mythe de Sisyphe* and the play *Caligula* as a cycle on the **[[absurd]]**:
the feeling that arises when a human being, who needs meaning, faces a world that gives none. The
absurd is not in us or in the world, but in their meeting. In *Le Mythe de Sisyphe*, Camus asks how
to live once that is recognised. His answer is neither despair nor religious hope but *lucidité*:
to look at the absurd clearly and keep living, in revolt and with a taste for life. The essay closes
on Sisyphus, condemned forever to push his rock up the mountain, whom Camus presents not as a
victim but as the model of the absurd hero.

Meursault is one reading of that idea. His *indifférence* shocks the court more than his crime; he
refuses to pretend to feelings he doesn't have, and in that sense he is honest to the point of
destruction. Readers have argued ever since about what he is: a man without feeling, a man of
*fatalisme* who lets things happen, a lucid hero of the absurd, or, as many recent critics stress, a
colonial Frenchman who kills a nameless Algerian and is tried less for that than for not crying at his
mother's funeral. Was the shooting the effect of the sun, something close to an *insolation*? The
novel suggests it and explains nothing.

### Example 2: the trial in French legal words

The second part of the novel is a trial before a *cour d'assises* (B2), the French court that tries
serious crimes with a jury. Its people and its stages have exact names:

- The prosecution is represented by *l'avocat général* (a magistrate, not a lawyer); the novel calls
  him simply *le procureur*, the general word. His speech is *le réquisitoire* (C1 honors).
- The defence lawyer's speech is *la plaidoirie*.
- *Les jurés*, ordinary citizens drawn by lot, decide with the judges on guilt and sentence.
- They can grant *des circonstances atténuantes*, which lower the sentence.
- In the novel, the prosecutor asks for *la peine capitale*, and Meursault is condemned to be
  guillotined. France abolished the death penalty in 1981.

Notice how the novel turns the procedure upside down: the *réquisitoire* is about Meursault's soul,
not his act, and his lawyer's *plaidoirie* seems to speak about someone else. In the passé composé,
Meursault watches his own trial as a spectator.

## Daoud's counter-investigation

In 2013 the Algerian journalist Kamel Daoud published *Meursault, contre-enquête* in Algiers
(Barzakh); the Paris edition followed in 2014 (Actes Sud), and it won the Goncourt prize for a first
novel in 2015. The narrator, Haroun, is the brother of the man Meursault killed. He gives the victim
a name, Moussa, and tells the story from the other side, as an old man talking in a bar in Oran. His
*contre-enquête* reverses Camus's novel point by point: the dead man has a family, a mother who
grieves, a life; and Haroun himself, in July 1962, as Algeria becomes independent, kills a Frenchman,
almost as absurdly. The book is both a tribute to Camus's style and a reply to its silence: a francophone
novel written back to the centre. Like Camus's, it is in copyright, and we describe it only.

## Common mistakes

- *Thinking the passé composé is "wrong" in a novel.* It is a choice, and *L'Étranger* made it famous.
- *Confusing narrator and author.* Meursault's indifference is not Camus's; the novel examines it.
- *Calling the prosecutor l'avocat de la partie civile.* The *avocat général* speaks for society;
  the victim's family has its own lawyer, if it takes part.
- *Saying absurde = ridiculous.* In Camus, *l'absurde* is a philosophical gap between our demand for
  meaning and a world that offers no answer.
- *Treating Daoud's book as a sequel.* It is a counter-narrative: the same events from the victim's
  side.

## Key points

- *L'Étranger* (Gallimard, 1942) is a first-person narration in the passé composé, with short
  sentences and few links: discours used for a récit.
- Sartre's 1943 essay showed how this cuts the narrative into separate moments without causes.
- The absurd is the meeting of our need for meaning with a world that offers none; *Le Mythe de Sisyphe*
  answers it with lucidity and revolt.
- The trial uses exact legal French: *avocat général, réquisitoire, plaidoirie, jurés, circonstances
  atténuantes, peine capitale*.
- Kamel Daoud's *Meursault, contre-enquête* (2013, 2014) gives the victim a name and a voice.

lessons.title: Nonobstant, le cas échéant: reading legal French
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is about specialised French: the language of law, science, economics and ideas that DALF
C2 dossiers draw on. The aim is to read these texts without losing the thread and reuse their
precision in your own writing.

This first lesson is about law. B2 (honors) gave you the formulas of contracts (*ci-après, en vertu
de, sous réserve de, le cas échéant*); C1 gave you *attendu que* and *ledit*. Here you learn how
French law is laid out, how a statute states a duty, how a court decision is built, and what a
losing party can do next. The theme is a tenant's deposit
dispute. The parties, the court and the judgment are invented; the rules are real and described in
general terms, as they stood in November 2026.

*This lesson is not legal advice.* Amounts, time limits and procedures change and depend on the
case. For a real dispute in France, go to an ADIL (*agence départementale d'information sur le
logement*, which gives free advice on housing), the court's *greffe* (clerk's office), or a
lawyer.

## How French law is laid out

Much of French law is gathered in codes: the Code civil, the Code pénal, the Code de
procédure civile, the Code du travail and dozens more. Some important statutes stand outside
them: the residential lease is governed by the *loi du 6 juillet 1989*, a statute with its own
numbered articles.

A code is divided, from the largest unit to the smallest, into *livres, titres, chapitres,
sections* and *articles*. An article may have several paragraphs, each an *alinéa*. Most modern
codes number their articles by part: an article of the legislative part, adopted by Parliament,
starts with *L.*; one of the regulatory part, made by government decree, starts with *R.* or
*D.* The Code civil is older than this system and keeps plain numbers.

| written | read aloud | means |
|---|---|---|
| *art. L. 211-3* | *l'article L. deux cent onze tiret trois* | an article of the legislative part |
| *art. R. 211-3* | *l'article R. deux cent onze tiret trois* | an article of the regulatory part |
| *art. 22, al. 2* | *l'article 22, alinéa 2* | the second paragraph of article 22 |
| *art. 22 in fine* | *l'article 22 in fine* | the end of article 22 |

*In fine* is Latin for "at the end" (of a text or a paragraph). Lawyers use two more Latin phrases
all the time: *de facto* (in fact, whatever the rules say) and *a contrario* (by the opposite
reasoning: if the law grants something to tenants of unfurnished flats, *a contrario* it doesn't
grant it, by that article, to others). Latin phrases are written without accents. Collectively
they are called **[[legal Latin]]**.

The decisions of the courts form *la jurisprudence*: case law. *Une jurisprudence constante* is a
settled line of decisions. It is not "jurisprudence" in the English sense of legal philosophy.

## The prescriptive present

French statutes state rules in the present indicative. The present here doesn't describe what
happens; it orders it. This is the **[[prescriptive present]]**.

- *Le preneur est tenu de payer le loyer.* (The lessee must pay the rent.)
- *Le dépôt de garantie est restitué dans un délai maximal de deux mois.* (The deposit shall be
  returned within two months at most.)
- *Le bail est résilié de plein droit.* (The lease is terminated as of right.)

A few verbs carry the force of the rule:

| form | force | example |
|---|---|---|
| present of a verb, often passive | duty | *Le dépôt est restitué …* |
| *être tenu de* + infinitive | duty | *Le bailleur est tenu de remettre une quittance.* |
| *pouvoir* | permission | *Le preneur peut donner congé à tout moment.* |
| *ne peut* (often without *pas*) | prohibition | *Le dépôt ne peut être supérieur à un mois de loyer.* |
| *est puni de* | penalty | *Le fait de … est puni de …* |

Contracts use the same present, and often *devoir* or the future as well (*le Preneur devra
justifier d'une assurance*): all three read as obligations. In a report, state a rule the same
way: *Le bailleur est tenu de …*, not *Le bailleur va devoir …*

## The formulas, one step further

Legal texts add these to the ones you know:

- *nonobstant* + noun (notwithstanding): *nonobstant toute clause contraire* (whatever the
  contract says to the contrary).
- *à défaut de* + noun (failing, in the absence of): *à défaut de paiement*.
- *de plein droit* (as of right, automatically, without anyone having to ask a judge).
- *à titre gracieux* (free of charge, as a favour): formal; *gratuitement* is everyday. *À titre
  onéreux* is the opposite: for payment.
- *ci-après dénommé « le Bailleur »* (hereinafter called "the Lessor"). The capital letter then
  marks the defined term.
- *caduc, caduque* (lapsed, no longer valid): *Faute d'avoir été acceptée dans le délai, l'offre
  est devenue caduque.* Outside law it means "obsolete": *un raisonnement caduc*.

## The people of a case

| word | who | everyday equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| *le bailleur, la bailleresse* | the lessor | *le propriétaire* (A1 honors) |
| *le preneur, la preneuse* | the lessee | *le locataire* (A1 honors) |
| *le cocontractant, la cocontractante* | the other party to a contract | *l'autre partie* |
| *le demandeur, la demanderesse* | who brings a civil case | — |
| *le défendeur, la défenderesse* | who answers it (civil) | *le prévenu* (B2) is the criminal defendant |
| *le requérant, la requérante* | who applies to a court, often by *requête* (written application) | — |
| *l'ayant droit* (pl. *les ayants droit*) | someone who holds a right through another (an heir, a family member) | — |
| *le justiciable* | anyone subject to the courts | *le citoyen*, *l'usager de la justice* |

A court is *une juridiction*; *le tribunal* (B2) is one kind, *la cour d'appel* and *la Cour de
cassation* are others. To rule is *statuer* (*statuer sur un litige*); to dismiss a claim is
*débouter* (*débouter quelqu'un de sa demande*: the person is the object, the claim follows *de*).
A court can add *une astreinte*, a daily penalty that runs until a party obeys. In everyday work
French *l'astreinte* also means being on call.

## How a decision is built

Every French decision has the same three parts: who and what (the parties, the facts and the
procedure so far), why (**[[the reasons]]**, *les motifs*), and what the court decides
(**[[the operative part]]**, *le dispositif*, which follows the words *Par ces motifs*). The statement of
reasons as a whole is *la motivation*: a new sense of a word you know as "motivation".

For two centuries the high courts packed their reasons into a single long sentence: the Cour de
cassation chained *attendu que …, attendu que …* and the Conseil d'État *considérant que …* The
**[[direct style]]** (*rédaction en style direct*) changed that. The Conseil d'État announced it in
December 2018 and applied it from 1 January 2019: one *considérant ce qui suit* at the top, then
numbered paragraphs of ordinary sentences. The Cour de cassation followed for all its judgments
from 1 October 2019, with numbered paragraphs under headings such as *Faits et procédure*,
*Examen du moyen* (or *des moyens*) and *Dispositif*. The stated aim was decisions that are easier
for the *justiciable* to read. Lower courts follow their own models.

![The first page of an invented judgment, divided into five zones: a header naming the court, the date and the two parties; a block of numbered paragraphs headed "Faits et procédure"; a longer block headed "Motifs de la décision"; a block starting "PAR CES MOTIFS" with verbs such as "condamne" and "déboute"; and a last line on the possible remedy.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Read the operative part first: it says who won what, in verbs in the present with the court as
subject: *condamne* (orders to pay), *ordonne*, *déboute*, *rejette*, *dit que* (rules that).

## Remedies

A losing party looks for *une voie de recours* (a means of appeal, a remedy). The everyday verb is
*faire appel* (B2); the legal phrase is *interjeter appel* (to lodge an appeal), before a *cour
d'appel*, which judges the facts and the law again. Above it, *le pourvoi en cassation* asks the
Cour de cassation to check only whether the law was correctly applied; it doesn't rehear the facts.

For small claims the first judgment is often final. As of November 2026, a civil claim of up to
5,000 euros is, as a rule, judged *en dernier ressort*: there is no appeal, only a *pourvoi*. Above that
amount, the judgment is *en premier ressort* and can be appealed. The time limits are counted from
the formal service of the judgment (*la signification*): generally one month for an appeal and
two months for a *pourvoi*. Each depends on the case: check before acting.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The path of a deposit dispute
  accDescr: The keys are returned and the exit inventory is made. The landlord has one or two months to return the deposit. The tenant sends a formal notice, then tries conciliation, then applies to the judge, who gives a judgment. Up to 5,000 euros the judgment is final and only a pourvoi en cassation is possible. Above 5,000 euros an appeal goes to the cour d'appel, whose decision can then go to the Cour de cassation.
  A["Remise des clés, état des lieux de sortie"] --> B["Délai légal : un ou deux mois"]
  B --> C["Mise en demeure"]
  C --> D["Tentative de conciliation"]
  D --> E["Saisine du juge"]
  E --> F["Jugement"]
  F -- "jusqu'à 5 000 euros : pas d'appel" --> G["Pourvoi en cassation"]
  F -- "au-delà de 5 000 euros" --> H["Appel devant la cour d'appel"]
  H --> I["Arrêt d'appel"]
  I --> G
```

## Reading: a deposit dispute judged in direct style

The deposit (*le dépôt de garantie*, the legal term for what everyday French calls *la caution*)
is governed by article 22 of the 1989 law (as of November 2026): for an unfurnished flat, at most one month's rent
excluding charges, returned within one month of the keys if the exit inventory matches the entry
one, two months if it doesn't, with 10 % of the monthly rent added for each month of delay begun.

> *Tribunal de proximité de Valombre — Juge des contentieux de la protection — Jugement du 5
> octobre 2026. Mme Inès Garnier contre M. Paul Delorme.*
>
> *Faits et procédure.* 1. Par contrat du 1er septembre 2022, M. Paul Delorme a donné à bail à
> Mme Inès Garnier un appartement non meublé, moyennant un loyer mensuel de 850 euros hors
> charges. Un dépôt de garantie du même montant a été versé à la signature. 2. Mme Garnier a
> donné congé et restitué les clés le 30 juin 2026. L'état des lieux de sortie, établi
> contradictoirement le même jour, ne relève que des « traces d'usure normale » sur les murs du
> séjour. Le bailleur a néanmoins conservé la totalité du dépôt, en invoquant la nécessité de
> repeindre la pièce. 3. Après l'échec d'une tentative de conciliation, Mme Garnier a saisi le
> tribunal par requête. La requérante demande la restitution du dépôt, la majoration prévue par
> la loi et 1 500 euros de dommages et intérêts. Le
> défendeur conclut au rejet de l'ensemble de ces demandes.
>
> *Motifs de la décision.* 4. En vertu de l'article 22 de la loi du 6 juillet 1989, le dépôt de
> garantie est restitué dans un délai maximal de deux mois à compter de la remise des clés,
> déduction faite, le cas échéant, des sommes dont le bailleur justifie qu'elles restent dues. 5.
> Il résulte de l'article 7 de la même loi que le preneur ne répond pas des dégradations dues à la
> vétusté. 6. En l'espèce, l'état des lieux de sortie ne mentionne aucune dégradation imputable à
> la locataire, et le bailleur, qui ne produit ni devis ni facture, ne justifie d'aucune somme
> restant due. En conservant l'intégralité du dépôt, il a de facto mis à la charge de Mme Garnier
> la remise en état d'un logement qu'elle a occupé près de quatre ans. 7. Le dépôt doit donc être
> restitué. N'ayant pas été rendu dans le délai légal, il est majoré de plein droit de 85 euros,
> soit 10 % du loyer mensuel, pour chaque mois de retard commencé. 8. Mme Garnier ne démontre pas un préjudice distinct de celui que
> répare déjà la majoration légale.
>
> *Par ces motifs*, le tribunal, statuant publiquement, par jugement contradictoire et en dernier
> ressort : condamne M. Delorme à payer à Mme Garnier la somme de 850 euros, majorée de 85 euros
> par mois de retard commencé depuis le 30 août 2026 jusqu'au complet paiement ; déboute Mme
> Garnier de sa demande de dommages et intérêts ; condamne M. Delorme aux dépens.

*Summary by part.*

- *Facts (1–3).* A flat let in 2022 (*donner à bail*: to let under a lease; *moyennant*: in
  return for). The tenant left on 30 June 2026; the exit inventory, drawn up with both present
  (*contradictoirement*), notes only normal wear, but the landlord kept the deposit to repaint.
  After failed conciliation, she applied to the court (*saisir le tribunal*) for the deposit, the
  increase and damages. He asks for everything to be rejected.
- *Reasons (4–8).* The rule; the tenant isn't liable for wear due to age (*la vétusté*); in this
  case (*en l'espèce*) he proves no sum is owed (*ne produit ni devis ni facture*: neither quote nor
  invoice), so he has in effect (*de facto*) made her pay to refurbish the flat. The deposit is
  returned with the increase, as of right. No separate harm (*préjudice*) is shown.
- *Operative part.* Ruling in public, after hearing both sides (*contradictoire*), with no
  appeal possible (*en dernier ressort*): 850 euros plus 85 euros per month begun; damages dismissed; he pays the costs (*les dépens*).

## A lease clause in plain French

Plain-language writers often rewrite a clause for the reader who must obey it. Here is
an invented termination clause (*clause résolutoire*), then a plain version of it.

> *Article 9 — Clause résolutoire. À défaut de paiement d'un seul terme de loyer ou de charges à
> son échéance, et dans le délai prévu par la loi après un commandement de payer demeuré
> infructueux, le présent bail sera résilié de plein droit, si bon semble au Bailleur, sans
> préjudice de tous dommages et intérêts. Le cas échéant, l'expulsion du Preneur pourra être
> ordonnée par la juridiction compétente.*
>
> *Version claire : Si vous ne payez pas un loyer ou des charges à la date prévue, le propriétaire
> peut vous faire remettre un commandement de payer. Si vous n'avez toujours pas payé à la fin du
> délai fixé par la loi, le bail peut prendre fin automatiquement, si le propriétaire le
> souhaite. Il peut aussi vous demander une indemnisation. Le juge peut alors ordonner votre
> départ.*

Article 9, termination clause: if a single instalment of rent or charges is not paid when due, and
within the period set by law after a formal demand for payment has had no effect, this lease will
be terminated as of right, if the Lessor so wishes, without prejudice to any damages. Where
applicable, the eviction of the Lessee may be ordered by the competent court. Plain version: if
you don't pay a rent or charges on the due date, the owner can have a formal demand delivered to
you. If you still haven't paid by the end of the period set by law, the lease can end
automatically, if the owner wishes. He can also ask you for compensation. The judge can then order
you to leave.

The plain version keeps every condition but changes the grammar: *vous* for *le Preneur*, verbs
for nouns (*si vous ne payez pas* for *à défaut de paiement*), short sentences. It also shows the
limits of a summary: the period was shortened by a reform in 2023, and a judge can still, under
conditions, grant time to pay and suspend the clause. Neither text tells the tenant that.
(*Le commandement de payer* is delivered by a *commissaire de justice*, the officer who serves legal
documents. *La résiliation* is the termination of a contract.)

## Common mistakes

- Reading the prescriptive present as a description: *Le dépôt est restitué dans les deux mois*
  states a duty, not a habit.
- Translating *la jurisprudence* as "jurisprudence": it is case law.
- *Débouter la demande*: it is the person who is *débouté*, not the claim (*débouter Mme X de sa
  demande*); a claim is *rejetée*.
- Confusing *le défendeur* (civil) with *le prévenu* (criminal), and *interjeter appel* (formal)
  with *faire appel* (everyday). Both pairs name the same thing in different settings.
- *Nonobstant que* + clause: it is archaic; modern legal French uses *nonobstant* + noun.
- Taking a summary for the rule. A plain version, or this lesson, never replaces the current text
  and advice on the case.

## Key points

- Codes go *livre, titre, chapitre, section, article, alinéa*; *L.* articles are legislative, *R.*
  and *D.* regulatory; the Code civil has plain numbers.
- Statutes state duties in the prescriptive present; *être tenu de* = must; *ne peut* = may not.
- *Nonobstant, à défaut de, de plein droit, à titre gracieux, caduc; in fine, de facto, a
  contrario* (no accents).
- A decision: facts, *motifs*, *dispositif* (*Par ces motifs … condamne, ordonne, déboute*). The
  direct style replaced *attendu que* (Cour de cassation, from 1 October 2019) and *considérant
  que* (Conseil d'État, from 1 January 2019).
- Remedies: *interjeter appel* (cour d'appel: facts and law), *le pourvoi en cassation* (law only);
  small claims are judged *en dernier ressort*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete

lessons.title: Il a été montré que: scientific and technical French
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 read the law; this one reads science and engineering. DALF C2 dossiers in the *sciences*
option, and many general ones, include a research summary, an expert report or an interview with
an engineer. Their French is not hard because of its grammar. It is hard because it packs
information into nouns, hides the people who did the work, qualifies every claim, and writes
numbers its own way.

The lesson covers the structure of a scientific article, the impersonal and passive voice of
science, chains of nouns, how to describe a device, and French conventions for numbers and units.
Hedging (*semblent indiquer, sous réserve de confirmation*) is C1 08's subject, and words built
from Greek and Latin roots are C1 16's: they are used here, not taught again. The theme is an
engineering report on converting a regional railway line to hydrogen trains. The line, the report
and its figures are invented; facts about real trains are dated and sourced.

## The shape of a scientific article

French research articles and many technical reports follow the international **[[IMRaD]]** order:
*introduction, matériel et méthodes, résultats, discussion*, preceded by an abstract (*le résumé*)
and followed by a conclusion and references. Each part has a job.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The IMRaD order of a scientific article
  accDescr: An abstract summarises everything. The introduction gives the state of the art and the question. Materials and methods say how the work was done, so that others can reproduce it. Results give what was measured, without comment. The discussion interprets the results and states their limits. The conclusion and references close the article.
  A["Résumé : l'essentiel, souvent en 150 à 300 mots"] --> B["Introduction : état de l'art, question"]
  B --> C["Matériel et méthodes : comment, pour être reproductible"]
  C --> D["Résultats : ce qui a été mesuré"]
  D --> E["Discussion : interprétation, limites"]
  E --> F["Conclusion, références"]
```

- The introduction sets out *l'état de l'art* (what is already known: the literature review) and
  the question.
- *Matériel et méthodes* describes the *protocole*. You met *le protocole* at C1 as official
  etiquette; in science it is the experimental procedure. The point of this section is
  *la reproductibilité*: another team must be able to repeat the work and get the same result. A
  *reproductible* result is one they can.
- *Résultats* reports what was measured, with figures and tables, and no interpretation.
- *Discussion* interprets, compares with other studies and states the limits.

## Impersonal and passive: the scientific voice

French science writing rarely says *j'ai mesuré*. It uses three devices, often together, which
this lesson calls the **[[scientific passive]]**.

| device | example | effect |
|---|---|---|
| passive with *être* | *Les mesures ont été réalisées sur un banc d'essai.* | the action, not the actor |
| impersonal *il* | *Il a été montré que … ; il apparaît que … ; il ressort de l'analyse que …* | a finding presented as a fact of the field |
| *on* and the *nous* of authors | *On observe une baisse … ; nous avons retenu trois scénarios.* | a general subject; the team, modestly |

Three details. *Il a été montré que* takes the indicative (it states a result). The pronominal
passive is common for what happens in general: *le rendement se mesure en pourcentage* (is
measured). And *nous* in an article is the authors, even when there is only one.

## Chains of nouns

Technical French turns actions into nouns and strings them together: *la mise en service de la
ligne après homologation du matériel roulant*. To read such a chain, find the verb behind each
noun and put back the people:

- *la mise en service* ← *mettre en service* (to put into service): the operator starts running
  trains;
- *l'homologation* ← *homologuer* (to approve officially): the safety authority approves the
  trains;
- *le matériel roulant*: the rolling stock, every vehicle that runs on the rails.

So: the line will open to passengers once the authority has approved the trains. When you write,
one or two nouns in a row are precise; four are a wall. Unpack them for a general reader.

## Describing a device

A **[[technical description]]** says what a thing is made of, what it does, and how. The verbs are
few and fixed:

- composition: *être constitué de, se composer de, comporter, être équipé de*;
- function: *permettre de* + infinitive, *servir à* + infinitive, *assurer la fonction de*;
- operation: *fonctionner, alimenter* (to supply with power), *convertir … en …*

> *La pile à combustible est constituée d'un empilement de cellules. Elle permet de convertir
> l'hydrogène en électricité, qui alimente les moteurs de traction. Une batterie assure la
> fonction de tampon : elle stocke l'énergie récupérée par le freinage régénératif.*

The fuel cell is made up of a stack of cells. It converts hydrogen into electricity, which powers
the traction motors. A battery acts as a buffer: it stores the energy recovered by regenerative
braking.

## Two trains: catenary and hydrogen

An electric train takes its power from an overhead line, *la caténaire*, through *le
pantographe*, the folding arm on its roof. A hydrogen train carries its own power: hydrogen in
tanks, produced elsewhere by *électrolyse* (splitting water with electricity), and *une pile à
combustible* that turns it back into electricity. Both use electric *traction* (haulage by
electric motors), and both can recover energy when they brake.

![Two trains side by side. On the left, an electric train under an overhead wire, with the folding arm on its roof touching the wire. On the right, a two-car hydrogen train with no wire above it: on the roof of the first car, the power car, a hydrogen tank and a fuel cell unit; in the second car, a battery.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In passenger service, the first hydrogen trains ran in Germany: two Alstom Coradia iLint trains
entered regular service in Lower Saxony on 17 September 2018, between Cuxhaven and Buxtehude, with
a range of up to 1,000 km, according to the maker. On a single-track line (*une voie unique*),
trains pass each other only at stations or loops, where *un aiguillage* (points, a switch) sends
each one onto its own track; *la signalisation* (signalling) keeps them apart. A train that runs
as one fixed unit is *une rame*; its vehicle with the motors is *la motrice*.

## Numbers and units in French

| rule | French | not |
|---|---|---|
| decimal comma | *3,5 km ; 0,27 kg* | 3.5 km |
| space between thousands | *12 500 habitants* | 12,500 |
| space before a unit and % | *25 % ; 140 km/h* | 25% |
| no plural on symbols | *5 kg, 40 kW* | 5 kgs |
| powers of ten | *10⁻³* (*dix puissance moins trois*) | — |

An **[[order of magnitude]]** (*un ordre de grandeur*) is a size to the nearest power of ten. *Un ordre
de grandeur de plus* means about ten times more; *du même ordre de grandeur* means comparable.
*Une grandeur*, in physics, is any measurable quantity (a speed, an energy, a mass); a quantity
that varies in a model is *une variable*, and one fixed for a given case is *un paramètre*. Ratios
are said as *deux fois plus élevé que* or *un facteur trois*. To say how much of the input
energy comes out as useful work, French says *le rendement* (efficiency), never *la performance*.

## Reading: a test report

> *Conversion de la ligne Vernais–Saint-Aubin à la traction hydrogène — Rapport d'essais
> (extraits)*
>
> *Résumé.* La ligne Vernais–Saint-Aubin, longue de 62 km, à voie unique et non électrifiée, est
> aujourd'hui exploitée en traction thermique. Le présent rapport évalue la faisabilité de sa
> conversion à l'hydrogène. Une chaîne de traction complète a été testée sur banc d'essai, et une
> modélisation de l'exploitation a été réalisée pour trois scénarios. Il apparaît que la traction
> hydrogène permettrait de supprimer les émissions locales sans électrifier la ligne, au prix d'un
> rendement global nettement inférieur à celui de la traction électrique directe. Ces résultats
> restent à confirmer en conditions réelles.
>
> *Résultats.* (1) Les mesures ont été réalisées sur le banc d'essai du centre technique, équipé
> de 48 capteurs. Chaque essai a été répété trois fois ; l'écart entre les séries n'excède pas 2
> %, ce qui confirme la reproductibilité du protocole.
>
> (2) Le rendement de la pile à combustible atteint 48 % à charge nominale. Rapporté à l'ensemble
> de la chaîne (électrolyse, compression et stockage, pile, moteurs), le rendement global s'établit
> à 26 %, contre environ 80 % pour un train alimenté par caténaire. Autrement dit, à service égal,
> la traction hydrogène consommerait environ trois fois plus d'électricité : l'écart est du même
> ordre de grandeur que celui que signale l'état de l'art.
>
> (3) Le freinage régénératif récupère 18 % de l'énergie de traction sur le profil de la ligne, qui
> compte onze arrêts. La batterie tampon, dimensionnée à 120 kWh, suffit à absorber les pointes de
> freinage observées.
>
> (4) La modélisation fait apparaître que la variable déterminante est le prix de l'hydrogène :
> au-delà de 9 euros par kilogramme, le coût d'exploitation dépasse celui de l'électrification
> partielle avec trains à batteries. Les autres paramètres (fréquence des circulations, masse de
> la rame) n'ont qu'une influence marginale.
>
> (5) Aucune modification de la signalisation ni des aiguillages n'est requise. La mise en service
> commerciale reste toutefois subordonnée à l'homologation du matériel par l'autorité de sécurité
> ferroviaire, qui exigera des essais en ligne sur au moins douze mois.
>
> *Discussion (extrait).* Ces résultats doivent être interprétés avec prudence. Les essais sur banc
> ne reproduisent ni les variations de température ni le profil exact de la ligne, qui comporte
> plusieurs rampes de 20 ‰. Par ailleurs, le rendement global retenu suppose un hydrogène produit
> sur place par électrolyse ; s'il devait être acheminé par camion, le bilan se dégraderait
> sensiblement. Il serait donc hâtif de conclure à la supériorité d'une solution : la comparaison
> avec des trains à batteries, rechargés sous une caténaire partielle, devra être approfondie lors
> de la phase suivante.

*Translation of the abstract.* The Vernais–Saint-Aubin line, 62 km long, single-track and not
electrified, is currently run with diesel traction. This report assesses whether it could be
converted to hydrogen. A complete traction system was tested on a test bench, and the line's
operation was modelled for three scenarios. It appears that hydrogen traction would remove local
emissions without electrifying the line, at the cost of an overall efficiency well below that of
direct electric traction. These results remain to be confirmed under real conditions.

*Summary of the results.*

1. Tests on a bench with 48 sensors (*les capteurs*), each repeated three times, varied by 2 % at
   most: the protocol is reproducible (*ne pas excéder*: not to exceed).
2. The fuel cell's efficiency is 48 % at rated load; the whole chain gives 26 %, against about 80 %
   with a catenary, so roughly three times as much electricity for the same service (*à service
   égal*), a gap in line with the literature.
3. Regenerative braking (*le freinage régénératif*) recovers 18 % of traction energy on a line with
   eleven stops; the 120 kWh buffer battery (*dimensionnée à*: sized at) is enough.
4. The model shows that the decisive variable is the price of hydrogen: above 9 euros per kilo,
   partial electrification with battery trains is cheaper. Other parameters have only a marginal
   influence.
5. Signalling and points need no change, but commercial service depends on (*est subordonnée à*)
   approval of the trains, after at least twelve months of trials on the line.

*Summary of the discussion.* Caution: the bench reproduces neither temperature changes nor the
line's 20 ‰ gradients (*les rampes*); the efficiency assumes hydrogen made on site, and trucking
it in would worsen the balance (*se dégrader*); it would be hasty (*hâtif*) to name a winner, and
battery trains charged under a partial catenary need further study.

Notice the voice: no person acts in the whole extract. *Il apparaît que* and *fait apparaître que*
present findings; *doivent être interprétés avec prudence* and *il serait hâtif de conclure* are the discussion's hedges; passives (*ont été réalisées, a été répété*) hide the team; the conditional
(*permettrait, consommerait*) marks projections; *restent à confirmer* is the abstract's hedge.

## Dialogue: the test engineer on local radio

The same findings sound different when an engineer explains them to the public: fewer nouns, more
verbs, and the hedges spelled out.

```dialogue
# Radio Vernais, le magazine des régions
Journaliste: Alors, ce train à hydrogène, il marche ?
= So, this hydrogen train: does it work?
Nadia Benali: Sur le banc d'essai, oui, très bien. Mais un banc, ce n'est pas une ligne : il faudra rouler un an avant l'homologation.
= On the test bench, yes, very well. But a bench isn't a line: we'll have to run for a year before approval.
Journaliste: On dit pourtant que l'hydrogène gaspille de l'énergie.
= People say hydrogen wastes energy, though.
Nadia Benali: C'est vrai qu'on perd beaucoup en route. Pour faire rouler le même train, il faut à peu près trois fois plus d'électricité qu'avec une caténaire.
= It's true that a lot is lost along the way. To run the same train, you need roughly three times as much electricity as with an overhead line.
Journaliste: Alors pourquoi ne pas électrifier ?
= Then why not electrify?
Nadia Benali: Parce qu'installer une caténaire sur soixante kilomètres de voie unique coûte très cher. Tout dépendra du prix de l'hydrogène.
= Because putting up an overhead line along sixty kilometres of single track is very expensive. It will all depend on the price of hydrogen.
```

Compare the registers: the report's *le rendement global s'établit à 26 %* becomes *on perd beaucoup
en route*, and *la variable déterminante est le prix* becomes *tout dépendra du prix*. Being able to
move between the two is part of C2 precision.

## Common mistakes

- *La performance* for efficiency: the word is *le rendement* (which also means yield or return in
  agriculture and finance).
- *Le matériel* for "material": *le matériel* is equipment (*le matériel roulant*); a material is
  *un matériau*.
- A decimal point or no space before a unit: *3,5 km*, *25 %*.
- Reading *une grandeur* as "greatness" in a physics text: it is a measurable quantity.
- *Une pile à combustible* is not a battery: it produces electricity from a fuel as long as fuel
  is supplied; *une batterie* (A2) stores it.
- Over-long noun chains in your own writing: unpack them with verbs.

## Key points

- IMRaD: *résumé, introduction* (with *l'état de l'art*), *matériel et méthodes* (the
  *protocole*, for *reproductibilité*), *résultats, discussion, conclusion*.
- The scientific voice: passives, impersonal *il* (*il a été montré que* + indicative), *on*, the
  authors' *nous*.
- Noun chains (*la mise en service après homologation*): find the verb behind each noun.
- Description: *être constitué de, permettre de, servir à, assurer la fonction de, alimenter*.
- Numbers: decimal comma, spaces before units and %, no plural on symbols; *un ordre de grandeur*
  ≈ a power of ten; *le rendement* = efficiency.
