lessons.title: Conjoncture, trésorerie, endettement: economic and financial French
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Economic and financial French fills the business pages, company reports and many DALF dossiers. At
C1 you read about growth, public debt and offshoring (*la conjoncture, le PIB, le déficit, la
dette publique*). This lesson adds the vocabulary of three worlds: the economy as a whole and its
central bank, the company and its accounts, and the markets. It also covers what happens to a
French company that can no longer pay its debts, the verbs that make figures move, and the
careful language of forecasts. The theme is a family bicycle maker that raises money, then nearly
goes under. The company, its figures and the article about it are invented.

## The economy: cycles, structures and the central bank

Economists separate two kinds of cause, and the adjectives are worth having exactly.

- *conjoncturel, conjoncturelle* (cyclical, short-term): tied to the current state of the economy
  (*la conjoncture*, C1). *Un ralentissement conjoncturel* should pass when the cycle turns.
- *structurel, structurelle* (structural): tied to how the economy or a firm is built.
  *Un déficit structurel* remains even when growth is normal; *le chômage structurel* doesn't
  fall with a recovery.

This pair (**[[cyclical and structural]]**) is the backbone of many economic arguments: a writer who
calls a problem *conjoncturel* is saying "wait"; one who calls it *structurel* is saying "reform".

*L'inflation* (B2) is a general rise in prices; *la déflation* is a general, lasting fall, which
sounds pleasant but discourages spending and investment (why buy today what will be cheaper
tomorrow?). Fighting both is the job of *la politique monétaire* (monetary policy), run in the euro
area by the European Central Bank (*la Banque centrale européenne*, *la BCE*). Its main lever is
*le taux directeur* (the key interest rate; in fact it sets several): what banks pay to borrow
from it and earn on what they leave with it. In July 2022, to
curb inflation, the BCE raised its key rates for the first time since 2011.

A budget or a trade balance ends in *un déficit* (C1) or its opposite, *un excédent* (a surplus):
*la balance commerciale est excédentaire*. States and large firms borrow on the markets, and *les
agences de notation* (credit rating agencies; one is *une agence de notation*) grade their ability to repay; a downgrade makes
borrowing dearer. When share prices collapse in a few days, the press speaks of *un krach* (a
crash), a word borrowed from German: *le krach de 1929* began on Wall Street in October of that
year.

## The company and its accounts

A company's year is its *exercice* (financial year): you met *l'exercice* as "exercise"; here it
is *l'exercice 2025*, which may or may not match the calendar year. At the end of each *exercice* a
company draws up its **[[financial statements]]** (*les comptes annuels*):

| statement | French | what it shows |
|---|---|---|
| balance sheet | *le bilan* (new sense: you know *le bilan* as "review") | what the firm owns (*l'actif*) and owes (*le passif*) on one day |
| income statement | *le compte de résultat* | income (*les produits*) and costs (*les charges*) over the year, and the result |
| cash flows | *le tableau des flux de trésorerie* | where the cash came from and went |

*La trésorerie* is the cash a firm actually has, or its cash management; *le chiffre d'affaires*
(B1) is its turnover. A firm can be profitable on paper and still run out of *trésorerie* if its
customers pay late. *L'endettement* is its debt load (*endetté*, B2, is the adjective); its
*solvabilité* is its ability to pay its debts in the long run. A gain made by selling an asset for
more than it cost is *une plus-value*; a loss is *une moins-value*.

![A simplified income statement for the invented company Cycles Lambert, financial year 2024, in millions of euros: turnover 38.6; operating costs minus 41.9; operating result minus 3.3; financial costs minus 1.1; exceptional items and tax plus 0.2; net result minus 4.2, shown as a loss.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The markets

A company listed on the stock exchange (*la Bourse*) has its shares (*les actions*) quoted every
day: *la cotation* is the listing, or the quoted price. Its owners are *les actionnaires*
(shareholders), who may receive *un dividende*, a share of the profit. *La capitalisation
boursière* (market capitalisation) is the share price times the number of shares. A company goes
public through *une introduction en Bourse* (a flotation, an IPO).

Before that, a young or growing firm often raises capital privately: *une levée de fonds* (a
fundraising round), *auprès d'un fonds d'investissement* (from an investment fund). Firms also
combine: *une fusion* (a merger: two become one) differs from *une acquisition* (a purchase: one
buys the other); the press often joins them as *une fusion-acquisition*. *La fusion* also keeps its
physical senses: melting, and nuclear fusion.

## When a company can't pay

Everyday French says a firm *fait faillite* (goes bankrupt). French law uses other words, and the
press is careful about them. Under the rules in force in November 2026, a firm in difficulty that can still pay may ask for a protective
procedure; one in *cessation des paiements* (unable to pay its debts that are due with the cash it
has) must declare it within 45 days. The court then opens one of two procedures:

- *le redressement judiciaire* (receivership): an observation period, up to 18 months in all,
  during which creditors (*les créanciers*) must wait and the firm keeps working;
- *la liquidation judiciaire* (compulsory liquidation), when recovery is clearly impossible: the
  firm's assets are sold and it closes.

The firm that owes is *le débiteur*, the one owed *le créancier*. As of November 2026, the court
is usually the *tribunal de commerce*, or in some cities, since 1 January 2025, a *tribunal des
activités économiques*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A French company that cannot pay its debts
  accDescr: When a company is in cessation des paiements, it must declare it within 45 days. The court opens a redressement judiciaire if recovery is possible, or a liquidation judiciaire if it is clearly impossible. At the end of the observation period of a redressement, the court adopts a recovery plan, orders the sale of the business, or orders liquidation.
  A["Cessation des paiements"] --> B["Déclaration au tribunal, sous 45 jours"]
  B --> C["Redressement judiciaire : période d'observation"]
  B --> D["Liquidation judiciaire : redressement impossible"]
  C --> E["Plan de redressement"]
  C --> F["Cession à un repreneur"]
  C --> D
```

## Making figures move

| verb | movement | example |
|---|---|---|
| *progresser* | rise steadily | *Les ventes progressent de 3 %.* |
| *s'envoler* | soar | *Le chiffre d'affaires s'est envolé.* |
| *stagner* (B2 honors) | stagnate | *La production stagne.* |
| *reculer* | fall back | *Le PIB a reculé de 0,2 %.* |
| *se replier* | ease, edge down | *L'action se replie de 1 %.* |
| *plonger* | plunge | *Le titre a plongé de 30 % en une séance.* |

Percentages and points are not the same. A rate that goes from 4 % to 6 % rises *de deux points*,
which is a rise of 50 %. Careful writers keep the two apart.

Forecasts are hedged: *la croissance devrait atteindre 1 %* (is expected to); *les analystes
tablent sur une reprise* (are counting on); *sous réserve que la demande se maintienne*
(+ subjunctive); *sauf retournement de conjoncture* (barring a turn in the economy).

## Reading: a business-press article

> *Cycles Lambert : de la levée de fonds au redressement judiciaire*
>
> (1) Il y a quatre ans, Cycles Lambert incarnait le renouveau industriel. Fondée en 1952 à
> Vaudrel et toujours contrôlée par la famille de son fondateur, la PME surfait sur l'engouement
> pour le vélo à assistance électrique : son chiffre d'affaires s'était envolé de 60 % en deux
> exercices, et elle avait bouclé en 2022 une levée de fonds de 12 millions d'euros auprès d'un
> fonds d'investissement régional. La direction évoquait alors une introduction en Bourse.
>
> (2) Le retournement a été brutal. Après les années fastes de la crise sanitaire, distributeurs
> et fabricants se sont retrouvés avec des stocks considérables, qu'ils ont écoulés à prix
> cassés. Dans le même temps, la hausse des taux directeurs engagée par la BCE à l'été 2022 a
> renchéri le crédit, pour les ménages comme pour les entreprises. Pour Cycles Lambert, dont
> l'endettement avait doublé pour financer une nouvelle usine, le cumul s'est révélé intenable.
>
> (3) Les comptes de l'exercice 2024 en portent la trace : le chiffre d'affaires a reculé de 31 %,
> le compte de résultat affiche une perte nette de 4,2 millions d'euros, et la trésorerie ne
> couvrait plus que trois semaines d'activité. Les actionnaires familiaux, qui avaient renoncé à
> tout dividende dès 2023, ont dû se rendre à l'évidence : l'entreprise ne pouvait plus payer ses
> dettes échues. La direction a déclaré la cessation des paiements, et le tribunal a ouvert une
> procédure de redressement judiciaire en septembre 2025.
>
> (4) Le redressement judiciaire n'est pas la faillite au sens où l'entend le langage courant.
> Pendant la période d'observation, les poursuites des créanciers sont suspendues et l'usine
> continue de produire. À son issue, le tribunal peut adopter un plan de redressement, ordonner la
> cession de l'activité ou prononcer la liquidation judiciaire.
>
> (5) Pour Cycles Lambert, l'issue semble aujourd'hui favorable. Un groupe néerlandais propose non
> pas une acquisition pure et simple, mais une fusion qui laisserait à la famille une
> participation minoritaire. Les banques, principaux créanciers, accepteraient d'étaler leurs
> créances sur huit ans. Reste à convaincre le fonds entré au capital en 2022 : la plus-value qu'il
> espérait réaliser lors de l'introduction en Bourse s'est muée en moins-value probable.
>
> (6) Au-delà du cas d'espèce, la mésaventure illustre une distinction chère aux économistes. Le
> recul des ventes était conjoncturel : il tenait à un cycle de surstockage qui semble s'achever.
> L'endettement excessif de l'entreprise, lui, était structurel : il découlait d'un pari pris au
> sommet du cycle. Les analystes du secteur tablent sur une reprise modérée en 2027, sous réserve
> que la consommation des ménages ne se replie pas de nouveau.

*Summary by paragraph.*

1. Four years ago the family-owned firm rode the e-bike craze (*surfer sur l'engouement*): turnover
   soared 60 % in two financial years, it closed (*boucler*) a 12-million-euro round in 2022, and
   talked of floating on the stock market.
2. The reversal: after the boom years of the pandemic, the trade sold off big stocks cheaply (*à
   prix cassés*), while the ECB's rate rises from summer 2022 made credit dearer (*renchérir*). With
   its debt doubled to build a factory, the combination was untenable.
3. The 2024 accounts: turnover down 31 %, a net loss of 4.2 million, cash for three weeks. The
   shareholders, who had given up dividends in 2023, had to face facts (*se rendre à l'évidence*):
   it could no longer pay debts that were due (*échues*). Receivership opened in September 2025.
4. Receivership is not bankruptcy in the everyday sense: creditors' actions are frozen, the factory
   works on, and the court will then choose a plan, a sale or liquidation.
5. A Dutch group proposes a merger rather than a takeover, leaving the family a minority stake; the
   banks would spread (*étaler*) repayment over eight years. The fund's hoped-for capital gain has
   turned (*s'est muée*) into a likely loss.
6. The fall in sales was cyclical (an overstocking cycle now ending); the excessive debt was
   structural (*découler de*: to stem from), a bet made at the top of the cycle. Analysts expect a
   moderate recovery in 2027, provided household spending doesn't fall back.

## From the annual report

Company reports open with a letter to the shareholders. Its language is formal and careful:

> *Mesdames, Messieurs les actionnaires, l'exercice 2025 a été le plus difficile de notre
> histoire. Notre solvabilité a été mise à l'épreuve, et nous avons dû recourir à une procédure
> qui protège l'entreprise le temps de la redresser. Nos débiteurs, distributeurs fragilisés par
> la crise, ont payé avec retard, ce qui a pesé sur notre trésorerie. Je veux le dire clairement :
> nos difficultés ne tiennent pas à la qualité de nos vélos, mais au poids d'une dette contractée
> trop vite.*

Ladies and gentlemen, shareholders: the 2025 financial year was the hardest in our history. Our
solvency was put to the test, and we had to turn to a procedure that protects the company while it
recovers. Our debtors, retailers weakened by the crisis, paid late, which weighed on our cash. I
want to say it clearly: our difficulties are not due to the quality of our bikes, but to the weight
of a debt taken on too fast.

## Common mistakes

- *La faillite* for every company failure: in a news report or a dossier, name the procedure
  (*redressement judiciaire, liquidation judiciaire*).
- Confusing *le créancier* (who is owed) with *le débiteur* (who owes).
- *Le bénéfice* (B1, profit) for *le chiffre d'affaires* (turnover), or *le bilan* for the income
  statement.
- "Rose by 2 %" for *a progressé de deux points*: points are not per cent.
- *Une fusion* and *une acquisition* used as synonyms.
- Calling a cyclical problem *structurel*, or the reverse: the adjective carries the argument.

## Key points

- *Conjoncturel* (cyclical) / *structurel* (structural); *l'inflation / la déflation*; *la
  politique monétaire* of the BCE and its *taux directeurs*; *un excédent / un déficit*; *les agences
  de notation*; *le krach*.
- Accounts: *l'exercice*, *le bilan* (balance sheet), *le compte de résultat*, *la trésorerie,
  l'endettement, la solvabilité, la plus-value*.
- Markets: *l'actionnaire, le dividende, la cotation, la capitalisation boursière, l'introduction en
  Bourse, la levée de fonds, la fusion, l'acquisition*.
- Difficulty: *la cessation des paiements* (declare within 45 days) → *le redressement judiciaire*
  or *la liquidation judiciaire*; *la faillite* is the everyday word; *le créancier / le débiteur*.
- Points ≠ per cent; hedge forecasts (*devrait, tabler sur, sous réserve que* + subjunctive).

lessons.title: Aporie, paradigme, dialectique: the language of ideas
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last specialised language of this module is the language of ideas: the vocabulary that
philosophy, the social sciences and the essay share, and that DALF C2 dossiers in the *lettres et
sciences humaines* option take for granted. At C1 you learned academic French (lesson 15) and the essay with its
*plan dialectique* (lesson 20). This lesson goes one level up:
the abstract nouns, the *-isms* and the adjectives of philosophy, and the grammar that makes
abstract writing precise: defining, distinguishing, generalising and nominalising. It ends with the
opposite skill, saying the same thing without jargon. The rhetoric of argument is lesson 22's.

The theme is a radio philosophy programme on whether progress is an illusion. The programme, its
host and its guests are invented; the thinkers they discuss are real, and their works are only
named and described.

## Words for thinking about thinking

Most of these nouns are cognates, so the danger is not that you won't recognise them but that you
will use them loosely. Each has a narrow sense.

*Being and knowing.* *L'ontologie* is the study of being: what exists, and how. *L'épistémologie*
is the theory of knowledge, and in French especially the philosophy of science (how science knows
what it knows). *L'essence* of a thing is what makes it what it is (*l'essence de la justice*);
careful: in everyday French, *l'essence* is petrol. *La finitude* is the condition of a being that
is limited, above all in time: human beings die, and know it. *L'altérité* is otherness: the fact
that the other is not me, and the respect that this calls for.

*Reasoning.* *Un axiome* is a starting point accepted without proof, often as self-evident (in
mathematics, a basic rule of a system); *un postulat* is a premise one asks the reader to grant,
and so is more open to dispute. *Une tautologie* says the same thing twice and so says nothing (*le
progrès, c'est aller de l'avant*). *Une antinomie* is a contradiction between two claims that each
seem justified. *Une aporie* is a problem with no way out, a reasoning that ends in an impasse.
*La dialectique* is reasoning that moves through opposition: a thesis meets its contrary, and the
tension leads to a new position (C1's *plan dialectique* applies this to the essay). *Un paradigme*
is a model or framework of thought; since the historian of science Thomas Kuhn (*The Structure of
Scientific Revolutions*, 1962), *un changement de paradigme* is a change in the whole way a field
sees its problems.

*Opinion.* *La doxa* is received opinion, what "everyone knows" without having examined it. *Un
lieu commun* is a commonplace idea or a platitude. Both are slightly pejorative in an essay: they
name what the writer is about to question.

## The -isms

![A concept map titled "Les -ismes". Four rows of opposed pairs: for knowing, empiricism (from experience) against rationalism (from reason); for the real, materialism (matter comes first) against idealism (mind comes first); for freedom, determinism (everything has causes) against free will (we choose freely); for values, universalism (the same for all) against relativism (depends on culture). Below, two positions on their own: existentialism (we make ourselves by our choices) and nihilism (no value holds).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The *-isms* come in pairs, and a C2 reader recognises the opposition behind each one:

- *l'empirisme* (all knowledge comes from experience) and *le rationalisme* (reason can know
  some things without experience);
- *le matérialisme* (matter comes first; mind depends on it) and *l'idéalisme* (ideas or the
  mind come first);
- *le déterminisme* (everything has causes that make it necessary) and *le libre arbitre* (C1);
- *l'universalisme* (some values hold for every human being) and *le relativisme* (C1 honors:
  values depend on the culture or the point of view);
- *l'existentialisme* (the philosophy associated with Sartre: human beings have no nature given
  in advance and make themselves by their choices), and *le nihilisme* (no value or meaning
  holds).

Beware of the everyday senses: *le matérialisme* also means caring about possessions, and *un
idéaliste* is someone with ideals. In a philosophy text, the technical sense wins.

## Four adjectives

- *transcendant* (transcendent): beyond the world or beyond experience. Spelt *-ant*; the
  philosophers' *transcendantal* (Kant) is a different word.
- *immanent* (immanent): within, belonging to the thing itself, the opposite of *transcendant*.
  Don't confuse it with *imminent* (about to happen).
- *inhérent à* (inherent in): part of the nature of: *les risques inhérents à toute innovation*.
- *intrinsèque* (intrinsic): in itself, independent of anything else: *la valeur intrinsèque
  d'une œuvre*; the opposite is *extrinsèque*.

## The grammar of abstraction

*Defining.* *La finitude désigne la condition d'un être limité. Par progrès, on entend ici …
Ce terme renvoie à … On appelle « doxa » l'ensemble des opinions reçues.* An essay that defines
its key **[[concept]]** (in argument, a word given an exact, stated meaning) before using it can't be
accused of playing on words.

*Distinguishing.* *Il convient de distinguer le progrès technique du progrès moral. Il ne s'agit
pas de nier la science, mais d'en mesurer les effets. L'homme en tant qu'espèce n'est pas l'homme en
tant qu'individu.* (*En tant que*: as, considered as.)

*Generalising.* French uses **[[the generic article]]**: the definite article for a whole class
(*L'homme est un être fini. Les sociétés modernes valorisent l'innovation.*), and sometimes the
indefinite for "any one" (*Un philosophe doit douter.*). English says "Man" and "modern societies"
without an article; French can't drop it. Many writers now prefer *l'être humain*
to *l'homme* for the species.

*Nominalising.* Abstract writing turns verbs and adjectives into **[[abstract nouns]]**: *fini →
la finitude, autre → l'altérité, progresser → le progrès, déterminer → le déterminisme*. This lets
a writer make an idea the subject of a sentence (*La finitude interdit …*). Used with measure, it
gives precision; piled up, it gives **[[jargon]]**: specialist vocabulary used where plain words would
do, which hides the reasoning instead of carrying it.

## The radio programme

*Summary of an invented programme, "Les Mardis de la pensée": "Le progrès est-il une illusion ?"*

The host, Claire Vasseur, opens with a commonplace (*un lieu commun*): nobody believes in progress
any more. The epistemologist Mehdi Laroche objects that science does progress, in a precise sense:
each paradigm explains more than the last, even if, as Kuhn argued, the change from one to the
next is not a smooth accumulation. The historian of ideas Anne Feuillet recalls the two founding
texts of the quarrel. In his *Discours sur les sciences et les arts* (1750), written for a prize
question of the Académie de Dijon, Rousseau argued that the progress of the sciences and arts had
not made people better; his *Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les
hommes* (1755) makes human perfectibility the source of both our gains and our misfortunes.
Condorcet, writing his *Esquisse d'un tableau historique des progrès de l'esprit humain* in
1793–1794 while in hiding during the Terror (it was published after his death, in 1795), saw the
improvement of humanity as having no fixed limit. Laroche calls the idea of a progress built into
history itself (*un progrès inhérent à l'histoire*) "a postulate, not a result". Feuillet ends with
Bergson (*L'Évolution créatrice*, 1907), the philosopher of lived time (*la durée*), for whom the
future is not written in advance.

## Reading: an essay extract

> *Le progrès, une idée à l'épreuve*
>
> (1) Qu'il y ait du progrès, la doxa contemporaine en doute volontiers ; que le progrès soit une
> illusion, c'est devenu un lieu commun. Il convient pourtant de distinguer deux affirmations que
> l'on confond trop souvent : l'existence de progrès particuliers, dans les techniques, la médecine
> ou le droit, et l'idée du Progrès, au singulier et avec une majuscule, selon laquelle l'histoire
> humaine irait, dans son ensemble, vers le mieux.
>
> (2) La première affirmation relève de l'observation : l'espérance de vie, la mortalité infantile,
> l'accès à l'écrit se mesurent, et leur évolution sur deux siècles ne laisse guère de doute. La
> seconde n'est pas un constat mais un postulat. Chez Condorcet, qui la soutient avec le plus de
> confiance, le perfectionnement de l'espèce est pensé sans limite fixée d'avance : il est posé
> comme un axiome dont découle tout le reste. On ne le démontre pas ; on le suppose.
>
> (3) C'est ce postulat que Rousseau, quelque quarante ans plus tôt, avait mis en cause. Non pas en
> niant que les sciences et les arts se développent, mais en refusant d'en conclure que les hommes
> en deviennent meilleurs. Le progrès des savoirs n'entraîne pas celui des mœurs : affirmer le
> contraire, c'est confondre deux ordres de réalité. On voit par là que la querelle n'oppose pas
> les amis et les ennemis de la science, mais deux conceptions de ce qui, en l'être humain, peut
> progresser.
>
> (4) Faut-il en conclure que le débat aboutit à une aporie ? Pas nécessairement. Une démarche
> dialectique permet de dépasser l'antinomie apparente entre ceux qui voient dans l'histoire une
> ascension et ceux qui n'y voient qu'une chute. Le progrès n'est ni une loi de l'histoire, comme
> le voudrait un déterminisme optimiste, ni une illusion, comme le prétend un nihilisme de salon :
> il est une tâche. Rien ne garantit qu'il ait lieu, et c'est précisément pourquoi il dépend de
> nous.
>
> (5) Cette conception a un coût : elle suppose que l'on renonce à l'idée d'un progrès inhérent à
> la marche du temps. Elle a aussi un mérite. Elle prend au sérieux notre finitude (nous ne verrons
> pas la fin de l'histoire, et nos choix ont des effets que nous ne maîtrisons pas) sans en faire
> une raison de désespérer. Elle oblige enfin à poser une question que l'idée du Progrès, par sa
> généralité même, permettait d'éluder : progrès pour qui ? L'altérité des autres peuples et des
> générations futures, dont le point de vue n'est jamais exactement le nôtre, interdit de juger du
> mieux à l'aune de nos seuls intérêts présents.

*Summary by paragraph.*

1. Received opinion (*la doxa*) doubts progress; "progress is an illusion" has become a
   commonplace. But two claims must be distinguished: particular advances, and the idea of Progress
   with a capital P, history as a whole moving towards the better.
2. The first is a matter of observation (*relever de*): life expectancy and literacy can be
   measured. The second is a postulate: in Condorcet, improvement is conceived as having no limit
   set in advance, an axiom from which everything else follows. It is assumed, not proved.
3. Rousseau, some forty years earlier, questioned that postulate: not by denying that knowledge
   grows, but by refusing to conclude that people become better. The quarrel is between two views
   of what in human beings can progress.
4. Is it an impasse (*une aporie*)? Not necessarily: a dialectical approach overcomes the apparent contradiction
   (*l'antinomie*) between ascent and fall. Progress is neither a law of history (an optimistic
   determinism) nor an illusion (a fashionable nihilism, *de salon*): it is a task, and depends on us
   because nothing guarantees it.
5. The cost: giving up the idea of a progress inherent in time. The merits: it takes our finitude
   seriously without despair, and it raises the question the grand idea avoided (*éluder*): progress
   for whom? The otherness of other peoples and future generations forbids judging the better by the
   yardstick (*à l'aune de*) of our present interests alone.

## Saying it without jargon

Here is a sentence of the kind a dossier sometimes contains, then a plain rewriting of the same
idea.

> *La problématisation de l'axiologie progressiste invite à une déconstruction de son paradigme
> ontologique, dont l'immanence téléologique se révèle intrinsèquement aporétique.*
>
> *L'idée que l'histoire va vers le mieux repose sur une hypothèse qu'on ne peut pas démontrer :
> elle suppose que le progrès fait partie de la nature même du temps. Or cette hypothèse mène à des
> difficultés qu'elle ne sait pas résoudre.*

Roughly: "The problematisation of progressive axiology invites a deconstruction of its ontological
paradigm, whose teleological immanence proves intrinsically aporetic." The plain version: "The idea
that history moves towards the better rests on an assumption that can't be proved: it assumes that
progress is part of the very nature of time. And that assumption leads to difficulties it can't
resolve."

The method: find the claim (here, "progress-as-law can't be proved and leads to problems"); give
each sentence a subject that acts; turn nouns back into verbs (*la problématisation* → *on se
demande si*); keep a technical term only if you need it, and define it the first time. The plain
version is longer, and better: a C2 reader is judged on precision, not on density.

## Common mistakes

- *Un axiome* and *un postulat* as mere synonyms for "idea": both are starting points of a
  reasoning, unproved.
- *Une aporie* for any difficulty: it is a problem with no solution in the terms set.
- *Transcendent* for *transcendant*: French spells it with *-ant*.
- *Immanent* confused with *imminent*.
- Dropping the generic article: *Homme est mortel* is impossible; say *L'homme est mortel*.
- *L'essence* read as petrol in a philosophy text, or the reverse at the pump.
- Mistaking density for depth: four abstract nouns in a row are a warning sign.

## Key points

- Being and knowing: *l'ontologie, l'épistémologie, l'essence, la finitude, l'altérité*.
  Reasoning: *l'axiome, le postulat, la tautologie, l'antinomie, l'aporie, la dialectique, le
  paradigme*. Opinion: *la doxa, le lieu commun*.
- The -isms come in pairs: *empirisme / rationalisme, matérialisme / idéalisme, déterminisme /
  libre arbitre, universalisme / relativisme*; *l'existentialisme, le nihilisme*.
- *Transcendant* (beyond) / *immanent* (within); *inhérent à*; *intrinsèque / extrinsèque*.
- Define (*X désigne, par X on entend*), distinguish (*il convient de distinguer, non pas … mais,
  en tant que*), generalise with the generic article, nominalise with measure.
- Rousseau (1750, 1755), Condorcet (*Esquisse*, published 1795), Bergson (1907): named and
  described, never quoted.
- Plain style: claim first, subjects that act, verbs for nouns, terms defined.

lessons.title: Ariane, Kourou, le CNES: the French of space
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 taught the voice of French science and engineering on the ground. Space is the field
where that voice is most public: launches are broadcast live with a commentary, missions have
press kits, and space law has its own statute. France has been a space power since the 1960s, and
Europe's launchers fly from French territory, so the vocabulary is French first and translated
afterwards. This lesson covers the institutions and their history, the words of a launch and of a
crewed mission, the debris problem, and the official terms that France recommends.

## French space, in dates

The French space agency, the CNES (*Centre national d'études spatiales*), was created on 19
December 1961. In 1964 France chose Kourou, in French Guiana, for its launch base: the *Centre
spatial guyanais* (CSG). The site is about five degrees north of the equator, so a rocket launched
eastward gets the most help from the Earth's rotation, and there is open sea to the east. The first
rocket left Kourou on 9 April 1968: Véronique, a sounding rocket. In 1975 European states founded
the European Space Agency (*l'Agence spatiale européenne*, ESA), whose headquarters are in Paris.

```timeline
title: French and European space, 1961–2024
event: 19 December 1961 | The CNES is created | Institutions
event: 1964 | Kourou, in French Guiana, is chosen as the launch site | Kourou
event: 9 April 1968 | First launch from Kourou: the Véronique sounding rocket | Kourou
event: 1975 | The European Space Agency is founded; its headquarters are in Paris | Institutions
event: 24 December 1979 | First flight of Ariane 1 | Ariane
event: 5 July 2023 | Last flight of Ariane 5, after 117 launches | Ariane
event: 9 July 2024 | First flight of Ariane 6 | Ariane
caption: Dates from the CNES and the Guiana Space Centre. Ariane 5's first flight, in 1996, failed.
```

The Ariane family made Europe independent for access to space. Ariane 1 first flew on 24 December
1979. Ariane 5, whose first flight in 1996 ended in failure, became the workhorse for commercial
satellites and made 117 launches until its last on 5 July 2023. Ariane 6 first flew on 9 July 2024.
Two French astronauts' missions are recent landmarks: Thomas Pesquet spent about six months on the
International Space Station from November 2016 to June 2017 (the *Proxima* mission, launched on a
Soyuz) and again from April to November 2021 (*Alpha*, on a SpaceX Crew Dragon), when he became
the first French commander of the station.

## The words of a launch

A rocket that puts objects into space is *un lanceur* (B1 honors), the **[[launch vehicle]]**. It
stands on *le pas de tir* (the launch pad). It is built in *étages* (stages: you met *l'étage* as
the floor of a building), each with its engines and propellants, dropped when empty. At the top,
*la coiffe* (the fairing: also, in everyday French, a traditional headdress) protects what the
rocket carries through the atmosphere, then splits open and falls away. What it carries is *la
charge utile*, the **[[payload]]**: one or more satellites, a probe, a capsule.

![A rocket standing on its launch pad beside a service tower. From top to bottom: a rounded nose cone, cut away to show a satellite inside; the upper stage; the main stage with two side boosters; the pad and its flame trench at the base.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The sequence has fixed words. *Le compte à rebours* (C1) runs down to zero; *la mise à feu*
(ignition) lights the engines; *la poussée* (thrust) lifts the rocket when it exceeds its weight,
and *le décollage* (B2 honors) follows. Stages separate one after another, the fairing is jettisoned,
and the last stage achieves *la mise en orbite* (placing in orbit) of the payload. *La poussée*
also has everyday senses: a push, and a surge (*une poussée de fièvre, une poussée de l'extrême
droite aux élections*).

Many telecommunications satellites go to *l'orbite géostationnaire*, the **[[geostationary orbit]]**:
a circular orbit above the equator, about 36,000 km up, where a satellite goes round in exactly the
time the Earth takes to turn. Seen from the ground it stays still, so a fixed dish can point at it.

### Example 1: a launch commentary

> *H0 plus deux minutes vingt : la poussée des propulseurs d'appoint diminue, la séparation est
> confirmée. L'étage principal poursuit son vol. Nous attendons maintenant le largage de la coiffe,
> qui interviendra au-dessus de cent kilomètres d'altitude, lorsque la charge utile n'aura plus
> besoin de protection. Largage de la coiffe confirmé. Tous les paramètres sont nominaux.*

"Liftoff plus two minutes twenty: the thrust of the side boosters is falling, separation is
confirmed. The main stage continues its flight. We are now waiting for the fairing to be
jettisoned, which will happen above a hundred kilometres, when the payload no longer needs
protection. Fairing jettison confirmed. All parameters are nominal."

How to read it: *H0* (*H zéro*) is the reference moment of the launch, around ignition and
liftoff, and times are counted from it. *Les
propulseurs d'appoint* are the side boosters; *le largage* is the release or jettisoning of
something (*larguer*: to drop). *Interviendra* is the formal *aura lieu*. *Nominal* means "as
planned", a technical sense French shares with English. And *lorsque* takes the future when the
main verb is in the future (*interviendra … lorsque la charge utile n'aura plus besoin*), where
English uses the present ("when the payload no longer needs").

## The words of a mission

The French have three words for space travellers. *L'astronaute* (B2) is the international and
most common word; *le cosmonaute* is used for Soviet and Russian crews; *le spationaute*, a French
coinage built on *spatial*, is used mainly for French and European astronauts. The Académie
française's dictionary records it and notes that *astronaute* is more common; FranceTerme, the
French government's terminology service, gives *astronaute* as its headword and *spationaute* as
an official synonym. In the press
you will see all three; in your own writing *astronaute* is the safe choice, and *spationaute*
is correct.

A crew vehicle that reaches the station performs *l'amarrage* (docking), which is also the
everyday word for mooring a boat (*amarrer*: to moor). The way home ends with *la rentrée
atmosphérique* (atmospheric re-entry), when friction with the air heats the capsule and slows it
down before the parachutes open.

### Example 2: a press release, unpacked

> *L'amarrage du vaisseau à la station est intervenu à 10 h 08, heure de Paris, à l'issue d'une
> phase d'approche automatique de vingt-huit heures. L'ouverture de l'écoutille, après
> vérification de l'étanchéité, est prévue en début d'après-midi.*

This is lesson 10's style: nouns where a story would put verbs. Unpack each one:

1. *L'amarrage … est intervenu à 10 h 08* → *le vaisseau s'est amarré à 10 h 08* (the craft docked
   at 10.08, Paris time).
2. *à l'issue d'une phase d'approche automatique de vingt-huit heures* → *après s'être approché
   automatiquement pendant vingt-huit heures*.
3. *L'ouverture de l'écoutille, après vérification de l'étanchéité* → *on ouvrira l'écoutille
   (the hatch) quand on aura vérifié qu'elle est étanche (airtight)*.

The release names no person at all: the docking, the approach and the opening simply "happen".
That is normal in the genre; in an article for the general public, you would put the crew and the
control centre back in.

## The debris problem

Every launch leaves objects in orbit: dead satellites, spent upper stages, fragments from
explosions and collisions. These *débris spatiaux* (space debris; *le débris spatial* in the singular, which is rarer) move
at several kilometres per second, so even a small one can destroy a satellite. The CNES's 2025
estimates count about 54,000 objects larger than 10 cm and about 1.5 million between 1 and 10 cm.

France regulates the problem by law. Under the *loi du 3 juin 2008 relative aux opérations
spatiales* (LOS), a launch, the control of a satellite in orbit or its return to Earth carried out
from France or by a French operator needs authorisation, and the CNES checks each request against
technical rules, which include limiting debris. A rule of this kind reads, in legal form (our
illustration, not the law's wording): *L'opérateur est tenu de limiter la production de débris
spatiaux*: the prescriptive present of lesson 09.

## Common mistakes

- *La charge payante*, a calque of "payload" sometimes seen: the standard term is *la charge
  utile*.
- *Le lanceur* and *la fusée* (B1 honors) are not quite the same: *la fusée* is the everyday word,
  *le lanceur* the technical one for a rocket that puts objects in orbit.
- *L'étage* read as "floor" in a launch commentary: it is a stage.
- *L'amarrage* translated as "mooring" in a space text: it is docking.
- Treating *spationaute* as wrong or *astronaute* as un-French: both are correct.
- *Les débris spatial*: the plural adjective is *spatiaux*.

## Key points

- The CNES (1961), Kourou (chosen 1964, first launch 1968), ESA (1975, Paris), Ariane 1 (1979),
  Ariane 5 (last flight 2023), Ariane 6 (first flight 2024); Thomas Pesquet's *Proxima*
  (2016–2017) and *Alpha* (2021).
- A launch: *le lanceur, le pas de tir, les étages, la coiffe, la charge utile, le compte à
  rebours, la mise à feu, la poussée, la mise en orbite, l'orbite géostationnaire*.
- A mission: *l'astronaute* (FranceTerme's headword), *le spationaute* (its synonym), *le cosmonaute*;
  *l'amarrage, la rentrée atmosphérique*.
- *Les débris spatiaux*; the LOS of 2008 makes French operators limit them.
- Space press releases nominalise: unpack the nouns into verbs and put back who acts.

lessons.title: Le Code civil de 1804: a style of law
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 taught you to read legal French as it is used today. This lesson looks at the text
behind much of it: the Code civil of 1804, which still governs persons, families, property and
contracts in France, and which writers have admired as a model of prose. You will see how it was
made, what it unified, how its style works, how its family law has been rewritten, and how far it
travelled. Its articles are described here in our own words, never quoted: if you want the wording,
read the current text on Légifrance, the official site of French law.

## Two Frances before the Code

Before the Revolution, France had no single private law. Roughly, the north was the land of **[[customary law]]** (*le droit coutumier*): each province or city had its own *coutume*, a body of
rules first handed down by usage and then written down, the most influential being the Coutume de
Paris. The south was the land of **[[written law]]** (*le droit écrit*): the *droit romain* (Roman
law), as compiled under the emperor Justinian and taught in the universities, applied there as the
common basis. A marriage, an inheritance or a sale could follow different rules a few days' ride
apart.

The Revolution wanted one law for one nation. Its assemblies tried several drafts of a civil code
in the 1790s, and none was adopted. The work was finished under Napoleon Bonaparte, then First
Consul.

## How the Code was made

In August 1800 Bonaparte appointed a commission of four lawyers: François Tronchet and Félix
Bigot de Préameneu, trained in the customary law of the north, and Jean-Étienne-Marie Portalis and
Jacques de Maleville, from the written-law south. The balance was deliberate: the Code would be a
compromise between the two traditions. Their draft was presented in 1801 with a *Discours
préliminaire*, mainly the work of Portalis. In it he argues, roughly, that a law-maker cannot
foresee every case, that laws should therefore lay down general principles rather than rules for
every detail, and that it falls to judges and jurists (*les juristes*) to apply them to the
infinite variety of real life.

The draft was debated at length in the Conseil d'État, where Bonaparte took part in many sessions,
and then adopted as thirty-six separate laws. A law of 21 March 1804 (30 ventôse an XII in the
Revolutionary calendar) gathered them into one *Code civil des Français* of 2,281 articles. This is
**[[codification]]**: bringing scattered rules together into one ordered, written code. The Code took
the name *Code Napoléon* in 1807; today it is simply *le Code civil*.

*La promulgation* of a law is the act by which the head of state makes it official and
enforceable (the verb *promulguer* is B2 honors). *Le législateur* is the lawmaker: in French
legal writing, the abstract author of the law (*le législateur a voulu …*), whoever actually drafted
it.

![A tree showing the structure of the Code civil des Français of 21 March 1804, 2,281 articles: a preliminary title on the publication, effects and application of laws; Book One on persons (civil status, marriage, divorce, parentage, paternal authority); Book Two on property (ownership, usufruct, easements); Book Three on the ways of acquiring property (inheritance, gifts, contracts, marriage settlements). A note adds Book Four on securities (2006) and says the 1804 titles are simplified.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The 1804 Code has a short preliminary title and three books: persons, property, and the ways of
acquiring property. Later reforms added books, for example a fourth on securities (*les
sûretés*) in 2006, but the 1804 skeleton is still recognisable.

## A style of law

The Code's articles are short, general and written in the prescriptive present of lesson 09. Many
are one sentence. They state a principle, not a list of cases, exactly as Portalis wanted. This is
why writers have admired them. In a draft of a letter to Balzac in October 1840, Stendhal said that while
writing *La Chartreuse de Parme* he read a few pages of the Code civil every morning to set his
tone: he wanted its plainness, with nothing added to charm the reader. The anecdote is often
repeated, and it fits: the Code's sentences are clear, exact and without ornament.

### Example 1: the principle of civil liability

One article of the Code, numbered 1382 for two centuries and 1240 since a reform of contract law in
2016, contains in a single sentence the whole basis of civil liability: whoever, by his fault,
causes damage to another person must repair it. Look at what the sentence does not say. It names
no kind of damage, no kind of fault, no amount. Judges have spent two centuries filling it in, and
the *jurisprudence* (lesson 09) on it fills volumes. That is the Code's method: the principle
in the text, the detail in the courts.

How to describe such an article in your own French, as a report or an essay would:

> *L'article 1240 du Code civil pose le principe de la responsabilité civile : quiconque cause un
> dommage à autrui par sa faute est tenu de le réparer.*

Notice the verbs of description: *poser le principe de, prévoir, disposer que, énoncer*. The
present (*pose, est tenu*) is both the present of description and the prescriptive present.

### Example 2: usufruct

*L'usufruit* (usufruct) is a right inherited from Roman law. The Code defines it as the right to use
and enjoy a thing that belongs to someone else, as the owner would, on condition of keeping it
intact. The holder, *l'usufruitier*, can live in a house or rent it out and keep the rent, but can't
sell the house itself. The owner, who keeps only the bare ownership (*la nue-propriété*), recovers the full right
when the usufruct ends, usually at the usufructuary's death. It is common in French families: after
a death, a surviving spouse often receives the usufruct of the home, and the children its bare
ownership.

In plain French: *L'usufruitier peut se servir du bien et en percevoir les revenus, mais il ne
peut pas le vendre, et il doit le conserver.*

## What changed: the family

The Code of 1804 built the family on the husband and father. *La puissance paternelle* (paternal
authority) gave the father power over his children, and the married woman was legally under her
husband's authority. Most of this was rewritten in the twentieth century.

```timeline
title: Rewriting the family in the Code civil
event: 1816 | Divorce, allowed since 1792, is abolished | Divorce
event: 1884 | The Naquet law brings divorce back, for fault only | Divorce
event: 1938 | Married women gain civil capacity | Couples
event: 13 July 1965 | Reform of marriage settlements: each spouse manages their own property | Couples
event: 4 June 1970 | Parental authority, shared by both parents, replaces paternal authority | Children
event: 3 January 1972 | Children born outside marriage gain equal rights | Children
event: 11 July 1975 | Divorce reform, including divorce by mutual consent | Divorce
event: 4 July 2005 | An ordinance removes the distinction between legitimate and natural parentage | Children
event: 18 November 2016 | Divorce by mutual consent without a judge becomes possible | Divorce
caption: Dates from vie-publique.fr; the 2016 law took effect on 1 January 2017.
```

The vocabulary followed the law. *L'autorité parentale* (parental authority) replaced *la puissance
paternelle* in 1970: the new term names a duty exercised by both parents in the child's interest,
not a power. *La filiation* (parentage, descent) is the legal link between a child and its parents;
the old distinction between *filiation légitime* and *filiation naturelle* disappeared in 2005. A
couple's *régime matrimonial* (marriage settlement, matrimonial property regime) decides who owns
what: since the 1965 reform the default for couples who sign no contract is *la communauté réduite
aux acquêts*, in which what each spouse earns during the marriage is shared and what each owned
before, or inherits, stays their own.

## How far it travelled

The armies of the Empire carried the Code across Europe, and many states kept it or copied it. It
remained in force in Belgium and Luxembourg after French rule ended; Belgium has been replacing it,
book by book, with a new Civil Code in recent years. It inspired codes in Italy, Spain, Portugal and
much of Latin America, and, beside Spanish sources, the civil code of Louisiana. In Québec, whose civil law descends from
the Coutume de Paris, the Civil Code of Lower Canada (1866) drew heavily on the French Code; it was
replaced by the Civil Code of Québec in 1994. Its influence elsewhere is often summed up as the
"civil law" tradition, opposed to the English "common law" of judge-made precedent: a simplification,
but a useful one.

## Common mistakes

- *Le droit écrit* means the Roman-law tradition of the south, not simply "written law" as opposed
  to oral rules: the customs of the north were written down too.
- *La puissance paternelle* in a modern text: it is historical; today's term is *l'autorité
  parentale*.
- *Le juriste* (a legal expert, any lawyer in the broad sense) is not *l'avocat* (a lawyer admitted
  to the bar, who can represent clients in court).
- *L'usufruit* is not ownership: the usufructuary uses and enjoys, the bare owner owns.
- Quoting an article from memory: describe it (*l'article X pose le principe de …*), or copy the
  current text from Légifrance.

## Key points

- Before 1804: *le droit coutumier* (north) and *le droit écrit*, based on *le droit romain*
  (south).
- Four drafters (Tronchet, Bigot de Préameneu, Portalis, Maleville), Portalis's *Discours
  préliminaire*, *la promulgation* of 21 March 1804: 36 laws, 2,281 articles, one code.
  *La codification* gathers rules into one code.
- The style: short, general articles in the prescriptive present; Stendhal's admiration (1840).
- Family law rewritten: *l'autorité parentale* (1970) replaced *la puissance paternelle*; *la
  filiation* equalised (1972, 2005); *le régime matrimonial* reformed (1965); divorce (1884, 1975,
  2016).
- Belgium, Luxembourg, Louisiana, Québec: the Code's reach, to be stated with care.

lessons.title: Essencerie, maquis, grin: French in sub-Saharan Africa
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 (honors) you met the francophone world as a map, and at B2 (honors) as a literature: *le griot* (the West
African storyteller and keeper of memory) and *la négritude* (the literary movement of Senghor and
Césaire). This module looks at the French that people actually speak and write in the four big areas
outside France, and lesson 16 then asks whether one of them is "the" standard. Nothing here ranks
varieties: Dakar French is not a faulty copy of Paris French, any more than American English is a
faulty copy of British English.

Africa is where French has most of its speakers. The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie
(OIF) counted 321 million French speakers in 2022 and 396 million in its 2026 report, about 65 % of
them in Africa. Much of that jump comes from a change of method: the 2026 report counts, for the first
time, children aged 6 to 9 who are schooled in French. Quote both figures, with the date and the
method note, never the 396 million on its own.

This lesson covers the status of French beside other languages, the ways African French makes new
words, the everyday words of town life, and the urban youth varieties of Abidjan and Yaoundé. Its
theme is a week in Dakar and Abidjan seen by a young journalist, Inès Faye (invented). The Maghreb is
lesson 14's subject, and the novelist Ahmadou Kourouma is honors lesson 16h1's.

## French among other languages

In most of francophone Africa, French is one language among many, and its job differs from place to
place. Linguists describe these jobs with a few terms:

- A **[[langue véhiculaire]]** (lingua franca) is a language used between people whose first languages
  differ: Wolof in Senegal, Dioula in much of Côte d'Ivoire, Lingala in Kinshasa, and French itself in
  many towns and offices.
- A **[[langue vernaculaire]]** (vernacular) is the language of a community, learned at home and used
  among its own speakers.
- A **[[national language]]** (*la langue nationale*) is a status a state gives to languages it
  recognises as belonging to the country; it may or may not make them official.

These categories overlap: Wolof is a vernacular for some Senegalese and a lingua franca for many
more. *Le plurilinguisme* (multilingualism) is the normal condition: a market trader in Dakar may use
Wolof, Pulaar, French and a little Arabic in one morning.

The legal status of French also varies, and it has changed recently. As of November 2026:

| country | status of French | other languages with a status |
|---|---|---|
| Senegal | official language (constitution of 2001) | national languages: Wolof, Pulaar, Serer, Diola, Malinké, Soninké and others once codified |
| Côte d'Ivoire | official language | about sixty languages, none of them official |
| Cameroon | official, with English | many national languages |
| DR Congo | official language | four national languages: Lingala, Kikongo, Swahili, Tshiluba |
| Mali | working language since the constitution of July 2023 | the national languages are now the official languages |
| Burkina Faso | working language since a constitutional revision adopted in December 2023 (promulgated in January 2024) | national languages made official |
| Niger | working language under the *Charte de la refondation* of March 2025 | Hausa named the national language, beside the country's other languages |

The changes in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger came from military governments that broke with France,
and press reports describe them as French being "demoted". French is still used in their
administrations and schools; what changed is the symbol, and how far daily practice follows remains to
be seen.

view: fit
