## How African French makes words

A word or use of French typical of Africa is an **[[Africanism]]** (*un africanisme*). Most are made with
the ordinary tools of French, which is why a reader from Paris can often guess them. Linguists group
them by process:

| process | base | result |
|---|---|---|
| suffix on a French base | *l'essence* (petrol) | *l'essencerie* (petrol station, Senegal) |
| suffix on a base usually traced to a French verb | *débiter* (to cut up meat), probably through Wolof *dibi* (grilled meat) | *la dibiterie* (grilled-meat stall, Senegal) |
| noun → verb | *le cadeau*, *l'ambiance* | *cadeauter*, *ambiancer* |
| shift of meaning | *gâter* (to spoil) | *gâter* = to break down: *ma voiture est gâtée* |
| shift of meaning | *le maquis* (scrubland; the Resistance) | *le maquis* = open-air restaurant (Côte d'Ivoire) |
| borrowing | words from West African languages | *le grin* (tea circle), *le boubou* |
| compound | *le taxi* + *la brousse* (the bush) | *le taxi-brousse* |
| metaphor | an office for a second job | *le deuxième bureau* (a man's mistress) |

![A chart of six ways African French makes words. Each row has a French base on the left, an arrow, and the new word on the right: essence to essencerie (suffix), cadeau to cadeauter (noun to verb), gâter « abîmer » (to spoil) to gâter « tomber en panne » (to break down) (new meaning), a word from a West African language to le grin (borrowing), taxi plus brousse to taxi-brousse (compound), and bureau to deuxième bureau (metaphor).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A few more from Senegal, recorded in the Dakar press: *enceinter* (to make pregnant), *descendre*
(to finish work: *je descends à 17 h*), *long* (tall, of a person). The suffix *-erie* is very
productive: it turns a product into the place that sells or makes it, as *la boulangerie* does in
France.

Two dictionaries record these words. The *Inventaire des particularités lexicales du français en
Afrique noire*, compiled by a team of researchers from many countries, was a large survey of the 1980s, later revised.
The *Dictionnaire des francophones* (DDF), launched online by the French Ministry of Culture in March
2021, brings it together with Belgian, Swiss, Québec and other sources, so that one search shows
where a word is used. When you meet an unfamiliar word in an Ivorian or Senegalese newspaper, look
there before you assume it is a mistake.

## Words of town life

**Getting about.** Between towns there is *le taxi-brousse* (plural *les taxis-brousse*), a shared car
or minibus that leaves when it is full. In Abidjan, *le gbaka* is a crowded minibus whose young
conductor shouts the destinations from the door, and *le woro-woro* (also written *wôrô-wôrô*) is a
shared taxi on a fixed route at a fixed fare.

**Eating out.** In Côte d'Ivoire *le maquis* is an open-air restaurant, often with music; in France the
same word means scrubland, and *le maquis* of 1940–1944 was the armed Resistance hiding in it. In
Senegal you buy grilled mutton at a *dibiterie*.

**Money and clothes.** *La tontine* is a rotating savings club: each member pays the same amount at fixed
intervals (often every month), and each time one member takes the whole pot. *La cherté* (the high
cost) is standard French, but *la cherté de la vie* is especially frequent in African newspapers. *Le boubou*
is a long, wide, flowing robe worn by men and women; *le pagne* is a length of printed cloth wrapped as
a skirt (and, in older French, a loincloth).

**People and talk.** *Le grin* is a group of friends, usually young men, who meet every day over tea in
Mali and Burkina Faso. *La palabre* is a long public discussion, traditionally under *l'arbre à
palabres* in the village; in France *des palabres* (usually plural) are endless talk. The noun is
normally feminine; some African usage makes it masculine. *Le marabout* is a Muslim holy man and
teacher; in some countries the word also covers a healer or a fortune teller. *L'ambianceur*
(feminine *l'ambianceuse*) is the life and soul of the party, the one who knows how to *ambiancer* a
room. *Cadeauter quelqu'un* is to give someone a present. *Présentement* (at present) is often
felt as old-fashioned or regional in France but is ordinary in Africa and Québec.

**A judgemental word.** *Le deuxième bureau* is a man's mistress, literally "the second office", as if
the affair were a second workplace. It is informal and it judges the woman as much as the man.
Recognise it; don't use it.

![A street scene in Abidjan with five labels: le gbaka (a minibus with a sliding door and its conductor at the door), le woro-woro (a small shared taxi), le maquis (an open-air restaurant with tables under a corrugated roof and a sign, Chez Tantie), le boubou (a man in a long, wide blue robe) and le pagne (a woman wearing a skirt of wrapped printed cloth).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Urban vernaculars: nouchi and camfranglais

An **[[urban vernacular]]** is a variety that young city dwellers build from French and the other
languages around them, often as a badge of belonging. Two are well known. You only need to recognise
them; nobody expects a foreigner to speak them.

- **Nouchi** grew up in the streets of Abidjan in the late twentieth century and is now heard in
  Ivorian music, advertising and the media. Its name is usually explained from Malinké (a word for a
  moustache, the mark of a tough guy). *On s'est enjaillés !* (from English *enjoy*) = We had a great
  time. *Yako !* = Sorry! (sympathy, not apology). *La go* = the girl, the girlfriend.
- **Camfranglais**, in Cameroon's cities, mixes French with English, Cameroon Pidgin English and
  local languages: *Le mbom-là ne pense qu'à tchop* = That guy only thinks about eating (*le mbom* =
  guy, *tchop* = to eat).

Some words travel between them (*la go* is also Cameroonian), so don't pin a word to one country
unless a dictionary does.

## Reading: Sept jours, deux métropoles

Inès Faye wrote this chronicle for an invented travel magazine. Read each paragraph, then its summary.

> **Lundi, Dakar.** Le chauffeur qui m'attend à l'aéroport s'arrête d'abord à une essencerie : « On
> fait le plein, après on est tranquilles », me dit-il en wolof puis en français, sans même s'en
> apercevoir. Première leçon de la semaine : ici, on passe d'une langue à l'autre comme on change de
> file sur l'autoroute. Le français est la langue officielle, celle des panneaux, des journaux et des
> tribunaux ; le wolof, celle de la rue, du marché et des taxis, la langue que la plupart des Dakarois
> ont en commun.

The driver stops at a petrol station and switches from Wolof to French without noticing. French is
the official language of signs, papers and courts; Wolof is the shared language of the street.

> Le soir, mon confrère Mamadou m'emmène dans une dibiterie de son quartier. Autour des grillades de
> mouton, la conversation tourne vite à la cherté de la vie : le riz, le loyer, le transport. Sa mère,
> raconte-t-il, a pu payer la rentrée de ses petits frères grâce à la tontine de sa rue : chaque mois,
> douze femmes versent la même somme, et chaque mois l'une d'elles emporte la cagnotte. « Une banque
> sans guichet ni intérêts », résume-t-il.

Over grilled mutton, talk turns to the cost of living; Mamadou's mother paid for school with her
street's savings club (*la cagnotte* = the pot; *la rentrée* = the start of the school year).

> Mercredi, je prends un taxi-brousse pour Thiès. Sept passagers, des sacs ficelés sur le toit, et un
> voisin en grand boubou bleu qui m'explique qu'il rend visite à son marabout, le maître coranique
> qui a instruit trois générations de sa famille. Nous aurions dû partir à huit heures ; nous partons
> à dix, quand la voiture est enfin pleine. Personne ne s'en plaint : le départ, ici, c'est le moment
> où l'on est au complet.

In a bush taxi to Thiès, a man in a blue boubou is going to see his family's Koranic teacher. The car
leaves two hours late, when it is full, and nobody minds.

> **Jeudi, Abidjan.** Pour traverser la ville, il faut apprendre une autre grammaire, celle des
> transports. Le gbaka, minibus bondé dont l'apprenti crie les destinations à la portière, relie les
> communes ; le woro-woro, taxi collectif à prix fixe, fait les trajets plus courts. Le soir, on dîne
> au maquis, sous les néons, de poisson braisé et d'attiéké.

Abidjan's transport has its own "grammar": the crowded minibus between districts, the shared taxi
for short trips. Dinner is grilled fish and *attiéké* (a cassava semolina) at a maquis (*l'apprenti*
= the conductor; *bondé* = packed).

> Au maquis, il y a toujours un ambianceur : vendredi, c'était Serge, un comptable qui, dès la deuxième
> chanson, avait ambiancé toute la terrasse. Mes voisins de table parlaient un français mêlé de
> nouchi que j'ai mis du temps à suivre ; « On s'est enjaillés ! » m'a lancé l'un d'eux en partant.
> Quand j'ai demandé qui était la jeune femme assise près d'un client, ma voisine a levé les yeux au
> ciel : « Son deuxième bureau. » Le mot fait rire, mais il juge.

An accountant livens up the whole terrace; the neighbours' French is mixed with nouchi. A woman calls
a customer's companion his "deuxième bureau": funny, the journalist notes, but judgemental.

> **Dimanche.** Avant mon départ, mon hôtesse m'a cadeautée : un pagne aux couleurs vives, « pour que
> tu reviennes ». Je rentre avec un carnet plein de mots que mon correcteur d'orthographe souligne en
> rouge et qui sont pourtant du français : un français qui se fabrique ici, présentement, sous nos
> yeux.

Her hostess gives her a bright pagne as a present. Her notebook is full of words her spellchecker
rejects, and which are French all the same, made in Africa now.

Notice *m'a cadeautée*: the direct object *me* is the journalist, a woman, placed before *avoir*,
so the participle agrees, exactly as in *elle m'a remerciée*.

## Dialogue: au maquis

```dialogue
# Au maquis, à Abidjan
Serveuse: Bonsoir ! Vous prenez quoi ? Ce soir, on a du poisson braisé et du poulet.
= Good evening! What will you have? Tonight there's grilled fish and chicken.
Inès: Un poisson braisé avec de l'attiéké, s'il vous plaît.
= A grilled fish with attiéké, please.
Serge: Pareil pour moi. Et mets-nous de la musique, on va ambiancer un peu !
= The same for me. And put some music on for us, we're going to liven things up a bit!
Serveuse: Doucement, il est à peine huit heures. Le DJ n'est pas là présentement : son gbaka est gâté sur la route de Yopougon.
= Easy, it's barely eight o'clock. The DJ isn't here at the moment: his minibus has broken down on the Yopougon road.
Inès: Gâté ? Il a eu un accident ?
= Spoilt? Has he had an accident?
Serge: Non : gâté, ça veut dire en panne. Ici, une voiture gâtée, c'est une voiture qui ne démarre plus.
= No: gâté means broken down. Here a gâtée car is a car that won't start.
Inès: Je note. Et le monsieur du fond, qui chante plus fort que la radio ?
= I'll write that down. And the man at the back, singing louder than the radio?
Serge: C'est notre ambianceur. Sans lui, le maquis serait une cantine.
= That's our party man. Without him, the maquis would be a canteen.
Serveuse: Et c'est lui qui paie la tournée ce soir : il vient de toucher sa tontine !
= And he's buying the round tonight: he's just collected his savings-club pot!
```

## Common mistakes

- **Treating an Africanism as an error.** *Essencerie* and *cherté de la vie* are correct French where
  they are used. In your own formal writing for a French reader, use the France word (*la
  station-service*) or gloss the regional one, as a journalist would.
- **Reading *gâter* or *le maquis* with the France meaning.** *Le moteur est gâté* means it has broken
  down, not that it has gone bad; *aller au maquis* in Abidjan is going out to eat.
- **Pinning a word to one country.** *Présentement* is African and Québec usage; *la go* is Ivorian and
  Cameroonian. Say where a word is *common*, not where it is *exclusive*.
- **Quoting the OIF's 396 million alone.** Give the date and the change of method.
- **Using *le deuxième bureau* as a neutral word.** It is informal and judgemental.

## Key points

- French in Africa is official, co-official or a working language beside national languages and
  lingua francas; Mali (2023), Burkina Faso (2023–2024) and Niger (2025) changed its status.
- **[[Africanisms]]** come from French's own tools: suffixes (*essencerie, dibiterie, ambianceur*),
  conversion (*cadeauter, ambiancer*), new meanings (*gâter, le maquis*), borrowings (*le grin*),
  compounds (*le taxi-brousse*) and metaphors (*le deuxième bureau*).
- Check unfamiliar words in the *Inventaire* or the DDF before calling them mistakes.
- Nouchi and camfranglais are urban vernaculars: recognise them, don't imitate them.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the
lesson. The regional ones are reviewed from French to English only: you need to understand them, not
to produce them.

lessons.title: Bled, kif-kif, darija: French in the Maghreb and languages in contact
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 looked at French beside the languages of sub-Saharan Africa. In the Maghreb (Algeria,
Morocco and Tunisia) French has no official status at all, yet it is everywhere: in universities,
banks, newspapers and the speech of millions of families on both sides of the Mediterranean. And
the contact has gone both ways: the everyday French of France is full of words from Maghrebi Arabic.

This lesson gives you the vocabulary linguists use for what happens when languages meet, the Arabic
words of informal French with their register, and the history behind them told in neutral, factual
terms. Its theme is one family between Marseille and Oran across three generations (invented). The
French-based creoles are honors lesson 16h2's subject.

## Languages of the Maghreb

Four languages share the region, each with its own domains:

- **Standard Arabic** (*l'arabe standard*) is the official language of all three countries: the
  language of the constitution, school textbooks, the mosque and the television news.
- **Darija** (*la darija*) is the spoken Arabic of daily life, different in each country and
  different enough from the standard that the two feel like separate registers or separate
  languages. Its speakers are *arabophones* (Arabic speakers).
- **Amazigh** (*l'amazigh*, often called *le tamazight*; long called "Berber", *le berbère*) is the older
  language of North Africa, spoken today in Kabylia, the Aurès, the Rif, the Atlas and elsewhere.
  Morocco made it an official language in its constitution of 2011 (an organic law on its use
  followed in 2019); Algeria, where it had been a national language since 2002, made it official in
  the constitutional revision of 2016.
- **French** came with colonisation and stayed after independence.

Arabic in the region is the textbook case of **[[diglossia]]** (honors lesson 16h2): a written standard
for formal use and a spoken variety for everything else. French adds a third layer.

![A diagram of the languages of the Maghreb. Four boxes surround a central label "Maghreb": standard Arabic (official texts, school, the mosque, the TV news), darija (home, street, songs, advertising), Amazigh (home in Kabylia, the Rif and the Atlas; official in Morocco since 2011 and Algeria since 2016) and French (universities, business, part of the press). A dashed double arrow between darija and French is marked "alternance codique".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**History in brief.** France conquered Algeria from 1830 and ruled it until 1962; Tunisia (1881–1956)
and Morocco (1912–1956) were protectorates. Algeria's war of independence lasted from 1954 to 1962.
Most of the Europeans of Algeria, *les pieds-noirs* (about a million people), left for France in
1962. *Les harkis* were
Algerians who served as auxiliaries in the French army during the war; some reached France, where
many were housed in camps for years, and thousands who stayed in Algeria were killed in reprisals
(estimates vary widely). *La décolonisation* (B2 honors: the end of colonial rule) was followed by
*l'arabisation*: policies that replaced French with Arabic as the language of schooling and
administration, most thoroughly in Algeria from the 1960s and 1970s. *La langue de scolarisation* (the
language of schooling) is a political choice everywhere in the region.

**French today** (as of November 2026; practice varies, and this is a sketch, not a census). In
Morocco and Tunisia French remains widely used in higher education, above all in science, medicine
and business, and in a large part of the press. In Algeria it is still common in the press and in
business, but governments have promoted Arabic and, recently, English; Algeria is not a member of the
OIF. In Lebanon (one paragraph is enough here) the constitution names Arabic as the official language
and allows a law to set the cases where French is used; many schools and universities teach in
French, others in English.

## Languages in contact

**[[Language contact]]** is what happens when speakers of two or more languages live side by side. It
leaves traces of several kinds:

- A **[[borrowing]]** (*un emprunt*, B1 honors) is a word taken from another language: *le toubib* (C1: doctor)
  and *le bled* came from Maghrebi Arabic.
- A **[[xénisme]]** is a borrowing still felt as foreign: a French newspaper puts *la chorba* (a Maghrebi
  soup) or *le hittiste* in italics and explains it. With time a xénisme may become an ordinary
  borrowing that nobody notices.
- **[[Interference]]** (*l'interférence*) is a feature of one language carried into another: the rolled r
  of some Maghrebi speakers of French, or an English speaker's *je suis chaud* for "I feel hot".
- A **[[substrate]]** (*le substrat*) is an earlier language whose traces survive in the one that replaced
  it: linguists see a Gaulish substrate in French (*le chêne*, *la boue*) and an Amazigh substrate in
  the Arabic of the Maghreb.
- **[[Code-switching]]** (*l'alternance codique*; the English term is also used in French) is switching
  between languages within one conversation, or within one sentence. It is a normal skill of
  bilingual speakers, not a sign that they speak neither language well: they switch for a quotation,
  a joke, a feeling, a word that fits better or to show who they are.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a borrowing settles into French
  accDescr: A foreign word, for example the darija word for a little, first appears in French as a xénisme, in italics and explained, like la chorba. It then becomes an ordinary informal borrowing without italics, like un chouïa. Finally it may become fully integrated and its origin forgotten, like l'algèbre or le sucre, which came from Arabic in the Middle Ages.
  A["A foreign word (darija: a little)"] --> B["Xénisme: in italics, explained (la chorba)"]
  B --> C["Ordinary borrowing, often informal (un chouïa)"]
  C --> D["Fully integrated, origin forgotten (l'algèbre, le sucre)"]
```

## Arabic words in the French of France

Many entered French through soldiers' slang in colonial Algeria, others through the families of the
Maghrebi *diaspora* (the communities living outside the region) and through rap. Almost all are
**informal**: fine with friends, out of place in a formal letter.

| word | meaning | register and origin | neutral French |
|---|---|---|---|
| *le bled* | the back of beyond; "back home" for families from the Maghreb | informal; Maghrebi Arabic *blad*, country, village | *le village, le pays* |
| *kif-kif* | same difference | informal, invariable; Arabic, "like like" | *pareil* |
| *la smala* | a big family, the whole tribe | informal; Arabic, a chief's household and camp | *la famille* |
| *la baraka* | luck, blessing | informal; Arabic, blessing | *la chance* (A2) |
| *le caïd* | the big shot; a gang boss | informal; Arabic, leader | *le chef* |
| *un chouïa* | a tad | informal; Maghrebi Arabic, a little | *un peu* |
| *le clebs* | mutt, dog | informal; Maghrebi Arabic, dog | *le chien* (A1) |
| *maboul, maboule* | nuts, crazy | informal; Arabic | *fou* |
| *le souk* | a souk (market); chaos | the market sense is neutral; *c'est le souk* is informal | *le marché; le désordre* |

*Le toubib* (C1) and *le seum* (C1 honors: frustration, slang) belong to the same family. Older
borrowings from Arabic came through medieval Latin, Italian and Spanish and are no longer felt as borrowings at
all: *l'algèbre, le chiffre, le sucre*.

Some words name things of the Maghreb itself and are neutral: *la médina* (the old walled town), *la
chorba* (a soup of meat, vegetables and spices; also spelt *chorbah* or *chourba*), *le hittiste*
(Algeria: a young unemployed man, usually explained from Algerian Arabic *hit*, wall: the young man
who spends the day leaning against one). *Le pataouète* is the popular French of the pieds-noirs of
Algeria, coloured by Spanish, Italian, Maltese and Arabic; descriptions differ on its exact mix.

## Reading: trois générations, deux rives

A student, Yasmine, interviewed her grandmother and her father for a university project on *la
double culture* (dual culture). This is an extract.

> **Fatiha, 77 ans, née à Oran.** — À l'école, avant 1962, tout se faisait en français ; à la maison,
> c'était la darija. Dans notre rue, il y avait des familles espagnoles qui parlaient pataouète : un
> français plein de mots espagnols, avec un accent qui chantait. Après l'indépendance, les pieds-noirs
> sont partis presque tous la même année. Mes petits frères, eux, ont fait leurs études en arabe :
> l'arabisation était passée par là. Moi, je suis arrivée à Marseille en 1975, avec mon mari et une
> valise. Et puis la smala a suivi, cousin par cousin !

Fatiha went to a French school before independence and spoke darija at home; her Spanish-origin
neighbours spoke pataouète. Her younger brothers were schooled in Arabic after independence. She
came to Marseille in 1975, and the rest of the family followed.

> **Karim, 48 ans, né à Marseille.** — Avec ma mère, je parlais darija ; dehors, français. L'été, on
> partait au bled, et là-bas on me trouvait un accent de Français ! Dans les années 1990, plusieurs de
> mes cousins d'Oran étaient hittistes : diplômés, sans travail, ils passaient la journée adossés au
> mur du quartier. Moi, j'ai eu la baraka : un bon lycée, un premier emploi. Au collège, mes copains
> qui n'avaient aucune famille au Maghreb disaient « kif-kif » et « un chouïa » sans savoir d'où ça
> venait.

Karim spoke darija with his mother and French outside; in Algeria he sounded French. In the 1990s
several cousins were young unemployed graduates; he had luck. His school friends used Arabic words
without knowing their origin (*adossés au mur* = leaning against the wall).

> **Karim.** — Avec mes enfants, j'ai fait l'inverse de ma mère : je leur parlais français, de peur
> qu'ils prennent du retard à l'école. C'est ma mère qui leur a transmis la darija, en cuisinant, en
> racontant des histoires, en les grondant aussi ! Aujourd'hui, je le regrette un peu. On croyait
> qu'il fallait choisir une langue pour réussir ; on sait maintenant qu'un enfant peut en apprendre
> deux, voire trois, sans que l'une chasse l'autre.

With his own children Karim spoke only French, fearing they would fall behind at school; their
grandmother passed on darija. He now regrets it: a child can learn two or three languages without one
pushing out the other.

> **Yasmine, 22 ans.** — Moi, je mélange. Avec ma grand-mère, je commence en français et je finis en
> darija quand je suis émue ; elle me répond « *saha* » quand je lui dis que j'ai réussi un examen. Ma
> mère est kabyle : à la maison, on entendait aussi l'amazigh, et j'apprends à l'écrire. Ce n'est pas
> du « mauvais français », c'est de l'alternance codique : je change de langue pour dire une émotion,
> pour faire rire, pour montrer qui je suis. Mes amis de la fac, qui n'ont aucune famille au Maghreb,
> me demandent même de leur apprendre des mots : la langue de ma grand-mère devient un peu la leur.

Yasmine mixes languages: she ends in darija when moved, and her grandmother says *saha* ("well
done", literally "health") when she passes an exam. Her mother is Kabyle, so Amazigh was heard at
home too. Her university friends ask her to teach them words.

> **Fatiha.** — La double culture, ce n'est pas être à moitié d'ici et à moitié de là-bas. C'est avoir
> deux maisons. Parfois les deux sont pleines, parfois les deux sont vides.

Dual culture, says Fatiha, isn't being half of each: it is having two homes, sometimes both full,
sometimes both empty.

> **Fatiha.** — Quand je rentre au bled, mes nièces trouvent que mon arabe sent Marseille ; à
> Marseille, ma voisine trouve que mon français sent Oran. Au début, ça me vexait. Maintenant, j'en
> ris : c'est la preuve que j'ai vécu des deux côtés.

In Algeria her nieces hear Marseille in her Arabic; in Marseille her neighbour hears Oran in her
French. It used to hurt; now she laughs: it proves she has lived on both shores.

## Dialogue: au marché de Noailles

Yasmine and her father shop at a Marseille market. Darija words are glossed in the translation.

```dialogue
# Au marché, à Marseille
Karim: Il me faut de la coriandre et un chouïa de piment pour la chorba de ce soir.
= I need some coriander and a tad of chilli for tonight's chorba.
Yasmine: Papa, la dernière fois tu en as mis bezzaf, mamie a pleuré !
= Dad, last time you put in loads (bezzaf, darija: a lot), granny cried!
Karim: Elle a pleuré de bonheur. Bon, pour la viande, on va chez Ahmed ou chez le boucher d'en face ?
= She cried with happiness. Right, for the meat, shall we go to Ahmed's or the butcher's opposite?
Yasmine: Kif-kif, les deux sont bons. Mais le samedi, chez Ahmed, c'est le souk.
= Same difference, they're both good. But on Saturdays Ahmed's is chaos.
Karim: Alors on prend celui d'en face. Inch'Allah, ta grand-mère sera contente.
= Then we'll go to the one opposite. God willing, your grandmother will be pleased.
```

Two kinds of switching appear: single words inside a French sentence (*bezzaf*) and a whole formula
(*inch'Allah*, God willing, which many French speakers of every background now use).

## Register in practice

The same news can be told with the loans or without them. A text message from Karim to his brother:

> *La smala débarque samedi, c'est le souk à la maison. Prends un chouïa de pain en plus.*

The family is descending on Saturday, the house is chaos, get a bit more bread. Rewritten for a
formal email to a caterer, every loan goes:

> *Toute la famille sera présente samedi et la maison sera très animée. Pourriez-vous prévoir un peu
> plus de pain ?*

Nothing is lost in meaning, but the first version tells the brother "this is us", and the second
tells the caterer "this is business". Choosing between them is a matter of register, not of correct
and incorrect French.

**Pronunciation.** *Caïd* has two syllables (ca-ïd), and so has *chouïa* (chou-ya); the end of
*clebs* sounds like "kleps", and the final *d* of *bled* is pronounced.

## Common mistakes

- **Using the informal loans in formal writing.** *Le bled*, *kif-kif*, *maboul* and *le clebs* are
  informal. In a report, write *le village d'origine*, *identique*, *fou*, *le chien*.
- **Calling code-switching a lack of French.** It is a skill; describe it as *l'alternance codique*.
- **Confusing darija and standard Arabic.** Darija is the spoken variety; standard Arabic is the
  official, written one.
- **Writing history with loaded words.** Name the facts and the dates (*les pieds-noirs*, *les
  harkis*, 1962) and say where estimates vary.
- **Writing *kif-kifs* or *maboule* for a man.** *Kif-kif* is invariable; *maboul* has the feminine
  *maboule*.

## Key points

- In the Maghreb, standard Arabic is official, darija is spoken, Amazigh is official in Morocco
  (2011) and Algeria (2016), and French has no official status but wide use.
- **[[Language contact]]** leaves **[[borrowings]]**, **[[xénismes]]**, **[[interference]]** and a **[[substrate]]**;
  **[[code-switching]]** is a normal bilingual skill.
- French's Arabic loans (*le bled, kif-kif, la smala, la baraka, le caïd, un chouïa, le clebs, maboul,
  le souk*) are informal; know their neutral equivalents.
- Tell the colonial history with dates and neutral terms.

lesson.

lessons.title: Joual, chiac, magasiner: Québec and Acadian French at C2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 (honors) you met *le dépanneur* (the corner shop), *magasiner* (to go shopping) and *le chum*
(buddy, boyfriend); at C1 (honors) *le char* (the car), *la tuque* (the woolly hat) and *à tantôt*
(see you later). This lesson goes further into the French of North America: how Québec French sounds,
a few points of its spoken grammar, the informal words that a visitor hears in the first hour, the
official terms the province coins, the laws that protect French, and the French of Acadia and
Louisiana. Its theme is an episode of a Montreal podcast and a visit to Moncton (hosts and podcast
invented). Belgium, Switzerland and the debate over one standard are lesson 16's subject.

About nine million people live in Québec, and French is the province's only official language. Québec
has its own standard usage: the news on Radio-Canada, the province's laws and its
novels are written in a French any reader of this course can follow, with some words of its own.
The differences are largest in informal speech.

## How it sounds

Descriptions of Québec pronunciation agree on a few features, found in many speakers (not all, and
more in informal speech):

- **[[Affrication]]**: before the vowels *i* and *u* (and the semivowels that go with them), *t* and *d*
  are pronounced with a little hiss: *tu* sounds like "tsu", *dire* like "dzire", *petit* like
  "p'tsi".
- **Diphthongs:** long vowels in a stressed syllable may glide: *père* can sound close to "paèr",
  *fête* to "faète".
- **Vowel length** still separates words that most speakers in France pronounce alike: *mettre* /
  *maître*, *patte* / *pâte*.
- **Lax vowels:** *i*, *u* and *ou* in a closed syllable are more open: *petite*, *musique*, *route*.

## Spoken grammar

- **Questions with *-tu*:** *Tu viens-tu ?* (Are you coming?), *C'est-tu loin ?* (Is it far?). The
  particle *-tu* marks a yes/no question, whatever the person (C1: recognition).
- ***Là* as a marker:** *Là, j'ai faim, là.* It frames and stresses the statement, much like "now" or
  "you know".
- **Gender of some anglicisms:** *la job*, *la business*, *une game* are common in Québec where France
  says *le job* (or *le boulot*). Usage varies; in formal Québec writing *l'emploi* is the safe word.
- **Address:** *tu* is used much more widely than in France, with colleagues and in shops.

## Words you will hear

| Québec | meaning | France, neutral |
|---|---|---|
| *ma blonde* | my girlfriend | *ma petite amie, ma copine* |
| *capoter* | to freak out (with joy or panic) | *paniquer, s'emballer* |
| *niaiser* | to fool around, to tease | *plaisanter, faire l'idiot* |
| *jaser* | to chat | *bavarder* |
| *achaler* | to bother, to pester | *embêter* |
| *pas pantoute* | not at all | *pas du tout* |
| *une piasse* (or *piastre*) | a dollar, a buck | *un dollar* |
| *dispendieux* | expensive | *cher* |
| *le cellulaire* | the mobile phone | *le portable* (A2) |
| *faire du pouce* | to hitchhike | *faire du stop* |
| *être tanné* | to be fed up | *en avoir assez* |
| *magané* | worn out, battered | *abîmé, épuisé* |
| *le traversier* | the ferry | *le ferry, le bac* |

Most are informal. Three are not: *dispendieux* and *le traversier* are standard in Québec and
appear in newspapers; *le cellulaire* is the ordinary word. *Dispendieux* exists in France too, but is
usually described as formal there. *Jaser* also exists in France with another meaning: to gossip. *Capoter* in
France means to overturn (a car) or to fall through (a deal).

Two institutions: *le cégep* (also written *Cégep* or *CÉGEP*, from *collège d'enseignement général et
professionnel*) is the college between secondary school and university; *la poutine* (chips, or fries,
with cheese curds and gravy) is a dish, now known well beyond Québec.

**The sacres.** A **[[sacre]]** is a Québec swear word built on a word of Catholic worship. The church
words are *le tabernacle, le calice* (chalice), *l'hostie* (the host), *le ciboire* (ciborium) and
*Christ*; the swear words come from them: *tabarnak, câlisse, ostie, ciboire, crisse*. They are among
the strongest words in Québec French, and they show how central the Church was to Québec life until
the 1960s. Learners should recognise them and never use them; the softened forms (*tabarouette,
câline*) are milder but still informal. *Le sacre* also has its standard French meaning: a
coronation.

## Official terms and the OQLF

The *Office québécois de la langue française* (OQLF) studies and proposes French terms, and its
*Grand dictionnaire terminologique* (GDT) records them. A few it also makes official, as a **Québec
official term**: either *un terme normalisé*, whose use is compulsory in the province's administration
and in some documents, or *un terme recommandé*, which is only advised. Most terms in the GDT are
neither: they are simply the ones the OQLF proposes and prefers. Where France often borrows English,
Québec tends to coin: *le clavardage* (online chat, from *clavier* + *bavardage*,
proposed by the OQLF in 1997) and the verb *clavarder*; *l'infolettre* (a newsletter); and three words
from C1 (honors), *le divulgâcheur* (spoiler), *l'égoportrait* (selfie) and *la baladodiffusion*
(podcasting). In France the official recommendation for online chat is *le dialogue en ligne* (2006),
though most people say *le chat* or *le tchat*.

## Laws and history

The *Révolution tranquille* (the Quiet Revolution) of the 1960s took schools, health care and social
services out of the Church's hands and built a modern Québec state; it also made the French language
a political cause. The *Charte de la langue française*, known as *la loi 101*, was sanctioned on 26
August 1977: it made French the language of the state, of work, of business and, for most children, of
school. In 2022 the *Loi sur la langue officielle et commune du Québec, le français* (Bill 96,
sanctioned on 1 June 2022) reformed it and tightened several of its rules.

**[[Joual]]** is the working-class French of Montreal, named after the way *cheval* sounds in it. It
became a literary language with Michel Tremblay's play *Les Belles-sœurs*, first performed at the
Théâtre du Rideau Vert in Montreal on 28 August 1968: a housewife who has won a million trading stamps
invites the women of her family and neighbourhood to help her stick them into booklets, and her
guests, eaten up by envy, end up stealing them. Writing a play in joual caused a scandal; it is now
seen as a turning point in Québec theatre.

## Acadia and Louisiana

*L'Acadie* was the French colony of the Maritimes. In 1755 the British began deporting the Acadians, a
deportation that lasted for years and that Acadians call *le Grand Dérangement*. Some went to
Louisiana, where their descendants are the Cajuns (*Cajun* comes from *Acadien*). Today New Brunswick
is Canada's only officially bilingual province: its first Official Languages Act dates from 18 April
1969. In Moncton many young *Acadiens* speak **[[chiac]]**, a French mixed with English words and
structures. In Louisiana *le cajun* (Cajun French) is supported by the CODOFIL (Council for the
Development of French in Louisiana), created by a state law in 1968.

Three invented lines of chiac, for recognition only:

- *Je vas watcher la game à soir.* — I'm going to watch the game tonight. (*à soir* = *ce soir*)
- *C'était right le fun, mais j'étais tired.* — It was really fun, but I was tired. (*right* = *très*)
- *Anyway, faut que je retourne back chez nous.* — Anyway, I've got to go back home. (*chez nous* =
  home)

```map

title: French in North America
view: fit
point: Montréal | 45.50, -73.57 | Québec
point: Québec | 46.81, -71.21 | Québec
point: Moncton | 46.09, -64.78 | Acadia

point: Lafayette | 30.22, -92.02 | Louisiana
caption: Grand-Pré (Nova Scotia) is one of the places from which Acadians were deported in 1755; Lafayette is the main town of Cajun Louisiana.
```

![A schematic map of French-speaking North America, not to scale. A river runs from the south-west to a gulf in the north-east. Two dots on the river are Montréal (upstream) and Québec City (downstream). A third dot, south of the gulf, is Moncton in New Brunswick. A separate box at the bottom shows Louisiana, with a dot for Lafayette above the Gulf of Mexico.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: Ça jase en ville, épisode 42

This is a written summary of an invented Montreal podcast (*un balado*) for its website.

> Sami ouvre l'épisode en racontant sa fin de semaine : il a fait du pouce jusqu'à Tadoussac avec sa
> blonde, puis ils ont pris le traversier pour franchir le Saguenay. « J'étais magané en revenant,
> mais ça valait la peine », résume-t-il. Mélodie, elle, avoue qu'elle est déjà tannée de l'hiver
> alors qu'il n'a pas encore commencé.

Sami hitchhiked to Tadoussac with his girlfriend and took the ferry; he came back worn out. Mélodie
is already fed up with a winter that hasn't begun.

> Le sujet du jour vient d'un auditeur, Thomas, un Lyonnais installé à Montréal depuis trois mois.
> Quand une collègue lui a dit d'arrêter de niaiser, il a cru qu'elle le traitait d'idiot ; quand une
> autre lui a demandé si son voisin l'achalait encore, il n'a rien compris. « Pas pantoute ! » lui
> a-t-on répondu quand il a demandé si on se moquait de lui. Mélodie rassure Thomas : à Montréal, on
> jase avec tout le monde, et personne ne lui en veut.

A listener from Lyon was puzzled by *niaiser* (he thought he was being called stupid) and *achaler*;
the hosts reassure him that people chat with everyone and nobody is cross with him.

> Deuxième partie : l'argent. Les animateurs comparent ce qu'on peut acheter avec vingt piasses à
> Montréal et à Paris. La poutine reste abordable ; le loyer, lui, est devenu dispendieux, et un
> forfait de cellulaire coûte plus cher qu'en France. Sami raconte qu'au cégep, il vivait avec
> cinquante piasses par semaine et qu'il capotait à chaque facture.

The hosts compare prices: poutine is still cheap, rent has become expensive, and phone plans cost more
than in France; at college Sami lived on fifty dollars a week and panicked at every bill.

> La troisième partie porte sur les mots de l'Office. Mélodie défend le clavardage : « On clavarde
> depuis presque trente ans, alors qu'en France on fait encore du chat ! » Sami, plus sceptique,
> reconnaît pourtant que l'infolettre du balado a plus d'abonnés depuis qu'elle ne s'appelle plus
> *newsletter*.

Mélodie defends the OQLF's *clavardage*; Sami is sceptical but admits that the podcast's newsletter
has more subscribers since it took a French name.

> Dans le courrier des auditeurs, une enseignante de Sherbrooke défend l'accent québécois : « Mes
> élèves disent "tsu" et "dzire" depuis toujours ; ce n'est pas une faute, c'est une prononciation. »
> Sami rappelle que les présentateurs de Radio-Canada parlent un français soigné sans pour autant
> imiter l'accent parisien. Mélodie conclut la séquence par une question qui reviendra dans un
> prochain épisode : à qui appartient la norme ?

A teacher from Sherbrooke defends the Québec accent: her pupils' affricated *tu* and *dire* are a
pronunciation, not a mistake. Radio-Canada's presenters speak careful French without a Paris accent.
Mélodie ends with a question for a later episode: who owns the norm?

> Entre deux rires, les animateurs rappellent d'où vient leur fierté linguistique. Leurs grands-parents
> ont connu le Québec d'avant la Révolution tranquille, où l'on travaillait souvent en anglais dans les
> grandes entreprises de Montréal ; leurs parents ont vu arriver la loi 101. « Nous, on est la
> première génération à trouver normal de tout faire en français », résume Mélodie.

The hosts' grandparents often had to work in English in Montreal's big firms before the Quiet
Revolution; their parents saw loi 101 arrive. Mélodie's generation is the first to find it normal to
do everything in French.

> Enfin, Mélodie revient de Moncton, où elle a enregistré des jeunes Acadiens. Elle a entendu du chiac
> au café, du français soigné à l'université et de l'anglais partout. « Le chiac, ce n'est pas une
> langue qui se perd, c'est une langue qui se défend autrement », conclut-elle. L'épisode se termine
> sur le souvenir du Grand Dérangement, que plusieurs de ses invités ont évoqué sans qu'elle le leur
> demande.

From Moncton, Mélodie brings back chiac in the café, careful French at the university and English
everywhere; for her chiac is a way of holding on to French, not of losing it. Several guests
mentioned the deportation of 1755 unprompted.

## Dialogue: avant l'enregistrement

The hosts talk before recording. The translation shows how informal Québec speech maps onto informal
France speech.

```dialogue
# Au studio, à Montréal
Mélodie: Sami, ton cellulaire sonne encore. Tu peux-tu le fermer ?
= Sami, your phone's ringing again. Can you turn it off?
Sami: C'est ma blonde. Elle capote : j'ai oublié les clés de l'auto chez nous.
= It's my girlfriend. She's freaking out: I left the car keys at home.
Mélodie: C'est pas pantoute surprenant. Bon, on commence-tu ?
= Not one bit surprising. Right, shall we start?
Sami: Deux minutes, là. Je suis encore magané de ma fin de semaine.
= Two minutes, OK? I'm still worn out from my weekend.
Mélodie: Arrête de niaiser, on a trente minutes à remplir !
= Stop fooling around, we've got thirty minutes to fill!
```

Notice *chez nous* (= home, whoever is speaking), *l'auto* (the neutral Québec word; *le char* is
informal) and the two *-tu* questions.

## Common mistakes

- **Using the sacres.** Recognise them; never use them, even as a joke.
- **Hearing *jaser* or *capoter* with the France meaning.** In Québec, *jaser* is to chat, not to
  gossip, and *capoter* is to freak out.
- **Thinking Québec French is old French.** It kept some older words (*la piastre, présentement*), but
  it has changed as much as the French of France, in other directions.
- **Calling chiac "broken French".** It is a contact variety with its own regular patterns.
- **Getting the dates wrong.** Loi 101: 1977; its reform: 2022; Grand Dérangement: from 1755.

## Key points

- Many Québec speakers have **[[affrication]]** (*tu* → "tsu"), diphthongs and long vowels.
- *-tu* questions and *là* are spoken markers; formal Québec writing uses the shared standard.
- Informal words: *capoter, niaiser, jaser, achaler, pantoute, la piasse, être tanné, magané*;
  standard Québec words: *dispendieux, le traversier, le cellulaire, l'infolettre, le clavardage*.
- **[[Joual]]** (Montreal) and **[[chiac]]** (Moncton) are varieties to recognise, and the **[[sacres]]** are
  explained, never used.
- Laws: the Charte de la langue française (1977, reformed 2022); New Brunswick's bilingualism (1969);
  CODOFIL in Louisiana (1968).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the
lesson. The regional ones are reviewed from French to English only.

lessons.title: Un français ou des français ? Belgium, Switzerland and the pluricentric norm
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A1 (honors) you learned *septante* and *nonante*; at B1 (honors) *le kot* (a student room), *la drache*
(a downpour) and *le natel* (a mobile phone); at C1 (honors) *le bourgmestre* (the mayor),
*la votation* (a popular vote), *la tirette* (a zip), *le GSM* (a mobile phone) and *la panosse* (a
floorcloth). This lesson adds the words of student life, the home and the town in Belgium and in
French-speaking Switzerland, and the vocabulary of Swiss direct democracy. Then it asks the question
behind the whole module: is there one correct French, spoken in Paris, or several, each correct in its
own place? Its theme is a debate between a student from Liège, a teacher from Geneva and an editor
from Paris (all invented). Québec was lesson 15's subject, and Africa lesson 13's.

French is one of Belgium's three official languages (with Dutch and German), spoken in Wallonia and
Brussels; in Switzerland it is one of four national languages (with German, Italian and Romansh),
spoken by about a quarter of the population, in *la Suisse romande* (French-speaking Switzerland).

## Belgium: student life, home and town

A Belgian student pays *le minerval* (the tuition fee) at the start of the year, keeps lecture notes
in *une farde* (a folder, a ring binder), goes to *une guindaille* (a student party, informal) on
Thursday night, and shuts herself away for *le blocus*: the weeks of study before the exams, when
nobody goes out. In France *le blocus* is only a blockade, and French students *révisent*.

At home you push down *la clenche* (the door handle or latch; also used in northern France) and cook
*des chicons* (endives; *l'endive* in most of France, though *chicon* is also northern French). The
*navetteur* (feminine *la navetteuse*) is a commuter who takes the train to Brussels every day. In the
town hall, the *bourgmestre* (C1 honors) works with the *échevins* (feminine *l'échevine*): aldermen,
each in charge of one area such as schools or roads, roughly what France calls an *adjoint au maire*.

Belgian administrative French has its own prepositions: *endéans* means "within" a period. A letter
from a commune may say *Veuillez répondre endéans les trente jours* (Please reply within thirty
days); a French administration would write *dans un délai de trente jours*.

## Switzerland: school, home and direct democracy

In the canton of Vaud, teenagers go to *le gymnase* (upper secondary school; elsewhere a gym, and in
Geneva the same school is *le collège*) and finish with *la maturité* (the school-leaving exam,
informally *la matu*; also "maturity" in general). At home they leave *du cheni* (clutter, a mess:
informal; also spelt *chenit*) in their rooms until a parent announces *la poutze* (a big clean,
informal, from German *putzen*: *faire la poutze*). At the supermarket the cashier offers you *un
cornet*: a paper or plastic carrier bag (elsewhere *un cornet* is a cone, for chips or ice cream).

![Four objects drawn as picture cards, numbered: a ring binder with papers, a door handle on a door, a long white and yellow endive, and a plastic carrier bag with handles.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Switzerland is a federation of twenty-six *cantons*, each with its own constitution, parliament and
schools; *cantonal* (feminine *cantonale*, plural *cantonaux*) describes what belongs to a canton:
*les impôts cantonaux*, *une école cantonale*. Citizens vote several times a year (*la votation*, C1
honors). With *une initiative populaire* (a popular initiative), 100,000 citizens can sign to put a
change to the federal constitution to the vote, if they collect the signatures within eighteen
months. *Romand* (feminine *romande*) means French-speaking Swiss: *la presse romande, les cantons
romands*.

| France | Belgium | Switzerland |
|---|---|---|
| *les frais d'inscription* | *le minerval* | *les taxes d'études* |
| *le classeur, la chemise* | *la farde* | *le classeur* |
| *les révisions* | *le blocus* | *les révisions* |
| *le sac (de caisse)* | *le sac* | *le cornet* |
| *l'adjoint au maire* | *l'échevin* | *le conseiller municipal* (varies by canton) |

## One norm or several?

For centuries, "good French" meant the French of Paris, described by the Académie française, the
grammarians and the dictionaries published in France (honors lesson 04h2). Everything else was a
*régionalisme*, a word to avoid. Linguists today describe French differently.

- A **[[regionalism]]** (*un régionalisme*) is a word, meaning or construction typical of one region:
  *septante* in Belgium, *le cornet* in Switzerland, *présentement* in Africa and Québec. France has
  regionalisms too: the floorcloth that most of France calls *la serpillière* is *la wassingue* in
  the north, as it is *la loque* in Belgium and *la panosse* in Switzerland.
- A **[[variety]]** (*une variété*) is any form of a language shared by a group: Belgian French, Québec
  French, the French of Dakar. The word is neutral: it doesn't say "dialect" or "mistake".
- A **[[pluricentric language]]** (*une langue pluricentrique*) has several standard centres, each with
  its own norms, dictionaries and institutions: English (Britain, the United States, Australia),
  German (Germany, Austria, Switzerland), and, more and more, French.
- An **[[endogenous norm]]** (*une norme endogène*) is a standard set from inside a community, by its own
  writers, media and schools; an **[[exogenous]]** one (*exogène*) is imported from outside. Québec,
  with the OQLF and its own dictionary Usito, is often described as having gone furthest towards
  an endogenous norm.
- **[[Reference French]]** (*le français de référence*) is the written standard shared by all: the
  French of international news, of treaties, of this course. A Belgian, a Swiss and a Senegalese
  journalist all write it, and each adds a few words of their own.

![Two diagrams side by side. On the left, "one centre": Paris in the middle, with arrows pointing out to Brussels, Geneva, Montréal and Dakar. On the right, "several centres": Paris, Brussels, Geneva, Montréal and Dakar as equal circles, each linked to a shared ring in the middle labelled "français de référence".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**[[Linguistic insecurity]]** (*l'insécurité linguistique*) is speakers' feeling that their own French is
not "good" French: the Belgian who apologises for *septante*, the Québécois who switches accent in
Paris. It has been studied in Belgium (notably by the Louvain linguist Michel Francard) and in
Québec, among other places. Its harsher cousin is **[[glottophobia]]** (*la glottophobie*): prejudice or
discrimination against people because of their accent or the way they speak, at school, in a job
interview or on television. The sociolinguist Philippe Blanchet proposed the term and set it out in
*Discriminations : combattre la glottophobie* (2016).

Two facts show that the centres don't always follow Paris. **The feminisation of job titles** came
earlier outside France: Québec from 1979 (*la professeure, l'auteure*), the Fédération
Wallonie-Bruxelles with a decree of 21 June 1993, Swiss administrations gradually in the 1980s and
1990s. France followed with government circulars, and the Académie française accepted the principle
only in a report of 2019. And since March 2021 the *Dictionnaire des francophones* (DDF) has put
the words of every country side by side, without marking any of them as the norm.

## Reading: Le bon français n'habite pas à Paris

An opinion piece by an invented Brussels columnist, Aline Dewez.

> On m'a appris, à l'école, à me méfier de ma propre langue. Un professeur soulignait en rouge
> « endéans » dans nos copies ; ma grand-mère, qui disait « endéans la semaine », passait à ses yeux
> pour une paysanne. J'ai mis vingt ans à comprendre que ma grand-mère parlait un français
> parfaitement correct, simplement belge.

The columnist was taught at school to distrust her own French; it took her twenty years to see that
her grandmother's Belgian French was perfectly correct.

> Les linguistes ont un nom pour ce malaise : l'insécurité linguistique. Elle est le fruit d'une
> idée ancienne, selon laquelle le bon français serait celui d'une ville, d'une classe et d'une
> époque. Or le français est aujourd'hui une langue pluricentrique : il a plusieurs centres, comme
> l'anglais ou l'allemand, et la majorité de ses locuteurs vivent hors d'Europe.

Linguists call this unease linguistic insecurity, the product of an old idea that good French belongs
to one city and one class. French now has several centres, and most of its speakers live outside
Europe.

> Faut-il pour autant renoncer à toute norme ? Évidemment pas. Une lettre administrative, un article
> de presse, un traité doivent pouvoir être lus de Bruxelles à Dakar ; c'est le rôle du français de
> référence. Mais une norme commune n'exige pas l'effacement des variétés. Le Suisse qui demande un
> cornet à la caisse ne commet pas de faute : il parle le français de Lausanne, comme le Parisien
> parle celui de Paris.

A shared standard is still needed for documents read across the francophone world, but it doesn't
require erasing the varieties: a Swiss asking for a *cornet* makes no mistake.

> L'histoire récente montre d'ailleurs que les centres ne suivent pas toujours Paris. Le Québec a
> féminisé les noms de métiers dès 1979, la Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles en 1993 ; l'Académie
> française n'a accepté le principe qu'en 2019. Et depuis 2021, le Dictionnaire des francophones range
> côte à côte les mots de Kinshasa, de Lausanne et de Lyon, sans décréter lequel est le bon.

The centres don't always follow Paris: Québec and Belgium feminised job titles long before the
Académie accepted it, and the DDF puts every country's words side by side without choosing.

> Qu'on me comprenne bien : je ne plaide pas pour que chacun écrive comme il parle. Je plaide pour
> qu'on cesse de corriger, chez les uns, ce qu'on trouve charmant chez les autres. Un élève de Namur
> qui écrit « endéans » dans une lettre administrative ne commet pas plus de faute qu'un Lyonnais qui
> écrit « dans un délai de » : chacun emploie le français de son administration.

She is not asking everyone to write as they speak, only that people stop correcting in some what
they find charming in others (*plaider pour* = to argue for): a pupil from Namur writing *endéans*
makes no more of a mistake than someone from Lyon writing *dans un délai de*.

> Reste un dernier obstacle, plus sournois : la glottophobie. On ne refuse pas un poste à quelqu'un
> parce qu'il dit chicon plutôt qu'endive, mais on sourit de son accent, on le trouve « sympathique »
> plutôt que « compétent ». Tant que les présentateurs des journaux télévisés auront tous le même
> accent, le message restera clair : il y a un français qui compte et des français qui amusent.

The last obstacle is glottophobia: people are not refused jobs for a word, but they are smiled at
for an accent, found "nice" rather than "competent" (*sournois* = insidious). While every news
presenter has the same accent, the message stays the same.

> Le jour où un étudiant de Liège pourra dire guindaille à la radio nationale française sans qu'on lui
> demande de traduire, nous saurons que le français est devenu ce qu'il prétend être : la langue de
> tous ceux qui la parlent.

When a Liège student can say *guindaille* on French national radio without being asked to translate,
French will have become what it claims to be: the language of all who speak it.

## Dialogue: le débat

```dialogue
# Un débat radiophonique
Manon (Liège): Quand je dis que je suis en blocus, mes amis français croient que je manifeste !
= When I say I'm in my study period, my French friends think I'm on a protest!
Claire (Paris): C'est bien le problème : un même mot, deux sens. Pour publier un livre lu partout, il faut une norme commune.
= That's exactly the problem: one word, two meanings. To publish a book read everywhere, you need a common standard.
Luc (Genève): Une norme commune, oui, mais pas forcément parisienne. Mes élèves écrivent un excellent français et disent quand même cornet.
= A common standard, yes, but not necessarily a Parisian one. My pupils write excellent French and still say cornet.
Claire (Paris): Je ne dis pas le contraire. Dans un roman, j'aime qu'on entende Genève. Dans un manuel, je préfère le français de référence.
= I'm not saying otherwise. In a novel I like to hear Geneva. In a textbook I prefer reference French.
Manon (Liège): Alors on est d'accord : la norme, c'est une question de lecteur, pas de capitale.
= Then we agree: the standard is a question of the reader, not of the capital.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Calling a regionalism a mistake.** *Endéans*, *le minerval* and *le cornet* are correct where they
  are used. Choose by your reader: in a text for France, use or gloss the France word.
- **Thinking France has no regionalisms.** Every variety has them; Paris French is one variety among
  others.
- **Mixing up *endogène* and *exogène*.** *Endo-* = inside, *exo-* = outside.
- **Writing *cantonals*.** The masculine plural is *cantonaux*.
- **Assuming one word, one country.** *Le chicon* is Belgian and northern French; *la tirette* is
  Belgian and Swiss. Say where a word is common.

## Key points

- Belgian words: *le minerval, la farde, la guindaille, le blocus, la clenche, le chicon, le
  navetteur, l'échevin, endéans*; Swiss words: *le gymnase, la maturité, le cheni, la poutze, le
  cornet, romand*; Swiss democracy: *le canton, cantonal, l'initiative populaire*.
- French is a **[[pluricentric language]]**: several centres share **[[reference French]]**, and each has
  its own **[[regionalisms]]** and, increasingly, an **[[endogenous norm]]**.
- **[[Linguistic insecurity]]** is the speaker's own doubt; **[[glottophobia]]** (Blanchet, 2016) is other
  people's prejudice.
- Québec (1979) and Belgium (1993) feminised job titles before France; the DDF (2021) treats every
  variety alike.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the
lesson. The Belgian and Swiss words are reviewed from French to English only.

lessons.title: Les Soleils des indépendances: Kourouma and the Malinké novel
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 showed how African French makes words of its own. This lesson shows a novelist who made a
whole style of it. Ahmadou Kourouma's *Les Soleils des indépendances* (1968) tells the fall of a
Malinké prince in a West African country after independence, in a French that carries the images,
proverbs and rhythms of Malinké. At B2 (honors) you met *la négritude*, the movement of Senghor and
Césaire, who wrote in a classical, even solemn French; Kourouma, a generation later, chose to bend
French instead. You'll learn the facts about the author and his two best-known novels, a retelling of
the first, and how to describe his style. Everything below is retold or described: no line of either
novel is quoted.

## The author

Ahmadou Kourouma was born in 1927 in the north of Côte d'Ivoire (sources give Boundiali or the
nearby village of Togobala) into a Malinké family; *le malinké* is both the people and their
language, one of the Mande languages. He served in the French colonial army in Indochina in the early
1950s, studied in Lyon, and worked as an actuary for banks and insurance companies. After
independence he was briefly imprisoned in Côte d'Ivoire, and he spent long years abroad, in Algeria,
Cameroon and Togo. He died in Lyon on 11 December 2003.

```timeline
title: Ahmadou Kourouma (1927-2003)
event: 1927 | Born in the north of Côte d'Ivoire
event: 1950-1954 | Serves with the French army in Indochina
event: 1960 | Côte d'Ivoire becomes independent
event: 1968 | Les Soleils des indépendances published in Montréal
event: 1970 | Le Seuil publishes the novel in Paris
event: 1990 | Monnè, outrages et défis
event: 1998 | En attendant le vote des bêtes sauvages
event: 2000 | Allah n'est pas obligé: prix Renaudot and Goncourt des lycéens
event: 11 December 2003 | Dies in Lyon
caption: Dates from encyclopaedia entries; the novels after 1970 were all published by Le Seuil.
```

The first novel's history is part of its legend. In the usual account, French publishers turned the
manuscript down; it won
a prize from the Montréal journal *Études françaises* and appeared in 1968 from the Presses de
l'Université de Montréal. Le Seuil took it up in 1970, and it has been read in France ever since.

## The story, retold

Fama Doumbouya is the last heir of the Doumbouya, the princely *dynastie* (dynasty) of the
Horodougou, whose capital is the village of Togobala. Colonisation took away his family's power, and
he fought the *colons* (the colonial settlers) in the hope that independence would give it back.
Independence gives him nothing. The new state is run by *le parti unique* (the single party), the
*chefferie* (chieftaincy) has lost its meaning, and Fama, ruined, lives in the capital by attending
funerals, where the gifts handed out to mourners keep him alive. His wife Salimata sells food at the
market. They have no children; Salimata is blamed and tries every remedy, prayer and *fétiche*
(charm), though the novel lets the reader suspect that the *stérilité* (infertility) is Fama's.

When his cousin Lacina, who had become chief of Togobala, dies, Fama goes back to the village for the
funeral rites. He finds a place in decay, and he inherits, as custom requires, one of his cousin's
widows, the young Mariam. Back in the capital, the two wives quarrel; Fama is drawn into the
discontent against the regime, arrested, tried and sent to prison. Freed with other prisoners when
the president decides on a show of reconciliation, he leaves for the north, tries to cross a border
that has been closed, and is fatally wounded. He dies on the way to Togobala, and with him, the
novel suggests, the dynasty.

## Malinkéisation

Critics call Kourouma's style the **[[malinkéisation]]** of French: Malinké ways of saying carried into
French words. It takes a few recognisable forms. The examples below are invented to show the kind of
thing; they are not Kourouma's sentences.

- **Words with a Malinké range of meaning.** The title is the clearest case: *soleil* stands for a
  day and, by extension, an era, so *les soleils des indépendances* are "the days" or "the age" of
  independence, not suns.
- **Images and proverbs as argument.** The narrator explains events with sayings, in the manner of an
  oral storyteller. An invented example: *le fleuve ne remonte pas vers sa source* (the river doesn't
  flow back to its source), to say that the past won't return.
- **A narrator who talks to the listener.** Comments, questions and asides break into the story, as
  in the *oralité* (B2 honors: oral tradition) of the griot: *Vous croyez que Fama s'est tu ? Pas du
  tout.*
- **Bold syntax.** Inversions, repetitions and comparisons drawn from village life, mixed with a crude
  humour that Paris novels of the 1960s rarely allowed.

The effect is a French that a reader from Paris understands, but in which he keeps hearing another
language. Critics describe this as **[[hybridity]]** (*l'hybridité*): a text that belongs fully to
neither culture and draws its force from both.

### Example 1: describing a sentence

Take this invented sentence in the manner of the novel: *Trois soleils plus tard, le village s'était
couché sans dire un mot, comme une vieille qui n'a plus de dents pour se plaindre.*

1. *Trois soleils plus tard*: *soleil* in the sense of "day", a transposed meaning.
2. *le village s'était couché*: a concrete verb for an abstract event (the village fell silent).
3. *comme une vieille qui n'a plus de dents*: a comparison taken from daily life, humorous and harsh
   at once.

A commentary would say: *La phrase transpose en français une image et un sens malinkés (le soleil
pour le jour) et emprunte à l'oralité sa comparaison familière.* — The sentence transposes into
French a Malinké image and meaning, and borrows its homely comparison from oral tradition.

### Example 2: the same event in reference French

The same moment in neutral reference French: *Trois jours plus tard, le village se tut.* Nothing is
wrong with it, and nothing is left of the voice. Comparing the two versions is the quickest way to
show, in an exam commentary, what Kourouma's French does: it doesn't break the rules of French so much
as fill French with another way of seeing.

## Allah n'est pas obligé

Kourouma's last completed novel, *Allah n'est pas obligé* (2000), won the prix Renaudot and the
Goncourt des lycéens the same year. Its narrator, Birahima, is a boy from Côte d'Ivoire who becomes
*un enfant-soldat* (a child soldier) in the civil wars of Liberia and Sierra Leone. He tells his story
in a mix of street French, Malinké words and borrowed swear words, and he explains difficult words as
he goes by looking them up in four dictionaries he carries: two French ones, the *Inventaire des
particularités lexicales du français en Afrique noire* and an English–French dictionary. The joke is
serious: the reader sees the boy building his own French between several norms, as the whole
francophone world does.

## The politics of writing in French

After independence, *l'africanisation* (Africanisation) meant replacing colonial staff and models
with African ones, in administration as in culture. For writers, the question was which language to
use. Some argued for writing in African languages; Kourouma wrote in French, but a French he had made
answer to Malinké thought. Readers then and now disagree on what that choice means: a conquest of the
colonial language, a compromise with it, or simply the language of a multilingual writer.

## Common mistakes

- **Quoting the novel from memory.** Retell and describe it; famous lines are easily misremembered.
- **Calling Kourouma's French "incorrect".** It is a deliberate style; describe its procedures.
- **Reading *soleil* literally in the title.** It means days, an era.
- **Confusing Kourouma with the Negritude poets.** They wrote a classical French; he transformed
  French from within.
- **Forgetting the dates:** 1968 in Montréal, 1970 at Le Seuil; *Allah n'est pas obligé*, 2000.

## Key points

- Kourouma (1927–2003), Ivorian, Malinké; *Les Soleils des indépendances* (Montréal 1968, Le Seuil
  1970); *Allah n'est pas obligé* (2000, Renaudot and Goncourt des lycéens).
- Fama, last of a *dynastie*, is ruined by independence, the *parti unique* and the end of the
  *chefferie*; his childless marriage mirrors the end of his line.
- **[[Malinkéisation]]**: Malinké meanings, images, proverbs and an oral narrator carried into French.
- **[[Hybridity]]** names a text that draws on two cultures at once.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the
lesson.

lessons.title: Les créoles à base française: French-based creoles
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 (honors) you met the word *le créole*. This lesson explains what a creole is: not a dialect of French,
not "broken French", but a language of its own that took most of its words from French and built a
grammar that French doesn't have. More than ten million people speak a French-based creole, most of
them in Haiti. You'll see where these languages are spoken and what status they have, how they arose, a
few of their structures (for recognition only), the relationship between creole and French, and the
ideas of *créolité* and *créolisation* that Caribbean writers made famous. Africa and the Maghreb were
lessons 13 and 14; this lesson stays in the Caribbean and the Indian Ocean.

## What a creole is

A **[[pidgin]]** (*un pidgin*) is a simplified contact language that people who share no language build
to trade or work together; nobody speaks it as a first language. A **[[creole]]** is a language born in
such a contact situation that has become the first language of a community, with a full grammar and
vocabulary. In the classic account, children growing up with a pidgin turned it into a creole; many
linguists now think creoles often formed faster and without a stable pidgin stage, and the question is
still debated.

The language that supplies most of a creole's words is its **[[lexifier]]** (*la langue lexificatrice*).
For the creoles of this lesson it is French, more precisely the popular and regional French of the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries spoken by sailors, settlers and overseers. The grammar, however,
is new: it owes something to the African languages of the enslaved and much to the contact itself.
That is why a French speaker recognises many words in a Haitian sentence but can't follow it.

## Where they are spoken

| place | creole | status (as of November 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Haiti | Haitian Creole (*kreyòl*) | official with French under article 5 of the 1987 constitution; spoken by nearly everyone, while far fewer people are fluent in French |
| Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana | Antillean and Guianese creoles | French overseas departments: French is the only official language; the creoles count among the regional languages of France and are taught in some schools |
| Réunion | Réunion Creole | as above |
| Mauritius | Kreol Morisien | the most widely spoken language; English and French dominate official use; in August 2026 the National Assembly set up a select committee to study introducing it in parliament |
| Seychelles | Seselwa | one of three national languages, with English and French (constitution of 1993) |
| Louisiana | Louisiana Creole | a small and endangered community language, distinct from Cajun French (lesson 15) |

A person who speaks a creole is *créolophone* (Creole-speaking; also a noun: *les créolophones*).

```map
base: world
title: Some French-based creoles
view: fit
point: Haiti (Port-au-Prince) | 18.54, -72.34 | Caribbean
point: Guadeloupe | 16.24, -61.53 | Caribbean
point: Martinique | 14.64, -61.02 | Caribbean
point: French Guiana (Cayenne) | 4.92, -52.31 | South America
point: Réunion | -20.88, 55.45 | Indian Ocean
point: Mauritius | -20.16, 57.50 | Indian Ocean
point: Seychelles | -4.62, 55.45 | Indian Ocean
point: Louisiana (Lafayette) | 30.22, -92.02 | North America
caption: Each point marks a place where a French-based creole is spoken; the creoles are separate languages, not one.
```

## How they arose

These creoles were born on the **plantation** (*la plantation*) of the colonial sugar and coffee
economy, between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. Enslaved Africans, brought from many
regions and speaking many languages, were made to work under French-speaking masters and overseers.
*L'esclavage* (slavery; the noun is masculine) shaped the language as it shaped everything else: the
creole was the language of the fields and of the enslaved community, French the language of power.

Resistance took many forms, among them *le marronnage* (marronage): escape from the plantation, by
individuals for a few days or by whole communities who founded free villages in the hills and forests.
Slavery was first abolished by the Revolution in 1794, restored by Bonaparte in 1802, and abolished
for good in the French colonies by the decree of 27 April 1848; that *abolition* is commemorated
every year in each overseas department, each on its own date. Haiti had freed itself earlier: its revolution led to
independence in 1804.

## A few structures (recognition only)

The examples are invented for this lesson. Haitian Creole spelling is phonetic (*ò* is an open o, *è*
an open e; *m* is a short form of *mwen*, I).

![A chart of three features of Haitian Creole, each with a French word above it. Row one: French "le livre" above Haitian "liv la", with the article after the noun highlighted, and "les livres" above "liv yo". Row two: three sentences with a marker before the verb: "m ap manje" (I am eating), "m te manje" (I had eaten), "m pral manje" (I am going to eat). Row three: the word "lakou", from French "la cour", with the old article fused into the noun.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- **The determiner comes after the noun.** *liv la* = the book; *liv yo* = the books; *yon liv* = a
  book (the indefinite stays in front).
- **Tense and aspect are marked by small words before an unchanging verb.** *Timoun yo ap jwe.* = The
  children are playing. *Manman m te achte yon liv.* = My mother had bought (or bought) a book. *Nou
  pral wè frè li.* = We're going to see his brother. The verb *manje* (to eat) never changes.
- **French articles fused into nouns.** *lakou* (yard, from *la cour*), *lekòl* (school, from *l'école*):
  the creole took the French article as part of the word.

The Antillean creoles work in a similar way with other markers: in Martinique *Man ka manjé* is "I'm
eating" and *Man ké manjé* "I'll eat".

### Example 1: decoding a sentence

*Pitit li yo te jwe nan lakou lekòl la.*

1. Find the nouns and their determiners: *pitit li yo* (her/his children: *pitit* = child, *li* = his
   or her, *yo* = plural); *lakou lekòl la* (the school yard).
2. Find the marker before the verb: *te* = anterior (past).
3. Put it together: *Ses enfants avaient joué (ou ont joué) dans la cour de l'école.* — Her (or his)
   children had played (or played) in the school yard.

The French words are all there (*petit, la cour, l'école*), but the order of the parts and the way
time is marked are not French: the lexifier gave the words, not the grammar.

## Creole and French: diglossia

**[[Diglossia]]** (*la diglossie*) is a situation in which two varieties share a society with different
roles: a "high" one for writing, school, law and formal speech, and a "low" one for home, friends and
daily life. The term was made famous by the American linguist Charles Ferguson in 1959, and Haiti was
one of his examples, with French high and Creole low. The same pattern held in the Antilles and
Réunion. It has been shifting for decades: Creole is now heard in Haiti's parliament and courts, on
radio and in schools, and novels, newspapers and dictionaries are written in it. Many speakers still
feel that serious things are said in French, a form of the linguistic insecurity you met in lesson 16.

### Example 2: reading a situation

A Martinican teacher speaks French in class and Creole with colleagues in the staffroom; her pupils
answer in French but joke in Creole. Described as a linguist would: *une situation de diglossie : le
français occupe les fonctions formelles, le créole les fonctions familières, et l'alternance codique
(leçon 14) est constante.* — a diglossic situation: French fills the formal roles, Creole the
informal ones, and code-switching (lesson 14) is constant.

## Créolité and créolisation

In 1989 three Martinican writers, Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau and Raphaël Confiant, published
*Éloge de la créolité*, a manifesto. Against the idea that Caribbean identity was French (assimilation)
or only African (as some read Negritude, B2 honors), they defined it as **[[créolité]]**: an identity made
of African, European, Asian and Amerindian elements mixed in the plantation world, with the creole
language at its centre. Chamoiseau's novel *Texaco* won the prix Goncourt in 1992.

The Martinican poet and thinker Édouard Glissant (1928–2011) preferred **[[créolisation]]**: the open,
never finished process by which cultures in contact produce something nobody could have predicted.
For Glissant the Caribbean was a laboratory of what was happening to the whole world. *Créolité* names
an identity; *créolisation* names a process.

## Common mistakes

- **Calling a creole a dialect of French.** It is a separate language with French as its lexifier.
- **Thinking there is one creole.** Haitian, Martinican, Réunion and Mauritian creoles are different
  languages; speakers of two of them may understand each other only in part.
- **Confusing pidgin and creole.** A pidgin has no native speakers; a creole does.
- **Mixing up *créolité* and *créolisation*.** The first is an identity (Bernabé, Chamoiseau, Confiant,
  1989); the second a process (Glissant).
- **Giving 1848 as the only date.** Slavery was abolished in 1794, restored in 1802 and abolished
  again in 1848.

## Key points

- A **[[creole]]** is a full language born of contact; French is the **[[lexifier]]** of the creoles of Haiti,
  the Antilles, Guiana, Réunion, Mauritius, the Seychelles and Louisiana.
- They arose on the **plantation** under slavery; *le marronnage* was one form of resistance;
  abolition came in 1848.
- Haitian Creole puts the determiner after the noun (*liv la*) and marks tense before the verb (*te,
  ap, pral*).
- **[[Diglossia]]** gave French the high roles and creole the low ones; the balance is shifting.
- **[[Créolité]]** (1989) is an identity; **[[créolisation]]** (Glissant) a process.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the
lesson.

lessons.title: Lire un dossier de 2 000 mots: selection, problématique and personal input
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C1 you wrote a synthèse: several documents condensed into one neutral text, with no opinion
and nothing from outside. The DALF C2 asks for the opposite gesture. You read a long dossier, and
then you *take sides*, in a genre the subject sets (an article, an éditorial, a report, a
speech), using the documents *and* what you know yourself. This lesson is about the reading and
the thinking that come before the writing: surveying a dossier fast, judging its sources, finding
a problématique, choosing what to keep and planning. Lessons 18 to 20 then teach the four genres.
The theme is the right to repair.

## The written paper in brief

The **[[DALF C2 written paper]]** (*compréhension et production écrites*), as FEI's sample papers
and the national certification registry describe it: 3 h 30; a **[[dossier]]** of about 2,000 words
(seven or eight documents in the samples); *two subjects*, of which you treat *one*; a
structured text of *at least 700 words* in the genre the subject names; a monolingual French
dictionary allowed. The paper is marked out of 50, and you need at least 10 of them. Check FEI's
current pages and your centre's instructions before the exam: formats change, and the paper's
own instructions always win over this course.

The registry describes what the paper looks for, which we can summarise: read long documents from
varied sources quickly, pick out what serves the problem you have chosen, link it to your own
contributions, and write a long, organised text whose tone is *committed* and whose line of
argument holds from start to finish.

| | C1 synthèse | C2 production écrite |
|---|---|---|
| your opinion | none | required, clear and argued |
| outside knowledge | forbidden | expected (*apports personnels*) |
| documents | all of them, faithfully | the useful ones, selected |
| form | a neutral text | a set genre with an addressee |
| length | 200–240 words | at least 700 words |

## Reading 2,000 words in fifty minutes

Read a 2,000-word dossier in three passes, each with its own purpose.

1. **[[Survol]]** (skimming): *survolez* the paratext only: titles, *chapôs*, sources, dates, authors,
   captions, the *légende* of an infographic. In ten minutes you know who speaks, where, when and
   roughly in favour of what. The subjects are already in your head: read them first.
2. **[[Balayage]]** (scanning): run your eyes over the documents looking only for what your subject
   needs: a figure, a date, an argument against.
3. **Repérage** (spotting) with a pencil: underline, number the arguments in the margin, write
   *+*, *−* or *?* beside each, and the subject's letter (A, B) beside what serves it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Working through a DALF C2 dossier
  accDescr: Read the two subjects first, then survey the paratext of the dossier, choose one subject, scan and spot what it needs, set a problématique and a line, select and rank, plan with personal input, write in the genre, then reread and count.
  A["Read the two subjects"] --> B["Survol: paratext only"]
  B --> C["Choose one subject"]
  C --> D["Balayage and repérage"]
  D --> E["Problématique and line"]
  E --> F["Select and rank, set aside"]
```
