lessons.title: Le DALF C2: the exam and a course review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson of the French course explains what C2 means, describes the **[[DALF C2]]**
and how it is marked, gives a strategy for each paper, reviews the course, and suggests how to
keep your French at this level afterwards. The two honors lessons that follow are full mock
papers.

## What C2 means

**[[CEFR C2]]** is the higher of the two "proficient user" levels (*utilisateur expérimenté*, C1) of
the CEFR, *le CECRL* in French (*Cadre européen commun de référence pour les langues*). In our
words, the global scale describes a C2 user who understands with ease almost everything they
hear or read, who can draw on several spoken and written sources and rebuild their arguments
into one coherent account, and who expresses themselves spontaneously, fluently and precisely,
telling apart fine shades of meaning even on complex subjects.

The Council of Europe's Companion Volume (2020) breaks this down into scales, each made of
**[[descriptors]]** (*les descripteurs*): short statements of what a learner can do at each level.
A set of descriptors used as a standard is *un référentiel* (a framework of standards; also a
benchmark). The rows that matter most for this course, summarised:

- **range and control:** a very wide vocabulary, idioms and colloquial language with their
  connotations, and word choice that is consistently right: *la justesse* (accuracy, the right
  word in the right place) more than rare words;
- **precision and flexibility:** fine shades of meaning, qualifiers, no ambiguity, and the
  ability to reformulate for emphasis or for another listener (modules 1 and 2);
- **long texts and talks:** structured, flowing, in the style the reader or listener expects,
  with the writer's own view clearly separated from the sources' (modules 5 and 6);
- **sociolinguistic appropriateness:** almost every social and cultural implication of what is
  said, and the language to persuade and negotiate (modules 1 and 4);
- **mediation:** passing meaning on between texts and people (below).

**[[Mediation]]** (*la médiation*, as a CEFR activity) is the work of making a text or an exchange
accessible to someone else: summarising several sources into one account, explaining what a
speaker implies, or what irony or understatement does in a text. The DALF C2's compte rendu of a
recording and its writing from a dossier are both mediation. (*La médiation* is also mediation in
a dispute, and *le médiateur* (B2) the mediator.)

C2 is not "native". A **[[near-native]]** speaker (*quasi natif*; the native speaker is *le
locuteur natif*) is one whose French a listener takes for a native's for a long stretch. The
Companion Volume describes C2 without making the native speaker its yardstick, and plenty of
natives would not meet every C2 descriptor. What C2 asks for is *l'idiomaticité*
(idiomaticity): language that is *idiomatique*, made of the *locutions figées* (set phrases)
and collocations a native would choose, used precisely.

## The DALF C2

The DALF (*Diplôme approfondi de langue française*) C2 is a diploma of the French Ministry of
Education; France Éducation international (FEI) designs the papers. Each level of the DELF and
DALF is a separate diploma, valid for life. What follows comes from FEI's sample papers, the
national certification registry (France Compétences) and an exam centre's information sheet
(CEL, académie de Nancy-Metz, March 2023). FEI's pages and the candidate's manual are the final
word: check them before you register.

| paper | time | points | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Compréhension et production orales* (individual) | about 1 h of preparation, then about 30 min with the jury | 50 | a long recording (about 15 minutes in the sample paper), heard twice; a compte rendu, an argued point of view, a debate (lessons 21–23) |
| *Compréhension et production écrites* (collective) | 3 h 30 | 50 | a dossier of about 2,000 words; two subjects, you treat one; one structured text of at least 700 words (article, éditorial, rapport, discours …: lessons 17–20) |

The written paper is an *épreuve collective* (C1), sat in a room with other candidates; the oral
is an *épreuve individuelle* (C1). The sample papers allow a monolingual French dictionary
(*dictionnaire unilingue*, C1). *La passation* is the sitting of a test (*la passation des
épreuves*; also a handover: *la passation de pouvoirs*).

![An overview chart of the DALF C2, from the sample papers. Two boxes side by side. Left: compréhension et production orales, an individual test, about 1 hour of preparation, about 30 minutes in front of the jury, a recording of about 15 minutes heard twice, then compte rendu, point de vue and débat; 50 points. Right: compréhension et production écrites, a collective paper, 3 hours 30, a dossier of about 2,000 words, two subjects with one to treat, one text of at least 700 words, article, éditorial, rapport, discours; 50 points. Below: total out of 100; pass with 50 out of 100 and at least 10 out of 50 in each paper; check FEI's pages, as the format can change.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Passing

The total is out of 100 and the pass mark (*le seuil de réussite*, C1) is 50, with at least 10
out of 50 in each paper: below 10, a paper fails the diploma whatever the total. The two papers
add up; neither is a gate to the other. Contrast the French *concours* (competitive exams for
schools and the civil service): there, candidates who pass the written papers are *admissibles*
(eligible for the oral), and *l'admission* (final success) is decided after the oral, in many
concours on the written and oral marks together. *Admissible* also means
acceptable (*une réponse admissible*).

### Older books

Until 2020 the DALF C2 came in two domains, *lettres et sciences humaines* or *sciences*. FEI's
change kit of October 2019 removed the choice from the March 2020 sessions. Older books and
some sample papers still show it; train with them, but check the format against FEI's current
sample papers:

- [DALF C2: description of the exam (FEI)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/article/dalf-c2)
- [Manuel du candidat DALF C2 (FEI)](https://france-education-international.fr/document/manuel-candidat-dalf-c2)

Each exam centre (often an Alliance française, an Institut français or a university) sets its
own dates, fees and deadlines and sends a *convocation* (A2). Centres' rules on who may register
vary: ask yours.

## How the papers are marked

Trained examiners mark both papers with marking grids. FEI's 2019 change kit announced new
production grids for its exams without naming C2; the current C2 grids and the split of the 50 points within each paper were not found in the sources
this course could read, so here are the qualities markers look at in general terms, as the
registry entry describes the skills:

- **oral:** the structure and content of the recording rendered faithfully, with the speakers'
  attitudes, relations and positions; a monologue that is organised and easy to follow; ease in
  the exchange, and the ability to hold the floor;
- **written:** fast reading of long documents; selection of what the chosen subject needs, linked
  to your own contributions; a long, organised text with a suitable, committed tone and a
  coherent line;
- **at both:** range, *justesse*, accuracy and register.

In some French competitive exams each paper is read by two markers, *la double correction* (double marking);
how the DALF organises its marking isn't described in what this course could read, so don't
build a strategy on it.

## Strategies for each paper

**The oral (lessons 21–23, honors 24h2).** The hour goes fast, especially if the two hearings
fall inside it: first hearing for structure and positions, the pause to number the ideas, second
hearing for examples and attitudes. Then regroup the notes by idea, write out only your first
sentence, your problématique and your last sentence, and list two objections you expect.

**The written paper (lessons 17–20, honors 24h1).** Lesson 17 suggests one way to divide 3 h
30 (advice, not an exam rule): 50 minutes to read the subjects, survey the dossier, choose and
select; 30 minutes to plan; 105 minutes to write straight onto the *copie* (B2); 25 minutes to
reread and count.
Write the word count if the paper asks for it, and follow its counting instructions: the editor
in this app counts *l'homme* as one word, an exam paper may not.

## A C2 holder's story

> J'ai passé le DALF C2 à trente-quatre ans, après dix ans à Lyon. Je parlais français tous les jours, au travail comme à la maison, et je croyais l'examen joué d'avance. Je me trompais. Ma première épreuve blanche a été une douche froide : à l'oral, j'ai restitué l'enregistrement dans l'ordre des interventions, sans un mot sur les attitudes ; à l'écrit, j'ai résumé le dossier au lieu de prendre position. Une enseignante chevronnée, qui préparait au diplôme depuis vingt ans, m'a fait remarquer autre chose : mes erreurs s'étaient fossilisées. J'oubliais l'accord du participe passé avec *avoir*, je confondais *près de* et *prêt à*, et personne ne me reprenait plus, puisque tout le monde me comprenait. J'avais atteint un palier.
>
> Pendant six mois, j'ai donc suivi une sorte de mise à niveau : un texte de sept cents mots toutes les deux semaines, corrigé par cette enseignante ; des émissions de radio écoutées deux fois, en prenant des notes ; un carnet de locutions figées que je réemployais exprès. J'ai travaillé la justesse plus que l'étendue : il ne s'agissait pas d'apprendre des mots rares, mais de choisir le mot exact.
>
> Le jour de la passation, j'étais plus aguerrie. L'enregistrement portait sur l'agriculture urbaine, et j'ai pris mes notes en colonnes, une par intervenant. Pendant le débat, un examinateur s'est fait l'avocat du diable ; j'ai su lui tenir tête sans perdre mon sang-froid. À l'écrit, j'ai choisi l'éditorial, le genre qui me permettait le mieux de m'engager.
>
> J'ai obtenu soixante-sept sur cent. Je ne me sens pas quasi native pour autant, et ce n'est pas ce que le diplôme demande. Mais je sais désormais repérer mes erreurs, et je continue à me perfectionner : le perfectionnement, en langue, n'a pas de fin.

In English: an invented candidate who had lived in Lyon for ten years expected an easy pass. Her
first mock exam showed two method errors (a turn-by-turn compte rendu, a summary instead of a
position) and, as a seasoned teacher (*chevronnée*) pointed out, fossilised errors that nobody
corrected any more: she had reached a plateau (*un palier*; also a landing on a staircase). Six
months of catching up (*une mise à niveau*: a text every two weeks, radio with notes, a notebook
of set phrases) left her more seasoned (*aguerrie*, literally hardened by battle) on the day. She
scored 67/100; she doesn't feel near-native, but she can now spot her errors and keeps improving.
*Une douche froide* is a cold shower, a nasty surprise; *joué d'avance* is a foregone conclusion.

**[[Fossilisation]]** (*la fossilisation*) is the process by which an error stops changing: it has
been understood so often that the speaker no longer hears it. Errors *se fossilisent* (fossilise)
most easily in fluent speakers who live in the language, which is why C2 learners often need feedback
more than input.

## The course in one chart

| skill | C1 lessons | C2 lessons |
|---|---|---|
| register | 01–04 (three registers) | 02 (six levels, shifted on purpose), 13–16 (regions) |
| the exact word | 13–16 (idioms, collocations) | 01 (paronyms, near-synonyms), 04 (scope, qualifiers) |
| agreement and the norm | B2 03, C1 93 (1990 spellings) | 03 (hard cases), 04h2 (who makes the norm) |
| tenses and moods | 05–07 | 05–06 (passé simple, literary subjunctives: recognition) |
| style | 04, 12h2 (rhetoric) | 07 (rhythm, word order), 08 (pastiche) |
| specialised French | 15 (academic) | 09–12 (law, science, economics, ideas) |
| long texts | 17–20 (synthesis, essay) | 17–20 (dossier, article, rapport, discours) |
| speaking | 21–23 (exposé, debate, lecture) | 21–23 (compte rendu, point of view, debate) |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The six modules of French C2
  accDescr: A top-down chain of six boxes, one per module, with a final box. Module 1, precision, register and the norm, lessons 01 to 04. Module 2, style and the literary tenses, 05 to 08. Module 3, specialised French, 09 to 12. Module 4, French across the French-speaking world, 13 to 16. Module 5, the long written text, 17 to 20. Module 6, speaking and the DALF C2, 21 to 24. Final box, the DALF C2, two papers, out of 100.
  M1["1. Precision, register, the norm (01–04)"] --> M2["2. Style, literary tenses (05–08)"]
  M2 --> M3["3. Specialised French (09–12)"]
  M3 --> M4["4. The French-speaking world (13–16)"]
  M4 --> M5["5. The long written text (17–20)"]
  M5 --> M6["6. Speaking and the DALF C2 (21–24)"]
  M6 --> D["DALF C2: two papers, out of 100"]
```

## After C2

There is no level above C2: what comes next is *le perfectionnement* (further training,
refinement; *l'amélioration*, B1, is improvement in general). To *perfectionner* your French
(to perfect, to improve it) at this level:

- **get feedback**, because input alone doesn't shift fossilised errors: a teacher, a writing
  group, a colleague who will correct you;
- **write for real readers**: letters to a newspaper, a blog, reports at work;
- **read across registers and regions**: a novel, a court decision, a Québec newspaper, a
  Belgian column. The course's reading list has books, radio and free classics for this level;
- **plan a *mise à niveau*** (refresher) whenever you've used French less for a while: a mock
  paper from FEI tells you quickly where you stand.

The *chevronné* or *aguerri* speaker (seasoned, experienced) is the one who keeps doing this.

## Pronunciation

- *Le CECRL*: usually said letter by letter, [se ə se ɛʁ ɛl].
- *Quasi* [kazi]: *quasi natif* [kazi natif]. *Aguerri* [ageʁi]: the *gu* is a hard [g].
- *L'idiomaticité* [idjɔmatisite]: six syllables.

## Common mistakes

- **C2 = native.** C2 is defined by what you can do, not by passing for a native.
- **Neglecting one paper.** Each needs at least 10 out of 50.
- **Training only with old books.** Their two domains are out of date since 2020.
- **Summarising the dossier.** At C2 the written text is engaged: a position, your own examples.
- **Admissible for "admissible as evidence" only.** In exams it means eligible for the next stage;
  it can also mean acceptable.
- **Stopping at the diploma.** Fossilised errors come back without feedback.

## Key points

- C2 is the higher proficient-user level: precision, range, flexibility, mediation, the
  integration of many sources into an engaged text or talk.
- DALF C2 (sample papers and registry): an oral (about 1 h of preparation, about 30 min, a
  recording heard twice, three parts) and a written paper (3 h 30, a dossier of about 2,000 words,
  one text of at least 700 words); 50 points each; pass with 50/100 and at least 10/50 in each.
- No domain choice since March 2020. The diploma is valid for life. Check FEI's pages first.
- After C2: feedback, real readers, every register; watch for fossilisation.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. Félicitations : vous avez terminé le tronc commun du cours de français C2, le dernier
du parcours !

lessons.title: Épreuve blanche: the written paper
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors lesson is a full mock of the **[[DALF C2]]** written paper, the *épreuve blanche* (mock
exam). The dossier and the two subjects are in the graded task at the end of the lesson: about
2,000 words of original documents on one question, whether short domestic flights should be
banned where a train exists. The lesson walks you through the reading, the choice of subject,
a model plan with a model introduction and conclusion for each subject, and a self-check list
for the whole course. Lessons 17 to 20 taught the method and the genres; this is where you put
them together, against the clock.

## The paper, in our words

As FEI's sample papers describe it: you have 3 h 30. You receive a dossier of about 2,000 words
(seven or eight documents in the samples) and two subjects. You treat one. You write one
structured text of at least 700 words, in the genre the subject names, for the reader it names,
using the dossier together with your own knowledge and taking a clear position. A monolingual
French dictionary is allowed in the samples. The paper is out of 50, and a mark below 10 fails the
diploma whatever the total. On the day, the paper's instructions win over anything here, including how
words are counted.

The mock follows that shape. The documents are original, and the outlets and authors are
invented and labelled so. The facts in document 1 about the French law are real; the figures in
document 5 are invented for the exercise and labelled as invented.

## Timing

One way to divide the 3 h 30 (advice, not an exam rule; it is the split lesson 17 suggests):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: One way to divide the three and a half hours
  accDescr: A top-down chain of five steps. First, 15 minutes to read both subjects, survey the dossier and choose. Second, 35 minutes to scan the documents, spot and select what the subject needs. Third, 30 minutes for the problématique and the plan, with the documents and your own examples placed in each part. Fourth, 105 minutes to write straight onto the answer sheet. Fifth, 25 minutes to reread, correct and count the words.
  A["0:00–0:15 Read both subjects, survey, choose"] --> B["0:15–0:50 Scan, spot, select"]
  B --> C["0:50–1:20 Problématique and plan, with own examples"]
  C --> D["1:20–3:05 Write straight onto the answer sheet"]
  D --> E["3:05–3:30 Reread, correct, count the words"]
```

An hour and three quarters of writing for at least 700 words leaves no time for a full draft: write from a
detailed plan, once.

## Reading this dossier

Survey first (lesson 17: titles, sources, dates, genres), then read for the subject you choose.
The eight documents, in one line each:

| document | genre and source | what it gives you | watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | fact sheet on the law | the real rule: the 2021 law, the 2023 decree, under 2 h 30 by direct train, three routes from Orly | the only document of record; cite it for facts |
| 2 | regional news report | a town with a subsidised *ligne aérienne* (air route) to Paris and no direct train | voices on both sides; the region must decide |
| 3 | economist's op-ed | the ban as a symbol; tax *le kérosène* (jet fuel) instead | one-sided by genre; a single author |
| 4 | interview with rail users | *le report modal* (modal shift) needs a better train first | an interest group: fair, but partial |
| 5 | infographic, invented figures | door-to-door times, prices, emissions | invented data: use it as the dossier's, not as real figures |
| 6 | essayist's column | *la honte de prendre l'avion* (flight shame): morality versus rules | ideas, no facts |
| 7 | science magazine | *les biocarburants* (biofuels), *le carburant d'aviation durable* (sustainable aviation fuel), *la compensation carbone* (carbon offsetting) | technology will be slow |
| 8 | readers' letters | a student, a retired woman, a railway worker | testimony, not proof |

Three things to notice. First, the documents disagree on what the problem is: emissions (1, 5,
7), fairness between territories (2, 8), method (3, 4, 6). Your problématique can come from that
disagreement. Second, *le trafic aérien* (air traffic) keeps growing, says document 7, so the
short-flight ban is small next to *l'aérien* (the air transport sector) as a whole: a good place
for your own knowledge. Third, document 4 and the letters in document 8 come from interested
parties: cite them as voices, not as neutral facts.

## Choosing a subject

The two subjects (in the task below) ask for different texts on the same dossier:

- **Subject 1, an éditorial** for the invented regional daily *L'Écho de Valbrume*, taking a
  position on a possible extension of the ban to journeys under four hours, which would end the
  town's air route. You speak for the paper, to its readers, with a strong line (lesson 18).
- **Subject 2, a rapport** for the president of the regional council, on whether to renew the
  subsidy for the Valbrume–Paris route or move the money to the *liaison ferroviaire* (rail link),
  with ranked recommendations (lesson 19).

Choose the one where you can build three parts with your own examples, not the one whose genre
you prefer. If you know a rail or air case of your own (a night train you have taken, a
country's policy you can describe accurately), the éditorial lets you use it more freely; if you
think in options and costs, the rapport is safer.

## Subject 1: a model plan for the éditorial

**Line:** yes to ending short flights, but train first. Title: *D'abord le train*.

1. **What the ban gets right** (concession). The short flight is the most emitting way to travel
   (doc. 5, doc. 2); the rule has real force as a signal (doc. 1, doc. 6). Own input: what you know
   of rail and air in another country.
2. **Why a ban alone would be unjust here.** No direct train (doc. 2); patients and firms (doc. 2,
   doc. 8); modal shift can't be decreed (doc. 4); one rule for unequal places (doc. 3).
3. **What we ask for.** A calendar: a direct, frequent, affordable train, then the end of the
   route; the subsidy moved to rail (doc. 8, doc. 4); a carbon price as well (doc. 3); technology
   won't come in time (doc. 7).

**Model introduction**

> **D'abord le train**
>
> Il est 7 h 05 : le petit avion de Valbrume décolle pour Paris, comme chaque matin. Peut-être plus pour longtemps. En étudiant l'extension de l'interdiction des vols courts aux trajets que le train assure en moins de quatre heures, le gouvernement place notre ville devant un dilemme qu'elle n'a pas choisi : renoncer à sa ligne aérienne au nom du climat, ou défendre un mode de transport dont personne ne conteste plus le coût pour la planète. Disons-le d'emblée : ce journal ne défendra pas l'avion à tout prix. Mais il refuse que Valbrume paie la première, et seule, une transition que l'État n'a pas préparée. Supprimer l'avion, oui ; mais d'abord le train.

**Model conclusion**

> La honte de prendre l'avion ne fera pas une politique, et l'interdiction seule pas davantage. Ce que Valbrume attend de l'État, ce n'est pas une dérogation, c'est un calendrier : un train direct, fréquent, à un prix raisonnable, puis, et seulement alors, la fin de la ligne aérienne. Si le gouvernement prend cet engagement, nous serons les premiers à saluer la mesure. S'il ne le prend pas, son interdiction n'aura de climatique que le nom.

In English: the introduction opens on a scene (the 7:05 flight), states the dilemma the
government's plan creates for the town, and takes the paper's line at once (*Disons-le
d'emblée*): not the plane at any price, but not Valbrume paying first and alone; the title comes
back as the last words. The conclusion turns document 6's phrase into a judgement, asks for a
calendar rather than an exemption, and ends on a conditional threat (*n'aura de climatique que le
nom*: will be climate policy in name only). The editorial *nous* is the paper speaking.

## Subject 2: a model plan for the rapport

**Line:** renew for a limited time, on a declining scale, and move the money to rail.

- Heading: addressee (*Madame la Présidente du conseil régional*), *Objet*, author's role, date.
- **I. État des lieux:** the route, its users and its cost to the region (doc. 2, doc. 5, doc. 8);
  the national rule and why it doesn't apply yet (doc. 1).
- **II. Analyse des deux options:** renewal (territorial access, health, firms: doc. 2, doc. 8)
  against redeployment (emissions, the train's capacity and prices, the case for a carbon price:
  doc. 3, doc. 4, doc. 5, doc. 7).
- **III. Préconisations,** ranked, each with a cost, an actor and a date (*l'échéancier*,
  C1): (1) renew for two years on a declining scale; (2) fund extra trains and a capped fare
  at once; (3) negotiate a direct train with the State and the operator; (4) an evaluation at
  mid-term before any final decision.

**Model introduction**

> Par lettre de mission, vous m'avez demandé d'examiner l'avenir de la subvention régionale accordée à la ligne aérienne Valbrume–Paris, qui arrive à échéance dans deux ans. La question se pose dans un contexte nouveau : depuis la loi « Climat et résilience » de 2021 et son décret d'application de 2023, l'État interdit les vols intérieurs lorsqu'un train direct et fréquent permet le même trajet en moins de deux heures trente, et le débat porte désormais sur un seuil plus élevé. La ligne de Valbrume n'est pas concernée à ce jour ; elle le serait si ce seuil était relevé. Le présent rapport dresse d'abord un état des lieux de la ligne et de ses usagers ; il analyse ensuite les deux options envisagées, le renouvellement de la subvention et le redéploiement des crédits vers le rail ; il formule enfin quatre préconisations, assorties d'un échéancier.

**Model conclusion**

> En définitive, le maintien de la ligne aérienne ne se justifie plus à long terme, mais sa suppression immédiate pénaliserait des usagers qui ne disposent pas, aujourd'hui, d'une alternative satisfaisante. Il est donc préconisé de renouveler la subvention pour une durée limitée et de manière dégressive, et d'en consacrer une part croissante à l'amélioration de la liaison ferroviaire, afin que le report modal soit possible avant d'être demandé. Une évaluation à mi-parcours permettrait à l'assemblée régionale de trancher en connaissance de cause.

In English: the introduction names the request (*par lettre de mission*), the context (the real
2021 law and 2023 decree, the debate on a higher threshold), the route's position under the
rule, and the plan in three steps. The conclusion gives the answer in one sentence each: no
long-term case for the route, no immediate cut; renewal that is limited and declining
(*dégressive*), money moved to rail, so that modal shift becomes possible before it is required;
a mid-term evaluation before the council decides. Impersonal throughout (*il est préconisé de*),
yet clearly committed: that is the C2 report.

## Self-check list for the whole course

Before you hand in, and before any real exam, check your text against the course:

- **Task (17–20):** the genre, the addressee and the stance the subject names; a title if the
  genre has one; at least 700 words, counted, the count written where the paper asks.
- **Dossier (17):** several documents used, combined by idea, cited by source (*selon
  l'économiste Bertrand Ancel*, *d'après l'infographie*), never copied; invented figures not
  presented as real ones; at least two examples of your own.
- **Line (18–20):** a position stated early, kept to the end, with the opposing view stated
  fairly and answered.
- **Precision (01, 04):** the exact word, no paronym slips; qualifiers that say how far a claim
  goes; no sentence that can be read two ways.
- **Register (02):** one register held throughout, shifted only on purpose.
- **The norm (03):** participle agreements, especially with *avoir* and a direct object placed
  before; *tout*, *même*, numerals.
- **Moods and tenses (C1 05–07):** the subjunctive where the verb or conjunction requires it; the
  conditional of hedging in the rapport.
- **Style (07):** varied sentence length, no repeated openings, a strong last sentence.
- **Specialised French (09–12):** terms used in their exact sense (*report modal, desserte,
  compensation carbone*).
- **Last ten minutes:** accents, agreements, homophones (*a / à, ou / où, ce / se*), punctuation and
  French spacing.

## Common mistakes

- **Summarising the dossier.** C2 asks for a committed text that uses the documents.
- **One document per part.** Plan by idea; each part draws on several documents.
- **Invented figures presented as facts.** Document 5's figures are the dossier's, and invented:
  write *selon l'infographie du dossier*.
- **The wrong genre.** An éditorial with headings and numbered recommendations, or a rapport
  with rhetorical questions and an editorial *nous*.
- **No count.** The editor counts as you type; an exam paper may ask you to write the count.

## Key points

- The mock follows the sample papers: 3 h 30, about 2,000 words of documents, two subjects, one
  text of at least 700 words in a set genre, with a position and your own knowledge.
- Read for disagreement between documents: it gives you the problématique.
- Cite by source, use several documents per part, add your own examples.
- The éditorial speaks for a paper with a strong line; the rapport answers a commissioning
  body with ranked, dated recommendations.
- Use the self-check list on every long text you write.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. Now write the paper: set a timer for 3 h 30.

```assignment
writing: fr6-m6-epreuve-ecrite
```

lessons.title: Épreuve blanche: the oral
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors lesson is a full mock of the **[[DALF C2]]** oral, on a new recording: a radio debate on
free public transport. The recording is split into the six listening questions of this lesson,
each a short extract with two speakers at most: do them first, twice each, taking notes in
columns (lesson 21), as if they were one fifteen-minute document. Then read the summary below,
prepare for about an hour, and compare your work with the models: a compte rendu, a plan for the
point of view, and a debate with the jury. The lesson ends with a self-assessment against the C2
descriptors.

![A chart of the DALF C2 oral as the sample paper describes it. On the left, listening and preparation, about one hour: a first hearing of about 15 minutes, a pause of about 3 minutes, a second hearing of about 15 minutes, and a box for notes, plan and key sentences, with a monolingual dictionary allowed. An arrow leads to the right: in front of the jury, about 30 minutes, three numbered rows: 1, compte rendu, about 5 to 10 minutes; 2, point de vue argumenté, about 10 minutes; 3, débat avec le jury, the rest of the time. Two notes at the bottom: the durations are those of the sample paper, so check FEI's current instructions; whether the two hearings are part of the hour is to be checked on the day.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The radio station, the city and the speakers are invented. The facts about real cities and the
French employers' levy are real, as stated below.

## The facts behind the debate

- **Dunkirk** made its bus network free for everyone in September 2018, and became the largest
  free network in France at the time.
- **Luxembourg** made public transport free nationwide on 1 March 2020, for residents,
  cross-border workers and tourists alike; first class on trains is still paid for.
- **Montpellier** made its network free for residents of the metropolitan area in December 2023.
- **Le versement mobilité** (mobility levy) is a tax on employers, private or public, with at least
  eleven employees, based on their payroll, inside the area of a transport authority that has adopted it.
  It is one of the main sources of funding for urban public transport, and it replaced the older
  *versement transport* under the 2019 mobility law.
- The body in charge of a local network is *l'autorité organisatrice* (the transport authority):
  a city, a metropolitan area or a region, which sets the *tarification* (fare structure) and
  chooses the operator.

Studies of free transport often report a modest shift from the car: part of the new passengers
used to walk or cycle. That is the heart of the debate.

## The recording: summary

> *Transports gratuits : cadeau ou mirage ?* Débat de Radio Estuaire, animé par Julien Marchal. Invités : Céline Arnaud, vice-présidente de la métropole de Rivemont chargée des mobilités ; Thomas Weber, économiste des transports ; Fatou Diallo, présidente de l'association d'usagers Bus pour tous ; Marc Lebrun, représentant des entreprises de la métropole.

1. **The project** (question 1). Rivemont will make its network free for residents next
   September. Céline Arnaud defends it as social justice and as a way to fill buses: fares cover
   only a small part of the cost, while *la billettique* (the ticketing system: machines,
   cards, inspection) and the fight against *la fraude* (fare dodging, by *les fraudeurs*) cost a lot.
2. **The economist** (question 2) points to an *effet d'aubaine* (windfall effect): many new
   passengers would have walked or cycled, or were already paying and simply stop paying. Citing
   Dunkirk, he says free transport raises ridership but rarely empties the roads.
3. **The users** (question 3). Fatou Diallo welcomes the idea but fears *la saturation*
   (overcrowding) at rush hour: "free, but standing". Her priority is *le cadencement*
   (a regular-interval timetable) and frequency; a *tarif solidaire* (an income-based concession
   fare) already helps the poorest.
4. **The employers** (question 4). Marc Lebrun recalls that firms already pay the *versement
   mobilité*; he is ambivalent: free transport helps staff get to work, but firms fear paying
   more for passengers who pay nothing.
5. **Who pays?** (question 5). The economist argues that the *titre de transport* (ticket, travel
   pass) also has a symbolic value: what is free is less respected and less funded. The
   vice-president answers that nobody says that of a free library; the economist rejects the
   comparison (*la comparaison ne tient pas*): a library is not overcrowded at rush hour, nor as
   costly as a bus network.
6. **The end** (question 6). The users and the employers agree on one point: investment in
   frequency first. The sticking point remains the timing: free transport now, or better service
   first?

## A model compte rendu (extract)

The full compte rendu would run five to ten minutes. Here are the opening and the transition,
with the plan announced; the middle is given as a plan.

> Le document que j'ai écouté est un débat radiophonique de Radio Estuaire consacré à la gratuité des transports publics, à partir d'un projet concret : celui de la métropole de Rivemont, qui rendra son réseau gratuit pour ses habitants à la rentrée. Quatre intervenants s'y opposent, puis s'y rapprochent : la vice-présidente chargée des mobilités, qui porte le projet ; un économiste des transports, sceptique ; la présidente d'une association d'usagers, favorable sur le principe mais réservée sur les moyens ; enfin un représentant des entreprises, dont la position est ambivalente. Je rendrai compte de ce débat en trois temps : les arguments en faveur de la gratuité, les objections qu'elle suscite, puis le point sur lequel les intervenants finissent par converger.
>
> […]
>
> Ce débat dépasse le cas de Rivemont. Il pose une question que je voudrais à présent discuter : la gratuité est-elle le meilleur usage de l'argent public consacré aux transports ?

The middle, by ideas: (1) for: justice, ridership, the cost of ticketing and fraud (the
vice-president); (2) against: the windfall effect and the modest shift from the car (the
economist, who *récuse* the vice-president's comparison with libraries), overcrowding (Fatou Diallo,
who *ironise* on standing passengers), the levy (the employers, who *prennent leurs distances*);
(3) the convergence on frequency, and the sticking point: timing.

## A model point of view: the plan

**Problématique:** *La gratuité est-elle le meilleur usage de l'argent public consacré aux
transports ?* **Position:** not as a first step; free transport is a goal, frequency is the
priority. **Plan:** problem, causes, solutions (lesson 22).

1. **The problem: a network that doesn't attract enough car drivers.** Fares are not the main
   obstacle for most drivers: time and comfort are. Example: the windfall effect (question 2);
   an example from your own city.
2. **The causes: frequency and capacity.** A bus every twenty minutes loses to the car whatever
   its price; overcrowding drives people away (question 3). An analogy: a free shop with empty
   shelves.
3. **The solutions, ranked.** First *le cadencement* and capacity; then targeted free fares
   (young people, low incomes: the *tarif solidaire*); full free transport last, where the
   network can absorb it, as a *corollaire* of good service rather than a substitute for it.

## A model debate

```dialogue
# Le débat : la gratuité des transports
M. Duval: Vous dites que la gratuité n'est pas une priorité. Mais le Luxembourg l'a instaurée à l'échelle d'un pays entier !
= You say free transport isn't a priority. But Luxembourg did it for a whole country!
Malik: C'est vrai, et c'est un exemple intéressant. Mais je rebondis sur votre mot « pays » : le Luxembourg est un petit pays aux moyens considérables, et son cas ne se transpose pas tel quel à une métropole française.
= True, and it's an interesting example. But I'll pick up on your word "country": Luxembourg is a small country with considerable means, and its case doesn't carry over as it stands to a French metropolitan area.
Mme Lemaire: La gratuité est aussi une question de justice. Les plus modestes ne peuvent pas attendre que le réseau soit parfait.
= Free transport is also a question of fairness. The least well-off can't wait for the network to be perfect.
Malik: J'en conviens, et c'est pourquoi je propose un tarif solidaire dès maintenant. Il vise ceux qui en ont besoin, sans effet d'aubaine pour ceux qui pouvaient payer.
= I grant that, which is why I'm proposing an income-based fare now. It targets those who need it, without a windfall for those who could pay.
M. Duval: Combien coûterait la gratuité totale à Rivemont ?
= How much would full free transport cost Rivemont?
Malik: Le débat ne donnait pas ce chiffre, et je ne vais pas en inventer un. Ce que l'on sait, c'est que la billettique et la lutte contre la fraude ont aussi un coût, qu'il faudrait déduire.
= The debate didn't give that figure, and I won't invent one. What we do know is that ticketing and the fight against fare dodging also have a cost, which would have to be deducted.
Mme Lemaire: Vous avez parlé d'un magasin gratuit aux rayons vides. L'image n'est-elle pas un peu forte ?
= You spoke of a free shop with empty shelves. Isn't that image a little strong?
Malik: Vous avez raison, je rectifie le tir : le réseau n'est pas vide, il est saturé aux heures de pointe. Mais l'idée demeure : la gratuité ne sert à rien si l'on ne trouve pas de place dans le bus.
= You're right; let me adjust that: the network isn't empty, it's overcrowded at rush hour. But the point stands: free fares are no use if you can't get on the bus.
M. Duval: Et si la gratuité attirait justement les automobilistes ?
= And what if free fares did attract drivers?
Malik: Alors je reverrais ma position, et volontiers. Mais les études citées dans le débat montrent plutôt un report modeste depuis la voiture. Je ne campe pas sur mes positions : je suis les résultats.
= Then I'd reconsider my position, and gladly. But the studies cited in the debate point rather to a modest shift from the car. I'm not digging my heels in: I'm following the results.
```

What the model shows: a concession turned into a proposal (*J'en conviens, et c'est
pourquoi …*), a trick question answered without inventing a figure, an image corrected without
giving up the argument, and the condition under which the candidate would change his mind.

```speak
# Free transport: key phrases
La gratuité est-elle le meilleur usage de l'argent public consacré aux transports ?
= Is free transport the best use of public money spent on transport?
Les études montrent plutôt un report modeste depuis la voiture.
= The studies point rather to a modest shift from the car.
Un tarif solidaire vise ceux qui en ont besoin, sans effet d'aubaine.
= An income-based fare targets those who need it, without a windfall effect.
La gratuité ne sert à rien si l'on ne trouve pas de place dans le bus.
= Free fares are no use if you can't get on the bus.
```

## Self-assessment against the C2 descriptors

Record yourself in the three parts (the speak blocks let you compare with a model voice), then
listen and check each line. In our words, from the Companion Volume's C2 rows:

- **Listening and notes:** I rendered every speaker's position and attitude, including the shifts,
  and nothing I said was not in the recording.
- **Compte rendu (mediation):** I regrouped the content by idea and explained what speakers
  implied or ironised, not only what they said.
- **Point of view (spoken production):** my talk flowed, its plan was audible, and a listener could
  recall my three main points afterwards.
- **Debate (formal discussion):** I held my position under objections, conceded what was fair, and
  answered hostile questions tactfully.
- **Range and precision:** I used precise verbs and qualifiers; I never had to hide a gap with a
  vague word.
- **Accuracy:** my grammar held even when I was thinking hard about the argument.

If a line is not yet true, go back to the lesson that teaches it: 21 for the first two, 22 for the
third, 23 for the fourth, module 1 for the last two.

## Common mistakes

- **Doing the questions once each.** The exam plays the recording twice: so should you.
- **Citing the real cities wrongly.** Dunkirk 2018, Luxembourg 2020, Montpellier 2023 (for
  residents): if you aren't sure of a date, leave it out.
- **The versement mobilité as a tax on passengers.** Employers pay it.
- **Effet d'aubaine for any benefit.** It is a benefit that goes to people who would have acted the
  same way without it.

## Key points

- Do the six listening questions as one long recording, twice, with notes in columns.
- Compte rendu by ideas, with attitudes; point of view with a plan that fits the question; debate
  moves from lesson 23.
- Real facts only if you are sure of them; never invent a figure in the debate.
- Assess yourself against the C2 descriptors, then return to the lesson that teaches each one.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Molière et la langue classique
topics: Classical French and words that changed
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French is often called *la langue de Molière*, as English is "the language of Shakespeare". This
lesson presents the man behind the phrase, the salons, the social ideals and comic types of his
age, the quarrels that nearly cost him his career, and the words of his century that still trip
up a modern reader. Lesson 05 taught you to read the **[[passé simple]]**; lesson 08 the
satire and pastiche of a period style. Here both meet a real author.

Nothing below is quoted from Molière. His plays are retold in modern French or in English, and his
famous lines are described, never copied. His verse is left to lesson 08h1.

## A life in dates

![A vertical timeline of Molière's life with ten dated rows: 1622, baptism in Paris; 1643, the Illustre Théâtre founded with the Béjart family; 1658, the troupe plays before Louis XIV; 1659, Les Précieuses ridicules; 1664, Tartuffe performed at Versailles, then banned; 1666, Le Misanthrope; 1669, Tartuffe finally authorised; 1670, Le Bourgeois gentilhomme at Chambord; 1673, Le Malade imaginaire and Molière's death; 1680, the Comédie-Française founded.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Jean-Baptiste Poquelin was baptised on 15 January 1622 at the church of Saint-Eustache in Paris.
His father held the office of upholsterer to the king, and the son studied with the Jesuits at the
Collège de Clermont. In 1643 he founded a company with the Béjart family, the Illustre Théâtre,
and soon took the stage name Molière. The company went bankrupt; Molière was briefly held for
debt. From 1646 he toured the provinces with part of the troupe for about twelve years.

On 24 October 1658 the troupe played before Louis XIV and settled in Paris, first at the
Petit-Bourbon, then, from January 1661, at the Palais-Royal. *Les Précieuses ridicules* opened on 18 November
1659, *L'École des femmes* in December 1662, *Le Malade imaginaire* on 10 February 1673. Molière
was taken ill during its fourth performance and died at home that
evening, 17 February 1673.

## Reading: Le rire et le pouvoir

> Fils d'un tapissier du roi, Jean-Baptiste Poquelin aurait pu reprendre la charge de son père. Il préféra le théâtre. En 1643, il fonda avec la famille Béjart l'Illustre Théâtre, qui fit faillite au bout de deux ans à peine ; c'est vers cette époque qu'il adopta le nom de Molière. Une douzaine d'années de tournées en province suivirent : la troupe y apprit son métier devant des publics de toute sorte.
>
> Revenu à Paris, Molière joua devant le jeune Louis XIV en octobre 1658 et obtint bientôt une salle. L'année suivante, *Les Précieuses ridicules* lui valurent un triomphe et ses premiers ennemis. Dès lors, presque chaque succès déclencha une querelle : on lui reprocha de railler les dévots, les médecins, les marquis, les pédants, bref tous ceux qui se prenaient au sérieux.
>
> Ce comédien ne se contentait pas d'écrire : il dirigeait la troupe, mettait en scène et tenait les grands rôles comiques. C'est d'ailleurs presque sur scène qu'il acheva sa vie : pris d'un malaise pendant la quatrième représentation du *Malade imaginaire*, il mourut chez lui le soir même. Sept ans plus tard, son ancienne troupe fusionna avec une troupe rivale pour former la Comédie-Française, que l'on appelle encore « la maison de Molière ».

*The son of an upholsterer to the king, Jean-Baptiste Poquelin could have taken over his
father's office. He preferred the theatre. In 1643 he founded the Illustre Théâtre with the
Béjart family; it went bankrupt after barely two years, and it was around then that he took the name
Molière. About twelve years of touring the provinces followed: there the troupe learned its trade
in front of every kind of audience.*

*Back in Paris, Molière played before the young Louis XIV in October 1658 and soon obtained a
theatre. The following year, Les Précieuses ridicules brought him a triumph and his first enemies.
From then on, almost every success set off a quarrel: he was accused of mocking the devout,
doctors, marquis, pedants, in short everyone who took themselves seriously.*

*This actor did not merely write: he ran the troupe, directed the plays and took the great comic
parts. Indeed, he ended his life almost on stage: taken ill during the fourth performance of Le
Malade imaginaire, he died at home that same evening. Seven years later his former troupe merged
with a rival company to form the Comédie-Française, which is still called "the house of
Molière".*

The narrative tenses are the passé simple (*préféra, fonda, fit, suivirent, apprit, obtint,
valurent, mourut, fusionna*), which you recognise and need not write; the background is in the
imperfect (*dirigeait, tenait*). *Aurait pu reprendre* is the conditionnel passé of an unrealised
possibility.

## Salons and préciosité

In the first half of the century, Paris society met in salons: the marquise de Rambouillet
received guests from about 1608, and after 1650 the novelist Madeleine de Scudéry led the most
admired circle. Her novel *Clélie* (1654–1660) contains the famous *Carte de Tendre*, a map of the
paths that lead to tender friendship. The salons cultivated refined feeling and speech. Modern critics call this taste **[[préciosité]]**, and
the women of these circles *les précieuses*; historians stress that few of them used the label
for themselves, and that much of what we "know" about their jargon comes from satirists such as
Somaize, whose *Dictionnaire des précieuses* appeared in 1660.

*Les Précieuses ridicules* (1659) is a one-act prose comedy. Two young women from the provinces,
newly arrived in Paris, dream of the elegant life they have read about in novels and turn away
two respectable suitors as too plain. The suitors take revenge: they send their valets, dressed
up as a marquis and a viscount, who dazzle the girls with absurd compliments until their masters
unmask and beat them. The comedy rests on a *quiproquo*: the girls take servants for noblemen.
In his preface Molière said he mocked only clumsy imitations of refinement.

## The honnête homme and the bel esprit

The century's social ideal was *l'honnête homme*, described in Nicolas Faret's manual of 1630 on
the art of pleasing at court: a man of good birth or good manners, cultivated without pedantry,
moderate in everything, at ease in conversation. Careful: *honnête* here does not mean "honest"
(A2) but "well-bred, accomplished". *Un bel esprit* is a person of wit and polish; from the
start the phrase could also be ironic, for someone who shows off.

*Le Misanthrope* (1666) puts the ideal on trial. Alceste rejects the polite lies of society and
demands total sincerity; yet he loves Célimène, a young widow who delights in salon gossip.
His friend Philinte, the honnête homme of the play, accepts people as they are. In one scene a
courtier reads Alceste a sonnet he has written and asks for an honest opinion, and gets it, which
starts a dispute. At the end Alceste resolves to flee the world. Is the misanthrope right or
ridiculous? The play leaves the question open.

## Comic types and the quarrel over Tartuffe

Molière drew on stock figures and gave them depth. *Le barbon* is the old man who wants to marry a
girl far too young for him: Arnolphe in *L'École des femmes* keeps his ward in ignorance so that
she will make a docile wife, and fails. *Le dévot* is a devout person; *le faux dévot* only plays
the part.

In *Tartuffe*, Orgon, a wealthy bourgeois, falls under the spell of a penniless man who passes
for a saint. He promises him his daughter and signs his property over to him. His wife, Elmire,
exposes the hypocrite by letting Orgon, hidden under a table, witness Tartuffe's advances to her.
Tartuffe then tries to evict the whole family, until an officer arrives in the king's name and
arrests him. Fittingly, the word *hypocrite* comes from the Greek for an actor.

The first version, probably in three acts, was played at Versailles on 12 May 1664 and banned at once. A
revised version, *L'Imposteur*, had a single performance on 5 August 1667 and was banned again;
the archbishop of Paris forbade the faithful to see or read it. Only on 5 February 1669 was the
play performed freely. Historians speak of a *cabale* of the devout behind these bans, and
often link it to a secret society of pious laymen, the Compagnie du Saint-Sacrement. Today *un
tartuffe* is any hypocrite.

## Monsieur Jourdain and the comédie-ballet

*Le Bourgeois gentilhomme* (1670) was created for the court at Chambord with music by Lully. A
rich merchant, Monsieur Jourdain, wants to become a gentleman and hires masters of music, dance,
fencing and philosophy. In the best-known scene, the philosophy master teaches him the difference between verse and
prose, and Jourdain is delighted to learn that his everyday speech has a learned name. In the finale he is made a dignitary of an invented Turkish order
in a mock ceremony, which lets his daughter marry the young man he had rejected.

This is a **[[comédie-ballet]]**: a comedy whose acts are framed by songs and dances that belong to
the plot. Molière invented the form with *Les Fâcheux*, played at Nicolas Fouquet's château of
Vaux-le-Vicomte on 17 August 1661, and ended with *Le Malade imaginaire* (music by
Marc-Antoine Charpentier).

## The parterre

In a 17th-century theatre, *le parterre* was the floor in front of the stage, where spectators,
mostly men, stood and paid the lowest price; nobles sat in boxes or even on stage. This loud,
judgemental public was courted by authors: in *La Critique de l'École des femmes* (1663)
Molière has a character defend its good sense against a scornful marquis. Today *un parterre* is mainly a flower bed,
and the theatre's floor seats are *l'orchestre*.

## Classical French and words that moved

**[[Classical French]]** (*le français classique*) is the language of the 17th and 18th centuries,
shaped by Vaugelas and the Académie (lesson 04h2). Most of it reads easily today, but a
modern reader notices three things. Object pronouns often stand before the verb that governs the
infinitive (*je le veux voir* for today's *je veux le voir*). Older editions write the imperfect
with *-oi-* (*il parloit*); the Académie adopted *-ai-* only in its 1835 edition, and most
modern editions modernise the spelling. And the **[[imperfect subjunctive]]** (lesson 06) is in
ordinary use.

The real trap is vocabulary. Some words kept their form and lost their force:

| word | classical sense | today |
|---|---|---|
| *l'ennui* | weariness, but also grief and deep worry | boredom |
| *étonner* | to stun, as if struck by thunder (Latin *extonare*) | to surprise |
| *la gêne* | torture, torment, then painful constraint | discomfort, embarrassment |
| *charmer* | to cast a spell on (*un charme* = a spell) | to delight |
| *formidable* | that inspires fear (Latin *formidare*, to dread) | terrific |

### Example 1: Reading a classical sense

These sentences were written for this lesson in a classical style:

- *La nouvelle de sa ruine l'étonna : il demeura immobile et sans voix.* — The news of his ruin
  stunned him: he stood motionless and speechless. (Read *étonner* as "struck dumb", not "surprised".)
- *Cet amour sans espoir était pour lui une gêne de chaque instant.* — This hopeless love was a
  constant torment to him. (Not "a constant inconvenience".)
- *Une armée formidable s'avançait vers la ville.* — A fearsome army was advancing on the town.

Ask each time whether the context calls for the strong old sense: fear, grief, magic or violence
around the word usually say yes. English *formidable* kept the old sense, so it is a false
friend.

### Example 2: From salon talk to plain French

Here is an invented sentence in the précieux manner, in its spirit but not taken from any text:

> Apportez-nous, je vous prie, la messagère muette des cœurs, et la fidèle compagne des veilles, que nous puissions écrire à la nuit tombante.

*Please bring us the silent messenger of hearts, and the faithful companion of late hours, so that we
may write as night falls.* Plain French: *Apportez-nous du papier et une bougie pour écrire ce
soir.* The précieux style replaces names with periphrases and turns objects into figures; the
satire lies in using that machinery for the most ordinary request.

## Why "la langue de Molière"?

The phrase is a periphrasis for French. It spread as Molière became the national author, read
in every school. It is mostly a compliment, sometimes ironic (*il maltraite la langue de
Molière*: he mangles French). It doesn't mean that Molière fixed the language: grammarians and
the Académie did that.

## Common mistakes

- *Le quiproquo* is pronounced like *kiproko*; plural *les quiproquos*. For an everyday
  misunderstanding say *le malentendu* (A2 honors); *un quiproquo* is when one person or thing is
  taken for another.
- *L'honnête homme* is not "an honest man", and *précieux* (A2 honors) still means precious: *la
  préciosité* is the style, *une précieuse* the salon lady.
- French *formidable* is positive; English "formidable" is not. Don't translate one by the other.
- *Le dévot* is devout, not devoted (*dévoué*); *un faux dévot* is a hypocrite.
- Don't call every play of Molière a comédie-ballet: *Le Misanthrope* and *Tartuffe* are not.
- Don't quote famous lines from memory in an essay: describe them, or check an edition.

## Key points

- Molière: baptised 15 January 1622 in Paris, died 17 February 1673; Illustre Théâtre 1643;
  provinces from 1646; before Louis XIV 24 October 1658; Comédie-Française 1680.
- Plays: *Les Précieuses ridicules* 1659, *L'École des femmes* 1662, *Tartuffe* 1664–1669,
  *Le Misanthrope* 1666, *Le Bourgeois gentilhomme* 1670, *Le Malade imaginaire* 1673.
- Préciosité: the refined language of the salons, mocked when it turns into jargon. The
  honnête homme: moderation and social grace. The comédie-ballet: comedy with music and dance.
- Classical French: pronouns before the governing verb, *-oi-* spellings in old editions,
  imperfect subjunctive in use, and words whose force has faded (*ennui, étonner, gêne,
  charmer, formidable*).

lessons.title: Hugo, Les Misérables et l'argot
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French C1 (04h3, honors) taught today's slang and verlan, and lesson 02 the informal and popular
registers. This lesson goes back to the century in which argot first entered great literature:
Victor Hugo's *Les Misérables*, a novel of convicts, street children and insurrection that
devotes a whole book to the language of the underworld. You will read the story retold in a
paragraph or two, follow Hugo into exile, and see which words of the 19th-century underworld
became ordinary French.

As in every literature lesson of this course, nothing is quoted from Hugo: the novel is retold
in original French, and Hugo's ideas are described in English.

## Hugo in brief

Victor Hugo was born in Besançon on 26 February 1802, the son of an officer of Napoleon's
armies. By thirty he led the Romantic movement: the première of his play *Hernani* in 1830
turned into a battle between old and young, and *Notre-Dame de Paris* followed in 1831. He was
elected to the Académie française in 1841 and made a peer of France in 1845. After the revolution
of 1848 he sat as a representative and moved steadily to the left. When Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte
seized power on 2 December 1851, Hugo tried to organise resistance, then fled.

## Nineteen years in exile

![A simplified map of the Channel area showing England with London, northern France with Paris, Belgium with Brussels, and the islands of Jersey and Guernsey. Red arrows mark Hugo's route into exile, from Paris to Brussels, Brussels to Jersey and Jersey to Guernsey (the key gives 1851, 1852 and 1855); a green arrow marks his return from Brussels to Paris in 1870.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Hugo reached Brussels in December 1851, and a decree of January 1852 banished him from France
with other representatives of the left: he was now *un proscrit*, and the measure a
*proscription*. In August 1852 he moved to Jersey, a British island off Normandy, and in
October 1855, expelled from Jersey with other French exiles, he settled on Guernsey, where he
bought Hauteville House. In exile he wrote the satirical poems of *Les Châtiments* (1853), *Les
Contemplations* (1856) and much of *Les Misérables*. In 1859 he refused the emperor's amnesty.
In August 1870 he left Guernsey for Brussels, and he returned to Paris on 5 September 1870, the day after the Republic was proclaimed. He died on 22
May 1885, and his body was taken to the Panthéon after a national funeral.

*L'exil* (B2 honors) is the state; *un exilé* is anyone who lives in exile; *un proscrit* has
been banished by an official act, often for political reasons.

## Les Misérables, the book

Hugo began a novel called *Les Misères* in 1845, set it aside in 1848 and finished it in exile.
*Les Misérables* was published in 1862 by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven et Cie, a Brussels firm;
the first volumes went on sale in early April. It has five parts named after characters and
places (*Fantine, Cosette, Marius*, then the idyll of the rue Plumet and the epic of the rue
Saint-Denis, and *Jean Valjean*) and filled ten volumes. Novel, history, sermon and essay at
once, it is the model of the **[[roman-fleuve]]**: Hugo stops the story for long digressions on
Waterloo, convents, the sewers of Paris and argot.

## Reading: Valjean, de Toulon à Paris

> En 1815, Jean Valjean sortit du bagne de Toulon après dix-neuf ans de peine : il avait volé un pain, puis tenté plusieurs fois de s'évader. Rejeté de partout, il fut accueilli un soir par un évêque, à qui il déroba son argenterie. Repris par les gendarmes, il fut sauvé par l'évêque lui-même, qui affirma la lui avoir donnée. Ce pardon le transforma.
>
> Quelques années plus tard, devenu sous un faux nom industriel et maire d'une petite ville, l'ancien forçat rencontra Fantine, une ouvrière que la misère avait réduite à tout vendre pour payer la pension de sa fille Cosette, confiée à des aubergistes cupides, les Thénardier. Il promit à la mourante de sauver l'enfant. Mais l'inspecteur Javert, qui l'avait connu au bagne, ne cessa de le traquer.
>
> Valjean arracha Cosette aux Thénardier et l'éleva en secret à Paris, où elle s'éprit de Marius, un jeune homme lié à des étudiants républicains. En juin 1832, pendant l'insurrection, Marius se battit sur une barricade, au pied de laquelle mourut Gavroche, un gamin des rues. Valjean le sauva en le portant, blessé, à travers les égouts. Javert, qu'il avait épargné, le laissa partir, puis se jeta dans la Seine.

*In 1815 Jean Valjean left the penal colony of Toulon after nineteen years: he had stolen a loaf
of bread, then tried several times to escape. Turned away everywhere, he was taken in one evening
by a bishop, whose silver he stole. Caught by the gendarmes, he was saved by the bishop himself,
who claimed to have given it to him. This forgiveness transformed him.*

*A few years later, having become, under a false name, a manufacturer and the mayor of a small
town, the former convict met Fantine, a worker whom poverty had driven to sell everything to pay
for the keep of her daughter Cosette, left with greedy innkeepers, the Thénardiers. He promised
the dying woman to save the child. But Inspector Javert, who had known him in the penal colony,
never stopped hunting him.*

*Valjean took Cosette away from the Thénardiers and brought her up in secret in Paris, where she
fell in love with Marius, a young man linked to republican students. In June 1832, during the
insurrection, Marius fought on a barricade, at the foot of which Gavroche, a street urchin, died. Valjean saved
him by carrying him, wounded, through the sewers. Javert, whose life he had spared, let him go,
then threw himself into the Seine.*

The novel ends with Valjean's death, Cosette and Marius at his side. The tenses are those of the
récit: passé simple for events (*sortit, déroba, transforma, promit, s'éprit, mourut*),
plus-que-parfait for what came before (*avait volé, avait réduite*). Note the agreement in *que
la misère avait réduite*: the direct object *que* stands for Fantine and comes before the verb.

## The bagne and its people

*Le bagne* is the penal colony with hard labour. Until 1748, convicts rowed the king's galleys;
then they were moved to prisons in the naval ports (Toulon, Brest, Rochefort), still called
*bagnes*, a word usually traced to the Italian *bagno*, a bath, after a prison set up in old baths.
From 1852 France shipped convicts to Guiana, and later to New Caledonia; transportation to Guiana
was abolished in 1938, though the last convicts came home only in the early 1950s. *Le forçat* first meant the galley slave, then any convict at hard labour;
*le bagnard* is the inmate of a bagne. In the novel both words name Valjean, and both brand him
for life: his yellow passport marks him as a freed convict wherever he goes.

## Barricades and street children

*La barricade* is usually traced to *la barrique*, a barrel: Parisians blocked streets with barrels filled
with earth as early as the 16th century. In 1830, 1832 and 1848 the barricade became the symbol
of the Paris uprising. The insurrection of 5–6 June 1832, after the funeral of the popular
general Lamarque, is the one Hugo chose: a small republican rising, crushed in two days.

Gavroche, the Thénardiers' neglected son, lives in the streets and sleeps inside the plaster
elephant of the Bastille. A whole book of the third part portrays *le gamin de Paris*: cheeky,
generous, mocking, fearless. The informal *titi* (*le titi parisien*) names the same figure.

## The book on argot

The seventh book of the fourth part is a study of argot. Hugo had already been attacked for
giving a thief argot to speak in *Le Dernier Jour d'un condamné* (1829), and he answers the
critics: in his view a novelist has the right, even the duty, to go down into the *bas-fonds*
and record the language of *la pègre*, because that language tells the truth about misery. He
treats argot as a real language with its own grammar and imagery, borrowing from many tongues and
changing constantly because it must stay secret. He traces its history and turns it into a
social question: argot, for him, is the language of poverty as much as of crime, and the remedy
is to fight poverty.

Hugo had sources. Eugène-François Vidocq, a former convict who became head of a police brigade,
published memoirs in 1828–1829 and a book on thieves with an argot glossary in 1837; critics
often see something of him in both Valjean and Javert. Later in the century, slang was also
called the **[[langue verte]]**, a name that appears in the titles of 1860s dictionaries; today the
phrase sounds old-fashioned, and *l'argot* (C1 honors) is the usual word.

*Argot* itself first named the underworld community, then its language. Several underworld
words passed into ordinary French, as dictionaries record: *la tronche*, the head in argot, is
now informal for a face; *cambrioler* comes from an argot word for a room and is now standard;
*le flic*, a policeman, is informal, its origin still debated.

### Example 1: The right word for the outcast

Choose by what the person did or suffered:

- *Hugo vécut en proscrit à Guernesey.* — Hugo lived as a banished man on Guernsey. (an official
  act of banishment)
- *Des milliers d'exilés politiques gagnèrent Londres.* — Thousands of political exiles reached
  London. (living abroad, forced or not)
- *Le bagnard portait un numéro sur sa casaque.* — The convict wore a number on his prison jacket.
  (an inmate of the bagne)
- *Les forçats ramaient sur les galères du roi.* — The galley slaves rowed the king's galleys.
  (the historical sense)

### Example 2: From argot to standard

An invented informal sentence: *Les flics ont reconnu la tronche du type qui avait cambriolé la
bijouterie.* In standard French: *Les policiers ont reconnu le visage de l'homme qui avait
cambriolé la bijouterie.* Only *cambrioler* stays: it has climbed all the way into the norm. In
a formal report you would write *les enquêteurs ont identifié l'auteur du cambriolage*.

## Common mistakes

- *Le bagne* is not a bath (*le bain*), and *le forçat* takes a cedilla.
- *Les bas-fonds* is plural only and masculine: *les bas-fonds de Paris*. Literally, the shallows
  of the sea; figuratively, the slums and the people who live on crime.
- *La pègre* is a collective: the underworld as a whole. For one criminal say *un truand* or *un
  malfaiteur*.
- *Les Misérables* keeps its *s*; *misérable* alone means wretched, or in old usage a villain.
- *Guernesey* and *Jersey* are the French names; the plural of *roman-fleuve* is *romans-fleuves*.
- Don't write *langue verte* as a modern label for slang in your own text unless you want an old
  flavour; say *l'argot*.

## Key points

- Hugo: born 26 February 1802 in Besançon, died 22 May 1885; Panthéon after a national funeral.
- Exile after the coup of 2 December 1851: Brussels, Jersey (1852–1855), Guernsey (1855–1870);
  return on 5 September 1870.
- *Les Misérables*: 1862, Brussels (Lacroix, Verboeckhoven et Cie), five parts; Valjean, Fantine,
  Cosette, Javert, Marius, Gavroche; the barricade of June 1832.
- The fourth part's seventh book studies argot as the language of misery; Vidocq's memoirs
  (1828–1829) were among the sources of the time; *la langue verte* is the old name.

lessons.title: Yourcenar, Mémoires d'Hadrien et la prose classique au XXe siècle
topics: The historical novel and its voice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 06 taught you to recognise the imperfect subjunctive and the classical sequence of tenses,
forms most modern writers have given up. Marguerite Yourcenar kept them, in novels published
after the Second World War, and made a name with a prose so measured that many readers place it
beside the 17th century's. This lesson presents her life, retells *Mémoires d'Hadrien* (1951),
the novel written as the dying emperor's letter, and shows how to read her long sentences. It ends
at the Académie française, which elected her as its first woman member.

Yourcenar's work is still in copyright: nothing here is quoted from it. The novel is retold and
its famous opening is described, never copied.

## A life in dates

![A vertical timeline of Marguerite Yourcenar's life with eight dated rows: 1903, birth in Brussels; 1937, French translation of Virginia Woolf's The Waves; 1939, departure for the United States; 1947, American citizenship and the legal name Yourcenar; 1951, Mémoires d'Hadrien; 1968, L'Œuvre au noir, prix Femina; 1980, first woman elected to the Académie française; 1987, death on Mount Desert Island, Maine.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Marguerite Cleenewerck de Crayencour was born in Brussels on 8 June 1903. Her mother died ten
days after her birth, and she was raised by her father, partly on the family estate of the
Mont-Noir, in French Flanders, taught at home and taken travelling across Europe. Her pen name,
Yourcenar, is an anagram of Crayencour less one *c*; she made it her legal name in 1947. In 1937
she translated Virginia Woolf's *The Waves* into French.

In 1939 she left for the United States with the American scholar Grace Frick, her companion until
Frick's death in 1979. She became an American citizen in 1947, and from 1950 the two women lived
in a house on Mount Desert Island, in Maine. *Mémoires d'Hadrien*, published by Plon in 1951, made
her famous; *L'Œuvre au noir*, a novel about a 16th-century physician and alchemist, won the
prix Femina in 1968. She died in Bar Harbor, on the same island, on 17 December 1987.

## Reading: Un empereur écrit à un adolescent

> Un empereur malade écrit à un adolescent. Hadrien, qui a passé soixante ans, sait que son cœur le lâche ; il adresse au jeune Marc Aurèle, qu'il a fait adopter par son successeur, une longue lettre où il fait le bilan de sa vie. Il y évoque son enfance, ses années de soldat sous Trajan, son accession à l'Empire, ses voyages incessants d'une province à l'autre, son amour de la Grèce, les villes qu'il a fondées, la paix qu'il a voulu maintenir aux frontières. Il y parle aussi d'Antinoüs, le jeune Grec qu'il a aimé et dont la mort dans le Nil a assombri ses dernières années.
>
> Yourcenar a lu tout ce que les historiens anciens rapportent d'Hadrien, mais elle invente la voix. Son pari tient en une question : comment un homme du IIe siècle se raconterait-il, s'il pouvait le faire sans mentir ? Il fallait que le lecteur oubliât la romancière pour n'entendre que l'empereur. D'où une prose ample et maîtrisée, où la mélancolie d'un homme qui va mourir se mêle à une sérénité patiemment conquise.

*A sick emperor is writing to a teenager. Hadrian, who is past sixty, knows that his heart is
failing; he sends young Marcus Aurelius, whom he has had adopted by his successor, a long letter
in which he takes stock of his life. In it he recalls his childhood, his years as a soldier under
Trajan, his accession to the Empire, his endless travels from one province to another, his love
of Greece, the cities he founded, the peace he tried to keep on the frontiers. He also speaks of
Antinous, the young Greek he loved, whose death in the Nile darkened his last years.*

*Yourcenar read everything the ancient historians report about Hadrian, but she invents the
voice. Her wager comes down to one question: how would a man of the 2nd century tell his own
story, if he could do it without lying? The reader had to forget the novelist and hear only the
emperor. Hence an ample, controlled prose, in which the melancholy of a man about to die mingles
with a serenity patiently won.*

The commentary is in the present, as a book review would be. *Qu'il a voulu maintenir* does not
agree: the direct object of *voulu* is the infinitive. *Il fallait que le lecteur oubliât* uses
the imperfect subjunctive (lesson 06), as Yourcenar herself would; today's everyday French says
*il fallait que le lecteur oublie*. Recognise it; don't write it.

## The novel

The letter opens with a visit from the emperor's doctor, which tells Hadrian how little time is
left. The six parts carry Latin titles; the first is taken from a short poem on the soul
attributed to Hadrian himself. The historical frame is accurate: Hadrian, born in 76 into a
family from Italica in Spain, reigned from 117 to 138, gave up some of Trajan's conquests,
travelled through almost every province, built a wall across northern Britain, loved Athens and
founded a city in Egypt in memory of Antinous, drowned in the Nile in 130. The revolt in Judaea
(132–135) darkens the last part. The book closes as the emperor, at peace, prepares to meet death.

Yourcenar added a notebook on the making of the novel. As she tells it there, she first wrote
versions in her twenties and destroyed them, and took the book up again for good after the war,
when a trunk of old papers sent from Europe gave her back a few surviving pages.

## Genre and voice

*Mémoires d'Hadrien* is a **[[historical novel]]** (*un roman historique*): a fiction set in a real
past, whose characters may be real. Its law is *la vraisemblance*: invented scenes must agree with
the documents and with what a man of that time could think. Yourcenar named her ancient sources in
her notes; her Hadrian never knows what a modern reader knows.

It is also a **[[first-person epistolary novel]]**: a single letter-writer, one addressee who never
answers, a past recalled in order from the edge of death. Compare *le roman épistolaire* (C1
honors), often a novel of many letters and voices. Don't confuse this voice with *le monologue
intérieur*: that technique, associated with Joyce and, in French, with Édouard Dujardin's novel
of 1887, follows thoughts as they come, without order or full syntax. Hadrian's reflections are
inward, but his sentences are composed, balanced and addressed to a reader.

Three words carry the book's tone. *L'hellénisme* is the love and study of Greek culture: Hadrian
speaks Greek, sees Greece as the measure of civilisation, and was nicknamed "the little Greek"
in his youth. *La sérénité*
is the calm he works towards; *la mélancolie*, the sadness of what is lost, colours every page.

## Classical prose in the 20th century

Yourcenar's sentence is the long **[[period]]** (lesson 07): it opens with subordinate clauses,
balances two or three members and closes on the main idea. Her vocabulary is precise and often
learned; her syntax keeps the literary subjunctive where most of her contemporaries had
abandoned it. Her *érudition* is vast, and an *érudit* reader enjoys checking her sources; yet
her style avoids display.

### Example 1: Reading a long period

This sentence was written for this lesson in the classical manner, not taken from Yourcenar:

> Quoique l'empereur eût beaucoup voyagé, et qu'il connût mieux que personne les frontières de l'Empire, ce fut dans un jardin de Tibur, à l'ombre, qu'il comprit enfin ce que ses conquêtes ne lui avaient pas appris.

Read it in three steps. First the concession: *Quoique … eût voyagé, et qu'il connût* (pluperfect
and imperfect subjunctive, recognition only; today: *ait voyagé, connaisse*). Then the cleft
*ce fut … que*, which puts the place in focus. The main idea comes last: what he understood.
*Although the emperor had travelled a great deal and knew the frontiers of the Empire better than
anyone, it was in a garden at Tibur, in the shade, that he at last understood what his conquests
had not taught him.*

### Example 2: The same idea in modern prose

A C2 writer can keep the rhythm without the old forms: *L'empereur avait beaucoup voyagé et
connaissait mieux que personne les frontières de l'Empire ; c'est pourtant dans un jardin de
Tibur qu'il comprit enfin ce que ses conquêtes ne lui avaient pas appris.* The concession moves
into *pourtant*, the subjunctives disappear, and the period still falls on its main idea.

## At the Académie française

On 6 March 1980 Yourcenar became the first woman elected to the Académie française, in the seat
of the writer Roger Caillois. She was received on 22 January 1981, welcomed by Jean d'Ormesson.
New members are received in a public session at which they give a *discours de réception*, their
first speech, praising their predecessor. Members are *académiciens* and *académiciennes*, and
traditionally wear *l'habit vert*, a coat embroidered with green olive branches. For
Yourcenar, Yves Saint Laurent designed a velvet cape with a shawl to cover her head. The
Académie's history and its role in the norm belong to lesson 04h2.

## Common mistakes

- *Mémoires* is masculine plural in the title (*les Mémoires d'Hadrien*): memoirs are *des
  mémoires*; *la mémoire* (A2 honors) is memory.
- *L'habit* is a garment or a costume here, not a habit (*l'habitude*, A2 honors).
- *La vraisemblance* is plausibility; *la ressemblance* is likeness.
- *L'érudition* is the noun, *érudit* the adjective (*une femme érudite*) and also a noun (*un
  érudit*, a scholar).
- *Hellénisme* takes an *h*; *Hadrien* is the French spelling of Hadrian.
- Don't call Hadrian's letter a *monologue intérieur*: it is composed and addressed to someone.

## Key points

- Yourcenar: born 8 June 1903 in Brussels, died 17 December 1987 in Maine; pen name an anagram
  of Crayencour; American citizen in 1947.
- *Mémoires d'Hadrien* (Plon, 1951): Hadrian's letter to the young Marcus Aurelius, a historical
  novel bound by vraisemblance, in the first person and in classical prose.
- Her style: long periods, precise and learned vocabulary, the imperfect subjunctive kept
  (recognition only).
- First woman elected to the Académie française (6 March 1980; received 22 January 1981).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Dossier : la traduction automatique va-t-elle remplacer les traducteurs ?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the course's capstone. It works like the written paper of the **[[DALF C2]]** (lessons 17
and 24h1): a dossier of documents on one question, and one long, engaged text written from it
with your own knowledge. The question is one that translators, publishers and the European
institutions argue about today: will **machine translation** (*la traduction automatique*,
translation produced by software without a human translator) replace human translators?

The full dossier, about 1,500 words in five documents, is in the graded task at the end of the
lesson. Here you get a guide to it: the facts, each document in brief with its key language, the
invented survey, a model plan and a checklist for the whole course. The authors, the interview
and the survey figures are invented; every fact about dates, companies and institutions is real
and dated. Translation procedures (*le calque, la modulation, le faux-sens*) belong to lesson
04h1: use them, they are not retaught here.

## The facts in brief

- *January 1954.* In New York, Georgetown University and IBM gave the first public demonstration
  of machine translation: an IBM 701 computer turned just over sixty prepared Russian sentences
  into English, with a vocabulary of 250 words and six grammar rules. The press was
  enthusiastic, and the researchers promised results within a few years.
