- *1966.* In the United States, the ALPAC committee reported that good machine translation was
  not in sight, and public funding collapsed.
- *Rules, then statistics.* For decades systems relied on hand-written rules; from the 1990s,
  statistical systems learned from millions of sentences already translated by humans. Google
  launched its translation service in 2006.
- *2016.* In September Google researchers presented a system built on a neural network (*un
  réseau de neurones*); on 15 November 2016 Google Translate applied it to eight language pairs,
  French–English among them, translating whole sentences rather than pieces.
- *2017.* Google researchers published the "Transformer" architecture, on which most of today's
  language models are built. In August a Cologne company that grew out of the online dictionary
  Linguee launched DeepL, first between seven European languages. The European Commission put its
  own system, eTranslation, into service.
- *Late 2022.* Chatbots built on large language models (*les grands modèles de langue*), which
  translate among many other tasks, opened to the general public.
- *2024.* According to the European Commission, its Directorate-General for Translation had 1,944
  staff, about 70 % of them in translation-related roles, and produced over 2.3 million pages, 30 % of
  them outsourced; eTranslation translated 763.5 million pages. The EU has 24 official
  languages.

These figures change every year: check the source's latest edition before you cite one.

## The words of the debate

*L'apprentissage automatique* (machine learning) is the family of methods by which a program
improves from examples rather than rules; *le modèle de langue* is a system trained to predict
the next word of a text. *La post-édition* is the correction of a machine translation by a
professional, *le post-éditeur* or *la post-éditrice*. *La localisation* adapts software, games
or websites to a market (dates, currencies, jokes, sometimes colours), and *le sous-titrage*
puts dialogue on screen, usually in one or two short lines. *La traductologie* is the academic study of
translation; *l'interprétariat* is the profession of the interpreter, who translates speech.
*La désintermédiation* is the removal of the middle person: here, a reader who no longer needs a
translator.

## Document 1: les repères

A chronology written for the dossier, in French, from the facts above. Note the journalistic
present for past events (*IBM présente, Google lance*), the dates at the head of each item and
the attributed figures (*selon la Commission européenne*). You may use these facts in your text,
in your own words.

## Document 2: l'entretien

```dialogue
# « Traduire, c'est d'abord lire » (entretien inventé)
Journaliste: Les logiciels de traduction ont-ils changé votre métier ?
= Have translation programs changed your work?
Claire Vasseur: Ils ont changé le marché plus que mon travail. Une machine produit une phrase correcte, rarement une phrase juste : elle ne sait pas qu'un personnage ment.
= They have changed the market more than my work. A machine produces a correct sentence, rarely a right one: it doesn't know that a character is lying.
Journaliste: Vous y voyez une menace ?
= Do you see it as a threat?
Claire Vasseur: Pour les débutants, certainement. Les petits travaux qui nous formaient sont les premiers automatisés. Mais les lecteurs savent reconnaître une voix.
= For beginners, certainly. The small jobs that trained us are the first to be automated. But readers can recognise a voice.
```

In short: an invented literary translator does not use machines for novels, finds post-editing
paid less and sometimes slower than translating, worries for beginners and for subtitling, but
saves time on checking facts and terms. Note *une phrase correcte / une phrase juste* (grammatical
versus right), the contrastive *En revanche* in the full text, and *assumer ses décisions et en
répondre* (to take responsibility for one's choices).

## Document 3: la tribune pour

*La machine ne remplace pas le traducteur, elle le libère*, by an invented head of a
localisation agency. His line: volumes are exploding (games, streaming, online trade); most of
these texts would never be translated by a human at all; post-editors check terminology, register
and the confident mistranslations of neural systems; rates per page fall, but hourly income
holds for well-equipped professionals, on condition that schools teach the tools and clients pay
for human review. Note the opening concession (*Chaque fois qu'une technique progresse, on
annonce la mort d'un métier*), the reportive conditional (*ce serait le tour des traducteurs*) and
*Encore faut-il que* + subjunctive (still, it is necessary that).

## Document 4: la tribune contre

*Ne laissons pas la langue aux machines*, by an invented conference interpreter who teaches
translation studies. Her line: a language model calculates the most probable sentence without
understanding it, and its errors are elegant, hence dangerous; disintermediation removes a
guarantor who signs and answers for the text; systems trained mostly on English push other
languages towards English turns of phrase (*adresser un problème* for *traiter un problème*);
underpaid post-editing drives out the best and discourages the young. She asks for labelling,
human translation of texts that engage lives or rights, and funded training. Note the rhetorical
question (*Qui répondra de l'erreur d'un logiciel gratuit ?*), *Il y a plus grave* (worse still),
and the closing ternary demand *Je demande que … , que … et que …* with subjunctives.

## Document 5: le sondage (chiffres inventés)

| Question (part des « oui ») | Grand public | Traducteurs |
|---|---|---|
| Utilise un outil de traduction automatique au moins une fois par mois | 64 % | 88 % |
| Ferait confiance à une notice médicale traduite sans relecture humaine | 21 % | 6 % |
| Veut qu'une traduction automatique soit toujours signalée | 72 % | 91 % |
| Pense que le métier aura disparu dans vingt ans | 38 % | 17 % |

![A grouped bar chart titled "Enquête inventée pour l'exercice". For four questions it shows the percentage answering yes among the general public and among translators. Uses a machine translation tool at least monthly: public 64 percent, translators 88 percent. Would trust an unrevised machine-translated medical leaflet: public 21 percent, translators 6 percent. Wants machine translation always labelled: public 72 percent, translators 91 percent. Thinks the profession will have disappeared in twenty years: public 38 percent, translators 17 percent.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The figures are invented. A precise C2 commentary states the contrast and its scope: *Si les
traducteurs utilisent ces outils plus que le grand public (88 % contre 64 %), ils sont aussi
nettement moins nombreux à leur faire confiance pour un texte à risque (6 % contre 21 %).* Avoid
"most people trust machines": the survey says the opposite for a medical leaflet.

### Example 1: Presenting both sides evenly

Before taking a position, state each side at its strongest, with its source:

> Pour Thomas Bérard, directeur d'une agence de localisation, la machine ne retire pas de travail aux traducteurs : elle permet de traduire des textes qui ne l'auraient jamais été. Inès Moreau, interprète de conférence, objecte qu'un logiciel ne répond pas de ses erreurs et que la désintermédiation supprime un garant.

*For Thomas Bérard, head of a localisation agency, the machine takes no work away from
translators: it makes it possible to translate texts that never would have been. Inès Moreau, a
conference interpreter, objects that software does not answer for its mistakes and that
disintermediation removes a guarantor.* Each claim is attributed, reformulated and set against
the other; nothing is copied.

### Example 2: From the dossier to your own line

An engaged C2 text then takes a qualified position, adds knowledge from outside the dossier and
says exactly how far its claim goes:

> Il serait naïf de croire que la traduction automatique épargnera tous les métiers de la langue ; il serait tout aussi faux d'annoncer leur disparition. Ce qui disparaît, c'est une certaine idée du traducteur comme simple convertisseur de mots. Ce qui reste, et qui pourrait bien gagner en valeur, c'est la responsabilité : celle de choisir, de vérifier et de signer.

*It would be naive to think that machine translation will spare every language profession; it
would be just as wrong to announce their disappearance. What is disappearing is a certain idea
of the translator as a mere converter of words. What remains, and may well gain in value, is
responsibility: that of choosing, checking and signing.* Note the paired conditionals, the
cleft *Ce qui …, c'est …* (lesson 07) and the hedge *pourrait bien*.

## The capstone task (graded)

*Le magazine culturel* Passerelles *(revue inventée) consacre un numéro au thème « Les langues à
l'heure des machines ». Vous rédigerez, au choix, un article pour ce numéro ou le discours que
vous prononcerez en ouverture d'une journée d'études organisée par une école de traduction. Vous
y répondrez à la question : la traduction automatique va-t-elle remplacer les traducteurs ? Texte
d'au moins 700 mots.*

A possible plan for the article (one of many):

1. Title and chapô; an attack (the 1954 promise of translation "within a few years").
2. What the machine has really changed: volume, speed, new uses (localisation, subtitling),
   with one example of your own.
3. What it does not do: understand, answer for a text, keep a voice; the risk of a French
   modelled on English.
4. Your qualified line: which tasks will shift, which will stay human, and on what conditions
   (labelling, training, pay).
5. A *chute* that opens: what this means for anyone who learns a language, including you.

For the speech, keep the same line but write for the ear (lesson 20): an address to the
students and teachers, an *exorde* that wins them, signposted parts, short sentences and a
*péroraison*.

```assignment
writing: fr6-h1-traduction
```

## Checklist for the whole course

| Check | Lessons |
|---|---|
| The exact word among near-synonyms and paronyms; no impropriety | 01 |
| Register held, or shifted on purpose | 02, 13–16 |
| Agreement in careful writing; numerals and invariables | 03 |
| Scope, qualifiers, no ambiguity | 04 |
| Literary tenses recognised in your sources, not needed in your text | 05, 06 |
| Rhythm, word order, adjective position, punctuation | 07 |
| Specialised formulas used only where they fit | 09–12 |
| Dossier read fast: selection, ranking, personal input | 17 |
| Genre: article (title, chapô, chute) or speech (address, exorde, péroraison) | 18, 20 |
| An engaged line, with objections answered | 21–23 |
| Length, word count, the paper's own instructions | 24, 24h1 |

## Common mistakes

- Treating the dossier as a list to summarise. At C2 you argue: select, rank and add your own
  knowledge.
- Presenting the invented survey figures as real. Say they come from the dossier, or leave them
  out.
- Copying sentences from the documents. Attribute and reformulate.
- Writing *la traduction automatique* as if it were one program. Name the kind (statistical,
  neural, a language model) or the service, with its date.
- Calques in your own French: *adresser un problème*, *faire sens* (lesson 04h1). Write *traiter
  un problème*, *avoir du sens*.
- Overclaiming: "machines understand texts", "translators will disappear". Qualify every forecast.

## Key points

- Dates: Georgetown–IBM (January 1954), ALPAC (1966), Google's neural system (2016), the
  Transformer and DeepL (2017), public chatbots on language models (late 2022).
- The dossier sets an agency head who sees the machine as a tool against an interpreter who sees
  a risk to quality, responsibility and the profession; a translator speaks from between them.
- The task: an article or a speech of at least 700 words, engaged, qualified, built from the
  dossier and from your own knowledge.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: The long written text: from dossier to article, report and speech
Speaking at C2 and the DALF C2
Honors: La langue et ses écrivains (language and its writers)

questions.stem: When was Tartuffe first performed freely, after five years of bans?
choices: On 12 May 1664, at Versailles
On 5 August 1667, under the title L'Imposteur
On 5 February 1669
On 14 October 1670, at Chambord
questions.explanation: The first version was played at Versailles on 12 May 1664 and banned at once; L'Imposteur had a single performance on 5 August 1667 and was banned again. Only on 5 February 1669 was the play performed freely. Chambord in October 1670 saw the first performance of Le Bourgeois gentilhomme.

questions.stem: Name the numbered events on this timeline of Molière's life.

image.alt: A vertical timeline from 1622 to 1680 with ten dated rows and empty boxes; five rows are numbered.

choices: Fondation de l'Illustre Théâtre
La troupe joue devant Louis XIV
Tartuffe joué à Versailles, puis interdit
Le Bourgeois gentilhomme, à Chambord
Fondation de la Comédie-Française
Élection à l'Académie française
Exil à Bruxelles
questions.explanation: In date order: 1643, the Illustre Théâtre with the Béjart family; 24 October 1658, the troupe plays before Louis XIV; 12 May 1664, Tartuffe at Versailles, then banned; 14 October 1670, Le Bourgeois gentilhomme at Chambord; 1680, the Comédie-Française, seven years after Molière's death. Molière was never a member of the Académie française, and exile in Brussels belongs to Hugo (lesson 91).

questions.stem: In Les Précieuses ridicules, the two young women take two valets for noblemen. What does French call this comic device?
choices: un vaudeville
une tirade
un parterre
un quiproquo
questions.explanation: Un quiproquo is a case of mistaken identity: one person taken for another. Le vaudeville (B2) is a light comedy genre, la tirade (B2) a long speech in a play, and le parterre the standing audience of a 17th-century theatre.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about préciosité are true, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: The marquise de Rambouillet received guests in her salon from about 1608.
Madeleine de Scudéry's novel Clélie contains the Carte de Tendre.
Somaize published a satirical Dictionnaire des précieuses in 1660.
The précieuses founded the Académie française to defend their jargon.
Molière said in his preface that he mocked all refinement, true or false.
questions.explanation: The Rambouillet salon (from about 1608), Scudéry's Clélie (1654–1660) with its map of Tendre and Somaize's satirical dictionary (1660) are all in the lesson. The salons did not found the Académie, and Molière's preface says the opposite of the last choice: he claimed to mock only clumsy imitations of refinement.

questions.stem: In a 17th-century text, "un honnête homme" most likely means…
choices: a man who never lies
a cultivated, moderate man at ease in society
a devout man who goes to church
a man of the middle class
questions.explanation: L'honnête homme is the century's social ideal (Faret, 1630): cultivated without pedantry, moderate, graceful in conversation. The modern sense of honnête, honest (A2), is a trap here. A devout man is un dévot; the middle class is la bourgeoisie.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: Le Bourgeois gentilhomme est une ___ : les chants et les danses y font partie de l'intrigue.
questions.explanation: Une comédie-ballet (plural les comédies-ballets) is a comedy framed and linked by songs and dances that belong to the plot. Molière invented the form with Les Fâcheux (1661); Le Bourgeois gentilhomme (1670) had music by Lully.

questions.topic: Classical French and words that changed
questions.stem: Match each word to the meaning it often had in 17th-century French.
choices: To stun, as if struck by thunder
Torture, torment
To cast a spell on
That inspires fear
To bore
questions.explanation: Étonner comes from Latin extonare (struck by thunder); la gêne first meant torture, then torment and painful constraint; charmer meant to bewitch (un charme was a spell); formidable meant fearsome (Latin formidare, to dread). Today they mean to surprise, discomfort, to delight and terrific. "To bore" is the modern sense of ennuyer, not a classical one.

questions.topic: Classical French and words that changed
questions.stem: A sentence written in the classical style reads: "Une armée formidable s'avançait vers la ville." What does "formidable" mean here?
choices: Terrific, wonderful
Enormous in number
Fearsome, dreadful
Well organised
questions.explanation: In classical French formidable keeps its Latin sense, that which inspires fear: a fearsome army. The modern French sense, terrific, would make no sense with an army bearing down on a town. "Enormous" is not the meaning of the word, even if a fearsome army may be large.

questions.stem: Listen. What happened during the fourth performance of Le Malade imaginaire?

audio.text: Le 17 février 1673, pendant la quatrième représentation du Malade imaginaire, Molière est pris d'un malaise. On le ramène chez lui, rue de Richelieu, où il meurt le soir même.

choices: Molière was arrested on the archbishop's orders
Molière was taken ill and died at home that evening
The play was banned after the performance
Louis XIV attended and granted Molière a pension
questions.explanation: The audio says that Molière was taken ill during the fourth performance, on 17 February 1673, was brought home to the rue de Richelieu and died that same evening. Nothing in it concerns a ban, an arrest or a pension.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the Tartuffe quarrel in order.
choices: The first version is played at Versailles and banned at once
L'Imposteur has a single performance and is banned
The archbishop of Paris forbids the faithful to see or read the play
The play is performed freely at last
questions.explanation: 12 May 1664: Versailles, then the ban; 5 August 1667: L'Imposteur, played once and banned; then the archbishop's prohibition, which targeted that revised version; 5 February 1669: the play is performed freely.

questions.stem: In a 17th-century theatre, who stood in "le parterre"?
choices: The nobles, on chairs placed on the stage
The actors waiting to go on
The musicians of the comédie-ballet
Spectators, mostly men, on the cheapest standing floor in front of the stage
questions.explanation: Le parterre was the floor in front of the stage, where spectators, mostly men, stood and paid the lowest price; it judged plays loudly. Nobles sat in boxes or even on stage. Today un parterre is mainly a flower bed, and the stalls are l'orchestre.

questions.topic: Classical French and words that changed
questions.stem: In classical French you may read "Je le veux voir." How does today's French say it?
choices: Je veux le voir.
Je le vois vouloir.
Je veux voir le.
Je le voulais voir.
questions.explanation: Classical French often put the object pronoun before the verb that governs the infinitive (je le veux voir); modern French puts it before the infinitive it belongs to: je veux le voir. Je le voulais voir changes the tense, je le vois vouloir means something else, and je veux voir le is not French.

questions.stem: In Le Misanthrope, which character embodies the moderation of the honnête homme?
choices: Alceste, who demands total sincerity
Célimène, who delights in salon gossip
Philinte, who accepts people as they are
Tartuffe, who passes for a saint
questions.explanation: Philinte, Alceste's friend, accepts the polite conventions of society: he is the honnête homme of the play. Alceste is the misanthrope who rejects them, and Célimène the young widow he loves. Tartuffe belongs to another play.

questions.stem: Today any hypocrite can be called by the name of Molière's false devout. Type the common noun: C'est un vrai ___ : il prêche la vertu et n'en pratique aucune.
questions.explanation: Un tartuffe (lower case as a common noun) is a hypocrite, after the title character of Tartuffe (1664–1669). The behaviour is la tartufferie. Un faux dévot would also describe him, but the blank takes one word.

questions.topic: Classical French and words that changed
questions.stem: What does the phrase "la langue de Molière" mean?
choices: The French of the 17th century only
The jargon of the précieuses
The verse of classical comedy
French, named after its most famous author
questions.explanation: La langue de Molière is a periphrasis for the French language as a whole, as "the language of Shakespeare" is for English. It does not mean that Molière fixed the language or that it is limited to his century; it can be ironic (il maltraite la langue de Molière).

questions.stem: Where and when was Les Misérables first published?
choices: In Paris, in 1845
On Guernsey, in 1856
In Paris, in 1870
In Brussels, in 1862
questions.explanation: Les Misérables was published in 1862 by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven et Cie, a Brussels firm; the first volumes went on sale in early April. 1845 is when Hugo began Les Misères; 1856 is Les Contemplations; 1870 is his return from exile.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this map of Hugo's exile.

image.alt: A simplified map of the Channel area with four numbered places linked by arrows: red arrows for the route into exile and a green arrow for the return.

choices: Paris
Bruxelles
Jersey
Guernesey
Genève
Le Havre
questions.explanation: Hugo left Paris (1) for Brussels (2) in December 1851, moved to Jersey (3) in August 1852 and, expelled from Jersey, to Guernsey (4) in October 1855; the green arrow is his return to Paris on 5 September 1870. Jersey is the larger island, closer to the Normandy coast; Guernsey lies further west and north.

questions.stem: Which word fits best? "Banni par un décret de janvier 1852, Hugo vécut dix-neuf ans en ___."
choices: proscrit
bagnard
titi
forçat
questions.explanation: Un proscrit has been banished by an official act, often for political reasons: exactly Hugo's case. Un bagnard and un forçat are convicts at hard labour, and un titi is a cheeky Paris street kid.

questions.stem: Put the stages of Hugo's exile in order.
choices: He reaches Brussels after the coup d'État
He settles on Jersey
He is expelled from Jersey and moves to Guernsey
He refuses the emperor's amnesty
He returns to Paris after the Republic is proclaimed
questions.explanation: December 1851 Brussels; August 1852 Jersey; October 1855 Guernsey (Hauteville House); 1859 the refused amnesty; 5 September 1870 the return, the day after the Republic was proclaimed.

questions.stem: In the reading, why had Jean Valjean spent nineteen years in the bagne?
choices: He had killed a gendarme
He had stolen a bishop's silver
He had fought on a barricade
He had stolen a loaf of bread, then tried several times to escape
questions.explanation: The reading says he had stolen a loaf of bread, then tried several times to escape, which lengthened his sentence. The bishop's silver comes after his release, and the barricade of 1832 much later; he never kills a gendarme.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about Les Misérables are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Javert had known Valjean in the bagne.
Gavroche is killed at a barricade in June 1832.
Valjean carries the wounded Marius through the sewers.
Cosette is the Thénardiers' daughter.
Fantine marries Marius at the end.
questions.explanation: Javert knew Valjean at Toulon and hunts him; Gavroche, the Thénardiers' son, is shot at the foot of the barricade in June 1832; Valjean saves Marius through the sewers. Cosette is Fantine's daughter, left with the Thénardiers, and it is Cosette who loves Marius; Fantine dies early in the novel.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: A penal colony with hard labour
First a galley slave, then any convict
The criminal underworld as a whole
The slums and the people who live there on crime
A banished political opponent
questions.explanation: Le bagne is the institution, le forçat the convict (first on the galleys), la pègre a collective noun for criminals, les bas-fonds (plural only) the lowest districts of a city. A banished political opponent is un proscrit.

questions.stem: Complete the old name for slang: au XIXe siècle, on appelait aussi l'argot « la langue ___ ».
questions.explanation: La langue verte was a common 19th-century name for slang, used in the titles of dictionaries of the 1860s. It sounds old-fashioned today; l'argot (C1 honors) is the usual word.

questions.stem: What does Hugo argue in the book on argot in the fourth part of Les Misérables?
choices: That argot is a passing fashion of young people
That argot is the language of misery as well as crime, and worth a novelist's study
That argot should be banned from literature
That argot was invented by the police to catch thieves
questions.explanation: Hugo answers critics who had attacked him for using argot: he treats it as a real language, born of poverty as much as of crime and constantly changing, and claims the novelist's right, even duty, to study it. He defends its place in literature rather than banning it.

questions.stem: Listen. What happened in June 1832, according to the speaker?

audio.text: Après les funérailles du général Lamarque, en juin 1832, de jeunes républicains dressent des barricades dans le centre de Paris. L'insurrection est écrasée en deux jours. C'est ce moment que Victor Hugo a choisi pour le grand épisode de son roman.

choices: A republican rising, crushed in two days, after a general's funeral
The revolution that overthrew King Charles X
The coup d'État of Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte
A strike of the workers of Montreuil-sur-Mer
questions.explanation: The audio describes the insurrection that followed General Lamarque's funeral in June 1832, when young republicans built barricades and were crushed in two days. The revolution of 1830 and the coup of December 1851 are other events; there is no strike in the audio.

questions.stem: Which of these words of underworld origin is now standard French, usable in a formal text?
choices: la tronche
le flic
cambrioler
le fric
questions.explanation: Cambrioler, traced to an argot word for a room, is now standard (un cambriolage, un cambrioleur). La tronche (face, head) and le flic (policeman) remain informal, and le fric (money) is informal too.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence in neutral French by replacing only the informal noun: "Il a fait une drôle de tronche en lisant la lettre."
accept: Il a fait une drôle de tête en lisant la lettre
Il a fait une drôle de mine en lisant la lettre
Il a fait une drôle de figure en lisant la lettre
Il a fait un drôle de visage en lisant la lettre
Il a fait une drôle de grimace en lisant la lettre
questions.explanation: La tronche is informal for the face or head. Neutral equivalents: une drôle de tête (the usual phrase), une drôle de mine, une drôle de figure, une drôle de grimace (a slightly different nuance: a grimace), or un drôle de visage (masculine, so un drôle de). The rest of the sentence stays as it is.

questions.stem: Who is Gavroche in Les Misérables?
choices: Valjean's adopted son
A police inspector
The bishop who forgives Valjean
A Paris street urchin, son of the Thénardiers
questions.explanation: Gavroche is the Thénardiers' neglected son, who lives in the streets and is shot at the foot of the barricade: the model of le gamin de Paris, informally le titi parisien. Valjean adopts Cosette, not Gavroche; Javert is the inspector.

questions.stem: Where does the word "barricade" most probably come from?
choices: From la barre, an iron bar across a door
From la barrique, a barrel, which Parisians filled with earth to block streets
From the name of an 18th-century engineer
From the English word barrier
questions.explanation: La barricade is usually traced to la barrique, a barrel: Parisians blocked streets with barrels filled with earth as early as the 16th century. The lesson mentions no engineer, and the French word is not borrowed from English.

questions.stem: Why can Les Misérables be called a roman-fleuve?
choices: Because it is set mainly on the banks of the Seine
Because it was first published in serial form in a newspaper
Because it is very long, filled ten volumes and stops the story for long digressions
Because Javert drowns himself in a river
questions.explanation: Un roman-fleuve is a very long novel or cycle, often in several volumes, that makes room for digressions: Les Misérables filled ten volumes and stops for Waterloo, convents, the sewers and argot. The Seine and Javert's death are details of the plot, not the reason for the label.

questions.stem: What happened on 6 March 1980?
choices: Mémoires d'Hadrien was published
Yourcenar received the prix Femina
Yourcenar became the first woman elected to the Académie française
Yourcenar gave her discours de réception
questions.explanation: On 6 March 1980 Yourcenar was elected to the Académie française, the first woman to be so; she was received, with her discours de réception, on 22 January 1981. Mémoires d'Hadrien came out in 1951, and the prix Femina was for L'Œuvre au noir in 1968.

questions.stem: Name the numbered events on this timeline of Marguerite Yourcenar's life.

image.alt: A vertical timeline from 1903 to 1987 with eight dated rows and empty boxes; five rows are numbered.

choices: Naissance à Bruxelles
Mémoires d'Hadrien (Plon)
L'Œuvre au noir, prix Femina
Première femme élue à l'Académie française
Mort dans le Maine
Prix Goncourt
Retour définitif en Belgique
questions.explanation: 1903, birth in Brussels; 1951, Mémoires d'Hadrien (Plon); 1968, L'Œuvre au noir and the prix Femina; 1980, the first woman elected to the Académie française; 1987, death in Bar Harbor, Maine. She never won the Goncourt and never moved back to Belgium: she lived on Mount Desert Island from 1950.

questions.stem: What form does Mémoires d'Hadrien take?
choices: A long letter from the dying emperor to the young Marcus Aurelius
An exchange of letters between Hadrian and Antinous
A diary kept by Hadrian's doctor
A third-person chronicle of Hadrian's reign
questions.explanation: The novel is one long letter from Hadrian, past sixty and ill, to the young Marcus Aurelius: a first-person epistolary novel with a single voice and an addressee who never answers. It opens with the doctor's visit, but the doctor is not the narrator.

questions.stem: In the reading, "Il fallait que le lecteur oubliât la romancière." What is the everyday modern equivalent of "oubliât"?
choices: oublie
oubliait
oubliera
ait oublié
questions.explanation: Oubliât is the imperfect subjunctive (lesson 06), recognition only. After a past main verb, modern French uses the present subjunctive for a simultaneous or later action: il fallait que le lecteur oublie. Oubliait is the indicative imperfect, wrong after il fallait que; ait oublié would mean the forgetting was already done.

questions.topic: The historical novel and its voice
questions.stem: Which of these describe how Yourcenar wrote Mémoires d'Hadrien, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: She read the ancient historians on Hadrian.
She invented the voice of the emperor.
She kept invented scenes consistent with the documents.
She wrote it in the form of an interior monologue without full syntax.
She wrote it in a single year, in 1951.
questions.explanation: Yourcenar read the ancient sources, invented Hadrian's voice and kept to la vraisemblance. The letter is composed and balanced, not an interior monologue, and the book took decades: drafts in her twenties, destroyed, then taken up again for good after the war.

questions.topic: The historical novel and its voice
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: The love and study of Greek culture
A calm that has been worked towards
Agreement with what is plausible or documented
Vast and detailed learning
Physical likeness between two people
questions.explanation: Hadrian's hellénisme, his sérénité before death and Yourcenar's érudition are all in the lesson; la vraisemblance is the law of the historical novel. A physical likeness is la ressemblance, a common confusion with vraisemblance.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: Les membres de l'Académie française portent traditionnellement l'___ vert.
questions.explanation: L'habit vert (masculine) is the embroidered coat of the members of the Académie française; endosser l'habit vert means to enter the Académie. Here habit means a garment, not a habit (l'habitude).

questions.topic: The historical novel and its voice
questions.stem: Why is Hadrian's letter not a "monologue intérieur"?
choices: Because it is written in the third person
Because it is composed, balanced and addressed to a reader, not a flow of raw thoughts
Because it contains no reflections on the emperor's feelings
Because interior monologue did not exist before 1951
questions.explanation: Le monologue intérieur follows thoughts as they come, without order or full syntax (Dujardin, 1887; Joyce). Hadrian's reflections are inward, but his sentences are composed and addressed to Marcus Aurelius. The letter is in the first person and full of feelings, and the technique dates from the late 19th century.

questions.stem: Put these events of Yourcenar's life in order.
choices: She translates Virginia Woolf's The Waves into French
She leaves for the United States with Grace Frick
Mémoires d'Hadrien is published by Plon
L'Œuvre au noir wins the prix Femina
She is received at the Académie française
questions.explanation: 1937 the translation of The Waves; 1939 the departure for the United States; 1951 Mémoires d'Hadrien; 1968 L'Œuvre au noir and the prix Femina; 22 January 1981 the reception at the Académie, after the election of March 1980.

questions.stem: Listen. Who welcomed Marguerite Yourcenar at the Académie française?

audio.text: Le 22 janvier 1981, sous la Coupole, Marguerite Yourcenar est reçue à l'Académie française. C'est Jean d'Ormesson qui prononce le discours d'accueil. Elle succède à l'écrivain Roger Caillois.

choices: Roger Caillois
Jean d'Ormesson
Yves Saint Laurent
Grace Frick
questions.explanation: The audio says that Jean d'Ormesson gave the welcoming speech on 22 January 1981. Roger Caillois is the predecessor whose seat she took, Yves Saint Laurent designed her outfit, and Grace Frick, her companion, had died in 1979.

questions.topic: The historical novel and its voice
questions.stem: Which sentence uses "vraisemblance" correctly?
choices: La vraisemblance entre la mère et la fille est frappante.
Il a acheté une vraisemblance au marché.
Elle a agi en toute vraisemblance de cause.
Ce détail nuit à la vraisemblance du récit : aucun Romain n'aurait pensé ainsi.
questions.explanation: La vraisemblance is plausibility: a detail that no Roman could have thought harms the story's plausibility. A likeness between mother and daughter is la ressemblance; the last two sentences are nonsense (the set phrase is en connaissance de cause).

questions.stem: Which phrase is correct?
choices: une femme érudition
une femme érudit
une femme érudite
une érudite femme savante
questions.explanation: Érudit is an adjective with the feminine érudite: une femme érudite. L'érudition is the noun (son érudition est immense). The last choice piles up two adjectives in an unnatural order and repeats the idea.

questions.stem: Rewrite in modern French, keeping "quoique": "Quoique l'empereur eût beaucoup voyagé"
questions.explanation: Eût voyagé is the pluperfect subjunctive, recognition only. After quoique, modern French uses the past subjunctive for an earlier action: quoique l'empereur ait beaucoup voyagé. Avait voyagé is wrong after quoique, which takes the subjunctive.

questions.stem: Which fact about the historical Hadrian appears in the lesson?
choices: He conquered Mesopotamia and kept it
He was born in Rome in 117
Antinous, the young Greek he loved, drowned in the Nile in 130
He was succeeded directly by Marcus Aurelius
questions.explanation: Antinous drowned in the Nile in 130, and Hadrian founded a city in his memory. Hadrian gave up some of Trajan's conquests rather than adding to them; he was born in 76 and reigned from 117; Marcus Aurelius was adopted by Hadrian's successor, Antoninus, and reigned after him.

questions.stem: Where does the name "Yourcenar" come from?
choices: From her mother's family
From a village in Flanders
From a character in one of her novels
From an anagram of her family name, Crayencour, less one c
questions.explanation: Yourcenar is an anagram of Crayencour less one c; she made it her legal name in 1947. Her mother, Fernande de Cartier de Marchienne, died ten days after her birth.

questions.stem: What did the Georgetown–IBM demonstration of January 1954 show?
choices: A computer translating whole books from French into English
The first neural network for translation
A speech translated live at the United Nations
An IBM 701 translating just over sixty prepared Russian sentences into English
questions.explanation: In January 1954 in New York, an IBM 701 translated just over sixty prepared Russian sentences into English, with a 250-word vocabulary and six grammar rules. Neural translation came in 2016; no whole books or live speeches were involved.

questions.stem: Put these milestones in order.
choices: The Georgetown–IBM demonstration
The ALPAC report
Google launches its translation service
Google Translate switches eight language pairs to a neural system
DeepL is launched
Chatbots built on large language models open to the public
questions.explanation: 1954 Georgetown–IBM; 1966 ALPAC; 2006 Google's service; 15 November 2016 the neural switch; August 2017 DeepL; late 2022 the public chatbots.

questions.stem: What is "la post-édition"?
choices: A second edition of a printed book
The correction of a machine translation by a professional
Translating a text after it has been published
The subtitling of a film after its release
questions.explanation: La post-édition (also postédition) is the revision of a machine translation by a professional, le post-éditeur or la post-éditrice. A second edition is une deuxième édition or une réédition; subtitling is le sous-titrage.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: Adapting software or a game to a market
Putting dialogue on screen in short lines
The profession of translating speech
The academic study of translation
Removing the go-between
Finding a word in a dictionary
questions.explanation: La localisation adapts language, dates, currencies and culture; le sous-titrage condenses dialogue into one or two short lines; l'interprétariat is the interpreter's profession; la traductologie is translation studies; la désintermédiation removes the intermediary. Looking a word up has no special name here.

questions.stem: Look at the invented survey. Which statements does it support? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A grouped bar chart of invented survey results for the general public and translators on four questions about machine translation.

choices: Translators use machine translation tools more often than the general public.
Translators are less willing than the public to trust an unrevised machine-translated medical leaflet.
Most of the general public would trust an unrevised machine-translated medical leaflet.
Most translators think their profession will have disappeared in twenty years.
Both groups mostly want machine translation to be labelled.
questions.explanation: 88 % of translators against 64 % of the public use the tools monthly; 6 % of translators against 21 % of the public would trust an unrevised medical leaflet, so only a minority of the public would; 72 % and 91 % want labelling; only 17 % of translators expect the profession to vanish. The figures are invented for the exercise.

questions.stem: What is the central argument of the opinion piece in favour of machine translation (Document 3)?
choices: Machines already translate literature better than people
Translators should refuse to use machines
Most texts the machine translates would never have been translated by a human, and human review still adds value
Post-editing should be paid less than translation
questions.explanation: The agency head argues that volumes are exploding, that the machine translates what no one would have paid a human to translate, and that post-editors add value by checking terms, register and errors. He admits that rates per page fall, but he does not say post-editing should be paid less; he asks clients to pay for human review.

questions.stem: What does the interpreter in Document 4 ask for?
choices: A ban on machine translation tools
Labelling of machine translations, human translation for texts that engage lives or rights, and funded training
The end of the European Union's translation service
Lower rates for post-editing
questions.explanation: She says explicitly that she does not ask for a ban: she wants machine translations labelled, texts that engage lives or rights translated and signed by humans, and training funded. Nothing in her text targets the EU service or asks for lower rates.

questions.stem: Complete: Un ___ de langue prédit le mot suivant d'un texte.
questions.explanation: Le modèle de langue (plural les modèles de langue) is a system trained to predict the next word of a text; un grand modèle de langue is a large language model.

questions.stem: Rewrite without the anglicism, keeping the rest of the sentence: "Nous devons adresser ce problème rapidement."
accept: Nous devons traiter ce problème rapidement
Nous devons régler ce problème rapidement
Nous devons résoudre ce problème rapidement
Nous devons aborder ce problème rapidement
Nous devons nous attaquer à ce problème rapidement
Nous devons nous occuper de ce problème rapidement
Nous devons nous pencher sur ce problème rapidement
Nous devons gérer ce problème rapidement
questions.explanation: Adresser un problème is a calque of English "to address a problem", which usage guides criticise. Write traiter, régler, résoudre, aborder, gérer, s'occuper de, se pencher sur or s'attaquer à ce problème, depending on the nuance (aborder: to start dealing with; résoudre: to solve).

questions.stem: Listen. What share of its translation work did the Commission's translation service outsource in 2024?

audio.text: Journaliste : En 2024, la direction générale de la traduction a produit plus de deux millions trois cent mille pages. Experte : Oui, et elle en a confié trente pour cent à des prestataires extérieurs ; le reste a été traduit en interne.

choices: About 10 %
Almost all of it
questions.explanation: The expert says 30 % was entrusted to outside providers, the rest done in-house. 70 % is the share of the service's staff in translation-related work, a different figure from the same 2024 brochure.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes the invented survey accurately and precisely?
choices: Les traducteurs rejettent la traduction automatique.
Le grand public fait confiance aux machines pour les textes médicaux.
Si les traducteurs utilisent davantage ces outils que le grand public, ils sont nettement moins nombreux à s'y fier pour un texte à risque.
Tout le monde pense que le métier de traducteur va disparaître.
questions.explanation: The accurate sentence states the contrast and its scope: translators use the tools more (88 % against 64 %) but trust them less for a risky text (6 % against 21 %). Translators do not reject the tools (they use them most); only 21 % of the public would trust an unrevised medical leaflet; and 38 % and 17 % are far from "everyone".

questions.stem: In the capstone task, how should you use the survey figures?
choices: As real national statistics, without naming the source
Only by copying the table into your text
Attributed to the dossier, or not at all, since they are invented
Not at all: a C2 text must not contain figures
questions.explanation: The survey is invented for the exercise: you may use it as part of the dossier, saying where it comes from, but never present it as real. Copying the table adds nothing, and figures are welcome in a C2 text when their source is clear.

questions.stem: In the model sentence "Ce qui reste, et qui pourrait bien gagner en valeur, c'est la responsabilité", what does "pourrait bien" do?
choices: It hedges the claim: a likely possibility, not a certainty
It expresses an order
It states a proven fact
It expresses a wish in the past
questions.explanation: Pourrait bien + infinitive presents something as quite possible without asserting it: a hedge that keeps the claim exact, as a C2 text should. A certainty would be the indicative (gagne en valeur); there is no order or past wish.

questions.stem: What did Google announce on 15 November 2016?
choices: The launch of DeepL
The first translation of Russian sentences by computer
The end of Google Translate
A neural translation system for eight language pairs, French–English among them
questions.explanation: On 15 November 2016 Google Translate applied its neural system to eight language pairs, including French–English, translating whole sentences at a time. DeepL is a different company (August 2017), and the Russian sentences belong to 1954.

questions.stem: Where does DeepL come from, according to the lesson?
choices: From a Cologne company that grew out of the online dictionary Linguee
From the European Commission's translation service
From Georgetown University
From a Paris translation agency
questions.explanation: DeepL was launched in August 2017 by a Cologne company that grew out of Linguee, first between seven European languages. The Commission's own system is eTranslation; Georgetown belongs to the 1954 experiment.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les météorologues annoncent un orage ___ sur la côte."
choices: imminent
éminent
immanent
émanant
questions.explanation: Imminent = about to happen. Éminent (distinguished) describes a person: un éminent spécialiste. Immanent (inherent) and émanant (coming from) are real words with other meanings.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les cambrioleurs sont entrés par ___ dans la pharmacie."
choices: infraction
effraction
réfraction
diffraction
questions.explanation: Entrer par effraction = to break in, by forcing a door or a window. L'infraction is any offence against the law; réfraction and diffraction are terms of physics.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il est ___ arriver à midi, mais son train a du retard."
choices: sensé
sencé
censé
censée
questions.explanation: Être censé + infinitive = to be supposed to. Sensé means sensible (une remarque sensée). Censée would agree with a feminine subject, but il is masculine; sencé is not a word.

questions.stem: Complete: "Selon l'enquête, l'accusé aurait ___ le crime en pleine nuit."
choices: perpétué
perpétrer
perpétuer
perpétré
questions.explanation: Perpétrer is used for a crime; perpétuer means to carry on (a tradition). After aurait, the past participle is needed (aurait perpétré), not an infinitive.

questions.stem: What does "dans toutes les acceptions du terme" mean?
choices: with every acceptance of the term
in every agreement of the contract
in every sense of the word
with every approval of the jury
questions.explanation: L'acception is the sense a dictionary gives a word. Its paronym l'acceptation means acceptance (l'acceptation d'une offre).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses recouvrer correctly?
choices: Elle a recouvré la vue après l'opération.
Il a recouvré le canapé d'un tissu bleu.
Le brouillard a recouvré toute la vallée.
Nous avons recouvré la table d'une nappe.
questions.explanation: Recouvrer = to regain or to collect (recouvrer la vue, la santé, une créance). To cover is recouvrir, whose participle is recouvert: il a recouvert le canapé, le brouillard a recouvert la vallée, nous avons recouvert la table.

questions.stem: Which verb fits best? "Depuis son arrestation, il ___ son innocence devant toutes les caméras."
choices: marmonne
bredouille
susurre
clame
questions.explanation: Clamer son innocence = to proclaim it loudly and publicly; devant toutes les caméras confirms the public, insistent manner. Marmonner (mumble), bredouiller (stammer in embarrassment) and susurrer (murmur softly) contradict it.

questions.stem: Which verb best describes passengers grumbling under their breath about a late train?
choices: clamer
maugréer
susurrer
ergoter
questions.explanation: Maugréer = to mutter with discontent (les voyageurs maugréaient contre le retard). Ergoter is to quibble over details, clamer to proclaim loudly, susurrer to murmur softly.

questions.stem: Which sentence would many usage guides criticise?
choices: Il faut pallier à ce manque de personnel.
Il faut pallier ce manque de personnel.
Il faut remédier à ce manque de personnel.
Il faut combler ce manque de personnel.
questions.explanation: Pallier takes a direct object (pallier un manque). Pallier à, probably modelled on remédier à, is widespread but criticised by many usage guides. Remédier à and combler are correct.

questions.stem: In its traditional sense, which careful usage keeps, what is "un raisonnement conséquent"?
choices: a long, substantial piece of reasoning
a consistent, logical piece of reasoning
a piece of reasoning with serious consequences
a piece of reasoning that comes afterwards
questions.explanation: Conséquent traditionally means consistent, logical (un homme conséquent acts in line with his ideas). The sense "large, substantial" (une somme conséquente) is common but criticised by many usage guides, which prefer considérable or important.

questions.stem: Which word means "long-winded"?
choices: prolifique
prodigue
prolixe
prolétaire
questions.explanation: Prolixe = long-winded, wordy (un orateur prolixe). Prolifique = productive (une romancière prolifique); prodigue = wasteful, lavish.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2 of the reading, why does M. Royer write to the paper?
choices: The paper named the wrong pharmacy.
The paper called a burglary an offence against parking rules.
The paper forgot to say when the burglary happened.
The paper wrote that a burglar entered "par infraction" instead of "par effraction".
questions.explanation: Il a raison : on entre par effraction. The columnist adds that the wrong word made the sentence say nothing: une infraction is any breach of the law.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of the reading, what does the columnist find "savoureux" about the "éminent danger" mistake?
choices: The mayor wrote in to complain about the mistake.
The translator who noticed it had made the same mistake.
By writing éminent, the paper praised the plan it meant to criticise.
The word imminent has disappeared from everyday French.
questions.explanation: Éminent is praise (distinguished), so the paper, sans le vouloir, a couvert d'éloges le projet qu'il voulait critiquer.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4 of the reading, what is the columnist's position on conséquent meaning "large"?
choices: A newspaper should prefer considérable or important, although the use is spreading.
The use is simply wrong and will never be accepted.
The use is now standard, so the reader's complaint is pointless.
The paper should have used prolixe instead.
questions.explanation: Je lui donne raison, avec une nuance: many usage guides criticise the use, it is spreading, and caution (la prudence) dictates considérable or important in a newspaper.

questions.stem: Listen to the reader's phone call to the paper. What is his attitude?

audio.text: Lecteur : Bonjour, je vous appelle au sujet de l'article de ce matin. Vous écrivez que le maire a « initié » le projet de tramway. Bon, je ne vais pas ergoter, tout le monde comprend. Mais enfin, on initie quelqu'un à quelque chose ; un projet, on le lance.

choices: He is furious and demands a correction on the front page.
He praises the article's precise vocabulary.
He says he did not understand the article.
He objects to the word, while admitting that its meaning is clear.
questions.explanation: Je ne vais pas ergoter, tout le monde comprend: he concedes the meaning is clear. Mais enfin, on initie quelqu'un à quelque chose: he still objects to initier for "to launch", a use many usage guides criticise.

questions.stem: Listen to two sub-editors. Why does Marc object to Lina's headline?

audio.text: Lina : Je mets « Le ministre bredouille » en titre. Marc : Bredouille ? Il a lu son texte sans une hésitation. Écris plutôt qu'il a éludé la question.

choices: Bredouiller is too informal for a headline.
Bredouiller suggests an embarrassment the minister did not show.
Bredouiller is a paronym that means to confuse.
The minister in fact shouted his answer.
questions.explanation: Il a lu son texte sans une hésitation: bredouiller (to stammer from embarrassment) gives him a state of mind he didn't show. Éluder describes only what he did.

questions.stem: Listen to the radio chronicle. What is the chronicler's attitude to the experts?

audio.text: Chroniqueuse : Chaque année, les mêmes experts nous rabâchent que la langue française se meurt. Chaque année, elle se porte à merveille. Je propose qu'on les laisse ressasser entre eux.

choices: Ironic: she finds their warnings tiresome and wrong.
Worried: she shares their fear for the language.
Neutral: she simply reports their view.
Admiring: she praises their persistence.
questions.explanation: Rabâcher (to keep repeating tiresomely) and the contrast elle se porte à merveille show that she thinks they are wrong; laissons-les ressasser entre eux dismisses them with irony.

questions.stem: Replace the criticised verb with a safe one, keeping the tense: "Les techniciens ont solutionné le problème en une heure." → "Les techniciens ont ___ le problème en une heure."
questions.explanation: Résoudre (participle résolu) is the verb usage guides prefer to solutionner; régler un problème is also correct.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence without the construction usage guides criticise: "Cette aide pallie à l'absence de transports."
accept: Cette aide pallie l'absence de transports
Cette aide remédie à l'absence de transports
Cette aide compense l'absence de transports
Cette aide supplée à l'absence de transports
Cette aide supplée l'absence de transports
Cette aide comble l'absence de transports
questions.explanation: Pallier takes a direct object: pallier l'absence de transports. Remédier à (which does take à) compenser, combler or suppléer (à) keep the meaning too.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: a liking, a tendency
a slope, an angle
a secret agreement
a crash
acceptance
questions.explanation: Inclination / inclinaison and collusion / collision are paronyms. Acceptance is l'acceptation, which is not in the list.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Le différend entre les deux pays porte sur la frontière.
Nul n'est censé ignorer la loi.
Voilà une proposition censée.
Ils ont un avis différend.
Elle a recouvré la santé.
questions.explanation: Le différend (noun, -end) is a dispute; censé + infinitive = supposed to; recouvrer la santé = to regain one's health. A sensible proposal is une proposition sensée, and the adjective is différent: un avis différent.

questions.stem: Name the word missing from each box of the paronym chart.

image.alt: Six boxes in three pairs, each with a French definition and an example phrase; the word at the top of each box is missing.

choices: éminent
imminent
l'effraction
l'infraction
perpétrer
perpétuer
prodigue
l'acception
questions.explanation: Read the definition and the example: distingué goes with éminent, sur le point d'arriver with imminent, forcer une entrée with l'effraction, une violation de la loi with l'infraction, commettre (un crime) with perpétrer, faire durer with perpétuer.

questions.stem: Give the noun, with its article, for a dispute between two parties (it sounds like the adjective "différent").
questions.explanation: Le différend is spelt -end: un différend commercial. For a dispute in court, le litige (B2) is the legal word.

questions.stem: Which register is this sentence in? "L'horodateur étant hors d'usage, un avis de paiement a néanmoins été établi à l'encontre de l'intéressé."
choices: soutenu
administratif
courant
familier
questions.explanation: The participle clause, the passive with no agent, à l'encontre de and l'intéressé hide the person: the administrative register. The soutenu would keep a personal voice (je n'en ai pas moins reçu un avis).

questions.stem: In a letter that says "Nous vous avisons que votre demande a été rejetée", who is "nous"?
choices: several officials who signed together
the writer and the reader together
the institution, speaking through one official
the writer as a literary narrator
questions.explanation: The administration's nous is a voice, not a group: one official signs, but the institution speaks. The passive (a été rejetée) also hides who decided.

questions.stem: What does "Le préfet a pris congé de ses hôtes" mean?
choices: The prefect took a day off from his hosts.
The prefect dismissed his guests.
The prefect thanked his hosts.
The prefect took leave of his hosts.
questions.explanation: Prendre congé de quelqu'un is the formal way to say goodbye and leave. Un jour de congé is a day off, a different sense of congé.

questions.stem: Which is the neutral equivalent of the informal "se gourer"?
choices: se tirer
se goinfrer
se tromper
se barrer
questions.explanation: Se gourer (informal) = se tromper (neutral). Se tirer and se barrer mean to leave; se goinfrer means to stuff your face.

questions.stem: What does "crevant" mean in "Ce sketch est crevant, j'ai pleuré de rire"?
choices: hilarious
exhausting
boring
too long
questions.explanation: Crevant has two informal senses, exhausting and hilarious; j'ai pleuré de rire (I cried with laughter) selects hilarious.

questions.stem: Which word belongs to the administrative register?
choices: mentionné
cité
évoqué
susmentionné
questions.explanation: Susmentionné (above-mentioned) is an administrative word: l'avis susmentionné. Mentionné, cité and évoqué are neutral and fit any register.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a register clash that is most likely a mistake rather than a deliberate effect?
choices: Le ministre a invité les grévistes à « se bouger », selon ses propres termes.
Monsieur le Maire, je me suis gouré de rue et je conteste l'amende.
Il a pris congé de la soirée vers deux heures, en emportant le fromage.
Après dix minutes de jargon administratif, l'humoriste conclut : « Bref, je me suis fait avoir. »
questions.explanation: An informal se gourer in a letter to the mayor, with nothing to mark it as a joke, reads as a slip: an incongruous word. The others are marked effects: an informal word quoted in guillemets, a humorous soutenu phrase for a guest leaving with the cheese, and a comedian's rupture de ton.

questions.stem: What is "une plaisanterie triviale"?
choices: a coarse joke
a clever joke
a short joke
a harmless joke
questions.explanation: Of jokes, words and scenes, trivial means crude, coarse. It can also mean commonplace (une idée triviale); the English sense "minor, unimportant" is common but criticised by some usage guides as an anglicism, and in maths une solution triviale is an obvious one.

questions.stem: What is "la gouaille"?
choices: a slang dictionary of the Paris suburbs
the cheeky, mocking wit associated with working-class Paris
a style of Parisian street song
the accent of southern France
questions.explanation: La gouaille is a manner, cheeky and mocking: la gouaille du titi parisien. Someone who has it is gouailleur, gouailleuse.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2 of the reading "Les mots ont-ils une classe sociale ?", what caused a scandal in 1829?
choices: a slang word in a classical tragedy
a poem by Victor Hugo
the plain word mouchoir spoken on stage
a novel written in spoken French
questions.explanation: The chronicle reports the story (on raconte) that in Vigny's adaptation of Othello the word mouchoir, spoken in full, caused a scandal. Hugo's poem came decades later and Céline's novel in 1932.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 4 of the reading, what separates a stylistic effect from a mistake?
choices: the age of the word
the speaker's social class
whether the word is in a dictionary
intention and dosage
questions.explanation: Ce qui distingue l'effet de style de la faute, c'est l'intention et le dosage: a deliberate rupture de ton stands out against a controlled text; an accidental word only shows the writer is lost.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 5 of the reading, when does speaking "like the people" become demagogic?
choices: whenever a politician uses an informal word
whenever a politician speaks simply
when popular speech is a costume worn to flatter an audience
when the audience does not understand the speech
questions.explanation: Parler simplement est une politesse; it becomes démagogique when le parler populaire n'est plus qu'un costume, enfilé pour flatter un auditoire qu'on méprise en privé.

questions.stem: Listen to Léa's voice message. Why did she leave the meeting?

audio.text: Léa : Salut, c'est Léa. Bon, la réunion de copro, je me suis barrée au bout d'une heure, j'en pouvais plus. Le syndic a rabâché les mêmes chiffres, et le voisin du troisième a engueulé tout le monde. Je te raconte ce soir.

choices: She could not take any more of it.
Her neighbour told her to leave.
She had to go back to work.
The meeting was cancelled.
questions.explanation: Je me suis barrée au bout d'une heure, j'en pouvais plus: she left because she couldn't stand any more. The neighbour shouted at everyone, but nobody sent her away.

questions.stem: Listen to the comedian. What creates the comic effect?

audio.text: Humoriste : Mesdames et messieurs, je tiens à vous aviser que l'intéressée, c'est-à-dire moi, s'est dûment acquittée de son loyer. Bref : j'ai plus un rond.

choices: a pun on the word loyer
an insult aimed at her landlord
slang from the first word to the last
a rupture de ton: administrative phrasing, then an informal punchline
questions.explanation: Je tiens à vous aviser, l'intéressée, s'est dûment acquittée: administrative French for paying the rent. Bref : j'ai plus un rond (I'm broke, informal) drops the register at once.

questions.stem: Listen to the interview. What bothers the linguist most about the mayor's language?

audio.text: Journaliste : Le maire a promis de « botter les fesses » aux fraudeurs. C'est démagogique ? Linguiste : Pas forcément. Le mot est familier, mais il l'a dit avec un sourire, comme entre guillemets. Ce qui me gêne davantage, c'est qu'il ne parle comme ça que pendant les campagnes.

choices: He used an informal expression.
He speaks like this only during election campaigns.
He smiled while he spoke.
He did not mention fraud.
questions.explanation: Ce qui me gêne davantage, c'est qu'il ne parle comme ça que pendant les campagnes: the register looks like a costume. The informal word itself, marked with a smile, is pas forcément démagogique.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows the vague "ils" for the authorities, typical of popular French?
choices: Ils m'ont encore augmenté les impôts, à la mairie.
Les agents ont dressé un procès-verbal.
Il est rappelé aux usagers que le stationnement est payant.
Nous vous informons que votre recours est recevable.
questions.explanation: Ils for an unnamed authority is a marker of popular speech. The other sentences name the agents, use the administrative impersonal (il est rappelé) or the institutional nous.

questions.stem: Rewrite in neutral (courant) French: "Je me suis gouré de jour."
accept: Je me suis trompé de jour
Je me suis trompée de jour
questions.explanation: Se gourer (informal) = se tromper (neutral). With être, the participle agrees with the speaker: trompé or trompée.

questions.stem: Rewrite in the administrative register with "aviser" in the passive: "On a prévenu les usagers de la fermeture." → "Les usagers ___ de la fermeture."
questions.explanation: Aviser quelqu'un de quelque chose (to notify) in the passive: les usagers ont été avisés de la fermeture. The passive removes the vague on, as the administration likes.

questions.stem: Match each informal word to its neutral equivalent.
choices: partir
dormir
la chambre
l'argent
les chaussures
la maison
questions.explanation: La maison is the neutral word for la baraque, which is not in the list.

questions.stem: Which features mark the administrative register? Select all that apply.
choices: the passive with no agent (un avis a été établi)
the institutional nous
dislocation (le parcmètre, il marchait pas)
set words such as susmentionné and dûment
pas without ne
questions.explanation: The passive, the institutional nous and set words like susmentionné and dûment belong to the administrative register. Dislocation and pas without ne mark informal and popular speech.

questions.stem: Put the six levels in the order of the lesson's register ladder, from the top (most formal) to the bottom.
choices: administratif
soutenu
courant
familier
populaire
argotique
questions.explanation: The ladder runs administratif, soutenu, courant, familier, populaire, argotique. The top two are both formal; the lower three shade into each other, and the last two are for recognition.

questions.stem: Name the register of each rung of the ladder.

image.alt: A ladder with six rungs, each holding one version of the same complaint with its markers highlighted; the register names are missing.

choices: administratif
soutenu
courant
familier
populaire
argotique
questions.explanation: From the top: un avis a néanmoins été établi (administratif); je n'en ai pas moins reçu (soutenu); j'ai quand même eu une amende (courant); je me suis quand même pris une amende (familier); ils m'ont collé trente-cinq balles (populaire); je me suis mangé une prune (argotique).

questions.stem: Give the formal two-word phrase meaning "to take one's leave" (as in "___ de ses hôtes").
questions.explanation: Prendre congé de quelqu'un is formal; partir and s'en aller are neutral, se barrer and se tirer informal.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les trois heures qu'il a ___ ne lui ont pas suffi."
choices: dormies
dormi
dormis
dormie
questions.explanation: Trois heures is a complement of duration (he slept for three hours), not a direct object, so the participle stays invariable.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les colis qu'il a ___ dépassaient tous dix kilos."
choices: pesé
pesée
pesés
pesées
questions.explanation: Here peser is transitive (he weighed the parcels): que stands for les colis, a masculine plural direct object placed before the verb, so pesés agrees.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les chaleurs qu'il a ___ l'été dernier ont épuisé les coureurs."
choices: faites
faits
faite
fait
questions.explanation: Il a fait (chaud) is impersonal: il refers to nothing and les chaleurs is not a direct object. The participle of an impersonal verb is always invariable.

questions.stem: Complete: "La plupart des coureurs ___ arrivés avant midi."
choices: est
était
sont
soit
questions.explanation: After la plupart des + plural noun, the verb is plural: la plupart des coureurs sont arrivés.

questions.stem: Complete: "Plus d'un coureur ___ abandonné avant la mi-course."
choices: a
ont
sont
avaient
questions.explanation: Plus d'un takes a singular verb (plus d'un coureur a abandonné), even though the meaning is plural; moins de deux, by contrast, takes a plural.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les meneurs d'allure portaient des maillots ___."
choices: bleus clairs
bleus clair
bleu clairs
bleu clair
questions.explanation: A compound colour (a colour plus a shade) is invariable: des maillots bleu clair. A simple colour agrees: des maillots bleus.

questions.stem: How do you write 4,280 in traditional spelling?
choices: quatre milles deux cents quatre-vingts
quatre mille deux cent quatre-vingts
quatre mille deux cents quatre-vingt
quatre mille deux cent quatre-vingt
questions.explanation: Mille never varies; cent loses its s because another number follows; quatre-vingts keeps its s because it ends the number. (The 1990 spelling hyphenates every part: quatre-mille-deux-cent-quatre-vingts.)

questions.stem: Complete: "Elle a couru une ___ avant de s'arrêter."
choices: demi-heure
demie-heure
demi heure
demie heure
questions.explanation: Before the noun, demi is invariable and joined with a hyphen: une demi-heure. After the noun it agrees in gender: une heure et demie.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ soit la distance, elle termine toujours la course."
choices: Quelque
Quelle que
Quel que
Quels que
questions.explanation: Quel que + être (whatever) is written in two words, and quel agrees with the subject of soit: la distance is feminine singular, so quelle que. Quelque in one word means some or about.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: La maison qu'ils ont faite construire est terminée.
La maison qu'ils ont faits construire est terminée.
La maison qu'ils ont fait construire est terminée.
La maison qu'ils ont faites construire est terminée.
questions.explanation: Fait followed by an infinitive is always invariable: la maison qu'ils ont fait construire; elle s'est fait couper les cheveux.

questions.stem: Following the 1990 recommendations, how is the participle written in "Mes jambes, je les ai ___ décider"?
choices: laissées
laissés
laissée
laissé
questions.explanation: The 1990 recommendations make laissé + infinitive invariable, like fait. Traditional grammar agrees it when the object performs the action (je les ai laissées décider), and that spelling is still accepted; laissés and laissée don't fit the feminine plural les jambes in either system.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of the race report, why is the participle invariable in "Les deux heures que j'ai couru seule"?
choices: Courir always takes être.
The speaker is a woman.
Deux heures is a duration, not a direct object.
The participle comes before the noun.
questions.explanation: Courir deux heures means running for two hours: a measure of time, so no agreement. With a real object (les risques qu'elle a courus) it would agree.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4 of the race report, what had kept the medical teams busy the previous year?
choices: the heat, with two hundred interventions
a storm, with eighty interventions
cramps among the half-marathon runners
hypothermia at the finish
questions.explanation: Les chaleurs qu'il a fait l'an dernier nous avaient valu deux cents interventions; this year, with cold rain, they made fewer than eighty, mostly for cramps and mild hypothermia.

questions.stem: Listen to the proofreader. What does she think of the journalist's sentence?

audio.text: Correctrice : Tu as écrit « la moitié des inscrits ont abandonné ». Journaliste : C'est faux ? Correctrice : Non, c'est correct, et le singulier aussi. Je voulais juste que tu choisisses en connaissance de cause.

choices: Only the singular is correct.
Only the plural is correct.
The sentence must be rewritten.
The plural is correct, and so is the singular.
questions.explanation: Après la moitié des, le singulier et le pluriel sont corrects: she only wants him to choose knowingly (en connaissance de cause).

questions.stem: Listen to the commentator. What has the runner achieved?

audio.text: Commentateur : Et voilà la marathonienne qui franchit la ligne d'arrivée ! Deux heures trente et une minutes : un chrono magnifique, quatre minutes sous son record personnel !

choices: a world record
a personal best, by four minutes
second place
the fastest time ever on this course
questions.explanation: Un chrono magnifique, quatre minutes sous son record personnel: she beat her personal best by four minutes.

questions.stem: Listen to the organiser. What was the main medical problem this year?

audio.text: Organisateur : Cette année, la déshydratation a pesé beaucoup moins lourd que les crampes. Il a fait frais, et nos ravitaillements ont surtout distribué des fruits.

choices: cramps
dehydration
falls on the wet road
sunburn
questions.explanation: La déshydratation a pesé moins lourd que les crampes: cramps counted for more. Peser lourd = to carry weight; il a fait frais explains why dehydration was rare.

questions.stem: Which phrase follows the usual rule for colour words?
choices: des chaussures marrons
des chaussures marron
des chaussettes vertes foncées
des drapeaux bleus-blancs-rouges
questions.explanation: Marron is a noun used as a colour, so it is invariable. Compound colours are invariable too: des chaussettes vert foncé, des drapeaux bleu-blanc-rouge.

questions.stem: Rewrite with the object before the verb: "Elle a reçu des médailles." → "Les médailles qu'elle ___"
questions.explanation: Que stands for les médailles, a feminine plural direct object now placed before the verb, so the participle agrees: a reçues.

questions.stem: Rewrite with "plus d'un" as the subject: "Plusieurs coureurs ont abandonné." → "Plus d'un coureur ___ abandonné."
questions.explanation: Plus d'un takes a singular verb: plus d'un coureur a abandonné.

questions.stem: Write 283 in letters (traditional or 1990 spelling).
questions.explanation: Cent has no s because a number follows it, and neither has vingt in quatre-vingt-trois. Traditional spelling hyphenates only below one hundred; the 1990 spelling hyphenates every part.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to the reason for its agreement.
left: les orages qu'il y a eu
la maison qu'ils ont fait construire
choices: a measure of time: no agreement
a direct object placed before: agreement
an impersonal verb: no agreement
fait + infinitive: no agreement
agreement with the subject
questions.explanation: Dormir is never transitive: les heures is a duration. Courir un danger is transitive, so courus agrees with que (les dangers). Il y a is impersonal; fait + infinitive never varies. Agreement with the subject is the être rule, used by none of these.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct in careful written French? Select all that apply.
choices: Une foule de supporters se pressait derrière les barrières.
Une foule de supporters se pressaient derrière les barrières.
La plupart des coureurs est arrivée.
Chacun a reçu sa médaille.
Plus d'un coureur ont abandonné.
questions.explanation: After une foule de, the verb may follow the form (singular) or the meaning (plural). Chacun takes the singular. La plupart des coureurs takes a plural (sont arrivés), and plus d'un a singular (a abandonné).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the marathon finish.

image.alt: A marathon finish: a runner with a bib crossing a line under an ARRIVÉE banner, a race clock, a pack of runners, a balloon on a pole above them, and a table with water bottles.

choices: le dossard
la ligne d'arrivée
le chrono
le peloton
le meneur d'allure
le ravitaillement
le podium
la foulée
questions.explanation: Le dossard is the number on the runner's chest; la ligne d'arrivée the line on the ground; le chrono the clock; le peloton the group behind; le meneur d'allure carries the balloon; le ravitaillement is the table of water and fruit.

questions.stem: In careful written French, what does "Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés" mean?
choices: No runner has arrived.
All the runners have arrived.
Some runners have arrived, but not all.
The runners have not all left yet.
questions.explanation: Careful writing reads the negation as applying to tous: not all. In speech the sentence can also be heard as "none", which is why a careful writer rewrites it.

questions.stem: Which sentence says clearly that no runner has arrived?
choices: Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés.
Les coureurs ne sont pas tous arrivés.
Certains coureurs ne sont pas arrivés.
Aucun coureur n'est arrivé.
questions.explanation: Aucun … ne leaves no doubt. Tous … ne … pas is ambiguous, and ne … pas tous and certains … ne … pas both mean that some have arrived.

questions.stem: What does "Il ne boit pas que de l'eau" mean?
choices: He drinks only water.
He doesn't drink water.
He drinks other things as well as water.
He never drinks anything.
questions.explanation: Ne … pas que = not only. Ne … que alone (il ne boit que de l'eau) = only.

questions.stem: What does "Il n'est pas toujours venu" mean?
choices: He hasn't always come.
He still hasn't come.
He has never come.
He always comes late.
questions.explanation: Pas toujours = not always. Toujours pas (il n'est toujours pas venu) = still not.

questions.stem: What does "Seul le maire a voté contre" mean?
choices: Even the mayor voted against.
The same mayor voted against.
The mayor himself voted against.
Only the mayor voted against.
questions.explanation: Seul before the noun phrase means only. Even = même le maire; the same = le même maire; himself = le maire lui-même.

questions.stem: What does "Je ne suis pas mécontent du résultat" usually mean?
choices: I'm angry about the result.
I'm pleased with the result.
I don't care about the result.
I haven't seen the result yet.
questions.explanation: A litotes says less to mean more: not displeased = pleased, said with modesty or understatement.

questions.stem: Why is "la peur de l'ennemi" ambiguous?
choices: The enemy may be the one who feels the fear or the one who causes it.
Ennemi may be singular or plural.
Peur may be read as a verb.
De may mean from a place.
questions.explanation: La peur de l'ennemi can be la peur qu'éprouve l'ennemi or la peur qu'inspire l'ennemi: the same group of words, two structures.

questions.stem: In "J'ai vu la photo du fils du ministre qui a fait scandale", which rewriting says that the photo caused the scandal?
choices: J'ai vu la photo du fils du ministre, lequel a fait scandale.
J'ai vu la photo du fils du ministre, laquelle a fait scandale.
J'ai vu la photo du fils du ministre, qui a fait scandale.
J'ai vu la photo du fils du ministre dont il y a eu scandale.
questions.explanation: Laquelle is feminine, and only photo is feminine, so it can refer only to the photo. Lequel points to the son or the minister; a comma before qui leaves the ambiguity.

questions.stem: Which formal qualifier means "in any event"?
choices: à proprement parler
tant soit peu
en tout état de cause
grosso modo
questions.explanation: En tout état de cause = in any event, whatever the case. À proprement parler = strictly speaking; tant soit peu = even slightly; grosso modo = roughly.

questions.stem: What does "la quasi-totalité des régions" mean?
choices: about half the regions
all the regions without exception
most of the large regions
almost all the regions
questions.explanation: La quasi-totalité = almost the whole: nearly all. La plupart (most) is vaguer.

questions.stem: What is "une réponse sibylline"?
choices: a short, curt answer
a crystal-clear answer
a cryptic, deliberately obscure answer
a long-winded answer
questions.explanation: Sibyllin (from the Sibyl's oracles) suggests chosen obscurity. Curt would be lapidaire, crystal-clear limpide, long-winded prolixe.

questions.stem: In praise of a writer, what is "un style lapidaire"?
choices: terse and striking
convoluted
vague
ornate
questions.explanation: Lapidaire = short and striking, like an inscription in stone. Of an answer it can also mean curt; convoluted is alambiqué.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2 of the fact-check, why is the 40 % figure accurate stricto sensu but misleading?
choices: It counts injuries as deaths.
It comes from another country.
It is a forecast, not a result.
It compares only one January with another.
