questions.explanation: La baisse de 40 % … compare janvier 2026 à janvier 2025. Over the whole year the fall is 19.6 %, and un mois n'est pas représentatif d'une année.

questions.stem: Which fact in paragraph 4 of the fact-check weakens the claim that the cameras caused the fall?
choices: The cameras were installed only in January.
Regions without cameras also saw deaths fall.
The minister later changed her figures.
Traffic increased during the year.
questions.explanation: Les deux régions sans radars ont d'ailleurs connu, elles aussi, une baisse: so other causes (fuel prices, less traffic, a mild winter) may be at work. Traffic in fact fell by about 6 %.

questions.stem: Why does paragraph 5 of the fact-check refuse to draw a conclusion from the Basse-Lorve region?
choices: The numbers are so small that the confidence interval is too wide.
The region has no cameras.
The figures for the region are false.
The region refused to publish its figures.
questions.explanation: Sur des effectifs aussi faibles (8 deaths, then 4), l'intervalle de confiance est si large that nothing can be concluded, and extrapolating to the country would be unwarranted.

questions.stem: Listen to the exchange on the radio. What does the fact-checker mean?

audio.text: Conseiller : Vous ne contestez pas que les radars sauvent des vies ? Vérificatrice : Je ne conteste rien de tel. Je dis que vos chiffres ne permettent pas de l'affirmer : le trafic a baissé la même année.

choices: She agrees that the cameras save lives.
The figures don't prove the claim, though she doesn't deny it.
She denies that the cameras save any lives.
She refuses to discuss the figures.
questions.explanation: Je ne conteste rien de tel: she turns aside the adviser's negative question, which tried to make the debate about something she never denied. Vos chiffres ne permettent pas de l'affirmer: the claim may be true, but the figures don't show it.

questions.stem: Listen to the minister. What is the effect of "ce n'est pas négligeable"?

audio.text: Ministre : Quinze vies de moins en un an, ce n'est pas négligeable. Je laisse chacun en tirer les conclusions.

choices: It admits that the result is negligible.
It contradicts the figure she gives.
It suggests that the result is significant without saying so outright.
It accuses the journalist of exaggerating.
questions.explanation: Ce n'est pas négligeable is a litotes: it lets the minister suggest "a big result" without making a claim that could be checked.

questions.stem: Listen to the journalist. What does she really think of the reply?

audio.text: Journaliste : Interrogé hier, le cabinet a répondu que les chiffres parlaient d'eux-mêmes. Voilà une réponse limpide… si l'on aime les énigmes.

choices: It is admirably clear.
It is rude to the press.
It is far too long.
It is obscure: limpide is ironic here.
questions.explanation: Voilà une réponse limpide… si l'on aime les énigmes: the afterthought turns limpide (crystal-clear) into irony. Les chiffres parlent d'eux-mêmes says nothing about which figures.

questions.stem: Rewrite so that the sentence can only mean "not all": "Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés." → "Les coureurs ___."
questions.explanation: Ne … pas tous puts tous inside the negation's scope, so only "not all" is possible.

questions.stem: Replace "à peu près" with a formal three-word qualifier: "Les deux projets coûtent ___ la même somme."
questions.explanation: Peu ou prou (formal or literary) = more or less. Grosso modo means the same but is two words and more common in speech.

questions.stem: Match each qualifier to its meaning.
choices: strictly speaking
in the broad sense
even slightly
in any event
roughly
questions.explanation: Roughly would be grosso modo or peu ou prou, which are not in the list.

questions.stem: Which problems does the fact-check find in the minister's claim? Select all that apply.
choices: a single month taken as if it represented the year
a sentence that could be heard in two ways
a correlation presented as a cause
a wrong number of regions with cameras
an invented death toll
questions.explanation: The article criticises the choice of January, the ambiguous Toutes les régions n'ont pas encore suivi, and the leap from correlation to causation. The minister gave no number of regions, and her death figures are real; they are just selected.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram: name each reading and give its unambiguous rewriting.

image.alt: Two diagrams for the sentence Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés: on the left, a runners circle overlapping an arrived circle; on the right, the two circles apart. The headings and the rewritings are missing.

choices: Lecture 1 : pas tous
Lecture 2 : aucun
Les coureurs ne sont pas tous arrivés.
Aucun coureur n'est arrivé.
Pas tous les coureurs sont arrivés.
questions.explanation: Overlapping circles mean some runners have arrived: "not all", rewritten Les coureurs ne sont pas tous arrivés. Separate circles mean no runner has arrived: "none", rewritten Aucun coureur n'est arrivé.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to write "The runners have not all arrived".
choices: Les coureurs
ne sont
pas
tous
arrivés.
questions.explanation: Tous comes after pas, inside the scope of the negation: Les coureurs ne sont pas tous arrivés.

questions.stem: Which procedure turns "as soon as he arrived" into "dès son arrivée"?
choices: modulation
calque
transposition
adaptation
questions.explanation: The verb arrived becomes the noun arrivée: a change of word class, which Vinay and Darbelnet call transposition.

questions.stem: Which procedure turns "it's not difficult" into "c'est facile"?
choices: modulation
transposition
borrowing
étoffement
questions.explanation: The point of view changes (not difficult → easy) while the meaning stays: a modulation.

questions.stem: "He limped out of the room" → "Il est sorti de la pièce en boitant" is an example of:
choices: a calque
an adaptation
a literal translation
a chassé-croisé
questions.explanation: English puts the manner in the verb (limp) and the direction in the particle (out); French swaps them: sortir (direction) en boitant (manner).

questions.stem: Which is the best translation of "Eventually, the minister agreed"?
choices: Éventuellement, le ministre a accepté.
Finalement, le ministre a accepté.
Actuellement, le ministre a accepté.
Définitivement, le ministre a accepté.
questions.explanation: Éventuellement means possibly, if need be: using it here would be a contresens. Actuellement means currently and définitivement for good.

questions.stem: Translating "a grim smile" as "un sourire triste" is:
choices: a faux-sens
a contresens
a non-sens
a calque
questions.explanation: Triste is close to grim but not exact (amer or sans joie would fit better): a slight inaccuracy, a faux-sens. A contresens gives a wrong or opposite meaning; a non-sens means nothing.

questions.stem: What does "Le film est actuellement à l'affiche" mean?
choices: The film is actually showing.
The film is currently showing.
The film will eventually be shown.
The film is definitely showing.
questions.explanation: Actuellement = currently, at the moment. Actually = en fait, en réalité.

questions.stem: Which phrase do usage guides prefer to the calque "être en charge de"?
choices: être en chargé de
être chargeant de
être chargé de
être à charge de
questions.explanation: Être chargé de (or responsable de) is the safe form. Être à charge means to be dependent on someone.

questions.stem: Why does a surtitle usually condense the sung text?
choices: Singers always sing more slowly than people read.
French is always shorter than the original language.
Theatres pay surtitlers by the word.
It has a line or two and only a few seconds of reading time.
questions.explanation: Space and reading time are the constraints: the surtitle keeps the event and the feeling and drops what the audience can see on stage.

questions.stem: Who are the "sourciers", in Jean-René Ladmiral's terms?
choices: translators who write for the target reader
translators who work only from Latin and Greek
translators who stay close to the source text
translators who specialise in surtitles
questions.explanation: Sourciers stay close to the source; ciblistes write for the target (cible) reader.

questions.stem: Listen to the translator. What did she do?

audio.text: Traductrice : Le client voulait « faire sens » partout dans la brochure. J'ai mis « avoir du sens ». Il ne s'en est même pas aperçu.

choices: She replaced a criticised calque with a safer phrase.
She kept the client's phrase everywhere.
She refused to translate the brochure.
She added a note explaining the phrase.
questions.explanation: Faire sens is a calque of "to make sense", common but criticised; she wrote avoir du sens, and the client did not even notice.

questions.stem: Match each procedure to its example.
choices: le week-end
gratte-ciel
il pleut des cordes
marcher jusqu'à la gare
dès son arrivée
questions.explanation: Dès son arrivée is a transposition, which is not in the list.

questions.stem: Translate with a chassé-croisé: "She swam across the lake." → "Elle a ___ le lac à la nage."
questions.explanation: French puts the direction in the verb (traverser) and the manner in an adverbial phrase (à la nage).

questions.stem: Translate "They ignored the warning" without the false friend: "Ils ___ l'avertissement."
questions.explanation: Ignorer means not to know: ils ont ignoré l'avertissement would mean they didn't know about it. Ne pas tenir compte de = to take no account of.

questions.stem: Which words are false friends for an English speaker? Select all that apply.
choices: éventuellement
actuellement
sensible
le téléphone
la table
questions.explanation: Éventuellement = possibly, actuellement = currently, sensible = sensitive. Le téléphone and la table mean what they seem to.

questions.stem: Give the French noun, with its article, for a slight error of meaning, less serious than a contresens.
questions.explanation: Le faux-sens is a near miss; le contresens a wrong meaning; le non-sens no meaning at all.

questions.stem: What did Vaugelas take as the model for his Remarques sur la langue françoise (1647)?
choices: the grammar of Latin
the speech of the Paris markets
the Académie française's finished dictionary
the usage of the most refined part of the royal court, checked against the best writers
questions.explanation: Vaugelas was a witness to usage, the usage of the court and the best authors of his day. The Académie's dictionary came only in 1694.

questions.stem: When was the ninth edition of the Académie française's dictionary completed?
questions.explanation: The ninth edition, begun in the 1980s, was completed in November 2024. 1694 is the first edition, 1935 the eighth, and 1992 the date of the ninth edition's first volume.

questions.stem: How is Le Bon Usage best described?
choices: a grammar with a prescriptive title and a largely descriptive method
a purely prescriptive list of errors
a dictionary of slang
an official text with legal force
questions.explanation: Grevisse and Goosse cite the writers who use a disputed form and those who condemn it, then give their own judgement.

questions.stem: Which work appeared in 16 volumes from 1971 to 1994 and is free online today?
choices: Littré's dictionary
the Trésor de la langue française
the Petit Robert
Vaugelas's Remarques
questions.explanation: The TLF, made at the CNRS in Nancy, is free online as the TLFi. Littré's dictionary was published from 1863 to 1872.

questions.stem: What does a descriptive grammar do?
choices: It tells you which forms to avoid.
It describes only pronunciation.
It records what speakers and writers do, with evidence.
It is published only by the Académie.
questions.explanation: Descriptive grammar describes usage without judging it; prescriptive (normative) grammar recommends and condemns.

questions.stem: In French typography, where does a non-breaking space go?
choices: after a full stop only
before a comma
inside brackets
before a colon
questions.explanation: French puts a non-breaking space before : ; ! ? (a thin one before ; ! ? in fine typography) and inside « ». Commas and full stops take no space before them.

questions.stem: Which is correct in French typography?
choices: en Janvier, le Français (the language)
en janvier, le Français (the language)
en janvier, le français (the language)
en Janvier, le français (the language)
questions.explanation: Months and languages take a lower case: en janvier, le français. A capital marks the people: les Français.

questions.stem: What gender is "espace" when printers speak of a non-breaking space?
choices: feminine: une espace insécable
masculine: un espace insécable
either, with no difference
it has no singular
questions.explanation: In typography espace is feminine (une espace fine); in everyday French it is masculine (un espace vert).

questions.stem: What force do the Académie française's recommendations on usage have?
choices: they bind every publisher
they are enforced by fines
they apply by law to all schools
prestige, but no legal force
questions.explanation: The Académie recommends; no one is fined for pallier à. Official state terminology is handled by a government commission in which the Académie takes part.

questions.stem: Name the typographic point marked by each number.

image.alt: A short French magazine paragraph: a heading beginning with an accented capital, a line ending with a novel title in italics, a line with a shaded space before a colon and a quotation in French guillemets, and a line with a narrow shaded space before an exclamation mark.

choices: la majuscule accentuée
l'italique
l'espace insécable
les guillemets
l'espace fine
le trait d'union
questions.explanation: The É of État is an accented capital; Le Rouge et le Noir is in italics; the space before the colon is a non-breaking space; « » are French guillemets; the narrow space before the exclamation mark is a thin space (une espace fine).

questions.stem: Match each work to its maker.
left: Grand Dictionnaire universel du XIXe siècle
choices: Vaugelas
Émile Littré
Pierre Larousse
Maurice Grevisse
Paul Robert
questions.explanation: Paul Robert made the Dictionnaire alphabétique et analogique, which is not in the list.

questions.stem: Write "état" with its capital and accent, as at the start of the heading "___ des lectures d'hiver".
questions.explanation: French capitals keep their accents: État, À bientôt, ÉCOLE.

questions.stem: Put these in chronological order, earliest first.
choices: Vaugelas's Remarques
the Académie's first dictionary
Littré's dictionary
Grevisse's Le Bon Usage
the last volume of the TLF

questions.stem: Give the French noun, with its article, for a person who writes dictionaries.
questions.explanation: Le or la lexicographe; the craft is la lexicographie.

questions.stem: Which verb is "naquit" the passé simple of?
choices: nager
naître
nuire
nouer
questions.explanation: "Naquit" is the passé simple of naître (il naquit en 1857: he was born in 1857), one of the irregular -i- stems. Nager gives nagea, nuire gives nuisit, nouer gives noua.

questions.stem: Which verb is "il vint" the passé simple of?
choices: voir
vivre
vaincre
venir
questions.explanation: The -in- stem belongs to venir and tenir and their compounds: il vint, il tint, il survint. Voir gives il vit, vivre gives il vécut, vaincre gives il vainquit.

questions.stem: What does "La rumeur crût de jour en jour" mean?
choices: The rumour grew from day to day.
The rumour was believed from day to day.
The rumour was born from day to day.
The rumour died down from day to day.
questions.explanation: With a circumflex, "crût" is the passé simple of croître (to grow). Without it, "crut" is the passé simple of croire (to believe), which would need a person as subject: "Il crut la rumeur".

questions.stem: Which of these is a passé antérieur?
choices: elle fût partie
elle était partie
elle fut partie
elle est partie
questions.explanation: The passé antérieur is être or avoir in the passé simple + the participle: "elle fut partie". With a circumflex, "elle fût partie" is a pluperfect subjunctive (lesson 06); "elle était partie" is the plus-que-parfait, "elle est partie" the passé composé.

questions.stem: What does this sentence from the reading mean? "À peine furent-ils arrivés au port qu'un agent leur proposa des billets à moitié prix."
choices: They arrived at the port because an agent had offered them half-price tickets.
As soon as an agent offered them half-price tickets, they set off for the port.
They had hardly arrived at the port when an agent offered them half-price tickets.
They had barely enough money for half-price tickets when they reached the port.
questions.explanation: "À peine" + passé antérieur with inversion, then "que" + passé simple: one event had only just ended when the next began. "Hardly … when" is the English frame. Nothing says the agent caused the journey.

questions.stem: Which text belongs to discours in Benveniste's sense?
choices: A letter: "Nous sommes arrivés hier ; je t'écris de l'hôtel."
A novel: "Ils arrivèrent le lendemain et descendirent à l'hôtel."
A chronicle: "Le navire leva l'ancre le 2 octobre."
A history book: "La crue survint dans la nuit du 3 au 4 juin."
questions.explanation: Discours addresses someone and ties events to the speaker's present: "je", "t'écris", "hier" and the passé composé. The other three are récit: third person and passé simple, cut off from the moment of writing.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of the reading, which verb describes the background rather than an event?
choices: survint
courut
accourut
pleuvait
questions.explanation: "Il pleuvait depuis huit jours" is in the imparfait: the setting, already going on when the events happen. "Survint", "courut" and "accourut" are in the passé simple: events in the foreground that move the story on.

questions.stem: A friend's email says: "Je reçus ta lettre hier et je fus très contente." What effect does this have?
choices: It is the normal way to give news in an email.
It sounds like a novel or a joke: an email would use the passé composé.
It is incorrect: the passé simple has no first person.
It is a regional form typical of Québec.
questions.explanation: The first person of the passé simple exists (je reçus, je fus) but belongs to literary memoirs; in an email, which is discours, it sounds bookish or playful. Normal email French is "J'ai reçu ta lettre hier et j'ai été très contente". Nothing about it is regional.

questions.stem: What does "Le maire fit sonner le tocsin sur-le-champ" mean?
choices: The mayor made a new alarm bell on the spot.
The mayor had the alarm bell rung at once.
The mayor heard the alarm bell ring at once.
The mayor stopped the alarm bell at once.
questions.explanation: "Fit" is the passé simple of faire; faire + infinitive is causative: he had someone ring the bell. "Sur-le-champ" means at once, on the spot.

questions.stem: Where are you least likely to meet the passé simple today?
choices: In a history book
In a newspaper obituary
In a fairy tale
In a phone conversation between friends
questions.explanation: The passé simple lives in written narrative: novels, tales, history books and some press genres such as obituaries. Conversation is discours and uses the passé composé.

questions.stem: Which form is the passé simple of commencer for "ils"?
choices: commencèrent
commençèrent
commencairent
commençairent
questions.explanation: Commencer takes ç only before a and o: il commença, nous commençâmes. Before è there is no need for a cedilla, so "ils commencèrent". The -èrent ending is the plural of every -er verb.

questions.stem: In "Il dit qu'il partirait le lendemain, et partit.", what tense is "dit"?
choices: The present
The imparfait
The passé simple, like "partit"
The passé composé without its auxiliary
questions.explanation: "Il dit" is identical in the present and the passé simple; context decides. Here the next verb, "partit", is a passé simple and "partirait" is a future in the past, so the whole sentence is a past récit.

questions.stem: In the invented book described in the lesson, what is the récit-cadre?
choices: The chronicle of the flood itself
Louise's letter from New York
The schoolteacher's account of finding the chronicle in an attic
The final pages on what became of the Morel children
questions.explanation: A frame story contains another story: here the teacher who finds the manuscript in 1912. The chronicle is the story inside the frame; the pages on the children are the épilogue; Louise's letter is a document inside the book.

questions.stem: Listen to the history programme. What does the speaker say about victims?

audio.text: Le 4 juin 1857, la Vaurelle sortit de son lit. En quelques heures, l'eau envahit le bourg ; le vieux pont, qui avait résisté à trois siècles de crues, céda avant l'aube. On ne compta, par miracle, aucune victime.

choices: There were none, which was remarkable.
Three people drowned before dawn.
Only the ferryman's family died.
The number of victims is unknown.
questions.explanation: The speaker says "On ne compta, par miracle, aucune victime": there were no victims at all, and "par miracle" stresses how surprising that was. The three centuries are the age of the bridge, not a number of dead.

questions.stem: Listen to two students talking about an essay. What is Claire's criticism?

audio.text: Claire : Dans ta rédaction, tu as écrit « je partis à l'aube ». C'est voulu ? Hugo : Oui, je voulais un ton de roman. Claire : Alors garde-le jusqu'au bout : deux lignes plus loin, tu passes au passé composé.

choices: The passé simple can't be used in the first person.
Hugo should write the whole essay in the present.
The passé simple is too informal for an essay.
Hugo switches from the passé simple to the passé composé for no reason.
questions.explanation: Claire accepts the passé simple as a choice ("C'est voulu ?") but asks Hugo to keep it to the end, because two lines later he moves to the passé composé. Mixing the systems by accident is the fault, not the first-person passé simple itself.

questions.stem: Listen to the end of a radio obituary. Why does the last sentence change tense?

audio.text: Il naquit à Saint-Étienne en 1931, signa son premier contrat à dix-sept ans et ne quitta jamais son club. Les supporters, eux, ne l'oublieront pas.

choices: The passé simple has no future form, so the speaker had no choice.
It moves from the finished life, told as récit, to the speaker's present and future.
The speaker made a grammatical mistake.
The last sentence reports what the supporters said.
questions.explanation: The life is told in the passé simple (naquit, signa, quitta): a story closed and cut off from now. "Les supporters, eux, ne l'oublieront pas" is discours: a future seen from the moment of speaking. The switch is a deliberate change of system.

questions.stem: Rewrite in the passé composé, as you would in a summary. "La crue survint dans la nuit." → "La crue ___ dans la nuit."
questions.explanation: Survenir takes être, and the participle agrees with la crue: "La crue est survenue dans la nuit."

questions.stem: Rewrite in the passé composé: "Dès qu'il eut aperçu l'eau, il courut à la mairie." → "Dès qu'il ___ l'eau, il ___ à la mairie."
questions.explanation: In discours the passé antérieur becomes a passé composé (a aperçu) and the passé simple a passé composé (a couru). The spoken passé surcomposé "a eu aperçu" (C1) is also accepted.

questions.stem: Rewrite in the passé composé: "Tout le village accourut." → "Tout le village ___ ."
questions.explanation: Accourir is one of the few verbs found with both auxiliaries: "a accouru" is the usual choice, "est accouru" is common in literary French. Both are correct.

questions.stem: Match each passé simple form to its infinitive.
choices: vivre
mourir
vaincre
s'asseoir
acquérir
acquitter
assister
questions.explanation: Vécut (-u- stem) is vivre, mourut is mourir, vainquit (-i- stem) is vaincre, s'assit is s'asseoir, acquit is acquérir. Acquitter would give acquitta and assister assista.

questions.stem: Put the events of the reading in the order in which they happen.
choices: Étienne s'éprend de Louise.
Les noces sont célébrées.
La crue survient.
Le vieux pont s'effondre.
Les Morel partent pour Le Havre.
questions.explanation: The story moves from the Saint-Jean ball (1856) to the wedding (2 June 1857), the flood the next night, the collapse of the bridge during the flood, and the departure in September.

questions.stem: Which of these forms are in the passé simple? Select all that apply.
choices: il prit
ils furent
il vint
qu'il vînt
il prend
nous parlâmes
questions.explanation: "Il prit" (prendre), "ils furent" (être), "il vint" (venir) and "nous parlâmes" (parler, with its circumflex) are passé simple. "Qu'il vînt" is an imperfect subjunctive (lesson 06), "il prend" a present.

questions.stem: Name the tense in each numbered box of the chart.

image.alt: A chart comparing récit and discours with five tense boxes blanked and numbered: the events in récit (1) and in discours (2), the second tense for what comes before in récit (3), and what comes after in récit (4) and in discours (5).

choices: passé simple
passé composé
passé antérieur
conditionnel
futur
présent
subjonctif imparfait
questions.explanation: Récit tells events in the passé simple, looks back with the plus-que-parfait and the passé antérieur, and looks ahead with the conditional (future in the past). Discours tells events in the passé composé and looks ahead with the future.

questions.stem: What is "qu'il fût"?
choices: the passé simple of être
the imperfect subjunctive of être
the conditional of être
the imparfait of être
questions.explanation: The circumflex and the que mark the imperfect subjunctive: "qu'il fût". The passé simple is "il fut" (no circumflex), the conditional "il serait", the imparfait "il était".

questions.stem: What does "Il eût fallu le prévenir." mean?
choices: He had to be warned.
He will have to be warned.
He must be warned now.
He should have been warned.
questions.explanation: With no que in front, "il eût fallu" is the conditionnel passé deuxième forme, the literary twin of "il aurait fallu": it would have been necessary. "He had to be warned" would be "il a fallu" or "il fallut".

questions.stem: How would modern standard French write "Je voulais qu'il vînt"?
choices: Je voulais qu'il vienne.
Je voulais qu'il venait.
Je voulais qu'il viendrait.
Je voulais qu'il soit venu.
questions.explanation: Modern French keeps the present subjunctive after a past main verb when the action is at the same time or later: "qu'il vienne". Vouloir que always takes the subjunctive, so "venait" and "viendrait" are wrong; "soit venu" would mean the coming had already happened.

questions.stem: What does "Eût-il su la vérité, il ne serait pas venu." mean?
choices: He knew the truth, so he didn't come.
Did he know the truth? He didn't come.
If he had known the truth, he wouldn't have come.
Although he knew the truth, he came.
questions.explanation: Hypothetical inversion with the literary form replaces si: "Eût-il su" = "S'il avait su". It is a condition contrary to fact: he didn't know, and he came. It is not a question and not a statement.

questions.stem: What does the writer mean? "Je finirai ce roman, dussé-je y passer l'hiver."
choices: I must spend the winter finishing this novel.
I spent the winter finishing this novel.
I will finish this novel, even if it takes me all winter.
I will finish this novel only if I can spend the winter on it.
questions.explanation: "Dussé-je" (imperfect subjunctive of devoir with inversion) means "even if I had to": a concession, not an obligation or a condition. Everyday French: "même si je dois y passer l'hiver".

questions.stem: What is the everyday equivalent of "ne fût-ce que"?
choices: ne serait-ce que
ne soit-ce que
n'était-ce que
ne fut-ce que
questions.explanation: "Ne fût-ce que" uses the imperfect subjunctive of être; today we use the conditional: "ne serait-ce que" (if only, even just). "Ne fut-ce que" without the circumflex is a spelling mistake, and the other two are not French formulas.

questions.stem: In Hortense's first letter, what did she fear? "je craignais même que mon manuscrit ne se fût égaré"
choices: That her manuscript had not got lost
That her manuscript would get lost in the future
That her publisher would lose it on purpose
That her manuscript had got lost
questions.explanation: After a verb of fearing, the ne is expletive: it has no negative meaning. The pluperfect subjunctive "se fût égaré" places the loss before the fear: she feared it had got lost (modern French: "que mon manuscrit se soit égaré").

questions.stem: Why does the columnist write "On eût dit un châtelain de 1850 recevant des cousins pauvres"?
choices: She is quoting a law of 1850.
The old-fashioned form fits the old-fashioned scene and mocks the minister's politeness.
Modern French has no other way to say "it was as if".
It is the usual form in Belgian French.
questions.explanation: The column works by contrast: literary forms from the world of châteaux describe a modern minister, and the gap is the joke. Modern French says "on aurait dit"; the columnist chooses "on eût dit" for effect.

questions.stem: Which form is a conditionnel passé deuxième forme?
choices: j'eus aimé
j'eusse aimé
j'aimasse
j'aimerais
questions.explanation: "J'eusse aimé" (= j'aurais aimé) has the shape of a pluperfect subjunctive and the meaning of a conditionnel passé. "J'eus aimé" is a passé antérieur, "j'aimasse" an imperfect subjunctive, "j'aimerais" a present conditional.

questions.stem: What does "Plût au ciel qu'il revienne !" express?
choices: A fact: it pleased heaven that he came back.
A fear: heaven forbid that he comes back.
The weather: it rained when he came back.
A wish: if only he would come back!
questions.explanation: "Plût au ciel que" is a frozen imperfect subjunctive of plaire: a literary wish, "if only". It has nothing to do with pleuvoir, although "il plut" can also mean "it rained" in the passé simple.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a subjunctive?
choices: Il fallait qu'elle eût du courage.
Elle eut du courage ce jour-là.
Dès qu'elle eut fini, elle partit.
Elle eut peur et se tut.
questions.explanation: After "il fallait que", "eût" with a circumflex is an imperfect subjunctive. In the other three, "eut" without a circumflex is the passé simple of avoir, alone or in a passé antérieur ("eut fini").

questions.stem: What does "Fût-elle ministre, elle devrait répondre." mean?
choices: Since she was a minister, she had to answer.
She was a minister and she answered.
Even if she were a minister, she would have to answer.
Was she a minister? She should answer.
questions.explanation: Hypothetical inversion with the imperfect subjunctive gives a concession: even if she were. Modern French: "Même si elle était ministre, elle devrait répondre."

questions.stem: Hortense writes: "je publierai ce livre, fût-ce à mes frais". What does she mean?
choices: She will publish it only if it costs her nothing.
Her publisher will pay for it.
She will publish the book even if she has to pay for it herself.
She is rich enough to publish it.
questions.explanation: "Fût-ce" (be it, even) introduces an extreme case she accepts: even at her own expense. Everyday French: "même à mes frais".

questions.stem: Listen to the column. What is the columnist's attitude to the reform?

audio.text: Le gouvernement promet une réforme ambitieuse. Ambitieuse, certes, fût-ce sur le papier. On eût aimé qu'elle le fût aussi dans les faits.

choices: Ironic: she suggests it is ambitious only on paper.
Enthusiastic: she praises its ambition.
Neutral: she simply reports the announcement.
Angry at the opposition, which blocks it.
questions.explanation: "Ambitieuse, certes, fût-ce sur le papier" grants the ambition only on paper, and "On eût aimé qu'elle le fût aussi dans les faits" says it is not ambitious in practice. The literary forms add a mocking solemnity.

questions.stem: Listen to two colleagues. What does Inès mean?

audio.text: Paul : Le rapport aurait dû être rendu en mars. Inès : Il eût fallu, pour cela, que quelqu'un le commandât. Paul : Tu es dure. Inès : Non, lucide.

choices: The report was commissioned in March.
She commissioned the report herself.
She thinks the report should be cancelled.
Nobody actually commissioned the report, so its delay is no surprise.
questions.explanation: "Il eût fallu, pour cela, que quelqu'un le commandât" = for that, someone would have had to commission it: nobody did. Paul finds her harsh; she calls herself clear-sighted ("lucide").

questions.stem: Listen to the extract from a speech. What does the speaker promise?

audio.text: Nous irons jusqu'au bout de cette enquête, dût-elle déplaire à certains, ne serait-ce que par respect pour les victimes.

choices: To stop the inquiry if it displeases anyone.
To complete the inquiry even if some people dislike it, if only out of respect for the victims.
To complete the inquiry only if the victims agree.
To show respect to the people the inquiry displeases.
questions.explanation: "Dût-elle déplaire à certains" = even if it displeases some people (a concession); "ne serait-ce que par respect pour les victimes" = if only out of respect for the victims. The speaker mixes a literary formula and its modern equivalent.

questions.stem: Rewrite in modern French: "Écrivez-moi, ne fût-ce que deux lignes." → "Écrivez-moi, ___ deux lignes."
questions.explanation: "Ne serait-ce que", with the conditional of être, is the current form of the literary "ne fût-ce que".

questions.stem: Rewrite in modern French: "Il eût fallu le prévenir." → "Il ___ le prévenir."
questions.explanation: "Il eût fallu" is the second form of the conditionnel passé; the ordinary form is "il aurait fallu".

questions.stem: Rewrite with si: "Eût-il su la vérité, il ne serait pas venu." → "S'il ___ la vérité, il ne serait pas venu."
questions.explanation: An unreal past condition takes si + plus-que-parfait: "S'il avait su la vérité". Never si + conditional ("s'il aurait su") in careful French.

questions.stem: Match each literary formula to the everyday French you would write.
choices: même
on aurait dit
qui que ce soit
si seulement
même si je devais
à condition que
questions.explanation: Each literary form has a modern equivalent: fût-ce = même; on eût dit = on aurait dit; qui que ce fût = qui que ce soit; plût au ciel que = si seulement; dussé-je = même si je devais. "À condition que" (provided that) matches none of them.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences follow the classical concordance? Select all that apply.
choices: Je doutais qu'il fût venu.
On voulait que le roman ne parût jamais.
Je voulais qu'il vienne.
Je ne crois pas que ce soit votre dessein.
Il voulait que je renonçasse à écrire.
questions.explanation: The classical concordance puts the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive after a past main verb: "fût venu", "parût", "renonçasse". "Je voulais qu'il vienne" is the modern concordance. "Je ne crois pas que ce soit" has a present main verb, so the present subjunctive is right in both systems.

questions.stem: Choose the imperfect subjunctive for each numbered box.

image.alt: A table of verbs with their passé simple tu form and imperfect subjunctive. In the qu'il column, four boxes are blanked and numbered: parler (1), finir (2), venir (3) and être (4).

choices: qu'il parlât
qu'il finît
qu'il vînt
qu'il fût
qu'il fut
qu'il venât
questions.explanation: Take the tu form of the passé simple, drop the -s, and give the third person a circumflex and a -t: tu parlas → qu'il parlât; tu finis → qu'il finît; tu vins → qu'il vînt; tu fus → qu'il fût. "Qu'il fut" lacks the circumflex; "venât" is not a form of venir.

questions.stem: Put the steps for forming the imperfect subjunctive in order.
choices: Take the tu form of the passé simple (tu vins).
Drop the final -s (vin-).
Add -sse, -sses, -ssions… (que je vinsse), or a circumflex and -t for il (qu'il vînt).
questions.explanation: The imperfect subjunctive is built on the passé simple: tu vins → vin- → que je vinsse, qu'il vînt.

questions.stem: Which device is used in "Il vint, il vit, il signa."?
choices: polysyndète
asyndète
période
hypotaxe
questions.explanation: Three clauses side by side with no linking word: asyndeton (l'asyndète), which speeds the sentence up. Polysyndeton would repeat "et"; a période is a long rising and falling sentence; hypotaxis subordinates.

questions.stem: What kind of sentence is "Silence."?
choices: une cadence majeure
une hypotaxe
un hiatus
une phrase nominale
questions.explanation: A sentence without a conjugated verb is a nominal sentence (une phrase nominale): it paints a scene in one stroke.

questions.stem: Which sound device is in "le fleuve, lent et lourd"?
choices: an alliteration in l
an assonance in e
a hiatus
a cacophony
questions.explanation: The consonant l is repeated (le, lent, lourd): an alliteration, which here slows the river down. An assonance repeats a vowel; there is no clash of vowels (hiatus) and nothing harsh (cacophony).

questions.stem: Which sentence ends on a cadence mineure?
choices: La pluie glissait sur les pavés, ruisselait le long des gouttières, se perdait lentement dans les caniveaux du quai.
Le fleuve s'assombrit, la ville se tait.
Elle avait tout prévu, tout préparé, tout vérifié avec soin : sauf lui.
Je marchais sans but.
questions.explanation: In a cadence mineure the last group is much shorter than those before it: after three long groups, "sauf lui" closes sharply. The rain sentence grows longer (cadence majeure), the river sentence balances two equal groups (binary), and "Je marchais sans but" is one group.

questions.stem: What device is used in "Au-dessus des toits scintillaient les premières étoiles."?
choices: hypotaxis: a subordinate clause comes first
a nominal sentence
stylistic inversion: the subject comes after the verb
polysyndeton
questions.explanation: The complement is fronted and the subject, "les premières étoiles", follows the verb, so it arrives last like a reveal. There is no subordinate clause and the sentence has a verb.

questions.stem: What does "un ancien élève" mean?
choices: a former pupil
an elderly pupil
a pupil at an old school
a pupil of ancient history
questions.explanation: Before the noun, ancien means former; after it, old (un quartier ancien). An elderly pupil would be "un élève âgé".

questions.stem: Which of these contains a hiatus?
choices: Viendra-t-il ?
Si l'on veut.
Le fleuve coule sous le pont.
Il alla à Arles.
questions.explanation: "Il alla à Arles" puts three vowel sounds in contact (a, à, A): a string of hiatuses. The t of "viendra-t-il" and the l' of "si l'on" exist precisely to avoid a hiatus, for euphony; in "Le fleuve coule sous le pont" every word meets the next at a consonant.

questions.stem: What does "blafard" mean in "la lumière blafarde des néons"?
choices: shimmering
pallid, sickly pale
muffled
bronze-gold
questions.explanation: Blafard is pale and dull, usually of light or a face. Shimmering is chatoyant, muffled feutré, bronze-gold mordoré.

questions.stem: How is "Comme il pleuvait, elle est partie." built?
choices: By parataxis: two clauses side by side with no link.
By hypotaxis: comme states the link of cause.
By asyndeton: a list without "et".
As a nominal sentence.
questions.explanation: The subordinate clause introduced by comme gives the cause: hypotaxis. The paratactic version would be "Il pleuvait. Elle est partie.", leaving the reader to supply the link.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2 of the reading, what does "des effluves de pain chaud, et de feuilles mouillées, et d'essence" do?
choices: It speeds the sentence up (asyndeton).
It is a nominal sentence.
It is a mistake: "et" should appear only once.
The repeated "et" makes the smells pile up (polysyndeton).
questions.explanation: Repeating the link is polysyndeton (la polysyndète): it slows down and accumulates. Asyndeton is the opposite, with no links. The repetition is a deliberate effect, not an error.

questions.stem: Which sentence places the adjective for a subjective, literary effect?
choices: D'étranges lueurs dansaient sur l'eau.
Une lumière verte éclairait la chaussée.
Il porte une veste propre.
Ce quartier ancien a été restauré.
questions.explanation: Étrange normally follows the noun; placed before it ("d'étranges lueurs"), it becomes an impression of the narrator. Verte classifies, and "une veste propre" and "un quartier ancien" use the ordinary position and meaning (clean, old).

questions.stem: What is the main fault of the overloaded rewriting in the lesson?
choices: It uses only parataxis.
It has no adjectives.
Every device is used at once, so nothing stands out.
It is in the passé simple.
questions.explanation: Four adjectives on one noun, three verbs that don't fit the mist, exclamations and abstract words: when everything shouts, nothing is heard. The flat version is the one made only of parataxis.

questions.stem: "Ton thé t'a-t-il ôté ta toux ?" is a well-known example of:
choices: euphony
assonance in a
cacophony
a period
questions.explanation: The run of t sounds and colliding syllables is harsh and comic: a cacophony (la cacophonie), the opposite of euphony.

questions.stem: Listen to the radio critic. What kind of prose is she describing?

audio.text: Sa prose ? Des phrases courtes, sèches, juxtaposées. Pas un « parce que », pas un « donc ». On avance par secousses, et c'est voulu.

choices: Paratactic prose with no stated links, used on purpose
Long periodic sentences full of subordinate clauses
Prose full of adjectives and alliterations
Careless writing that the critic condemns
questions.explanation: "Des phrases courtes, sèches, juxtaposées. Pas un « parce que », pas un « donc »" describes parataxis. "Et c'est voulu" shows she sees it as a deliberate choice, not carelessness.

questions.stem: Listen to two colleagues working on a speech. What does Léa suggest?

audio.text: Léa : Ton discours finit sur « et c'est ainsi que, tous ensemble, nous construirons demain ». Marc : C'est beau, non ? Léa : C'est long. Termine sur « Ensemble. » Un mot. Ça claque.

choices: Adding more subordinate clauses to the ending
Adding an alliteration in s
Removing the word "ensemble"
Ending on a single short word for impact
questions.explanation: Léa finds the ending too long and proposes to finish on "Ensemble." alone: a very short last element, a cadence mineure or chute, that "claque" (hits hard).

questions.stem: Listen to the sentence. What rhythm opens it?

audio.text: Lente et grise, la ville s'endormait ; le fleuve, lui, veillait.

choices: A ternary rhythm: three growing groups
A binary rhythm: two balanced adjectives
A period with three subordinate clauses
A nominal sentence
questions.explanation: "Lente et grise" balances two adjectives: a binary rhythm. The whole sentence then sets two clauses against each other on either side of the semicolon.

questions.stem: Rewrite with the complement first and the subject after the verb: "Les premières étoiles scintillaient au-dessus des toits."
accept: Au-dessus des toits scintillaient les premières étoiles
Au-dessus des toits, scintillaient les premières étoiles
questions.explanation: Fronting the place complement allows a stylistic inversion: "Au-dessus des toits scintillaient les premières étoiles." The subject arrives last.

questions.stem: Rewrite as parataxis, with two clauses and no linking word: "Comme il pleuvait, elle est partie."
questions.explanation: Parataxis drops comme and sets the clauses side by side: "Il pleuvait. Elle est partie." The reader supplies the cause. A semicolon, comma or colon between them is also paratactic.

questions.stem: Translate with the adjective in the right place: "a former pupil" (one person).
questions.explanation: Ancien before the noun means former: "un ancien élève" (or "une ancienne élève"). After the noun, "un élève ancien" would mean an old pupil.

questions.stem: Match each device to its example.
choices: Il vint, il vit, il signa.
Et la pluie, et le vent, et la nuit.
Novembre, déjà.
le fleuve, lent et lourd
Comme il pleuvait, elle est partie.
questions.explanation: Asyndeton: no links; polysyndeton: the link repeated; nominal sentence: no verb; alliteration: a repeated consonant (l). The comme sentence is hypotaxis, which isn't in the list.

questions.stem: Which of these are nominal sentences? Select all that apply.
choices: Silence.
Novembre, déjà.
Personne.
Je marchais sans but.
La nuit est tombée.
questions.explanation: "Silence.", "Novembre, déjà." and "Personne." have no conjugated verb. "Je marchais sans but" and "La nuit est tombée" have one.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the period.

image.alt: The period diagram with three labels blanked and numbered: the bracket under the three rising clauses (1), the high point of the arc (2), and the bracket under the short final clause (3).

choices: protase (montée)
acmé
apodose (descente)
hémistiche
polysyndète
questions.explanation: The rising part made of subordinate clauses is the protase; the high point, where the main clause is about to come, is the acmé; the short falling main clause is the apodose.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a rhythm analysis in order.
choices: Cut the sentence into groups at the pauses.
Count the syllables of each group.
Compare the lengths (growing, shrinking, equal).
Say what effect each choice has on the meaning.
questions.explanation: Groups first, then their length, then the comparison that names the cadence, and finally the effect, which turns an observation into an analysis.

questions.stem: Which definition fits "le pastiche"?
choices: A copy of someone else's text signed as one's own
An imitation of a manner (an author, a genre, a period) that copies none of its sentences, often in admiration
An imitation whose main aim is to mock by exaggerating
The reuse of a slogan to turn its message against it
questions.explanation: A pastiche imitates a way of writing, as a game or a homage. Signing a copy is plagiarism; mocking by exaggeration is parody; turning a slogan is détournement.

questions.stem: What does "l'emphase" mean in French?
choices: emphasis, stress
a firm opinion
a short summary
pomposity, bombast
questions.explanation: L'emphase is a false friend: it means pomposity (parler avec emphase). Emphasis in the English sense is l'insistance or la mise en relief.

questions.stem: What do you call a trivial subject told in the noble style of the epic?
choices: héroï-comique
burlesque
farce
épopée
questions.explanation: The mock-heroic (l'héroï-comique) raises a low subject with a high style, as Boileau's Le Lutrin does. The burlesque does the reverse; the farce is low in both; the epic is high in both.

questions.stem: Scarron's Virgile travesti makes the heroes of the Aeneid talk like market people. This is:
choices: héroï-comique
a pastiche of Boileau
burlesque
an epic
questions.explanation: A noble subject (the Aeneid) in a low style is burlesque, a travestissement that pulls the great down. Héroï-comique is the reverse: a trivial subject in a noble style.

questions.stem: What does Raymond Queneau's Exercices de style (1947) do?
choices: It imitates the openings of 99 famous novels.
It collects 99 parodies of political speeches.
It tells one trivial anecdote in 99 different ways.
It retells the Iliad in slang.
questions.explanation: Queneau takes one minor incident on a Paris bus and retells it 99 times in different styles and forms: proof that style is a choice made on top of a story.

questions.stem: What does French copyright law (Code de la propriété intellectuelle, art. L122-5, 4°) say about parody?
choices: Once a work has been made public, its author can't forbid parody, pastiche or caricature that respect the laws of the genre.
No one may imitate the style of a living author.
A whole novel may be copied if it is called a pastiche.
Only works in the public domain may be parodied.
questions.explanation: The exception covers parody, pastiche and caricature "compte tenu des lois du genre"; courts have generally looked for humour, no risk of confusion and no intent to harm. Copying a whole work remains infringement (contrefaçon), whatever it is called.

questions.stem: In the model pastiche, what is "une eau venue des cimes"?
choices: A deliberate anachronism
A verbal tic of the narrator
A cliché of the administrative style
A periphrasis for mineral water, a marker of the noble style
questions.explanation: The noble style avoids everyday words and replaces them with roundabout expressions: water from the mountain tops for a bottle of mineral water.

questions.stem: Which item in "Le combat de la caisse numéro sept" is a deliberate anachronism?
choices: le char
la carte de fidélité
les victuailles
la Muse
questions.explanation: A loyalty card has no place in an ancient epic: its arrival in the goddess's mouth is the joke. Char, victuailles and the Muse belong to the old epic vocabulary that the pastiche imitates.

questions.stem: In the memo, why "une cliente se serait insérée dans la file"?
choices: The conditional makes a polite request.
The conditional reports a fact that has not been confirmed.
The conditional expresses a wish.
The conditional gives an order to staff.
questions.explanation: This is the conditional of hearsay (C1): the memo reports what is said without vouching for it, a typical marker of administrative and press caution.

questions.stem: Which adjective describes a style swollen with rare words and long sentences?
choices: mièvre
feutré
diaphane
ampoulé
questions.explanation: Ampoulé (turgid) is said of a pompous, inflated style. Mièvre is soppy, feutré muffled, diaphane translucent.

questions.stem: A writer who puts "en fait" in every paragraph without noticing has:
choices: un tic de langage
une mise en abyme
un anachronisme
une contrefaçon
questions.explanation: A word repeated without thinking is a verbal tic (un tic de langage): exactly what a pastiche writer exaggerates.

questions.stem: Which of these is a détournement?
choices: A novel written entirely in the manner of the 1840s serials
A forged painting sold as an original
A protest poster that reuses a brand's slogan to attack the brand
A respectful allusion to a teacher's book
questions.explanation: Détournement keeps the shape of a known text or image and changes its message. The novel is a pastiche, the forgery the work of a faussaire, the allusion a hommage.

questions.stem: What does "mièvre" mean in "Les dialogues amoureux sont un peu mièvres"?
choices: pompous
violent
soppy, sentimental without force
witty
questions.explanation: Mièvre is sweet and sentimental without strength. Pompous is pompeux; witty would be spirituel.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mise en abyme?
choices: A play whose characters stage a play that mirrors their own story
A play told in reverse order
A play with no ending
A play that copies another play line by line
questions.explanation: A mise en abyme is a work inside the work that reflects it, like a play within a play. Copying another play line by line would be plagiarism.

questions.stem: Listen to the radio host. Why were three texts eliminated last year?

audio.text: Pour notre concours de pastiches, une seule règle : un style d'époque, un sujet d'aujourd'hui. Et attention : pas une phrase recopiée. Le jury a éliminé l'an dernier trois textes qui n'étaient que des collages.

choices: They were written in a modern style.
Their subjects were too old-fashioned.
They were too short.
They were collages of copied sentences, not pastiches.
questions.explanation: The rule is "pas une phrase recopiée": a pastiche imitates a manner without copying sentences. The three texts were "des collages", assemblies of borrowed sentences.

questions.stem: Listen to Sami and Jeanne. What worries Sami?

audio.text: Sami : Ta parodie du ministre, c'est drôle, mais tu ne risques rien ? Jeanne : La loi protège la parodie, tant que personne ne peut la prendre pour un vrai discours et que je ne cherche pas à nuire. Sami : Avec ton titre en grosses lettres, « Discours officiel », je n'en suis pas sûr.

choices: Parody is always illegal in France.
The title might make readers take the parody for a real speech.
Jeanne copied the minister's speech word for word.
The minister could sue Jeanne for imitating his style.
questions.explanation: Jeanne recalls the conditions (no confusion, no intent to harm). Sami fears her title, "Discours officiel", creates exactly the confusion the law excludes.

questions.stem: Listen to the critic. What does she think of the novel's style?

audio.text: L'auteur ne parle pas : il déclame. Chaque phrase est un monument, chaque adjectif une statue. On sort de ce roman épuisé, comme d'un musée sans bancs.

choices: It is sober and precise.
It is bombastic and exhausting.
It is soppy and sentimental.
It is full of slang.
questions.explanation: "L'auteur ne parle pas : il déclame", sentences like monuments, adjectives like statues, a museum with no benches: the critic attacks the emphase of the style, which tires the reader.

questions.stem: Rewrite in ordinary word order, subject first: "Devant lui s'étirait la file."
questions.explanation: The pastiche uses inversion as an epic marker. In ordinary order the subject comes first: "La file s'étirait devant lui."

questions.stem: Rewrite in plain modern French, in the passé composé: "Soudain survint l'adversaire." → "Soudain, l'adversaire ___ ."
questions.explanation: In plain French the subject comes first and the event takes the passé composé: "Soudain, l'adversaire est arrivé" (or est survenu, est apparu, a surgi).

questions.stem: Complete with the false friend of "emphasis" that means pomposity: "Il a lu son discours avec beaucoup d'___ : de grands mots, une voix solennelle, aucune idée."
questions.explanation: L'emphase is pomposity, not emphasis: "avec beaucoup d'emphase".

questions.stem: Match each term to what it does.
choices: imitates a manner, often admiringly
mocks a model by exaggerating it
copies a text and signs it as one's own
reuses a known text for another message
tells a noble subject in a low style
questions.explanation: Pastiche plays, parody mocks, plagiarism hides its model, détournement changes the message. A noble subject in a low style is the burlesque.

questions.stem: Which features mark the administrative style of the memo in the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: the impersonal il (Il est rappelé que …)
the passive voice
nouns instead of verbs (l'application, une dérogation)
epic similes
exclamations (Ô perfidie !)
questions.explanation: The memo relies on the impersonal il, the passive and nominalisation, plus the conditional of hearsay. Epic similes and exclamations are markers of the mock-heroic model, not of the memo.

questions.stem: Name the genre in each numbered square.

image.alt: A two-by-two grid of subject (low or noble) against style (low or noble), with the genre names blanked and numbered: noble subject in a low style (1), noble subject in a noble style (2), low subject in a low style (3), low subject in a noble style (4).

choices: burlesque
épopée
farce
héroï-comique
roman-feuilleton
circulaire administrative
questions.explanation: Noble subject, low style: burlesque. Noble subject, noble style: the epic. Low subject, low style: farce. Low subject, noble style: mock-heroic (héroï-comique).

questions.stem: Inside a line of verse, how many syllables does "une belle nuit" have?
questions.explanation: Before a consonant the e muet counts: u-ne-bel-le-nuit, five syllables. In conversation the two e's usually drop, giving three.

questions.stem: In verse, what happens to the e of "une" in "une aube"?
choices: It is elided before the vowel and doesn't count.
It counts as a full syllable.
It counts only at the end of the line.
It is pronounced like é.
questions.explanation: Before a vowel or a mute h the e muet is elided: "une aube" begins u-nau…

questions.stem: "Le vieux lion dormait au soleil de midi" has twelve syllables only if:
choices: lion is counted as one syllable (synérèse)
vieux is counted as two syllables
lion is counted as two syllables (diérèse)
midi loses a syllable
questions.explanation: Le (1) vieux (2) li (3) on (4) dor (5) mait (6) | au (7) so (8) leil (9) de (10) mi (11) di (12): the diérèse on li-on gives twelve. With lion in one syllable the line has eleven.

questions.stem: Where does the caesura fall in a classical alexandrine?
choices: After the fourth syllable
Wherever there is a comma
After the sixth syllable
After the eighth syllable
questions.explanation: The classical alexandrine splits into two hemistichs of six syllables; the sixth must end a word. A comma elsewhere is a pause, not the caesura.

questions.stem: What makes a rhyme masculine?
choices: The line doesn't end in an e muet.
The rhyming words are masculine nouns.
The rhyme shares three sounds.
The line has twelve syllables.
questions.explanation: Masculine and feminine refer to the ending: a feminine rhyme ends in an e muet (ville, docile), a masculine one doesn't (gris, cri), whatever the gender of the word.

questions.stem: How rich is the rhyme "lumière / chaumière"?
choices: pauvre
suffisante
embrassée
riche
questions.explanation: The two words share [mjɛʁ], three sounds or more: a rime riche. Embrassée names a pattern (abba), not a quality.

questions.stem: In "Elle avait attendu tout l'hiver sur le quai / Son fils. Le printemps vint, et le navire aussi.", what is "Son fils"?
choices: a caesura
a rejet
a hemistich
a diaeresis
questions.explanation: The object of "attendu" runs over the end of the line (enjambment) and the sentence stops after two words: a rejet, which gives "Son fils" its weight.

questions.stem: What is the structure of a sonnet?
choices: Three quatrains and a couplet
Two quatrains and two tercets
Four tercets and two single lines
Fourteen lines in one stanza
questions.explanation: The French sonnet has fourteen lines: two quatrains, then two tercets. (The English Shakespearean sonnet ends with a couplet, which is another form.)

questions.stem: Which of these original lines is an octosyllable?
choices: Le soir tombe sans bruit sur les toits de la ville.
Le vent pousse un journal le long du mur, docile.
Un dernier tram s'éloigne.
La nuit descend sur le jardin.
questions.explanation: La (1) nuit (2) des (3) cend (4) sur (5) le (6) jar (7) din (8): eight syllables. The first two lines are alexandrines (twelve); "Un dernier tram s'éloigne" has six, since the final e doesn't count.

questions.stem: Listen to the line. Where does the caesura fall?

audio.text: Le dernier tram s'en va, le quai devient tout gris.

choices: After "va"
After "tram"
After "quai"
After "dernier"
questions.explanation: Le (1) der (2) nier (3) tram (4) s'en (5) va (6) | le (7) quai (8) de (9) vient (10) tout (11) gris (12): the caesura falls after the sixth syllable, "va", at the end of a word and at a comma.

questions.stem: Count the syllables of this line as verse (the final e doesn't count): "Une belle robe blanche". Give the number.
questions.explanation: U (1) ne (2) bel (3) le (4) ro (5) be (6) blanche (7): every inner e muet is before a consonant, so it counts; the final e of blanche doesn't.

questions.stem: Match each rhyme scheme to its name.
choices: rimes plates
rimes croisées
rimes embrassées
rimes riches
questions.explanation: Plates (or suivies) go two by two, croisées alternate, embrassées enclose one pair inside the other. Riche is a quality, not a pattern.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the scansion.

image.alt: The original alexandrine Le soir tombe sans bruit sur les toits de la ville cut into twelve numbered syllables, with five blank labels: under syllables 1 to 6 (1), above the bar after syllable 6 (2), under syllables 7 to 12 (3), pointing to the syllable be (4), and pointing to the greyed final le (5).

choices: premier hémistiche
césure
second hémistiche
e muet compté
e final non compté
diérèse
rejet
questions.explanation: The bar after the sixth syllable is the caesura, which divides the line into two hemistichs. The e of "tombe" counts before the consonant of "sans"; the final e of "ville" doesn't count.

questions.stem: Which statements about the original quatrain of Example 4 are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its rhymes are croisées (abab).
Feminine and masculine rhymes alternate.
Every line has twelve syllables.
All its rhymes are riches.
It ends with a rejet.
questions.explanation: Ville, gris, docile, cri gives abab, feminine (ville, docile) alternating with masculine (gris, cri), in four alexandrines. Both rhymes are suffisantes, not riches, and the last line ends a sentence with no rejet.

questions.stem: In which tense is L'Étranger mainly narrated?
choices: the passé simple
the présent
the passé composé
the imparfait
questions.explanation: Camus tells the story in the passé composé, the tense of discours, where a classical novel would use the passé simple. That choice is central to the book's style.

questions.stem: Who tells the story of L'Étranger?
choices: An all-knowing narrator in the third person
Marie, years later
Meursault himself, in the first person
The prosecutor, at the trial
questions.explanation: It is a first-person narration: we see only what Meursault sees and says, and he rarely explains his motives.

questions.stem: What counts most against Meursault at his trial?
choices: His behaviour at his mother's funeral
A previous criminal conviction
The chaplain's testimony
A written confession
questions.explanation: The court talks more about the funeral (he didn't cry, he smoked, he went to see a comedy the next day) than about the killing. The chaplain comes only after the sentence.

questions.stem: In a French cour d'assises, who is l'avocat général?
choices: The defence lawyer
The president of the court
The lawyer of the victim's family
The magistrate who represents the prosecution
questions.explanation: Despite the name, l'avocat général is a magistrate of the prosecution, not a lawyer; the novel calls him simply le procureur. The defence speaks through its own lawyer, and the victim's family may have one too.

questions.stem: What is "la plaidoirie"?
choices: The prosecutor's speech
The defence lawyer's closing speech
The jury's verdict
The investigating judge's report
questions.explanation: La plaidoirie is the defence's speech; the prosecutor's is le réquisitoire.

questions.stem: What did Sartre argue in his 1943 essay on L'Étranger?
choices: That the novel should have been written in the passé simple
That the passé composé and the short sentences cut the story into separate moments without causal links
That Meursault is a portrait of Camus himself
That the novel is a pastiche of a specific American novel
questions.explanation: Sartre's "Explication de L'Étranger" analysed how the tense and the short sentences isolate each moment; he compared the technique to that of American novelists such as Hemingway, without calling the book a pastiche.

questions.stem: For Camus, what is "the absurd"?
choices: Anything ridiculous or silly
The belief that everything is predetermined
A style of comic theatre
The gap between our need for meaning and a world that gives none
questions.explanation: The absurd arises from the meeting between a human being who wants meaning and a world that offers none. Fatalism is another idea, and the everyday sense of absurde (ridiculous) is not Camus's.

questions.stem: Who tells the story in Kamel Daoud's Meursault, contre-enquête?
choices: Haroun, the brother of the man Meursault killed
Meursault's son
Marie, years later
A French investigating judge
questions.explanation: Daoud gives the victim's family a voice: Haroun tells the story from the other side and names his brother Moussa.

questions.stem: Why does Daoud give the victim a name?
choices: Because Moussa is his name in Camus's novel
Because Moussa is the narrator's own name
Because Camus never names him and calls him only "the Arab"
Because it is the name of Camus's publisher
questions.explanation: Camus's novel leaves the victim nameless; Daoud's counter-investigation starts from that silence and names him Moussa.

questions.stem: What are "les circonstances atténuantes"?
choices: Aggravating circumstances
The facts of the crime
Mitigating circumstances, which lower the sentence
The right to appeal
questions.explanation: Atténuer means to lessen: the jury may grant mitigating circumstances. Meursault's jury grants none.

questions.stem: Retell in the first person and the passé composé, as Meursault would: "Il gravit le talus." → "J'___ le talus."
questions.explanation: Gravir takes avoir and its participle is gravi: "J'ai gravi le talus." The passé simple "il gravit" becomes a passé composé, and the third person a first person.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: chaplain
juror
sunstroke
capital punishment
defence lawyer
questions.explanation: L'aumônier visits Meursault in his cell, les jurés decide with the judges, une insolation is sunstroke, and la peine capitale is the death penalty. The defence lawyer is l'avocat de la défense.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on the schematic map of the novel.

image.alt: A schematic map with four blank labels: the sea along the top (1), the town on the coast to the east (2), the beach to the west on the coast (3), and an inland place to the south-west (4).

choices: La Méditerranée
Alger (la prison, le tribunal)
La plage du cabanon
L'asile de vieillards (Marengo)
Oran
Paris
questions.explanation: Meursault lives, is imprisoned and is tried in Algiers; the old people's home is at Marengo, 80 km away according to the novel; the beach with Masson's hut is a bus ride from Algiers. Oran is where Daoud's narrator talks, not a place on this map.

questions.stem: Which features describe the style of L'Étranger? Select all that apply.
choices: first-person narration
short sentences with few linking words
the passé composé as the narrative tense
long periods with many subordinate clauses
a narrator who explains every motive
questions.explanation: Meursault tells his own story in the passé composé, in short, mostly paratactic sentences, and rarely explains why he acts. Long periods and full explanations are the opposite of this style.

questions.stem: What does this sentence from a statute express? "Le preneur est tenu de payer le loyer aux termes convenus."
choices: A duty of the lessee: he must pay the rent on the agreed dates
A description of what tenants usually do
Advice to tenants, which they may ignore
A promise about the future, made by the landlord
questions.explanation: Statutes and contracts state rules in the present indicative: the prescriptive present. "Être tenu de" + infinitive means "must". The sentence orders; it does not describe a habit or give advice.

questions.stem: A lease says: "La majoration est due nonobstant toute clause contraire." What does "nonobstant toute clause contraire" mean?
choices: unless a clause of the contract says otherwise
whatever any clause of the contract says to the contrary
in accordance with the clauses of the contract
provided that no clause forbids it
questions.explanation: "Nonobstant" + noun means "notwithstanding, despite": the increase is owed even if a clause says the opposite. "Unless a clause says otherwise" is the reverse meaning ("sauf disposition contraire").

questions.stem: A reference reads "art. R. 211-3". What does the R tell you?
choices: It is an article of the legislative part, adopted by Parliament
It is an article of the Code civil, which numbers by part
It is an article of the regulatory part of a code, made by government decree
It is an article that has been repealed
questions.explanation: "L." marks the legislative part of a modern code (adopted by Parliament); "R." and "D." mark the regulatory part (decrees). The Code civil is older than this system and uses plain numbers.

questions.stem: Complete the operative part of a judgment: "Le tribunal ___ Mme Garnier de sa demande de dommages et intérêts."
choices: rejette
condamne
ordonne
déboute
questions.explanation: "Débouter quelqu'un de sa demande" takes the person as object and the claim after "de": only "déboute" fits the frame. "Rejeter" takes the claim itself ("rejette la demande"); "condamner" is "condamner quelqu'un à"; "ordonner" is "ordonner quelque chose à quelqu'un".

questions.stem: In a civil case, who is "le défendeur"?
choices: The party against whom the claim is brought
The person prosecuted in a criminal court
The lawyer who defends a client
The judge who decides the case
questions.explanation: "Le défendeur" (feminine "la défenderesse") answers a civil claim brought by "le demandeur". The defendant in a criminal court is "le prévenu" (B2); the lawyer is "l'avocat".

questions.stem: What does "la jurisprudence" mean in "selon une jurisprudence constante"?
choices: legal philosophy
case law: the decisions of the courts
the area a court has authority over
the law faculty of a university
questions.explanation: "La jurisprudence" is case law; "une jurisprudence constante" is a settled line of decisions. It is not the English "jurisprudence" (legal philosophy). A court's area of authority is its "compétence" or "juridiction".

questions.stem: Since 1 October 2019, how does the Cour de cassation write its judgments?
choices: As one long sentence built on "attendu que"
In Latin formulas, as in the eighteenth century
In numbered paragraphs of ordinary sentences, under headings
As a summary drafted by the parties' lawyers
questions.explanation: The "direct style" replaced the chain of "attendu que" with numbered paragraphs under headings such as "Faits et procédure", "Examen du moyen" and "Dispositif". The Conseil d'État had made the same change, dropping "considérant que", from 1 January 2019.

questions.stem: You want to know at once who won a case. Which part of the decision do you read first?
choices: les motifs
les faits et la procédure
l'en-tête, with the names of the parties
le dispositif, after "Par ces motifs"
questions.explanation: The operative part ("le dispositif") follows "Par ces motifs" and states what the court decides: "condamne, ordonne, déboute, rejette". The reasons ("les motifs") explain why; the facts say what happened.

questions.stem: Under the rules described in the lesson (November 2026), a civil judgment on a claim of 2,000 euros is usually given "en dernier ressort". What can the losing party do?
choices: Only lodge a pourvoi en cassation; there is no appeal
Interjeter appel before the cour d'appel within one month
Ask the same judge to hear the facts again
Nothing: no remedy exists against such a judgment
questions.explanation: A judgment "en dernier ressort" can't be appealed; the only remedy left is the pourvoi en cassation, which checks the law, not the facts. As a rule, claims of up to 5,000 euros are judged this way. Check any real case: thresholds and time limits change.

questions.stem: What does the Cour de cassation examine when it receives a pourvoi?
choices: The facts and the law, all over again
Only whether the law was correctly applied
Only the amount of damages
Only whether the lawyers were competent
questions.explanation: The Cour de cassation judges the law, not the facts: it checks whether the lower court applied the rules correctly. A cour d'appel, by contrast, judges the facts and the law again.

questions.stem: What does "caduque" mean here? "Faute d'avoir été acceptée dans le délai, l'offre est devenue caduque."
choices: accepted automatically
doubled as a penalty
lapsed: no longer valid
suspended until a judge decides
questions.explanation: "Caduc, caduque" means lapsed, no longer valid (in legal French), or obsolete in general use: the offer wasn't accepted in time, so it no longer exists.

questions.stem: In paragraph 6 of the reading, the court says the landlord "a de facto mis à la charge de Mme Garnier la remise en état" of the flat. What does "de facto" convey?
choices: That the law expressly makes the tenant pay to refurbish the flat
That she agreed in writing to pay for the repainting
That the judge is uncertain about the facts
That in practice, though no rule allowed it, he made her pay to refurbish the flat
questions.explanation: "De facto" means "in fact, whatever the rules say": by keeping the whole deposit without proving any damage, he put the cost of the repainting on her, which the law (no liability for wear due to age) does not allow.

questions.stem: Why does the court dismiss Mme Garnier's claim for 1,500 euros of damages (paragraph 8 of the reading)?
choices: She shows no harm beyond the one the statutory increase already compensates
She applied to the wrong court
Her claim was made too late
The landlord had already paid her the damages
questions.explanation: Paragraph 9: "Mme Garnier ne démontre pas un préjudice distinct de celui que répare déjà la majoration légale." The 10 % increase per month of delay already compensates the delay; she proves no separate harm.

questions.stem: The landlord kept the deposit. Which word would a judgment use for him?
choices: le proprio
le bailleur
le preneur
le locataire
questions.explanation: "Le bailleur" is the legal term for the person who lets property. "Le proprio" is informal; "le preneur" (legal) and "le locataire" (everyday) both name the tenant, the other party.

questions.stem: Which sentence states the rule as a statute would?
choices: Le proprio va vous rendre la caution dans les deux mois.
Le dépôt de garantie serait restitué dans un délai de deux mois.
Le dépôt de garantie est restitué dans un délai maximal de deux mois.
Le dépôt de garantie a été restitué dans un délai de deux mois.
questions.explanation: Statutes use the prescriptive present: "est restitué" orders the return. The near future with "proprio" is informal speech; the conditional ("serait") reports or supposes; the passé composé ("a été restitué") reports a past fact.

questions.stem: Listen to the legal chronicle. What does the chronicler insist on at the end?

audio.text: Chroniqueuse : Vos droits au quotidien. Marc a quitté son appartement il y a trois mois. L'état des lieux de sortie était identique à celui d'entrée, et il attend toujours son dépôt de garantie. Que dit la loi ? Le bailleur avait un mois pour le rendre. Passé ce délai, la somme est majorée de dix pour cent du loyer par mois de retard commencé. Mais attention : ce n'est pas un conseil personnalisé. Renseignez-vous auprès de l'ADIL de votre département.

choices: That tenants should stop paying their rent until the deposit is returned
That the landlord in the question has broken criminal law
That the 10 % increase is no longer in force
That this is general information, and that listeners should get advice on their own case
questions.explanation: The chronicle ends: "ce n'est pas un conseil personnalisé. Renseignez-vous auprès de l'ADIL de votre département." She gives the general rule (one month, then 10 % per month begun) and sends listeners to free advice for their own case.

questions.stem: Listen to Julie and Thomas. What does Thomas imply about Julie's brother?

audio.text: Julie : Le juge a débouté mon frère. Il va faire appel. Thomas : Faire appel ? Pour huit cents euros ? Le jugement a été rendu en dernier ressort : il n'a que le pourvoi. Et la Cour de cassation ne rejugera pas les faits.

choices: He can't appeal, and a pourvoi wouldn't reopen the facts, so his chances are slim
He should appeal at once, before the month runs out
He has already won his case on appeal
He should sue the judge for damages
questions.explanation: Thomas points out that the judgment was given "en dernier ressort": no appeal, only a pourvoi, and "la Cour de cassation ne rejugera pas les faits". His ironic "Pour huit cents euros ?" adds that the stakes are small.

questions.stem: Listen to the lawyer. What is her attitude to the direct style?

audio.text: Avocate : Pendant deux siècles, nos arrêts tenaient en une seule phrase de deux pages. Le justiciable devait s'armer de patience, et d'un dictionnaire. Depuis 2019, la Cour écrit enfin comme tout le monde : des paragraphes numérotés, des phrases courtes. On ne va pas s'en plaindre.

choices: She regrets the old style and finds the new one too simple
She welcomes it, and mocks the old single-sentence judgments
She thinks it changed nothing for the justiciable
She is worried that judgments are now too short to be valid
questions.explanation: Her irony targets the old style ("une seule phrase de deux pages", "s'armer de patience… et d'un dictionnaire"), and "On ne va pas s'en plaindre" (we're not going to complain) shows approval of the change.

questions.stem: Complete the set formula of a judgment with the present participle of the verb meaning "to rule": "Le tribunal, ___ publiquement, par jugement contradictoire et en dernier ressort, …"
questions.explanation: "Statuer" = to rule; the formula is "Le tribunal, statuant publiquement, par jugement contradictoire et en dernier ressort". "Contradictoire" means both sides were heard.

questions.stem: Reformulation: rewrite in everyday French with a single adverb in place of the formal phrase. "La cave est mise à disposition à titre gracieux." → "La cave est mise à disposition ___."
questions.explanation: "À titre gracieux" is the formal phrase for "free of charge"; the everyday adverb is "gratuitement" ("gratis", "sans frais" and the more formal "gracieusement" are also accepted). The opposite is "à titre onéreux".

questions.stem: Reformulation: rewrite with the legal verb, so that the person is the object. "Le juge a rejeté la demande de la locataire." → "Le juge a ___ la locataire de sa demande."
questions.explanation: "Débouter quelqu'un de sa demande": the person is débouté, the claim follows "de". The participle agrees with nothing here because the auxiliary is avoir and the object follows: "a débouté la locataire".

questions.stem: Reformulation: rewrite in everyday French. "Elle a interjeté appel du jugement." → "Elle a ___ appel du jugement."
questions.explanation: "Interjeter appel" is the legal phrase; "faire appel" (B2) is the everyday one: "Elle a fait appel du jugement."

questions.stem: Put the divisions of a French code in order, from the largest to the smallest.
choices: le livre
le titre
le chapitre
la section
l'article
l'alinéa
questions.explanation: A code is divided into "livres", then "titres", "chapitres", "sections" and "articles"; an article may have several paragraphs, each an "alinéa": "l'article 22, alinéa 2".

questions.stem: Match each person in a case with what they do.
choices: lets a property under a lease
rents a property under a lease
answers a civil claim
applies to a court by written application
holds a right through another person
is prosecuted in a criminal court
questions.explanation: In everyday French the bailleur is "le propriétaire" and the preneur "le locataire". The défendeur answers a civil claim brought by the demandeur; the requérant applies by "requête"; an ayant droit holds a right through someone else (an heir, for example). The criminal defendant is "le prévenu".

questions.stem: Which of these are voies de recours (means of challenging a judgment)? Select all that apply.
choices: l'appel
le pourvoi en cassation
l'astreinte
la clause résolutoire
le dispositif
