cards.back: The honnête homme (Faret, 1630): cultivated without pedantry, moderate, graceful in society; not "an honest man". Un bel esprit: a wit, often ironic. Plural les beaux esprits.

Played at Versailles on 12 May 1664 and banned; L'Imposteur played once on 5 August 1667 and banned; performed freely from 5 February 1669. A cabale of dévots, often linked to the Compagnie du Saint-Sacrement.

cards.front: Comic types: le barbon, le dévot, le misanthrope
cards.back: Le barbon: the old man who wants a young wife (Arnolphe). Le faux dévot: the hypocrite (Tartuffe). Le misanthrope: Alceste, who rejects polite lies (1666).

Comedy framed by songs and dances that belong to the plot. First: Les Fâcheux (Vaux-le-Vicomte, 17 August 1661). Le Bourgeois gentilhomme (Chambord, 14 October 1670, Lully); Le Malade imaginaire (1673, Charpentier).
In a 17th-century theatre, the standing pit in front of the stage, cheapest and mostly male, loud in its judgements. Today a flower bed; theatre stalls are l'orchestre.

cards.front: Words that moved since the 17th century
cards.back: Ennui: grief, worry → boredom. Étonner: to stun (thunder) → to surprise. Gêne: torture → discomfort. Charmer: to bewitch → to delight. Formidable: fearsome → terrific.
cards.topic: Classical French and words that changed

cards.back: French of the 17th–18th centuries: pronoun before the governing verb (je le veux voir), -oi- imperfects in old editions (until the Académie's 1835 edition), the imperfect subjunctive in use.
cards.topic: Classical French and words that changed

cards.back: Born 26 February 1802 in Besançon; Hernani 1830; Académie française 1841; died 22 May 1885; national funeral and the Panthéon.
After the coup of 2 December 1851: Brussels (December 1851), Jersey (August 1852), Guernsey (October 1855, Hauteville House). Refused the 1859 amnesty; back in Paris on 5 September 1870.
Un proscrit is banished by an official act (often political); un exilé lives in exile; la proscription is the act of banishment; l'exil is the state.
Published in Brussels by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven et Cie; five parts, ten volumes; begun as Les Misères in 1845, finished in exile. A roman-fleuve with long digressions.
Valjean leaves the Toulon bagne (1815), is forgiven by a bishop, becomes a mayor, promises Fantine to save Cosette, is hunted by Javert, saves Marius from the June 1832 barricade through the sewers.

cards.front: Le bagne, le bagnard, le forçat
cards.back: Le bagne: penal colony with hard labour (naval ports after 1748; Guiana from 1852; transportation abolished 1938). Le bagnard: its inmate. Le forçat: first a galley slave, then any convict.
Gavroche, the Thénardiers' son, lives in the streets and is shot at the foot of the barricade. Le gamin de Paris; informal le titi parisien.

Part IV, book 7: argot as a real language of misery as well as crime, constantly changing because it must stay secret; a novelist may study the bas-fonds and la pègre. Vidocq's memoirs (1828–1829) were a source of the time.
An old name for slang, common in the 19th century; today old-fashioned. The usual word is l'argot. Underworld words now ordinary: la tronche (informal), cambrioler (standard), le flic (informal).
Born Marguerite Cleenewerck de Crayencour in Brussels on 8 June 1903; died in Bar Harbor, Maine, on 17 December 1987. Pen name an anagram of Crayencour (legal name in 1947).
Left for the United States in 1939 with Grace Frick; American citizen in 1947; from 1950 at Petite Plaisance on Mount Desert Island, Maine.
Translation of Virginia Woolf's The Waves (1937); Mémoires d'Hadrien (Plon, 1951); L'Œuvre au noir (1968, prix Femina).
One long letter from the dying emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138) to the young Marcus Aurelius: a first-person epistolary novel, opening with the doctor's visit; six parts with Latin titles.
Childhood, Trajan's wars, accession, travels, love of Greece (l'hellénisme), the wall in Britain, Antinous drowned in the Nile (130), the revolt in Judaea (132–135), death faced with sérénité.
Fiction set in a real past; its law is la vraisemblance: invented scenes must agree with the documents and with what people of the time could know.
cards.topic: The historical novel and its voice

cards.back: Le monologue intérieur renders thoughts as they come, without order (Dujardin, 1887; Joyce). Hadrian's letter is inward but composed, balanced and addressed to a reader.
cards.topic: The historical novel and its voice

cards.back: Long periods that close on the main idea; precise, learned vocabulary (érudition); the imperfect subjunctive kept (recognise it: qu'il oubliât = qu'il oublie).
First woman elected (6 March 1980), in Roger Caillois's seat; received on 22 January 1981 by Jean d'Ormesson. For the ceremony Yves Saint Laurent designed her a velvet cape with a shawl.

cards.front: L'habit vert, l'académicien, le discours de réception
cards.back: L'habit vert: the members' embroidered coat. Un académicien, une académicienne: a member. Le discours de réception: the new member's first speech, praising the predecessor.
January 1954, New York: Georgetown University and IBM; an IBM 701 translated just over sixty prepared Russian sentences into English (250 words, six rules). ALPAC (1966) then ended most US funding.

September 2016: Google researchers present a neural system; 15 November 2016: Google Translate applies it to eight pairs (French–English included). 2017: the Transformer; DeepL (August, Cologne); the EU's eTranslation.
European Commission DG Translation: 1,944 staff (about 70 % in translation-related roles), over 2.3 million pages, 30 % outsourced; eTranslation: 763.5 million pages. 24 official languages.
La post-édition: a professional's correction of a machine translation (also postédition). Le post-éditeur, la post-éditrice: who does it.

cards.front: Apprentissage automatique, réseau de neurones, modèle de langue
cards.back: Machine learning (learning from examples, not rules); neural network (plural réseaux de neurones); language model (predicts the next word; un grand modèle de langue).
Adapting software or games to a market; subtitling (one or two short lines on screen); the interpreter's profession (speech); the academic study of translation.
Removing the go-between: here, readers who no longer use a translator. The "against" side calls the translator a guarantor who answers for the text.

For (agency head): the machine translates what no human would have been paid to translate; post-editors add value. Against (interpreter): elegant errors, no one answers for them, English calques, underpaid post-editing.
An article or a speech of at least 700 words: engaged, qualified, built from the dossier and your own knowledge; sources attributed, invented figures never presented as real.
Denotation (what exactly they name), connotation (what they suggest), collocation (which words they go with), construction (which preposition or object), register and frequency.
distinguished (un éminent spécialiste) / about to happen (un danger imminent)
a break-in (entrer par effraction) / any offence against the law (une infraction au code de la route)
to commit a crime (perpétrer un attentat) / to carry on, keep alive (perpétuer une tradition)
supposed to, always + infinitive (il est censé venir) / sensible (une remarque sensée)
a dispute, noun in -end (un différend commercial) / different, adjective. For a dispute in court, le litige.
a sense of a word / acceptance; a liking, a tendency / a slope, an angle
to regain, to collect a debt (elle a recouvré la vue) / to cover (recouvert)
pallier à (→ pallier un manque), conséquent = large (→ considérable), solutionner (→ résoudre), initier un projet (→ lancer). Say "criticised by many usage guides", not "wrong".
mumble indistinctly / stammer in embarrassment / murmur softly, intimately (literary) / proclaim loudly (clamer son innocence)
mutter in discontent / quibble over details / keep going over (thoughts, grievances) / keep repeating tiresomely (mildly informal)
administratif, soutenu, courant, familier (productive); populaire, argotique (recognise; produce only in quotation). The lower levels shade into each other.
Administratif hides the person (passive, impersonal, l'intéressé) and uses set phrases; soutenu is a writer's formal French with a personal voice.

cards.front: se barrer, se tirer / partir / prendre congé
cards.back: to leave: informal / neutral / formal (prendre congé de quelqu'un)

cards.front: roupiller, la piaule, la baraque, le pognon, les godasses
cards.back: informal for: dormir, la chambre, la (grande) maison, l'argent, les chaussures

cards.front: se gourer, engueuler, se goinfrer, crevant
cards.back: informal: se tromper; to bawl out (rather rude); to stuff your face; exhausting or hilarious
administrative: to notify; to pay, to fulfil; duly; above-mentioned
A deliberate jump to another register for humour, irony, quotation or complicity. It works because the rest is controlled; by accident, the word is merely incongru.
commonplace (une idée triviale) or crude, coarse (une plaisanterie triviale). "Minor, unimportant" is common but criticised by some as an anglicism; une solution triviale is standard in maths.

cards.front: la gouaille, le parler, le clin d'œil
cards.back: cheeky, mocking popular wit (Paris); a way of speaking (le parler jeune); a nod to the reader, literally a wink
être: with the subject. avoir: with a direct object placed before. Pronominal: with its direct object (elle s'est essoufflée; elle s'est foulé la cheville).

cards.front: les heures qu'il a dormi / les colis qu'il a pesés
cards.back: A measure (time, price, weight, distance) is not an object: no agreement. A real object placed before: agreement.
Impersonal verbs (les chaleurs qu'il a fait) and fait + infinitive (la maison qu'ils ont fait construire). Laissé + infinitive: invariable in 1990 spelling, agreement still accepted.

cards.front: la plupart des / une foule de / plus d'un
cards.back: plural (la plupart des coureurs sont arrivés) / singular or plural / singular (plus d'un coureur a abandonné)
une demi-heure but deux heures et demie; nu-pieds but les pieds nus; à mi-course; des semi-marathons
simple: agree (des maillots bleus); compound: invariable (bleu clair); nouns as colours: invariable (marron), except rose, mauve, fauve, écarlate, pourpre. Orange: usually invariable.
quatre-vingts, deux cents (multiplied and final) but quatre-vingt-trois, deux cent trois, quatre-vingt mille; mille never varies; page quatre-vingt.
quelle que soit la distance (whatever: quel agrees with the subject of être) / quelque cinq mille litres (about: invariable), quelques coureurs (some)
le dossard (race number), le peloton (pack), la foulée (stride), le ravitaillement (refreshment point), le meneur d'allure (pacer), le chrono (race time), à mi-course (halfway)

cards.front: Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés.
cards.back: Careful writing reads "not all"; speech may hear "none". Clear: Les coureurs ne sont pas tous arrivés / Aucun coureur n'est arrivé.
only (il ne boit que de l'eau) / not only (il ne boit pas que de l'eau)

cards.front: Seul le maire / le seul maire / même le maire / le même maire
cards.back: only the mayor / the only mayor / even the mayor / the same mayor

cards.front: pas vraiment / vraiment pas; toujours pas / pas toujours
cards.back: not really / really not; still not / not always
Saying less to mean more: ce n'est pas mal (it's good), je ne suis pas mécontent (I'm pleased).

cards.front: Four ways to remove a structural ambiguity
cards.back: Change the word order; use a relative with lequel / laquelle; repeat the noun; add punctuation.

cards.front: stricto sensu, au sens large, en tout état de cause
cards.back: in the strict sense (Latin, no accents) / in the broad sense / in any event (formal)

cards.front: peu ou prou, grosso modo, tant soit peu
cards.back: more or less (formal) / broadly, roughly (common) / even slightly (formal)
crystal-clear; with one meaning only; terse (praise or curt); cryptic, deliberately obscure; convoluted
Two things varying together does not prove one causes the other. Also: l'écart-type (standard deviation), l'intervalle de confiance (confidence interval), faire l'amalgame (to lump together wrongly).
Direct: borrowing, calque, literal translation. Oblique: transposition, modulation, equivalence, adaptation (Stylistique comparée du français et de l'anglais, 1958).
Change of word class: as soon as he arrived → dès son arrivée.
Change of viewpoint: it's not difficult → c'est facile; wet paint → peinture fraîche.
Same situation, different words: il pleut des cordes. Adaptation replaces an unfamiliar situation (a Fourth of July barbecue → un barbecue du 14 Juillet).
swim across → traverser à la nage; he limped out → il est sorti en boitant. English verb = manner, French verb = direction.
Adding words French needs: walk to the station → marcher jusqu'à la gare; the train to Lyon → le train à destination de Lyon.
a wrong meaning / a slight inaccuracy / no meaning at all
currently (not actually), possibly (not eventually), for good (not definitely)
sensitive (not sensible: sensé); not to know (to ignore: ne pas tenir compte de); to check (to control: maîtriser)
en charge de → chargé de, responsable de; faire sens → avoir du sens; adresser un problème → traiter, aborder. Common and criticised.
Translators who stay close to the source text / who write for the target reader (terms of Jean-René Ladmiral). Les belles infidèles: polished 17th-century translations.
Remarques sur la langue françoise (1647): short notes on doubtful points, with the usage of the court and the best writers as the model. The first remarqueur.
Letters patent 1635; first dictionary 1694; ninth edition completed November 2024. Prestige, not law.
Littré: published 1863–1872, quotations from great writers. Pierre Larousse: Grand Dictionnaire universel (1866–1876). Paul Robert: analogical dictionary (1950s–1960s).
Maurice Grevisse, 1936; revised by André Goosse from the 12th edition (1986); 16th edition 2016. Prescriptive title, largely descriptive method.
Trésor de la langue française: 16 volumes, 1971–1994, about 100,000 words; free online as the TLFi.
Prescriptive: what you should write. Descriptive: what people write, with evidence. Most works mix both.
Non-breaking space before : ; ! ? (a thin one before ; ! ? in fine typography) and inside « ». In typography, une espace (feminine).
Accented capitals (État, À); lower case for months, days, languages (le français, en janvier); italics for titles and foreign words.

cards.front: Passé simple: the three ending sets
cards.back: -er: -ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent (il parla). -ir/-re: -is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent (il finit, il vendit). -u- verbs: -us, -us, -ut, -ûmes, -ûtes, -urent (il fut). Plus venir/tenir: il vint, ils vinrent.
fit (faire), dit, vit (voir), mit, prit, naquit (naître), vainquit (vaincre), s'assit, acquit (acquérir), vêtit, rompit.
fut, eut, sut, put, dut, crut (croire), lut, plut (plaire, pleuvoir), vécut (vivre), mourut, conclut, résolut.
Il crut = he believed (croire). Il crût = it grew (croître). Only the circumflex separates them.
Passé simple of avoir/être + participle: il eut fini, elle fut partie. After quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, après que, and in À peine fut-elle arrivée que …
Events cut off from the present, third person: passé simple (events), imparfait (background), plus-que-parfait and passé antérieur (before), conditional (after). Novels, tales, history books.
A speaker addresses someone, tied to the present: présent, passé composé, imparfait, plus-que-parfait, futur; every person. Letters, conversation, most press.
Passé simple (or passé composé) = events that move the story on. Imparfait = setting, states, habits, what was going on. Il pleuvait depuis huit jours (background). La crue survint (foreground).

cards.front: Retelling a récit in your own French
cards.back: Use the passé composé or the présent: La crue survint → La crue est survenue. Dès qu'il eut aperçu l'eau, il courut → Dès qu'il a aperçu l'eau, il a couru.
Avoir is usual (ils ont accouru); être is common in literary French (ils sont accourus). Both are correct; the drills use avoir.

cards.front: Imperfect subjunctive: how to form it
cards.back: Tu passé simple without -s + -sse, -sses, -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent; for il, a circumflex + -t: tu parlas → que je parlasse, qu'il parlât; tu vins → qu'il vînt.

cards.front: il fut / qu'il fût; il eut / qu'il eût
cards.back: No circumflex: passé simple (he was, he had). Circumflex: imperfect subjunctive, or with a participle a pluperfect subjunctive (qu'il eût fini).
Classical: Je voulais qu'il vînt; Je doutais qu'il fût venu. Modern: Je voulais qu'il vienne; Je doutais qu'il soit venu.
Same shape as the pluperfect subjunctive, meaning of the conditionnel passé: il eût fallu = il aurait fallu; on eût dit = on aurait dit; j'eusse aimé = j'aurais aimé.

cards.front: S'il l'eût su, il fût venu
cards.back: Classical hypothetical = S'il l'avait su, il serait venu. Never si + conditional in modern careful French.
Verb before subject, no si: Eût-il su la vérité, il ne serait pas venu (had he known). Fût-elle ministre … (even if she were). Dût-il y passer la nuit … (even if it takes him all night).
Be it, even / even just, if only. Write: même / ne serait-ce que.
Even if I had to (imperfect subjunctive of devoir + inversion; é for euphony). Write: même si je devais.
If only … (a literary wish). Write: si seulement …

cards.front: Literary forms in a modern column
cards.back: Used for ironic contrast: old-fashioned grammar for old-fashioned behaviour (On eût dit un châtelain de 1850). In your own writing, use the modern equivalents unless the irony is obvious.
Binary: two balanced groups (lent et lourd). Ternary: three groups (Il hésita, se retourna, partit), the classic rhetorical number.
Majeure: each group longer, the sentence opens out. Mineure: a short last group, the sentence closes sharply (tout prévu, tout vérifié : sauf lui).
A long sentence that rises through subordinate clauses (protase), peaks (acmé) and falls in a shorter main clause (apodose).
Alliteration: a repeated consonant sound (le fleuve, lent et lourd). Assonance: a repeated vowel sound (la pluie fine glissait sur la vitrine).
Euphony: pleasant sounds (the t of viendra-t-il). Cacophony: harsh clash (Ton thé t'a-t-il ôté ta toux ?). Hiatus: vowels meeting (il alla à Arles).
Parataxe: clauses side by side, no subordination (Il pleuvait. Elle est partie.). Hypotaxe: subordination states the link (Comme il pleuvait, elle est partie.).
Asyndète: no links, speeds up (Il vint, il vit, il signa). Polysyndète: the link repeated, accumulates (Et la pluie, et le vent, et la nuit).
A sentence with no conjugated verb: Novembre, déjà. Silence. Puis un rire. It paints a scene in strokes.
Often subjective or literary (d'étranges lueurs, un pâle sourire). Some change meaning: un ancien élève (former) / un quartier ancien (old); un cher ami / un repas cher.
Cut into groups, count syllables, compare lengths, listen for sounds, look at the links, then say what each choice does to the meaning.
Pastiche: imitates a manner, often admiringly, copying no sentence. Parodie: mocks a model by exaggerating it or changing its subject.
Plagiat: copies and signs as one's own. Hommage: respectful allusion. Détournement: reuses a known text, slogan or image to give it another message.

Code de la propriété intellectuelle, art. L122-5, 4°: once a work has been made public, its author can't forbid parody, pastiche or caricature within 'the laws of the genre' (courts generally look for humour, no confusion, no intent to harm).
Burlesque: noble subject, low style (Scarron, Le Virgile travesti). Héroï-comique (mock-heroic): trivial subject, noble style (Boileau, Le Lutrin, 1674).
Pomposity, bombast, not emphasis (= l'insistance, la mise en relief). Its adjectives: pompeux, grandiloquent, ampoulé, boursouflé.
A work inside the work that mirrors it: a play within a play, a novel about a writer writing that novel.

cards.front: Turning a style into a recipe
cards.back: Lexicon, syntax, tenses, rhythm and sound, figures, point of view, clichés and tics. Then choose four or five markers and keep them steady.
Invocation, epic epithets (le fier Gérard), periphrases (une eau venue des cimes), inversions, epic similes, passé simple, gods stepping in, and deliberate anachronisms (la carte de fidélité).
Impersonal il (Il est rappelé que), passive, nominalisation (l'application, une dérogation), conditional of hearsay (se serait insérée), set formulas (sont invités à veiller à).
Queneau, Exercices de style (1947): one anecdote, 99 ways. Proust's Lemoine pastiches (most in Le Figaro, 1908-1909; Pastiches et mélanges, 1919). Reboux and Muller, À la manière de… (from 1908).
Counts before a consonant (u-ne-bel-le-nuit: 5), elided before a vowel or mute h (u-nau…), never counted at the end of the line.
Diérèse: two vowels as two syllables (li-on). Synérèse: as one (lion, hier, pied). The count of the line shows which the poet chose.
Twelve syllables, a caesura after the sixth (which must end a word), two hemistichs of six.
Décasyllabe: ten syllables, often 4 + 6, the line of medieval epic. Octosyllabe: eight, no fixed caesura, light and quick.
Enjambement: the sentence runs past the end of the line. Rejet: a short piece carried over to the next line, then the sentence stops (… sur le quai / Son fils.).
Feminine: the line ends in an e muet (ville, docile). Masculine: it doesn't (gris, cri). Nothing to do with the gender of the word. Classical poetry alternates them.
Pauvre: one shared sound (ami / pli). Suffisante: two (gris / cri). Riche: three or more (lumière / chaumière). Manuals draw the lines slightly differently.
Plates: aabb. Croisées: abab. Embrassées: abba.
Fourteen lines: two quatrains (classically abba abba) and two tercets (often ccd eed or ccd ede).
Albert Camus (1913-1960), Gallimard, 1942. First-person narration by Meursault, in the passé composé. Nobel Prize for Camus in 1957.

cards.front: Why the passé composé matters in L'Étranger
cards.back: It is the tense of discours: each event is set down beside the moment of speaking, without the causal chain of the passé simple. Short sentences and few links add to the effect.

'Explication de L'Étranger' (Cahiers du Sud, 1943): the tense and the short sentences cut the story into separate moments with no causal links; he compared the technique with American novelists such as Hemingway.
The gap between our need for meaning and a world that gives none. Le Mythe de Sisyphe (1942) answers it with lucidity and revolt, not despair or hope.

cards.front: Who's who in a cour d'assises
cards.back: L'avocat général (prosecution, a magistrate; le procureur in the novel), the defence lawyer's plaidoirie, the prosecutor's réquisitoire, les jurés with the judges.
Mitigating circumstances, which lower the sentence. Meursault's jury grants none.
Capital punishment (= la peine de mort). Meursault is sentenced to the guillotine. France abolished the death penalty in 1981.
Kamel Daoud (Barzakh, Algiers, 2013; Actes Sud, 2014; Goncourt du premier roman 2015). Haroun, the victim's brother, names him Moussa and tells the story from the other side.

cards.front: How is a French code divided?
cards.back: Livre → titre → chapitre → section → article → alinéa (a paragraph of an article: l'article 22, alinéa 2).
L. = legislative part (adopted by Parliament); R. or D. = regulatory part (decrees). The Code civil keeps plain numbers.
Statutes state duties in the present: Le preneur est tenu de payer le loyer. Le dépôt est restitué dans les deux mois. Être tenu de = must; ne peut = may not.
Notwithstanding (+ noun): nonobstant toute clause contraire = whatever the contract says. Formal; malgré is everyday.

cards.front: de plein droit / à titre gracieux
cards.back: De plein droit = as of right, automatically. À titre gracieux = free of charge (formal for gratuitement); à titre onéreux = for payment.

cards.front: in fine, de facto, a contrario
cards.back: In fine = at the end (of a text); de facto = in fact, whatever the rules say; a contrario = by the opposite reasoning. No accents.
Legal terms for le propriétaire (lessor) and le locataire (lessee). Feminines: la bailleresse, la preneuse.
Le défendeur (la défenderesse) answers a civil claim; le prévenu is the defendant in a criminal court.
Débouter quelqu'un de sa demande = to dismiss someone's claim (the person is the object). A claim itself is rejetée.

cards.front: The three parts of a decision
cards.back: The facts and procedure; the reasons (les motifs); the operative part (le dispositif, after Par ces motifs: condamne, ordonne, déboute).
Conseil d'État: from 1 January 2019 (no more considérant que). Cour de cassation: from 1 October 2019 (no more attendu que). Numbered paragraphs.

cards.front: interjeter appel vs le pourvoi en cassation
cards.back: Appeal: the cour d'appel judges facts and law again. Pourvoi: the Cour de cassation checks only the law. Small claims (up to 5,000 euros, as a rule) are judged en dernier ressort: pourvoi only.
A daily penalty added to a court order until it is obeyed (sous astreinte de 20 euros par jour). At work: being on call.
Case law (une jurisprudence constante = settled case law). Not legal philosophy.
Résumé → introduction (état de l'art) → matériel et méthodes (protocole) → résultats → discussion → conclusion, références.
Passive (les mesures ont été réalisées), impersonal il (il a été montré que + indicative), on, the authors' nous.
Être constitué de, se composer de, comporter; permettre de, servir à, assurer la fonction de; alimenter, convertir … en …
La mise en service après homologation du matériel roulant = the line opens once the trains are approved. Find the verb behind each noun.
Decimal comma (3,5 km), space before units and % (25 %), space between thousands (12 500), no plural on symbols (5 kg).
A power of ten: un ordre de grandeur de plus ≈ ten times more; du même ordre de grandeur = comparable.
Efficiency (useful energy out / energy in); also yield and return. Never la performance.

cards.front: la pile à combustible vs la batterie
cards.back: A fuel cell makes electricity from hydrogen as long as it is supplied; a battery stores electricity.
The overhead line of an electric railway, and the folding arm on the train's roof that touches it.

cards.front: une grandeur, une variable, un paramètre
cards.back: A measurable quantity (physics); a quantity that varies in a model; one fixed for a given case.
Cyclical (should pass when the cycle turns) vs structural (comes from how the economy or firm is built).
From 4 % to 6 %: + deux points, which is a rise of 50 %.
The central bank's key rate (the BCE in the euro area), the main tool of la politique monétaire.

cards.front: le bilan vs le compte de résultat
cards.back: Bilan = balance sheet (owns / owes on one day). Compte de résultat = income statement (income and costs over the exercice).
The cash a firm actually has, or its cash management. A profitable firm can still run out of it.
Fusion: two companies become one. Acquisition: one buys the other. Together: une fusion-acquisition.
Créancier (créancière) = who is owed; débiteur (débitrice) = who owes.
Cessation des paiements → declare within 45 days → redressement judiciaire (observation, then plan, sale or liquidation) or liquidation judiciaire. Faire faillite is everyday.
Progresser, s'envoler (soar), stagner, reculer, se replier (ease), plonger (plunge).
La croissance devrait atteindre …; les analystes tablent sur …; sous réserve que + subjunctive; sauf retournement de conjoncture.
Capital gain / capital loss on selling an asset. Plus-value also means added value.
Both are unproved starting points. Axiome: accepted as self-evident or as a basic rule; postulat: a premise one asks the reader to grant.
Says the same thing twice; two claims that each seem justified contradict each other; a problem with no way out.
Received opinion; a commonplace. Slightly pejorative: you name them to question them.
The study of being; the theory of knowledge (in French especially the philosophy of science).
Empirisme / rationalisme; matérialisme / idéalisme; déterminisme / libre arbitre; universalisme / relativisme.
Beyond the world or experience / within the thing itself. Spelt -ant; immanent ≠ imminent.
Part of the nature of (inhérent à toute innovation) / in itself, independent of anything else (opposite: extrinsèque).
X désigne …; Par X, on entend …; X renvoie à …; On appelle X …
L'homme est un être fini; Les sociétés modernes …; Un philosophe doit douter. French can't drop the article.
Find the claim; give each sentence a subject that acts; turn nouns back into verbs; keep and define only the terms you need.
Rousseau, Discours sur les sciences et les arts (1750): knowledge doesn't make people better. Condorcet, Esquisse (written 1793–1794, published 1795): improvement without a set limit.
CNES created 19 December 1961; Kourou chosen 1964, first launch 9 April 1968; ESA founded 1975, headquarters in Paris.
Ariane 1: first flight 24 December 1979. Ariane 5: last flight 5 July 2023 (117 launches). Ariane 6: first flight 9 July 2024.
Le lanceur: les étages, les propulseurs d'appoint, la coiffe (fairing) over la charge utile (payload); it stands on le pas de tir.
Compte à rebours → mise à feu → décollage → séparation des propulseurs → largage de la coiffe → mise en orbite.
About 36,000 km above the equator; the satellite turns with the Earth and seems still from the ground.
Astronaute: most common, FranceTerme's headword (spationaute is its synonym). Spationaute: French coinage, correct. Cosmonaute: Soviet and Russian crews.
Docking (also mooring a boat); atmospheric re-entry.
Proxima (November 2016 to June 2017, Soyuz); Alpha (April to November 2021, Crew Dragon): first French commander of the space station.
Les débris spatiaux; the loi du 3 juin 2008 relative aux opérations spatiales (LOS): authorisation, technical rules checked by the CNES.
Before 1804: customs in the north (Coutume de Paris); Roman law (droit romain) in the south.

cards.front: The making of the Code civil
cards.back: Commission of August 1800: Tronchet, Bigot de Préameneu (north), Portalis, Maleville (south). Promulgation 21 March 1804: 36 laws, 2,281 articles.
Laws can't foresee everything: they should state general principles; judges and jurists apply them.
In a draft letter to Balzac (October 1840) he said he read a few pages of the Code each morning to set the tone of La Chartreuse de Parme.
The right to use and enjoy another's property and take its income, while keeping it intact; the owner keeps la nue-propriété.
1965 marriage settlements; 4 June 1970 l'autorité parentale replaces la puissance paternelle; 1972 and 2005 equal filiation; divorce 1884, 1975, 2016.
L'article 1240 pose le principe de … / prévoit que … / dispose que … / énonce … Never quote from memory.

glossary.definition: The refined taste of the Paris salons in the first half of the 17th century (the marquise de Rambouillet from about 1608, Madeleine de Scudéry after 1650): delicacy in feeling and in speech, elaborate compliments and periphrases. Its excesses were mocked by satirists and by Molière in Les Précieuses ridicules (1659). By extension, any affected style.

The French of the 17th and 18th centuries, after the grammarians and the Académie française had set the standard. A modern reader understands most of it, but meets object pronouns placed before the verb that governs an infinitive (je le veux voir), -oi- spellings of the imperfect in older editions, the imperfect subjunctive in ordinary use, and words whose meaning has since weakened (ennui, étonner, gêne, charmer).
glossary.topic: Classical French and words that changed

glossary.definition: A form created by Molière in 1661 (Les Fâcheux): a spoken comedy whose acts are framed and linked by songs and dances that belong to the plot, usually written with a court composer (Lully for Le Bourgeois gentilhomme, 1670; Charpentier for Le Malade imaginaire, 1673).

A very long novel, or a cycle of novels in many volumes, that follows characters or a society over years or generations and makes room for digressions. The term became current in the 20th century; it is also applied to earlier works such as Hugo's Les Misérables (1862).
An old name for slang (l'argot), common in the 19th century and used in the titles of dictionaries of the 1860s. Today it sounds old-fashioned or literary; l'argot is the usual word.

A novel set in a real past, whose characters may be historical figures, and whose invented scenes must agree with the documents and with what people of that time could know and think (la vraisemblance). Examples: Dumas's Les Trois Mousquetaires, Yourcenar's Mémoires d'Hadrien (1951).
glossary.topic: The historical novel and its voice

glossary.definition: A novel written as a letter (or letters) by one narrator to one addressee who does not reply, so that the whole story comes through a single voice that knows who it is writing to. Mémoires d'Hadrien is one long letter from the dying emperor to the young Marcus Aurelius. Compare the epistolary novel of many letters and correspondents.
glossary.topic: The historical novel and its voice

glossary.definition: A word that shares its core meaning with another but cannot replace it everywhere. Two near-synonyms can differ in denotation (what exactly they name), connotation, collocation, construction, register or frequency: murmurer and susurrer both mean to speak softly, but susurrer is literary and intimate.

A word that looks or sounds like another but means something else: la conjecture (a guess) and la conjoncture (the economic situation), éminent and imminent, effraction and infraction. The wrong one is a real word, so a spell checker will not catch it.

What a word suggests on top of what it names: approval, contempt, irony, an era or a social group. Économe (thrifty) and avare (miserly) name the same habit with opposite connotations. Dictionaries give the denotation; the connotation shows in their examples.

A word used in a sense it does not have, or that careful usage questions: pallier à for pallier, conséquent for "large", solutionner for résoudre, initier for "to launch". Many usage guides criticise these uses; several are common and some dictionaries record them, so say who criticises a use rather than calling it wrong.

A sentence with a gap used to show how near-synonyms differ: put each candidate in the gap and see which a native speaker would accept. In "Pris de court, le témoin a ___ une excuse", bredouillé and marmonné fit; clamé does not.

Moving from one level of language to another, either to suit a new reader (the same incident told to a council and to a friend) or within one text for effect (humour, irony, quotation, complicity). Deliberate shifts within a text are called ruptures de ton.

A sudden, deliberate jump to another register inside a text: an administrative account of a trivial mishap that ends with a slang phrase, or a formal word for a silly thing. It works only when the rest of the text is clearly controlled; the same jump by accident is an incongruous word.

The level of French that dictionaries mark pop.: features associated with working-class speech and frowned on by the norm, such as dislocation (le parcmètre, il marchait pas), a vague ils for the authorities, à for possession (la voiture à Paul) or si j'aurais. It sits between familier and argotique; learners recognise it and produce it only in quotation.

The French of official letters and forms: the passive and the impersonal (un avis a été établi, il est rappelé que), the institutional nous, nouns rather than verbs, and set words such as aviser, s'acquitter de, dûment, susmentionné, l'intéressé. It aims at legal safety rather than elegance, unlike the soutenu.

The verb form used in compound tenses and the passive (couru, pesé, fait, arrivée). With être it agrees with the subject; with avoir it agrees with a direct object placed before the verb; a pronominal verb agrees with its direct object.
Être or avoir, the verbs that form the compound tenses (elle est arrivée, il a couru). The auxiliary decides which agreement rule the past participle follows.

A verb such as coûter, valoir, peser, mesurer, courir, vivre, dormir or durer that can take a complement of price, weight, distance or time. That complement is not a direct object, so the participle does not agree with it (les heures qu'il a dormi). Used transitively, the same verbs agree (les colis qu'il a pesés).
A verb used only with an il that refers to nothing: il faut, il y a, il pleut, il fait chaud. Its past participle is always invariable: les chaleurs qu'il a fait, la tempête qu'il y a eu.

A noun singular in form that names a group: la foule, la moitié, une dizaine, la plupart. After some (une foule de, la moitié des) the verb may be singular or plural; after la plupart des it is plural.

A word whose form never changes: mille, the prefixes mi- and semi-, compound colours (bleu clair) and most nouns used as colours (marron, orange). Some words are invariable only in one position: demi and nu before the noun, tout as an adverb, quelque meaning "about".

A word that sounds like another: vert, verre, ver, vers; couru, courus, courue, courues. Agreement creates many homophones (-é, -er, -ez, -ait), so a test such as replacing the verb with vendre helps choose the spelling.
The noun or pronoun that a relative pronoun stands for: in les médailles qu'il a gagnées, the antecedent of que is médailles, which is why gagnées agrees with it.
In French grammar, the word after être, devenir, sembler, paraître … that describes the subject (elle est devenue avocate; ils semblent fatigués). An attribut agrees with the subject.
In French grammar, an adjective placed directly next to its noun (une course difficile, un ciel gris), as opposed to an attribut after a verb. It agrees with its noun.

The part of a sentence a word applies to. The scope of a negation or of tous, seul, même can change the meaning: Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés is read "not all" in careful writing but can also be heard as "none".

A sentence whose words can be grouped in two ways: la peur de l'ennemi (the fear the enemy feels, or the fear of the enemy), la photo du fils du ministre qui a fait scandale (which caused the scandal?). It is removed by word order, a relative with lequel, a repeated noun or punctuation.

Saying less in order to mean more, usually with a negation: Ce n'est pas mal (it's good), Je ne suis pas mécontent (I'm pleased). It can be polite, ironic or modest, and in an argument it can suggest a claim without making it.

A word or phrase that sets the limits of a claim: à proprement parler, stricto sensu, au sens large, en tout état de cause, peu ou prou, grosso modo, quasi, tant soit peu. Qualifiers make a statement exact rather than vague.

Rewriting a sentence so that it has only one meaning (French désambiguïser, or in everyday prose lever l'ambiguïté), for example Les coureurs ne sont pas tous arrivés or Aucun coureur n'est arrivé instead of Tous les coureurs ne sont pas arrivés.
In translation, changing the word class while keeping the meaning: as soon as he arrived (verb) becomes dès son arrivée (noun). One of the oblique procedures described by Vinay and Darbelnet (1958).
In translation, changing the point of view: it's not difficult becomes c'est facile; wet paint becomes peinture fraîche. One of the oblique procedures described by Vinay and Darbelnet.
In translation, rendering the same situation with entirely different words, as with idioms, proverbs and exclamations: it's raining cats and dogs becomes il pleut des cordes; ouch becomes aïe.

In translation, the double transposition between English and French verbs of movement: English puts the manner in the verb and the direction in a particle (swim across), French the direction in the verb and the manner in an adverbial (traverser à la nage). Outside translation, a to-and-fro of people or traffic.

A word or construction translated part by part from another language: gratte-ciel from skyscraper, être en charge de from "in charge of". Some calques are fully accepted; calques of syntax (faire sens, adresser un problème) are criticised by usage guides.

A word that looks like a word in another language but means something else: actuellement (currently, not actually), éventuellement (possibly, not eventually), sensible (sensitive), définitivement (for good), ignorer (not to know).
Grammar that says what you should write: it recommends, advises against and condemns. Usage guides, school grammars and the Académie française's Dire, ne pas dire are prescriptive.

Grammar that says what speakers and writers actually do, with evidence, without judging. Most reference works mix both attitudes: Le Bon Usage quotes writers for and against a use and adds its own judgement.

One of the 17th-century authors of Remarques or Observations on doubtful points of French usage, beginning with Vaugelas (1647) and continued by writers such as Ménage and Bouhours. They created the habit of judging usage one point at a time.

A space that keeps the characters on either side on the same line. French typography puts one before : ; ! ? (a thin one before ; ! ? in fine typography) and inside the guillemets « ». Printers make espace feminine in this sense: une espace insécable.

The past tense of the written récit: il parla, elle finit, ils vinrent. It presents events as complete and cut off from the present, mostly in the third person, in novels, tales, history books and some press genres. Recognition only in this course: read it, and write the passé composé or the présent when you retell.

The passé simple of avoir or être + the past participle (il eut fini, elle fut partie). It marks an event completed just before another one in the passé simple, after quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, après que, and in à peine … que (À peine fut-elle arrivée que l'orage éclata). Recognition only.

In Émile Benveniste's analysis (1959), the system of tenses that tells past events as if they told themselves, cut off from the moment of writing and with no I or you: passé simple for events, imparfait for the background, plus-que-parfait and passé antérieur for what came before, conditional for what came after. Benveniste called it histoire. The opposite system is discours.

In Benveniste's analysis, any utterance in which a speaker addresses someone and ties what is said to the speaker's present: conversation, letters, most press. Its tenses are the présent, the passé composé, the imparfait, the plus-que-parfait and the future; every person is possible. The opposite system is récit. (For the speech as a genre, see discours (genre).)

The division of work between the tenses of a narrative. The foreground holds the events that follow one another and move the story on (passé simple, or passé composé in discours); the background holds the setting, states, habits and what was going on (imparfait). The imparfait narratif breaks the rule on purpose, putting a foreground event in a background tense.

A literary subjunctive formed from the tu form of the passé simple without -s, + -sse, -sses, -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent, and for il a circumflex + -t: que je parlasse, qu'il parlât, qu'il fût, qu'il eût, qu'il vînt. Used in classical concordance after a past main verb. Only the third person singular is still met often. Recognition only.

Avoir or être in the imperfect subjunctive + the past participle: qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie. The past of the imperfect subjunctive in classical concordance (Je doutais qu'il fût venu). The same form serves as the conditionnel passé deuxième forme. Recognition only.

The rule of classical prose that puts the subjunctive in the imperfect or pluperfect after a main verb in a past tense or the conditional: Je voulais qu'il vînt; Je doutais qu'il fût venu. Modern French keeps the present and past subjunctive whatever the main tense (Je voulais qu'il vienne).

aliases: second form of the past conditional
glossary.definition: A literary form identical to the pluperfect subjunctive with the meaning of the conditionnel passé: il eût fallu = il aurait fallu; on eût dit = on aurait dit; j'eusse aimé = j'aurais aimé. Found in literary narrative and in set phrases. Recognition only.

A condition or concession expressed by putting the verb before its subject, without si: Eût-il su la vérité, il ne serait pas venu (had he known); Dût-il y passer la nuit, il finira (even if it takes him all night). English does the same with had he known, were she to.
A rhythm of two balanced groups: lent et lourd; Le fleuve s'assombrit, la ville se tait. It suggests order, symmetry or opposition.
A rhythm of three groups: Il hésita, se retourna, partit. The classic rhetorical number: it feels complete, and becomes a cadence majeure when the groups grow longer.

A long, built sentence that rises through several subordinate clauses (the protase) to a high point (the acmé) and falls in a shorter main clause (the apodose): Quand …, quand … et que …, la ville, lentement, se taisait. The grand form of French oratorical prose.

The way a sentence's groups change in length towards the end. In a cadence majeure each group is longer than the one before and the sentence opens out; in a cadence mineure the last group is shorter and the sentence closes sharply (tout prévu, tout vérifié : sauf lui).
The repetition of a consonant sound in nearby words: le fleuve, lent et lourd. It should echo the meaning (an s for wind or a whisper).
The repetition of a vowel sound in nearby words: la pluie fine glissait sur la vitrine (i).
A pleasant flow of sounds. French grammar itself serves it (the t of viendra-t-il, the l' of si l'on, cet before a vowel). Its opposite is cacophony, a harsh or comic clash of sounds.
Two vowel sounds meeting, between words or inside a word: il alla à Arles, il a été, poète. Classical verse forbade it between words; careful prose avoids piling them up.
Placing clauses side by side without subordinating one to another: Il pleuvait. Elle partit. The reader supplies the link; the effect is sober, fast, sometimes brutal.
Subordination: one clause depends on another and the link is stated (Comme il pleuvait, elle partit). The syntax of explanation and nuance.

Leaving out the linking words between items or clauses: Il vint, il vit, il signa. It speeds a sentence up. Its opposite, polysyndeton (la polysyndète), repeats the link (et … et … et) to insist and accumulate.
A sentence built around a noun, with no conjugated verb: Novembre, déjà. Silence. Puis un rire. It sets a scene in a few strokes, as stage directions and headlines do.

A text written in the manner of an author, a genre or a period, without copying its sentences, usually as a game or a homage. It relies on the reader recognising the model. French law allows pastiche, parody and caricature within 'the laws of the genre' (Code de la propriété intellectuelle, art. L122-5, 4°).
An imitation that mocks its model by exaggerating its features or applying them to an unsuitable subject. Pastiche plays with a manner; parody makes fun of it.

A noble subject told in a low, familiar style, which pulls the great down: Scarron's Virgile travesti (from 1648) retells the Aeneid with heroes talking like market people. The reverse of the mock-heroic.

A trivial subject told in the noble style of the epic, so that the gap makes us laugh: in Boileau's Le Lutrin (1674) a quarrel between churchmen over a lectern becomes an epic war. The reverse of the burlesque.
Pompous, inflated language. In French, l'emphase means bombast, not emphasis (emphasis = l'insistance, la mise en relief). Its adjectives: pompeux, grandiloquent, ampoulé, boursouflé.

A work inside the work that mirrors it: a play within a play, a novel about a writer writing that novel. The image comes from heraldry (a small shield at the centre, the abyme, of a larger one); André Gide first applied it to literature, in his journal for 1893.
Reusing a known text, slogan or image to give it another meaning, often political or satirical (an advertising slogan turned against the brand). The word also means a hijacking.

French verse is measured by syllables, not stresses. The e muet counts before a consonant (u-ne-bel-le-nuit), is elided before a vowel or mute h, and never counts at the end of the line (nor does a final -es or the -ent of a verb).
The twelve-syllable line of classical French verse, with a caesura after the sixth syllable dividing it into two hemistichs of six. The line of French tragedy and of much 19th-century poetry.
Each half of a line divided by a caesura; in the classical alexandrine, two hemistichs of six syllables.
The main pause inside a line of verse. In the classical alexandrine it falls after the sixth syllable, which must end a word. Romantic poets loosened it.
In verse, pronouncing two touching vowels as two syllables (li-on, pas-si-on), to fill the count or give a word weight. The count of the line shows whether the poet chose it.
In verse, pronouncing two touching vowels as one syllable, as in speech (lion, hier, pied in one syllable). The opposite of diaeresis.
A sentence running on past the end of a line into the next. When only a short word or two spill over before the sentence stops, that piece is a rejet, and it gains weight.
A poem of fourteen lines: two quatrains and two tercets. In the classical French sonnet the quatrains rhyme abba abba (rimes embrassées) and the tercets often ccd eed or ccd ede.

In Camus, the feeling that arises when a human being who needs meaning faces a world that gives none: not in us or in the world, but in their meeting. Le Mythe de Sisyphe (1942) answers it with lucidity and revolt rather than despair or hope.
A story told by one of its characters, who says je: the reader knows only what the narrator knows or chooses to say. L'Étranger is told by Meursault himself.

glossary.term: passé composé as a narrative tense
glossary.definition: Using the passé composé, the tense of discours, to tell a whole story. Camus did it in L'Étranger (1942): each event is set down next to the moment of speaking, without the causal chain of the passé simple, which gives the narration its flat, detached presence.

The present indicative used in statutes and contracts to state a rule or a duty, not to describe what happens: Le preneur est tenu de payer le loyer (the lessee must pay the rent); Le dépôt de garantie est restitué dans un délai de deux mois (shall be returned). Être tenu de = must; pouvoir = may; ne peut = may not.

The part of a court decision that states what the court decides, after the words Par ces motifs: condamne (orders to pay), ordonne, déboute (dismisses), rejette, dit que. Read it first: it says who won what.
The part of a court decision that explains why the court decides as it does: the rules, then their application to the facts (en l'espèce). The statement of reasons as a whole is la motivation.

Latin phrases used in French legal writing, written without accents: in fine (at the end of a text), de facto (in fact), de jure (by law), a contrario (by the opposite reasoning), ipso facto, ad hoc, sui generis.

The way French high courts now write their decisions: numbered paragraphs of ordinary sentences instead of one long sentence built on attendu que or considérant que. The Conseil d'État applied it from 1 January 2019, the Cour de cassation from 1 October 2019.
The usual order of a scientific article: Introduction, Methods (matériel et méthodes), Results (résultats), and Discussion, with an abstract (résumé) before and a conclusion and references after.

The voice of French science writing, which hides the person who acts: the passive (les mesures ont été réalisées), the impersonal il (il a été montré que + indicative, il apparaît que), on (on observe), and the nous of the authors.

A text that says what a device is made of (être constitué de, se composer de, comporter, être équipé de), what it does (permettre de, servir à, assurer la fonction de) and how it works (fonctionner, alimenter, convertir … en …).
A size given to the nearest power of ten. Un ordre de grandeur de plus = about ten times more; du même ordre de grandeur = comparable. Ratios: deux fois plus élevé que, un facteur trois.

Two kinds of economic cause. Conjoncturel (cyclical) problems come from the current state of the economy and should pass when the cycle turns; structurel (structural) ones come from how an economy or a firm is built and remain in normal times (un déficit structurel, le chômage structurel).

The accounts a company draws up for each financial year (l'exercice): le bilan (balance sheet: what it owns and owes on one day), le compte de résultat (income statement: income, costs and result over the year) and le tableau des flux de trésorerie (cash flows).
In argument, a word given an exact, stated meaning, so that it can be used without ambiguity. Define it before using it: X désigne …, par X on entend …, on appelle X …

The article used for a whole class rather than particular things: the definite article (L'homme est un être fini; Les sociétés modernes valorisent l'innovation) or the indefinite for any one member (Un philosophe doit douter). English often has no article here; French can't drop it.

A noun for a quality, state or idea, often formed from a verb or an adjective: fini → la finitude, autre → l'altérité, progresser → le progrès. Abstract nouns let an idea be the subject of a sentence; too many in a row become jargon.

Specialist vocabulary used where plain words would do, which hides the reasoning instead of carrying it. To rewrite it: find the claim, give each sentence a subject that acts, turn nouns back into verbs, and keep and define only the technical terms you need.
A rocket that puts objects into space (le lanceur): built in stages (les étages), with the payload under a fairing (la coiffe) at the top. Ariane 6 is a launch vehicle; la fusée is the everyday word.
What a launch vehicle carries into space (la charge utile): one or more satellites, a probe or a capsule.

A circular orbit about 36,000 km above the equator (l'orbite géostationnaire), where a satellite goes round in the time the Earth takes to turn, so it seems still from the ground. Used by many telecommunications satellites.
Gathering scattered rules into one ordered, written code (la codification). The Code civil of 21 March 1804 codified French private law by combining thirty-six laws into one code of 2,281 articles.

Law based on the customs of a province or city (le droit coutumier), first handed down by usage and then written down. Before 1804 it governed northern France; the Coutume de Paris was the most influential.

Le droit écrit: before 1804, the law of southern France, based on Roman law (le droit romain) as compiled under Justinian. The name refers to this Roman tradition, not to the fact of being written: northern customs were written down too.

A word or use of French typical of Africa: l'essencerie (petrol station, Senegal), cadeauter (to give a present to), gâter in the sense of to break down. Most are made with French's own tools: suffixes, conversion, new meanings, borrowings, compounds and metaphors.

A language used between people whose first languages differ: Wolof in Senegal, Dioula in much of Côte d'Ivoire, Lingala in Kinshasa, French in many African towns. The same language can be a vernacular for some speakers and a lingua franca for others.
The language of a community, learned at home and used among its own speakers. Compare langue véhiculaire, the language used between communities.

A status a state gives to languages it recognises as belonging to the country. National languages may or may not be official: Senegal lists several national languages while French is its official language; Mali made its national languages official in 2023.
A variety that young city dwellers build from French and the other languages around them, often as a sign of belonging: nouchi in Abidjan, camfranglais in Cameroon. Taught for recognition only.
What happens when speakers of two or more languages live side by side. It leaves borrowings, xénismes, interference, substrates and code-switching.
A word taken from another language: le toubib and le bled from Maghrebi Arabic, le week-end from English. An old borrowing may no longer be felt as foreign at all (l'algèbre, le sucre).
A borrowed word still felt as foreign, usually printed in italics and explained (la chorba, le hittiste in a French newspaper). With time it may become an ordinary borrowing.
A feature of one language carried into another: a pronunciation (a rolled r), a construction or a meaning (an English speaker's je suis chaud for j'ai chaud).
An earlier language whose traces survive in the language that replaced it: a Gaulish substrate in French (le chêne, la boue), an Amazigh substrate in the Arabic of the Maghreb.

Switching between languages within one conversation or one sentence: a single word (bezzaf), a formula (inch'Allah) or whole sentences. A normal skill of bilingual speakers, used for a quotation, a joke, a feeling or to show who they are.
The working-class French of Montreal, named after the way cheval sounds in it. Michel Tremblay's play Les Belles-sœurs (1968) made it a literary language.
The French of many young Acadians in and around Moncton (New Brunswick), mixed with English words and structures (C'était right le fun). Taught for recognition only.

In Québec, a swear word built on a word of Catholic worship (the tabernacle, the chalice, the host). Among the strongest words in informal Québec French: recognise them, never use them. In standard French le sacre is also a coronation.

A French term that the Office québécois de la langue française (OQLF) has made official: either normalised (un terme normalisé), and then compulsory in the province's administration and in some documents, or recommended (un terme recommandé). Most terms in the OQLF's Grand dictionnaire terminologique are neither: they are proposed or preferred terms without official status. Québec tends to coin French terms where France borrows English.
Pronouncing t and d with a little hiss before i and u, as many Québec speakers do: tu sounds like tsu, dire like dzire.

A language with several standard centres, each with its own norms, dictionaries and institutions: English (Britain, the United States, Australia), German (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) and, more and more, French (Paris, Brussels, Geneva, Montréal, Dakar).
A standard set from inside a community, by its own writers, media, schools and dictionaries; an exogenous norm is imported from outside (for most francophones, long the norm of Paris).
Speakers' feeling that their own French is not good French: the Belgian who apologises for septante, the Québécois who changes accent in Paris. Studied in Belgium and Québec, among other places.

Prejudice or discrimination against people because of their accent or the way they speak. The term was proposed by the sociolinguist Philippe Blanchet and set out in his book Discriminations : combattre la glottophobie (2016).
The written standard shared across the francophone world: the French of international news, treaties and textbooks. Each country adds a few words of its own.
A word, meaning or construction typical of one region: septante in Belgium, le cornet (carrier bag) in Switzerland, présentement in Africa and Québec. Paris French has regionalisms too.
Any form of a language shared by a group: Belgian French, Québec French, the French of Dakar. A neutral word: it says neither dialect nor mistake.
In literature, the quality of a text that belongs fully to neither of two cultures or languages and draws its force from both, as Kourouma's French does with Malinké.

Critics' name for Kourouma's style: Malinké meanings, images, proverbs, syntax and an oral narrator carried into French. The title Les Soleils des indépendances uses soleil in the Malinké sense of day or era.

A full language born in a contact situation that has become the first language of a community. French-based creoles (Haiti, the Antilles, French Guiana, Réunion, Mauritius, the Seychelles, Louisiana) take most of their words from French but have grammars of their own.
A simplified contact language that people with no shared language build to trade or work together; it has no native speakers. A creole does.
The language that supplies most of a creole's vocabulary: French for Haitian Creole. The lexifier gives the words, not the grammar.

A situation in which two varieties share a society with different roles: a high one for writing, school and law, a low one for home and daily life. Made famous by Charles Ferguson (1959); Haiti (French and Creole) and Arabic (standard and spoken) are classic cases.

The Caribbean identity defined in Éloge de la créolité (1989) by Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau and Raphaël Confiant: a mixed identity, neither only French nor only African, with the creole language at its centre.
Édouard Glissant's word for the open, never finished process by which cultures in contact produce something unpredictable. Créolité names an identity; créolisation a process.

The collective written paper of the DALF C2, as FEI's sample papers describe it: 3 h 30, a dossier of about 2,000 words, two subjects of which the candidate treats one, and one structured, committed text of at least 700 words in a set genre (article, éditorial, report, speech …). Marked out of 50. Check the current paper's instructions.

In the DALF C2 written paper, the set of documents (articles, interviews, extracts, infographics) on one theme from which the candidate writes. Unlike the C1 corpus, it is used selectively: the candidate keeps what serves the chosen subject and adds personal input.

What the writer brings beyond the documents: examples from one's own country, experience and reading, and general knowledge. Required at C2, forbidden in a C1 synthèse. One developed example is worth more than a list of names.

Judging a document before using it: its genre (news, opinion, advertising, institutional), its author and their position, its date, its outlet and its interest. A partial source can be used if it is named for what it is.

The first, fast pass over a dossier: only the paratext (titles, chapôs, authors, sources, dates, captions, the légende of an infographic), to know who speaks, where, when and roughly for what. From survoler, to skim.

The second pass over a dossier: running the eyes over the documents for the information one subject needs (a figure, a date, an argument against), without reading everything. It is followed by repérage, marking with a pencil.

The article in which a newspaper gives its own position on an issue of the day, in the voice of the paper (nous), often written or signed by the editor. It takes a stance from the first lines and keeps it, using rhetorical questions, controlled irony, concession and rebound, and a final call or warning.
A short, personal opinion column signed by one writer, often ironic: a mood more than a demonstration. Contrast the éditorial, which speaks for the newspaper.

The whole set of titles of a press article: the surtitre (a short line above the headline giving the topic or place), the titre, any sous-titre, the chapô and the intertitres that break up a long text.
The bold paragraph under a headline that sums up the article in two or three sentences and makes the reader want to go on. Press spelling of le chapeau.
The first sentence of an article, which must hook the reader: a scene, a figure, a quotation, a paradox, never a generality or a marronnier.

In a press article, the last sentence: a phrase that closes the text and stays with the reader, often by echoing the attaque. (In stylistics the word also names a short sentence that ends a run of long ones.)
In press jargon, a story that comes back every year at the same time (the first heatwave, back to school, holiday traffic). An attaque that could open a marronnier is a weak attaque.

An argued text written for a commissioning body (the commanditaire) that has to decide: header, introduction (object, terms of reference, scope, method), constat, analysis, ranked préconisations with cost, feasibility and deadline, conclusion and annexes, under numbered headings, in an impersonal, measured but committed style.
The person or body that orders a report (a mayor, a board, a minister) and sets its task in a lettre de mission: the report is addressed to it and must give it something to decide.
In a report, the section that states the facts and figures observed, before any judgement: what is happening, where, how much. Analysis and recommendations come after it.

A formal recommendation in a report. At C2 each one is numbered and ranked, and says what should be done, by whom, at what cost (chiffrage), how feasibly and by when (échéance), usually in the conditional or an impersonal form (il conviendrait de, il est proposé de).
Comparing one's situation and solutions with those of other organisations or towns to learn from them. The recommended French term for benchmarking, from parangon (a model).

A text written to be heard: someone speaks, on an occasion, to people who are present. It addresses the audience by precedence, wins its goodwill, follows a structure the ear can follow (exorde, narration, confirmation, réfutation, péroraison) and uses figures of repetition and address. (Lesson 5's discours, the speech-like mode opposed to the récit, is a different notion.)

Latin for winning the audience's goodwill: the moment in the opening of a speech (the exorde) where the speaker makes the audience well disposed, by modesty, a shared memory, a compliment or thanks. Written without accents.

In rhetoric, the appeal through the speaker's character: the image of competence, honesty and goodwill that the speech builds (Je suis né dans cette vallée …). One of Aristotle's three appeals, with pathos and logos.
In rhetoric, the appeal to the audience's feelings: a person, a scene, a memory. In everyday French le pathos often means overdone emotion, so it is used with measure.
In rhetoric, the appeal to reason: facts, figures, causes and consequences, logical steps.

The figure that repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive sentences or clauses (Cette ligne, ce sont … Cette ligne, ce sont …), to hammer an idea and give the ear a beat. Not to be confused with grammatical anaphora, a word that points back to something already said.
The figure of turning to address someone or something directly, present, absent or dead (Vous, les ouvriers du chantier …; Et vous, Marcel …). Also the name of the punctuation mark.

The figure that makes the absent, the dead or a thing speak (Si ces rails pouvaient parler, ils nous diraient …). Rousseau's first Discours (1750) has a famous one, in which a Roman consul returns to speak.

In the press, an opinion piece by authors from outside the newspaper, often a collective with signatories listed: credentials in the first lines, a precise demand and a call to action. The paper publishes it without endorsing it.

A public declaration of principles by a group, which often founds or speaks for a movement. It goes beyond a single demand; famous French manifestos are named by their number of signatories (the Manifeste des 343, 1971).

The part of a tribune or speech that asks someone to do something precise: an authority to decide, readers to sign or join, other professions to act. A good one names who, what and by when, so that it can be checked later.

The French school method of analysing a literary passage in two or three axes (claims about what the text does and how), each in sub-parts that quote briefly and analyse, with an introduction (amorce, présentation, problématique, annonce du plan) and a conclusion (bilan, ouverture). In the lycée it is now called le commentaire.

The overall effect a text aims at, also called its registre: lyrique (a personal feeling), élégiaque (a gentle lament for a loss), pathétique (pity), tragique (inescapable fate), épique (grandeur and struggle), comique, among others.

The set of words in a text that belong to one theme (water, the senses, absence). Listing them with their line numbers (a relevé) shows what a text insists on, and crossing two fields often gives an axe.
Genette's term for the point of view from which a story is perceived: zéro (an all-knowing narrator), interne (through one character's eyes) or externe (only what an outside observer could see).

The act of producing an utterance, studied through its marks: who speaks, to whom, where and when (personal pronouns, tenses, words like ici and demain, modalisers). In a narrative, it shows for instance when the narrator's voice gives way to a character's thought.

The figure that attaches an adjective to a word other than the one it logically describes: le chemin pensif (the walker is pensive), une cigarette nerveuse (the smoker is nervous). It lets a mood spread to the setting.

A spoken report of a recording's content, the first part of the DALF C2 oral: it presents the document and its speakers, announces a plan by ideas, attributes every position and attitude to its speaker with precise verbs (souligner, minimiser, récuser, ironiser), adds no opinion, and ends with a transition to the speaker's own point of view. About five to ten minutes in the sample paper.

What a speaker in a recording defends or rejects, and how that position moves during the discussion: conceding, coming round to a proposal (se rallier à), distancing oneself from an ally (prendre ses distances avec). A C2 listener notes each stance and each shift (l'inflexion).

The manner in which a speaker says something (with irony, anger, reluctance, ambivalence), named by the reporting verb chosen: ironiser sur, fustiger, minimiser, récuser, s'indigner, concéder. The verb must match the speaker: saying someone fustige when they only doubted distorts the recording.

A three-part plan for a yes-or-no question with strong arguments on both sides: thesis, antithesis, then a third part (le dépassement) that goes beyond both rather than splitting the difference. Its risk is a lukewarm "yes and no" at the end.
Reasoning from a general rule to a particular case: if the rule is true and the case falls under it, the conclusion follows. The syllogism is its classic form.
Reasoning from several observed cases to a general rule. It is only as strong as its cases: one counter-example (le contre-exemple) can weaken it.

A deduction in three steps: two premises and a conclusion that follows from them (every A is B; C is A; so C is B). If both premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion is true; most objections attack a premise.

Reasoning that supposes the opposite view is true, follows it to its consequences and shows that they are absurd, so the view must be rejected: if every noise at night were banned, there could be no night buses or concerts.
A statement an argument starts from (la prémisse). A conclusion is only as sound as its premises; in French the word has an accent and a double s.
A consequence that follows directly from what has just been shown (le corollaire): if the night is a common good, it has a cost.

The moves a speaker uses when a view is challenged: clarify the question, concede what is fair and rebound (j'en conviens, mais …), defuse a hostile question (désamorcer), admit what one doesn't know and offer what one does, and hold one's ground (je maintiens que …).

An answer that avoids the question (l'esquive): drowning it in details (noyer le poisson), dodging it outright (botter en touche), stating the obvious (enfoncer des portes ouvertes) or empty official talk (la langue de bois). Named calmly, it can be answered by recentring.

Someone who defends a view they don't hold, to test the other side's argument (se faire l'avocat du diable). Examiners in a debate may do it; the answer is to treat the objection seriously, not personally.

The French diploma at CEFR level C2, from the French Ministry of Education, with papers designed by France Éducation international. In the sample papers: an oral (a long recording heard twice, about an hour of preparation, about 30 minutes in three parts) and a written paper (3 h 30, a dossier of about 2,000 words, one text of at least 700 words), 50 points each; pass with 50/100 and at least 10/50 in each. Valid for life.

aliases: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
glossary.definition: The higher of the two proficient-user levels of the Council of Europe's framework (le CECRL): understanding almost everything with ease, rebuilding arguments from several sources into one coherent account, and expressing oneself spontaneously, fluently and precisely, with fine shades of meaning. It is defined by what a user can do, not by comparison with a native speaker.

In the CEFR, the activity of making a text or an exchange accessible to someone else: summarising several sources, explaining what a speaker implies, or what irony or understatement does. The DALF C2 compte rendu and the dossier-based text are mediation tasks.
A short statement of what a learner can do at a given level on one CEFR scale (le descripteur). A set of descriptors used as a standard is a framework (un référentiel).

Describing a speaker whose language a native listener takes for a native's for long stretches (quasi natif). Not the same as C2: the CEFR describes C2 by what a user can do, not by passing for a native speaker.

In language learning, the process by which an error stops changing because it no longer prevents understanding and nobody corrects it (la fossilisation; the errors se fossilisent). It often affects fluent speakers most; feedback, more than further input, is what usually shifts it.

references.title: The DALF C2 and the long text
references.body:
## The DALF C2 at a glance

As described in FEI's sample papers and the national certification registry (check FEI's current
pages and the candidate's manual before you sit the exam: formats change).

| paper | time | points | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compréhension et production orales (individual) | 1 h preparation, then about 30 min with the jury | 50 | listen to a long recording (about 15 minutes in the sample papers), heard twice; present its content; give an argued point of view on the problem it raises; debate with the jury |
| Compréhension et production écrites (collective) | 3 h 30 | 50 | read a dossier of about 2,000 words; choose one of two subjects; write one structured text of at least 700 words in the genre the subject asks for (article, éditorial, rapport, discours …) |

Total out of 100; pass mark 50; at least 10 out of 50 in each paper. Monolingual French
dictionaries are allowed in the sample papers. Since March 2020 there is no choice between a
humanities and a sciences domain. The diploma is valid for life.

## The written paper: a method

1. **Read the two subjects first** (genre, addressee, publication or occasion, the question).
2. **Survey the dossier** (*survol*): titles, chapôs, sources, dates, captions, figures.
3. **Choose a subject** you can argue with the documents *and* with your own knowledge.
4. **Scan** (*balayage*) for what the subject needs; **select** and rank (*hiérarchiser*); set
   aside what doesn't serve (*écarter*). You need not use every document.
5. **Set a problématique and a line** (an engaged position, unlike C1's synthèse).
6. **Plan** in two or three parts, with your own examples (*apports personnels*).
7. **Write** in the genre's form; cite documents by their source, in your own words.
8. **Reread** (moods, agreement, accents, register, connectors) and **count** (write the count if
   the paper asks for it; follow the paper's counting instructions).

## Genre checklists

| genre | must have | tone and features |
|---|---|---|
| **article** | a title (often a *surtitre* and a *chapô*), an *attaque* that hooks, *intertitres* if long, a *chute* | informative and argued; sources attributed (*selon, d'après*); concrete examples |
| **éditorial** | a title; a clear stance from the first lines; a strong ending | the paper's voice (*nous*), rhetorical questions, irony with control, a call or a warning |
| **rapport** | addressee (*commanditaire*), object, method; *constat*, analysis, *préconisations* (ranked, with cost, feasibility, *échéance*); conclusion; headings and numbering | impersonal, measured but committed; *il ressort de, il conviendrait de, eu égard à* |
| **discours** | an address (*Mesdames et Messieurs …*), an opening that wins the audience (*captatio benevolentiae*), a clear structure for the ear, a *péroraison* | short sentences, repetition, ternary rhythm, apostrophe, signposting; written to be heard |
| **tribune** (20h1) | a title; the signatories' credentials; a clear demand; a call to action | engaged, collective *nous*; facts and values |

## The oral: three parts

| part | aim | tips |
|---|---|---|
| 1. compte rendu of the recording (about 5–10 minutes in the sample paper) | report the content faithfully, by ideas, with each speaker's position and attitude | name the document and the speakers; use precise reporting verbs (*souligner, nuancer, ironiser, minimiser, récuser, se rallier à*); no opinion yet |
| 2. point de vue argumenté (about ten minutes) | defend your own view on the problem the recording raises | announce a problématique and a plan; examples from your own culture; signpost; conclude |
| 3. débat avec le jury | discuss, defend, nuance | listen to the whole question; reformulate it; concede what is fair, then rebound; admit what you don't know and offer what you do |

## Phrases by function

| function | phrases |
|---|---|
| presenting a recording | *Il s'agit d'un extrait de …; Le document donne la parole à …; Trois intervenants s'y opposent sur …* |
| reporting a stance | *X déplore que …; Y s'insurge contre …; Z prend ses distances avec …; W ironise sur …; V minimise …* |
| moving to your view | *Ce débat soulève une question plus large : …; C'est sur ce point que je voudrais prendre position.* |
| structuring | *Dans un premier temps …; J'en viens à …; Reste à savoir si …; Pour conclure …* |
| conceding and rebounding | *J'en conviens, mais …; C'est de bonne guerre, toutefois …; Vous avez raison de souligner …, encore faut-il …* |
| defusing a hard question | *Si je comprends bien votre question, …; Je ne prétends pas être spécialiste de …, mais …* |
| backtracking with grace | *Je me suis peut-être mal exprimé : …; Je rectifie : …* |

## What C2 means, in a few lines

At C2 you understand almost everything you hear or read, combine many sources into one coherent
account, and express yourself fluently and precisely, with fine shades of meaning, in any
register. The Companion Volume (Council of Europe, 2020) describes it scale by scale; lesson 24
summarises the rows that matter for the DALF.

references.title: French across the French-speaking world
references.body:
Figures and statuses change: each one below is dated, and lessons say "as of November 2026".
Regional words are labelled by where they are common, not where they are exclusive; many travel
(*présentement* is African and Québec usage, *la clenche* Belgian and northern French).

## How many speakers

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) counted 321 million French speakers in
2022 and 396 million in its 2026 report, 65 % of them in Africa; much of the rise comes from a new
